**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 1 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿Glory be to the One who took His servant by night from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque, whose surroundings We have blessed, that We might show him some of Our signs. Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing.﴾

The opening with the word of glorification (al-tasbih, "Glory be to God") without any preceding statement that requires exalting God above what is unfitting for Him indicates that a wondrous report is about to be received by the listeners. It points to the great power of the speaker and the exalted rank of the one spoken of.

The phrase of glorification in a statement that contains nothing suggesting likeness to creation or deficiency unbefitting God's majesty, such as ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, above what they describe﴾ [al-Saffat: 180], must be understood as used for more than mere exalting of God (tanzih). That more is wonder at the report being related, as in His saying ﴿It is not for us to speak of this. Glory be to You! This is a tremendous slander﴾ [al-Nur: 16], and in the verse of al-A'sha:

*"I said, when his boasting came to me: Glory be to the one from 'Alqama, the boaster!"*

Since this statement comes from God and the glorification is issued by Him, the meaning is to make the listeners marvel. Wonder is impossible in its literal sense for God, but this is not because such a figurative sense is disregarded in the figures of eloquent speech, since it can be reduced to a figure of speech, just as the expression of hope (ra'a) appears in God's speech, as in ﴿so that you may succeed﴾. Rather, it is because it is not proper for a speaker to marvel at his own act. So the sense of wonder here is of the kind of their saying: "Do you marvel at what so-and-so said, such and such?"

The rationale for this usage is that the original purpose of glorification is upon the appearance of what indicates the refutation of what is not befitting for God. Since the appearance of what indicates great power removes doubt about God's power and about associating partners with Him, it is fitting for the one who reflects to utter the glorification of God, that is, His exaltation above incapacity.

The original form of the expressions of glorification is the phrase "Glory be to God" (subhan Allah), from which the word "sabhala" was derived. The usage of its forms occurs with pronouns, as in "Glory be to You" (subhanaka) and "Glory be to Him" (subhanahu), and with the relative pronoun, as in ﴿Glory be to the One who created all the pairs﴾ [Ya Sin: 36], and this verse is of that kind.

The expression of the Exalted Essence by means of the relative clause rather than by the proper name serves to call attention to what the relative clause conveys by way of alluding to the rationale of this wonder and its exaltation, namely that momentous event and the great favor. It also indicates that the account of the Night Journey (isra') had spread among the people: the Muslims believed in it, and the polytheists denied it.

[Page 11]

In this there is an incidental (idmaj) elevation of the status of Muhammad (ﷺ), and an affirmation that he is a messenger from God, and that he was given of the proofs of the truthfulness of his call what they could not deny. The Night Journey was a disclosure to him of something unseen on earth, and it is the most excellent place after the Sacred Mosque.

And (asra) is a dialectal form of (sara), meaning "to travel by night." So the hamza here is not for transitivity, since transitivity is achieved by the preposition "bi-" (with). Rather, (asra) is a verb beginning with a hamza that is synonymous with (sara), like (aban) being synonymous with (ban), and like (anhaja al-thawb) meaning (nahaja), that is, "it wore out." So ﴿asra bi-'abdihi﴾ is in the same position as ﴿God took away their light﴾ [al-Baqara: 17].

Al-Mubarrad and al-Suhayli had a subtle point in distinguishing transitivity by the hamza from transitivity by the preposition "bi-": the second is more eloquent, because in its original formation it implies that the agent shares the action with the object. So the original sense of (dhahaba bihi) is that he took him along with him, as God said, ﴿and he traveled with his family﴾ [al-Qasas: 29]. The Arabs said: "he overwhelmed them with abuse" (ashba'ahum shatman), and "they went off with the camels" (rahu bil-ibil). In this there is a delicate point appropriate to the present context, in that He said ﴿asra bi-'abdihi﴾ rather than ﴿sara bi-'abdihi﴾. It alludes to the fact that God was with His messenger during his journey by His care and His guidance, as He said, ﴿for indeed you are under Our eyes﴾ [al-Tur: 48], and He said, ﴿when he said to his companion: Do not grieve, for God is with us﴾ [al-Tawba: 40].

So the meaning is: the One who made His servant one who journeys by night, that is, one who travels, and this is like His saying, ﴿So travel with your family during a part of the night﴾ [Hud: 81].

Since the (suru) was specifically the travel of the night, His saying "by night" (laylan) indicates that the journey to the Farthest Mosque took place within part of a night. Otherwise mentioning it would have been mere emphasis, and "benefit is better than repetition," as they say.

In this there is an indication that it was a journey that breaks customary norms, since it covered the distance between the starting point and the destination in part of a night. Also, it was so that mention of the night would lead to its indefiniteness, which conveys magnification.

Thus the indefiniteness of "laylan" (a night) is for magnification, by the indication of the care taken in mentioning it, together with knowledge of it from the verb "asra," and by the indication of its not being made definite. That is, it is a great night in view of its being made the time for that great journey. So indefiniteness here stands in the place of what indicates magnification. Do you not see how the magnification had to be conveyed by a special form in His saying ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during the Night of Decree. And what will make you know what the Night of Decree is?﴾ [al-Qadr: 1–2], since the Night of Decree came in a non-indefinite form?

[Page 12]

The (abd, servant) which is attributed to the pronoun of majesty here refers to Muhammad (ﷺ), as is the established usage of the Qur'an, for the word "servant" never occurs attributed to a third-person pronoun referring to the Exalted except with the meaning of the Prophet (ﷺ). Also, the report of the Night Journey to Jerusalem had spread among the Muslims, and its denial had spread among the polytheists, so the intended referent of "His servant" became known.

The attribution is an attribution of honor, not of definition, because the quality of servanthood to God is established for all creatures, so attributing it does not serve to define.

The Sacred Mosque is the Ka'ba and the courtyard surrounding the Ka'ba in Mecca, set aside for worship connected with the Ka'ba, such as circumambulating it, performing seclusion (i'tikaf) at it, and prayer.

The original meaning of "masjid" is the name of a place of prostration. The original meaning of "haram" is a forbidden matter, and because it is derived from the root (harm), with a fatha and then a sukun, which means prohibition, and it is synonymous with (haram). So describing a thing as "haram" means that its use is prohibited in a manner appropriate to it, as in ﴿Carrion is forbidden to you﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 3], that is, the eating of carrion, and the verse of 'Antara:

*"It is forbidden to me, and would that it were not forbidden!"*

That is, its approach is prohibited, because she is his father's wife, and that is reprehensible among them. It can also mean what is prohibited from having any action performed upon it, and it is specified by mention of the object to which it relates. Sometimes its object is not mentioned when custom indicates it, and from this is their saying "the sacred month" (al-shahr al-haram), that is, in which fighting is forbidden according to their custom.

[Page 13]

Sometimes the object is omitted for the purpose of generalization, so it is from omission for generality, and it returns to customary generality. So in such expressions as "the Sacred House" (al-bayt al-haram), what is meant is what is protected from the aggression of aggressors, the raids of kings and conquerors, and the performing of injustice and evil within it.

And "haram" is the form fa'al in the sense of maf'ul (passive participle), like their saying "a woman who is ḥaṣān," that is, protected by her chastity from people.

So the Sacred Mosque is the place prepared for prostration, that is, for prayer, and it is the Ka'ba and the courtyard made a sanctuary for it. Its extent varies in size and narrowness according to the ages, due to the number of people in it for circumambulation, seclusion, and prayer.

In the pre-Islamic period the Quraysh built their houses around the Sacred Mosque, and Qusayy placed near it the Council House (Dar al-Nadwa) for the Quraysh, and they used to sit in it around the Ka'ba. So it became confined when the houses of the clans of the Quraysh surrounded it, and each clan made its houses adjacent to one another. The collection of houses is called a "shi'b" (valley/quarter), with a kasra on the shin. Each clan used to approach the Sacred Mosque through the exit of its houses. There was no wall surrounding the Sacred Mosque, and the passages between the houses of the clans were called "gates" (abwab), because one would enter through them to the Sacred Mosque, such as the Gate of the Banu Shayba, the Gate of the Banu Hashim, the Gate of the Banu Makhzum, which is the Gate of al-Safa, the Gate of the Banu Sahm, and the Gate of the Banu Taym. Sometimes some gates were known by a direction close to them, such as the Gate of al-Safa, which is called the Gate of the Banu Makhzum, and the Gate of al-Hazwara, named after a place where there was a market for the people of Mecca called al-Hazwara. I do not know whether they were gates that were closed, or were openings in the open space, since "bab" (gate) is applied to what lies between two barriers.

The first person to build a wall to protect the Sacred Mosque was 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may God be pleased with him), in the year seventeen after the Hijra.

[Page 14]

It was given the title "the Mosque" because Ibrahim (peace be upon him) established it for the establishment of prayer in the Ka'ba, as God related of him: ﴿Our Lord, that they may establish prayer﴾ [Ibrahim: 37]. When the hanifiyya (pure monotheism) became extinct, and the people of the pre-Islamic period abandoned prayer, they forgot its description as "the Sacred Mosque," and began to say "the Sacred House." As for the statement of 'Umar: "I vowed in the pre-Islamic period to perform seclusion for one night in the Sacred Mosque," he referred to it by its name in Islam.

So this descriptive title came to predominate, and it became a proper name by dominance in the terminology of the Qur'an. I do not know that it was known by this name in the pre-Islamic period, nor was the Mosque of Jerusalem known by it in the period of its sanctity among the Children of Israel. The reason for this has been mentioned previously at His saying ﴿So turn your face toward the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Baqara: 144] in Surat al-Baqara, and at His saying ﴿that they barred you from the Sacred Mosque﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 2] at the beginning of Surat al-Ma'ida.

Its status as a proper noun comes from the whole of the descriptive phrase and the described noun together, and both are defined by the article "al-." So the first part is like "al-najm" and the second part is like "al-sa'iq," and definiteness is achieved by the two together. The grammarians did not count this type among the kinds of proper nouns by dominance, and perhaps they considered it as belonging to the definite with the article, but it must be counted as such, because its status as a proper noun has come about through both.

The Farthest Mosque (al-Masjid al-Aqsa) is the mosque known as Bayt al-Maqdis, located in Iliya' (Jerusalem), and it is the mosque built by Sulayman (peace be upon him).

"Al-Aqsa" means "the farthest," and what is meant is its distance from Mecca, as indicated by making it the endpoint of the journey from the Sacred Mosque. It is a descriptive attribute that revealed itself here, because of the added emphasis on the miraculous nature of this journey and its being beyond customary norms, since it covered a long distance in part of a night.

With this descriptive attribute that occurs for it in the Qur'an, the whole of the descriptive phrase and the described noun became a proper noun by dominance over the Mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis, just as "al-Masjid al-Haram" became a proper noun by dominance over the Mosque of Mecca. I reckon that this proper name is one of the innovations of the Qur'an, for the Arabs did not describe it with this attribute, but when they heard this verse they understood from it that it meant the Mosque of Iliya'. There was no other mosque of a divine religion at that time apart from these two.

[Page 15]

In this description in the form of the superlative (taf'il), considering the original sense of its formation, there is a hidden miracle of the Qur'an, indicating that between the two mosques there would be a great mosque, the Mosque of Taba (Medina), which is far from the Sacred Mosque, so that the Mosque of Bayt al-Maqdis would then be farther than it.

Thus the verse refers to all three mosques that are excellent in Islam above all Islamic mosques, which are explained by the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Journeys should not be undertaken except to three mosques: the Sacred Mosque, the Farthest Mosque, and my mosque."

The benefit of mentioning the starting point and the endpoint of the Night Journey with His saying ﴿from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque﴾ is twofold. The first is the explicit statement of covering a great distance within part of a night, because each of the adverbial phrase "laylan" and the two prepositional phrases ﴿from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque﴾ is connected to the verb "asra," so this connection implies simultaneity, so that it is known that it belongs to the category of miracles.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 1 (part 2 of 3):

The second point: it is an indication that God, exalted is He, makes this night journey a symbol that Islam gathered together what the laws of tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness) and the hanifiyyah (the pure monotheistic faith of Abraham) brought, from the time of Ibrahim (Abraham), upon him be peace, which proceeded from the Masjid al-Haram, to what branched out from it of laws whose seat was Bayt al-Maqdis, and then to its final form, which also appeared from Makkah. The hanifiyyah proceeded from the Masjid al-Haram and branched out in the Masjid al-Aqsa, then returned to the Masjid al-Haram, just as the night journey returned to Makkah, because every journey by night is followed by a return. By this, the last part was made to correspond with the first (radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr).

From here the connection becomes clear between the revelation of the social legislation in this surah, in the verses that open with His saying, ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isra': 23]. In them is ﴿And do not kill the soul which God has forbidden, except by right﴾ [al-Isra': 33], and ﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner﴾ [al-Isra': 34].

[Page 16]

﴿And give full measure when you measure, and weigh with an even balance﴾ [al-Isra': 35]. This is an indication that this religion would become a religion that governs among people, and whose rulings are implemented.

The Masjid al-Aqsa is the second mosque that Ibrahim built, as has been reported from the Prophet ﷺ. In the two Sahihs, it is related from Abu Dharr who said: "I said: O Messenger of God, which mosque was placed on earth first? He said: The Masjid al-Haram. I said: Then which? He said: The Masjid al-Aqsa. I said: How much time was between them? He said: Forty years."

This report makes clear that the Masjid al-Aqsa is from the building of Ibrahim, because the interval was specified by a period that falls within the lifetime of Ibrahim, upon him be peace, and its mention is linked with the mention of the Masjid al-Haram.

This is among the matters that the People of the Book neglected to mention, and it is among what God singled out His Prophet with knowledge of. The Torah bears witness to it: it came in the Book of Genesis, in chapter twelve, that when Abraham entered the land of Canaan, which is the land of Palestine, he pitched his tent in the mountain east of Bethel (Bayt Il, a town about eleven miles north of Jerusalem, whose name among the Philistines was Luz, and which Jacob named Bethel, as in chapter twenty-eight of the Book of Genesis), and west of the land of Ai (a Hebrew town known now as al-Tayyibah), and built there an altar to the Lord.

They apply the word "altar" (madhbah) to the mosque, because they offer sacrifices in their places of worship. 'Umar ibn Abi Rabi'ah said:

A doll beside a monk, a priest,
they fashioned it in the altar niche of the sanctuary.

That is, the place of the altar in the mosque, because the mihrab is the place of worship. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿While he was standing in prayer in the mihrab﴾ [Al 'Imran: 39].

There is no doubt that the mosque of Ibrahim is the place which Dawud (David), upon him be peace, intended to place the tent upon and to build his mihrab upon it, or God inspired him with that. He is also the one who instructed his son Sulayman (Solomon), upon him be peace, to build the mosque upon it, that is, the Temple. The historians of the Hebrews, among them Yusifusus (Josephus), have mentioned that the mountain where Ibrahim lived in the land of Canaan was named Nabu, and that it is the mountain upon which Sulayman built the Temple, which is the mosque containing the Rock.

[Page 17]

The story of Sulayman's building of it is detailed in the First Book of Kings among the books of the Torah.

It was subjected to destruction three times. The first: when Bukhtanasar (Nebuchadnezzar), king of Babylon, destroyed it in the year 578 BC. Then the Jews renewed it under Persian rule.

The second: the Romans destroyed it during the time of Titus after long wars between them and the Jews, and it was rebuilt. Then Hadrian completed its destruction in the year 135 AD, and erased its traces, so that nothing remained of it but ruins.

The third: when the queen Helena, mother of the emperor Constantine, king of the Romans (Byzantium), became Christian and became firmly attached to Christianity, and her heart was saturated with hatred of the Jews, because of what she believed about their killing of the Messiah. During her visit to Jerusalem, she ordered that the ruins of the Temple of Sulayman be cleared, and that what remained of its pillars and the like be removed, so that a church could be built with them over the tomb of the Messiah, as they claim, at a place they supposed to be the place of the tomb. The Christian historians doubt that this place is the place where the Messiah is said to have been buried. She named it the Church of the Resurrection. She also ordered that the site of the Masjid al-Aqsa be made a dumping ground for the town's refuse and rubbish, so the place of the Rock became a garbage heap, where rubbish piled up over it and covered it, and slid down over its steps.

When the Muslims conquered the rest of the land of al-Sham in the time of 'Umar, and 'Umar ibn al-Khattab came to witness the conquest of the city of Iliya, which was known before as Urushalim (Jerusalem),

[Page 18]

it came to be called Iliya' (with a kasra on the hamzah and a kasra on the lam), and this was its well-known name among the Arabs when the Muslims conquered Palestine. Iliya' is the name of a prophet of the Children of Israel who lived in the early ninth century BC. Al-Farazdaq said:

Two houses: the House of God, we are its custodians,
and a house high above Iliya', exalted.

The treaty was concluded between 'Umar and the people of that city, who were Christians. 'Umar said to one of their patricians named Safronius: "Show me the mosque of Dawud." He went with him until he reached the place of the gate, where the refuse had slid down over the steps of the gate. 'Umar strained himself until he entered and looked, and said: "God is greatest! By Him in whose hand is my soul, this is the mosque of Dawud, of which the Messenger of God ﷺ told us that he was taken on the night journey to it." Then 'Umar and the Muslims began to sweep the refuse away from the Rock until all of it was exposed. 'Umar went toward the direction of the mihrab of Dawud and prayed in it. Then he departed from the city of al-Quds to Palestine.

No mosque was built there until the time of 'Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, who ordered the beginning of the construction of the dome over the Rock and the restoration of the Masjid al-Aqsa. He entrusted the building to Raja' ibn Haywah al-Kindi, one of the scholars of Islam. This began in the year 66 AH, and the completion of it was in the year 73 AH.

'Umar was the first Muslim to pray in it, and he gave it the sanctity of mosques.

Therefore, the naming of that place as the Masjid al-Aqsa in the Qur'an is a Qur'anic naming, in which account was taken of what it had been before, because the status of being a mosque does not cease from the land of a mosque. The naming is according to what it was, and it is a subtle indication that it would be a mosque in the fullest reality of mosques.

Muslims faced it in prayer from the time when prayer became obligatory, which coincided with the night of the Isra', until sixteen months after the Hijrah. Then facing it was abrogated (nusikha), and the Ka'bah became the Islamic qiblah.

[Page 19]

I have seen that a Christian traveler named Arkulf (Arculf) visited al-Quds in the year 670 CE, that is, thirty-four years after the caliphate of 'Umar. He claimed that he saw a mosque built by 'Umar in a square shape of planks and large tree trunks, and that it could hold about three thousand people.

It appears that the attribution of the Masjid al-Aqsa to 'Umar ibn al-Khattab is a delusion of the Christians, who confused 'Umar's uncovering of the site of the mosque with its construction. If Arkulf was truthful in what he mentioned, that he saw a square place of planks and tree pillars, then that was something the Muslims of the land had made to protect that place from desecration.

His saying ﴿the surroundings of which We have blessed﴾ is a description of the Masjid al-Aqsa. The description is given with a relative clause (mawsuliyyah), in order to make the described thing well known by the content of the relative clause, so that it is as if the described thing were already known by the clause among the hearers. The purpose is to convey that its surroundings are blessed.

The form of the verb here (bara-kna, with the sense of mufa'alah) is for emphasis on the multiplication of the action, like 'Afakaka Allah (God grant you well-being).

Barakah (blessing) is the increase of good and bounty in this world and the Hereafter, through abundance of reward for those who pray in it, and the answering of the supplications of those who supplicate in it. The mention of barakah has already passed at His saying ﴿blessed and a guidance for the worlds﴾ [Al 'Imran: 96] in the surah of Al 'Imran.

The Masjid al-Haram has been described with the like of this in His saying ﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds﴾ [Al 'Imran: 96]. The reason for restricting the description of the Masjid al-Aqsa in this verse to the mention of this blessing is that the fame of the Masjid al-Haram for blessing, and for its being the station of Ibrahim, is known to the Arabs. As for the Masjid al-Aqsa, people had forgotten all of that: the Arabs have no knowledge of it, the Christians obliterated its traces out of their hatred for the Jews, and the Jews had distanced themselves from it and despaired of its return to them. Therefore, there was a need to inform of its blessing.

[Page 20]

The word hawla (around) indicates a place near the place of the noun to which hawla is attached.

That the blessing is around it is a kinayah (indirect expression) for the blessing being in it all the more, because if it has come about around it, then it has surpassed what is in it. Within this are the subtlety of implication (talazum), the subtlety of what the speech implies (fahwa al-khitab), and the subtlety of exaggeration through multiplication. Close to this is the saying of Ziyad al-A'jam:

Indeed, generosity, manliness, and liberality
are within a dome pitched over the son of al-Hashraj.

In the word hawla in this verse there is a fine appropriateness that the word fi in Ziyad's verse does not have, because the adverbial sense of fi is more general. His saying "in a dome" is a kinayah for its being within the one who dwells in the dome, but it does not convey its spreading out and exceeding of it to what is around it.

The causes of the blessing of the Masjid al-Aqsa are many, as the word hawla indicates. Among them: its founder was Ibrahim, upon him be peace. Among them: the blessing that reached it through the prophets who prayed in it, from Dawud and Sulayman and those after them from the prophets of the Children of Israel. Then through the arrival of the Messenger 'Isa (Jesus), upon him be peace, and his proclamation of the call to God in it and in what surrounds it. Among them: the blessing of those prophets buried around it, for it is established that the graves of Dawud and Sulayman are around the Masjid al-Aqsa. The greatest of these blessings is the Prophet's ﷺ arrival there, that arrival which was beyond the customary, and his praying in it with all the prophets.

His saying ﴿so that We might show him of Our signs﴾ gives the reason for the night journey as the will to show the divine signs. It is a reason by one of the wisdoms for which God granted His Prophet the favor of the night journey. The night journey has many wisdoms, which become clear from the narration of the night journey reported in the Sahih. The most important and most comprehensive of them is showing him of the signs of God, and the proofs of His power and mercy. That is, so that He would show him of the signs, and then he would inform them of what they had asked him about concerning the description of the Masjid al-Aqsa.

The particle of purpose (lam al-ta'lil) does not restrict the aim of what it governs to what follows it. Rather, the reason mentioned was limited to showing the signs because this reason is more closely connected to honoring the one taken on the journey and to attention to his station, since showing the signs increases the certainty of the one who sees them

[Page 21]

beyond the certainty that already existed before seeing. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And thus We showed Ibrahim the dominion of the heavens and the earth, that he might be among the certain﴾ [al-An'am: 75].

For God's natural disposition (fitrah) made the perception of sensible things more firm than the perception of demonstrative conclusions. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿And when Ibrahim said, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." He said, "Have you not believed?" He said, "Yes, but that my heart may be assured"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 260]. For this reason, God did not say after this reason: "Has your heart not been assured?", because the assurance of the heart is of wide scope with no limit. God made Ibrahim speak of the wisdom of prophethood. Likewise He hastened to show Muhammad ﷺ the signs before he asked Him for them, in abundance of favor.

'Ali ibn Hazm al-Zahiri said, and he excelled:

But for direct witnessing there is a subtle meaning,
for which Kalim (Moses) asked for the seeing.

Know that strengthening the certainty of the prophets is among the divine wisdoms, for in proportion to the strength of their certainty they rise further above the level of ordinary humans, attain to the knowledge of the realm of realities, and become equal in this field to the ranks of the angels.

As for the change of style from the third person in the relative pronoun and its two pronouns to the first person in His saying "We blessed..." and "that We might show him of Our signs," this is an instance of the rhetorical device of iltifat (shift of grammatical person), which is frequently employed in the speech of eloquent writers. This matter has already been discussed in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿You alone do we worship﴾ [al-Fatihah: 5], in the surah of al-Fatihah. The iltifat here has subtle features. Among them: since the Exalted Essence was brought to mind through the sentence of glorification and the relative clause, the position of absence became a position of witnessing, so it was appropriate to change the pronoun to pronouns of witnessing, which is the position of speaking in the first person.

Among them also is an allusion to the fact that the Prophet ﷺ, upon arriving at al-Masjid al-Aqsa, had moved from the station of inferring the unseen realm to the station of his arrival in the realm of witnessing.

Among them too is a preparation and paving the way for the intended referent of the pronoun in His saying ﴿Indeed, He is the Hearing, the Seeing﴾. It would thus readily occur that this pronoun refers to someone other than the one to whom the pronoun of "We show him" referred, because the norm is the consistency of pronouns, and because returning to the iltifat in close proximity is not the best practice.

So His saying ﴿Indeed, He is the Hearing, the Seeing﴾ — the more apparent view is that both pronouns refer to the Prophet ﷺ. This was said by some exegetes, and al-Tibi found it closer to the correct reading. However, the majority of exegetes hold that it refers to God, exalted is He, and perhaps its capacity to carry both meanings is intended.

Verses may come to bear several meanings, and their bearing of multiple meanings is intended in order to multiply the meanings of the Qur'an, so that each person takes from it according to the measure of his understanding, as we mentioned in the ninth introduction. In any case, the position of (inna) is for emphasis and causal explanation, as the separation of the sentence from what precedes it indicates.

It is either a causal explanation for the attribution of the verb (nuriyahu, "We show him") to its agent, or a causal explanation for its connection to its object. This conveys that this showing is from the category of wisdom, which is giving what is fitting to one who deserves it, and thus it is from the bestowal of wisdom upon one who is worthy of it.

The causal explanation is more fitting on the interpretation that the pronoun refers to the Prophet ﷺ, for there is no need to explain the attribution of the act to God, exalted is He, since it is established and known. What requires explanation is the granting of that wondrous showing to one whom the polytheists doubted would attain it, and whom they reckoned could not bear it as one like him.

Moreover, the sentence contains a restrictive construction, by defining the predicate with the definite article and with the pronoun of separation, a emphatic restriction, and it is a restriction qualifying an attribute, a restriction of the specifying type aimed at correcting a mistaken belief: that is, he is the one who perceives what he heard and saw, not the liar, nor the one who imagines, as the polytheists claimed. This restriction supports the return of the pronoun to the Prophet ﷺ, for it is the one suited to the rebuttal, and the polytheists would not dispute that God is Hearing and Seeing, unless one interprets it as meaning that He is the one who makes His messenger hear and see, whom you have denied, which reverts to exonerating the Messenger from lying and imagination.

Then, the two attributes, if they refer to the Prophet ﷺ, remain in their original derivational sense, for the intensification of the strength of his hearing and seeing, and his capacity to receive those astonishing witnessings, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He, ﴿The sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾ [al-Najm: 17], and His saying ﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he sees?﴾ [al-Najm: 12].

As for if they are attributes of God, exalted is He, it is fitting that they be interpreted as meaning "the one who causes to hear and the one who causes to see," that is, the one capable of making His servant hear and see, as in the saying of 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib:

"Is it from Rayhanah, the caller, the Hearing?" — that is: the one who makes hear.

The early scholars differed concerning the Isra' (night journey): was it with the body of the Messenger of God ﷺ from Makkah to Bayt al-Maqdis, or was it with his spirit in a dream, which is a complete spiritual witnessing, and the dreams of the prophets are true? The majority said: it was a night journey with the body while awake. 'A'ishah, Mu'awiyah, al-Hasan al-Basri, and Ibn Ishaq, may God be pleased with them all, said that it was a night journey with his spirit in a sleep-vision, and the dreams of the prophets are revelation.

The majority argued that the mention of it as a favour in the verse, and the denial of it by the Quraysh, are two proofs that the report of it was only about it being with the body. All agreed that the Quraysh asked the Prophet ﷺ to describe to them landmarks in Bayt al-Maqdis and on its route, and he described them to them as they were, and he described to them a caravan of Quraysh on a specified route and on a specified day, and they found it just as he had described to them.

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, the Prophet ﷺ said: "While I was in al-Masjid al-Haram, between sleeping and waking, Jibril came to me..." to the end of the hadith. This is more authentic and clearer than what has been narrated in another hadith, that the Isra' was from his house, or from the house of Umm Hani' bint Abi Talib, or from the Shi'b of Abi Talib.

The sound position is to understand that these are a different night journey, namely the one recorded in the hadith of the Mi'raj to the heavens, which is not what is meant in this verse. So the Prophet ﷺ had two honours: the first is the Isra', which is mentioned here, and the second is the Mi'raj, which is mentioned in the hadith of the two Sahihs at length and in other hadiths. It has been said that it is the one alluded to in the surah of al-Najm.

﴿And We gave Moses the Book and made it a guidance for the Children of Israel: "Do not take besides Me a guardian."﴾ It is a conjunction (*ʿatf*) upon the clause ﴿Glory be to He who took His servant by night﴾ (17:1) and so on. It is therefore an independent sentence (*jumla ibtidāʾiyya*), and the implied sense is: Allah took His servant Muhammad (ﷺ) by night, and He gave Moses the Book. These are two great favours upon a great portion of mankind. This is a transition to another theme, prompted by the mention of the Farthest Mosque (al-Masjid al-Aqsa), for the phases of the Farthest Mosque represent the phases through which the condition of the Children of Israel, as a whole, passed, with its stages of righteousness and corruption, of rising and decline, so that the Muslims may take a lesson from this and either follow their example or beware.

It is also linked to the words ﴿That We might show him of Our signs﴾ (17:1). Among the signs of Allah given to the Prophet (ﷺ) is the sign of the Qur'an, so it is as though it were said: "And We gave him the Qur'an." Then ﴿And We gave Moses the Book﴾ means the Torah, as His words after this confirm: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ (17:9), meaning to the way that is more upright than the way of the Torah, although both are guidance. This is in keeping with the night journey (*isrāʾ*) of the Prophet (peace be upon him), that he might see of the signs of Allah the Most High, which correspond to the condition of Moses (peace be upon him) when he was given prophethood. He was given prophethood at night, while he was travelling with his family from the land of Madyan, when he perceived a fire from the side of the mountain, and also to his condition when he was taken by night to converse with his Lord with the verses of the Book.

"The Book" refers to the one known to have been given to Moses (peace be upon him), namely the Torah. The pronoun in ﴿and made it﴾ refers to the Book, and describing it as "a guidance" is hyperbole, because guidance comes through acting upon what it contains, so it is treated as though it were guidance itself, like His words in the Qur'an: ﴿a guidance for the God-conscious﴾ (2:2).

He specified the Children of Israel because they are the addressees of the law of the Torah and no others. The "making" in His words ﴿and made it﴾ is the making of obligation (*taklīf*), and they are what is meant by "mankind" in His words: ﴿Say: "Who sent down the Book which Moses brought as a light and guidance for mankind?"﴾ (6:91), because "mankind" may be applied to some of them. Moreover, what is guidance for one group of mankind is suitable for anyone who has not been addressed by another book to benefit from its guidance. For this reason, He the Most High said: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance and light﴾ (5:44).

The majority of readers read ﴿that you not take﴾ with the *tāʾ* of address (*tattakhidhū*), in accordance with the original form when reporting statements that contain a prohibition. The particle *anna* is then explanatory (*tafsīriyya*), explaining what the word "Book" contains of the meaning of statements, and the explanation covers only part of what the Book contains, restricting itself to the most important part of it, which is monotheism (*tawḥīd*). Abu ʿAmr alone read it with the *yāʾ* of the third person, on the basis of reporting the speech by its meaning. Alternatively, *anna* may be a verbal particle (*maṣdariyya*) governing the genitive with an elided *lām*, a regular ellipsis (*ḥadhf muṭṭarid*), and the sense is: "We gave them the Book so that they would not take besides Me a guardian."

The *wakīl* is the one to whom affairs are entrusted, and what is meant by it is the Lord, because the servants rely upon Him in their affairs. That is, "do not take a partner to whom you turn for refuge." The use of *wakīl* for Allah is known in the language of the Children of Israel, as Allah relates of Jacob and his sons: ﴿So when they gave him their covenant, he said: "Allah is Witness over what we say"﴾ (12:66).

[Page 25]

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 17, verse 3:**

﴿O offspring of those whom We carried with Noah; indeed he was a grateful servant.﴾ It is permissible that this be a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) at the end of the narrative, not included within the explanatory clause (al-jumla al-tafsiriyya, the clause explaining the preceding verse). The accusative of (dhurriyyata) is then in the construction of specification (ikhtisas), to add clarification about the Children of Israel, a clarification intended as an allusion (ta'rid) to them because they did not give thanks for the blessing. It is also permissible that it be part of the explanatory clause, meaning: while they are the offspring of those whom We carried with Noah, peace be upon him,

[p. 26]

or that it be in the vocative (nida') by an implied vocative particle, meaning: O offspring of those whom We carried with Noah, intended to exhort them to give thanks for God's blessing and to avoid disbelief in Him by taking partners besides Him.

Al-haml (carrying) means placing one thing upon another in order to transport it. The intended meaning is carrying in the ship, as He said: ﴿We carried you in the flowing ship﴾ [al-Haqqah 69:11], meaning: the offspring of those whom We rescued from the Flood along with Noah, peace be upon him.

The clause ﴿indeed he was a grateful servant﴾ serves to give the reason for the prohibition against taking a guardian (wakil) besides God, because their forefathers were carried with Noah by a blessing from God upon them for their deliverance from drowning. Noah was a grateful servant, and those who were carried with him were grateful like him. That is, follow their example, and do not be ungrateful for God's blessings.

It is also possible that this clause is part of the explanatory clause, so it would be something God addressed to the Children of Israel. It is also possible that it is an appended closing remark (mudhayyila) to the clause ﴿And We gave Moses the Book﴾ [al-Isra' 17:2], in which case it is an address to the people of the Qur'an. Know that in choosing to describe them as the offspring of those who were carried with Noah, peace be upon him, there are great meanings: reminder, exhortation, and allusion. This is because the Children of Israel are descendants of Sam (Shem) son of Noah, and Sam was among those who boarded the ship.

The reason He did not say "offspring of Noah," although they are that as well, is to incorporate (idmaj) a reminder of the blessing of saving their ancestors from drowning.

In it there is a reminder that God saved Noah and those with him from destruction because of his gratitude and their gratitude, as an exhortation to emulate those people.

In it there is also an allusion that if they associate partners with God, a punishment and total annihilation will surely soon befall them, as in His saying: ﴿It was said, "O Noah, descend with peace from Us and blessings upon you and upon nations among those with you. And there are nations We will provide for, then a painful punishment will touch them from Us."﴾ [Hud 11:48].

[p. 27]

In it also is that the offspring of Noah were of two groups: a righteous, obedient group, who are those whom he carried with him in the ship, and an arrogant, disbelieving group, who is his son who drowned. Thus Noah, peace be upon him, was an example of the father of both groups. The Children of Israel were descendants of the righteous group, so if they follow him they will be saved, but if they deviate, they have inclined toward the other group and will soon perish. This parallel is the point behind choosing the mention of Noah from among their other forefathers, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, peace be upon them all, since this meaning is absent in those. It has been mentioned in this surah that the Children of Israel were annihilated twice because of their corruption on earth and their arrogance twice, and that this was the recompense for their neglect of God's promise to Noah, peace be upon him, when He rescued him.

The emphasis of Noah being ﴿a grateful servant﴾ by the particle (inna) treats them as if they were ignorant of that. Either it is to affirm their being led to follow him, if the clause is an address to the Children of Israel as part of the explanatory clause, or it is to treat them as if they were ignorant of it, until they became entangled in corruption and deserved annihilation and the loss of their dominion. From this it transitions to an allusion to the idolaters among the Arabs, that they do not follow Noah, because their example and the example of the Children of Israel in this context are identical in all their conditions. So the emphasis is considered with respect to the allusive meaning.

The meaning of Noah being a servant is that he acknowledged servitude to God, not being arrogant by associating partners. His being grateful means that he was intensely thankful to God by carrying out His commands. It is narrated that he used to frequently praise God.

Following the example of righteous forefathers is something human souls are naturally inclined to, and it is a matter of rivalry among nations, such that opposing it is considered something that provokes doubt about the validity of one's lineage.

Noah, peace be upon him, was an example of perfection of soul, and the Arabs knew this and were moved to follow him. Al-Nabigha said:

*You found trust, and it did not betray it;*
*Thus was Noah, who never betrayed.*

[Page 28]

﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Scripture: "You will surely cause corruption on the earth twice, and you will surely become exceedingly arrogant. So when the promise of the first of them came, We sent against you servants of Ours of great might, and they went through the homes, and it was a promise fulfilled."﴾ This is conjoined (ʿaṭf, grammatical coordination) to the clause ﴿And We gave Moses the Scripture﴾ [al-Isra' 17:2], meaning: We gave Moses the Scripture as guidance, and We made clear to the Children of Israel in the Scripture what would befall them because of opposing the guidance of the Torah, to inform this nation that God did not withhold guidance and counsel from those people. The connection is therefore evident.

The word qaḍāʾ (decree) means judgment, which is determination. The meaning of its being "in the Scripture" is that the decree was mentioned in the Scripture. The verb qaḍaynā is followed by the preposition (ilā, "to"), because qaḍaynā is made to carry the implicit meaning (taḍmīn) of ablaghnā ("we conveyed"), i.e., "We decreed and conveyed," as in His saying ﴿And We conveyed to him that matter﴾ [al-Hijr 15:66] in Surat al-Hijr. Thus "the Scripture" may refer to the Book of the Torah, and the definiteness is definiteness of reference (ʿahd), since He has just mentioned "the Scripture." It is found in several places, some of which are close to what is in this verse but in summary form (see Chapters 26, 28 and 30 [of the book of Isaiah/Ezekiel, as cited]). The shift from the pronoun to the explicit word "the Scripture" is therefore only for the sake of emphasis.

It is also possible that "the Scripture" refers to some of their religious books, so the definiteness of "al-Kitab" is definiteness of genus (jins), not definiteness of prior mention, because it is not the Scripture mentioned earlier in ﴿And We gave Moses the Scripture﴾ [al-Isra' 17:2]. When the name "the Scripture" was made explicit, it suggested that it is another of their books, namely the books called the books of the prophets: Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel, which are in the second rank after the Torah. Likewise the book of the prophet Malachi. The corruption twice is mentioned in the book of Isaiah and the book of Jeremiah.

[Page 29]

In the book of Isaiah there are warnings in chapters 5 and 10, and the first of the two occasions is mentioned in the book of Jeremiah in chapter 2, chapter 21 and elsewhere. The word "the Scripture" does not mean a single book, for a singular noun definite by the article of genus may refer to a plurality. It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: "al-Kitab is more than the books." It is also possible that "the Scripture" refers to the Torah and the books of the prophets, and for this reason too the explicit noun was used instead of a pronoun.

The clause ﴿You will surely cause corruption on the earth twice, and you will surely become exceedingly arrogant﴾ explains the clause ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Scripture﴾. Whatever the case, the second-person pronouns in this clause prevent "the Scripture" in His saying ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Scripture﴾ from meaning the Preserved Tablet or the Book of God, that is, His knowledge.

This verse alludes to great events between the Children of Israel and their enemies from two great nations: events between them and the Babylonians, and events between them and the Romans. These are divided accordingly into two types: one type in which their events with the Babylonians are included, and the other type, their events with the Romans. He expressed the two types by "twice," because each occasion of them contains several battles.

The first occasion is the totality of a sequence of events called in history the Babylonian Captivity, namely the campaigns of Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon and Assyria, against the land of Jerusalem. The first campaign was in the year 606 BCE; he took many groups of Jews captive, and this is called the First Captivity. Then he attacked them again in a campaign called the Second Captivity, which was greater than the first, in the year 598 BCE. He took captive the king of Judah and a great multitude of the Israelites, and took the gold that was in the Temple of Solomon and the precious vessels within it.

The Third Captivity, the destructive one, was in the year 588 BCE, when Nebuchadnezzar attacked them and took captive the whole people of Judah, burned the Temple of Solomon, and Jerusalem remained a ruin and a waste. Then they rebuilt it, as will come at His saying ﴿Then We gave you the return against them﴾ [al-Isra' 17:6].

[Page 30]

As for the second occasion, it is the series of Roman campaigns against the land of Jerusalem, and its explanation will come at His saying ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter comes﴾ [al-Isra' 17:7], and so on.

Attributing the corruption to the pronoun of the Children of Israel indicates that it is corruption by the majority of them, such that the whole nation is considered corrupt, even though it is not free of righteous people.

The "exaltation" (ʿuluww) in His saying ﴿and you will surely become exceedingly arrogant﴾ is a metaphor (majaz) for insolence and disobedience, like His saying ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh exalted himself in the land﴾ [al-Qasas 28:4], His saying ﴿Indeed, he was among the extravagant transgressors﴾ [al-Dukhan 44:31], and His saying ﴿Do not exalt yourselves over me, but come to me in submission﴾ [al-Naml 27:31]. Pride and insolence are likened to exalting oneself over something, because of the possession it implies, as a comparison of an intelligible thing to a perceptible one (tashbih maʿqul bi-mahsus).

The original form of "you will surely become exceedingly arrogant" (lataʿlunna) is lataʿluwunna, and the original form of "you will surely cause corruption" (latufsidunna) is latufsidunna.

The word "promise" (waʿd) is a verbal noun used with the meaning of the passive participle, i.e., "the promised thing of the first of the two occasions," meaning the time appointed for the first occasion of corruption and exaltation, as in His saying ﴿So when the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it level﴾ [al-Kahf 18:98].

Similar to this is His saying ﴿and it was a promise fulfilled﴾, meaning carried out and executed.

The construction of "promise" with "the first of them" is explicative (bayaniyya), meaning the promised thing which is the first of the two occasions of corruption and exaltation.

The verb "sent" (baʿatha) is used in the sense of creating the march toward the land of Israel and preparing its causes, as if it were a command to march against them, as already mentioned in His saying ﴿He will surely send against them until the Day of Resurrection those who will afflict them with terrible punishment﴾ [al-Aʿraf 7:167] in Surat al-Aʿraf. It is a sending of creation and subjugation, not a sending by revelation and command.

The verb "sent" is followed by the preposition of elevation ("against") because it is made to carry the implicit meaning of domination (taslit), as in His saying ﴿He will surely send against them until the Day of Resurrection those who will afflict them with terrible punishment﴾ [al-Aʿraf 7:167].

"Servants" (ʿibad) means those who are owned. These are servants of created-ness. Most often one says "servants of God," and one also says "slaves" ('abid) without an addition, as in His saying ﴿And your Lord is not unjust to the slaves﴾ [Fussilat 41:46]. When what is meant is those owned by slavery, one says only "slaves." The intended "servants of God" here are the Assyrians, the people of Babylon, who are the soldiers of Nebuchadnezzar.

"Might" (basʾ) means strength and severity in war. He described them by "of great might" because of their strength in their kind, as in the verse of Surat Sulayman: ﴿They said: "We are people of strength and people of great might"﴾ [al-Naml 27:33].

The clause "they went through" (fajasu) is coordinated (ʿaṭf) to "We sent" (baʿathna), so it is among the things decreed in the Scripture. Jaws means penetrating into the lands and traversing their roads going and returning, to seek out what is in them. Here it is meant as the pursuit of combatants, so it is a going-through of harm and mistreatment, by the indication of the context.

"Through" (khilal) is a noun that comes in the pattern of plurals and has no singular. It is the middle of a thing through which one passes, as He said ﴿Then you see the rain coming out from its midst﴾ [al-Nur 24:43].

The definiteness in "the homes" (al-diyar) is definiteness of reference (ʿahd), meaning "your homes," and this is the origin of making the article (al-) a substitute for the omitted genitive pronoun. They are the homes of the land of Jerusalem. Nebuchadnezzar's army entered it, killed the men, took captives, destroyed the homes, burned the city, and burned the Temple of Solomon with fire. The word "homes" includes the Temple of Solomon, since it was their house of worship. All the Children of Israel were taken captive, and by this the lands of the Jews were emptied of them. This is indicated by His saying in the following verse ﴿and that they might enter the Temple as they entered it the first time﴾ [al-Isra' 17:7].

"Through" (khilal) is a noun that comes in the pattern of plurals and has no singular. It is the middle of a thing through which one passes, as He said ﴿Then you see the rain coming out from its midst﴾ [al-Nur 24:43].

The definiteness in "the homes" (al-diyar) is definiteness of reference (ʿahd), meaning "your homes," and this is the origin of making the article (al-) a substitute for the omitted genitive pronoun. They are the homes of the land of Jerusalem. Nebuchadnezzar's army entered it, killed the men, took captives, destroyed the homes, burned the city, and burned the Temple of Solomon with fire. The word "homes" includes the Temple of Solomon, since it was their house of worship. All the Children of Israel were taken captive, and by this the lands of the Jews were emptied of them. This is indicated by His saying in the following verse ﴿and that they might enter the Temple as they entered it the first time﴾ [al-Isra' 17:7].

[Page 32]

﴿Then We gave you back the return [of victory] over them, and We supported you with wealth and sons, and made you greater in manpower.﴾ ﴿If you do good, you do good for yourselves; and if you do evil, then it is for them.﴾ [al-Isra' 17:6–7]

The clause "fa-jasu" (and they roamed through your homes) is coordinated with the clause that is part of the answer to "idha" (when) in His words "fa-idha ja'a wa'du ula-humaa" (so when the promise of the first of the two came). It is also part of what was decreed in the Book. Its form is past, but its meaning is future, because "idha" (when) is an adverb of future time. It was put in the past form to affirm that this event will certainly occur. The meaning is: We will send against you servants of Ours, and they will roam through [your land]. We will give you back the return of victory over them, support you with wealth and sons, and make you greater in manpower.

"Thumma" (then) indicates both a gradation in rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi) and a delay in time (al-tarakhi al-zamani).

"Al-radd" means to restore. The verb "radadna" (We gave back) is in the past form, following the common pattern in the answer to "idha," just as its condition is in the past form in His words "fa-idha ja'a wa'du ula-humaa, ba'athna" (so when the promise of the first of the two came, We sent). That is, "idha yajii, yab'athu" (when it comes, He sends). "Al-karra" is a return to the place from which one departed.

Thus His words "'alayhim" (against them) is a settled adverbial phrase (zarf mustaqirr) functioning as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "al-karra" (the return), because the return of the Children of Israel to Urshalim (Jerusalem) came about through the triumph of the king of Persia over the king of Babylon.

This is because the Children of Israel, after they had spent more than forty years in captivity under the Babylonians, repented to God and regretted what they had neglected. God then gave the kings of Persia power over the kings of Babylon, the Assyrians. The king Kurash (Cyrus) of Persia fought the Babylonians and defeated them, so their authority weakened. Then Daryush (Darius), king of Persia, attacked them and conquered Babylon in 538 BCE. In 530 BCE he permitted the Jews to return to Urshalim and renew their state. That was a victory they achieved over the Babylonians, who had been helpers of the Persians against them.

The promise of this victory also appears in the Book of Isaiah (Ashi'ya) in chapters 10, 11, 12, and elsewhere, and in the Book of Jeremiah (Armiya) in chapters 28 and 29.

His words "wa-amdadnakum bi-amwalin wa-banina wa-ja'alnakum akthara nafiran" (and We supported you with wealth and sons, and made you greater in manpower) are part of what was decreed and promised. It occurs in chapter 29 of the Book of Jeremiah: "Thus says the Lord, God of Israel, to all who were carried away captive from Urshalim to Babil: Build houses and dwell in them; plant gardens and eat their fruit; take wives and beget sons and daughters; multiply there and do not diminish."

"Nafiran" is a specifying accusative (tamyiz) of "akthar," and it clarifies the respect in which they are greater. "Al-nafir" is a collective noun (ism jam') for the group of people who go out with a man from his people and kin. From this comes Abu Jahl's saying: "Neither in the caravan nor in the company" (la fi al-'ir wa la fi al-nafir).

The comparative in "akthar" is a comparison with themselves, meaning: We made you greater than you were before the exile (al-jala'). This suits the context of divine favor. A group of exegetes said: "akthar nafiran" means greater in manpower than your enemies who expelled you from your homes. That is, [God] destroyed most of the Babylonians in their wars with the Persians, so that the number of the Children of Israel in the land of captivity became greater than the number of the Babylonians.

His words "in ahsantum ahsantum li-anfusikum wa-in asa'tum fa-laha" (if you do good, you do good for yourselves; and if you do evil, then it is for them) are part of what was decreed in the Book, of what the Children of Israel were addressed with. It is a rendering of what appears in chapter 29 of the Book of Jeremiah: "Pray for it [the city] to the Lord, for in its peace you will have peace." It also appears in chapter 31: "The Lord says, I will plant the house of Israel and the house of Judah, and it will be that as I watched over them to uproot, tear down, destroy and ruin, so I will watch over them to build and plant in those days. They will no longer say: The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge. Rather, each one will die for his own sin; everyone who eats sour grapes, his teeth will be set on edge."

The meaning of "in ahsantum ahsantum li-anfusikum" (if you do good, you do good for yourselves) is: We restore to you the return for the sake of repentance and the renewal of the generation. You are now in a state of blessing. If you do good, your recompense will be good. If you do evil, it is to your own harm. Just as We destroyed those before you for their sins, We have shown you kindness by accepting your repentance. So beware of evil, lest you come to the fate of those before you.

[Page 33]

Repeating the verb "ahsantum" is a means of emphasis (tanwih). He did not say "in ahsantum fa-li-anfusikum" (if you do good, then it is for yourselves). This is like the verse of al-Ahwas:

fa-idha tazulu tazulu 'an mutakhammitin
tukhsha bawadiruhu 'ala al-aqran

(So when he departs, he departs from one in a furious rage, whose sudden outbursts are feared by his equals.)

Abu al-Fath Ibn Jinni said in his commentary on the verse of al-Ahwas in al-Hamasa: The construction "fa-idha tazulu tazulu" is permitted only because a preposition is attached to the second verb, which gives the phrase its meaning. A similar case is God's saying: "These are the ones whom We misled; We misled them as We ourselves were misled" (al-Qasas 28:63). If He had said "These are the ones whom We misled; We misled them," the statement would convey nothing, just as your saying "The one whom I struck, I struck" conveys nothing. Abu 'Ali [al-Farisi] had refused in this verse what we had taken (in the original, "ajaznahu," we permitted it). However, the matter in it, in my view, is as I have explained to you. End of quote.

The apparent reason for Abu 'Ali's refusal in this verse is that he held it permissible for "aghwayna-hum" (We misled them) to be an emphatic restatement of "aghwayna" (We misled). His words "kama ghawayna" (as We ourselves were misled) would then be a resumptive explanatory clause (istinaf bayani), because the relative pronoun is predicated of a subject, which is the demonstrative "haa'ulaa'" (these). The sentence is thus complete with that. This is unlike the verse of al-Ahwas and Ibn Jinni's example: "The one whom I struck, I struck." So Abu 'Ali's refusal comes down to this: what Ibn Jinni took is not as definitively required in the verse as it is in the verse of al-Ahwas.

The style of repeating a verb when one intends to attach something to it is an eloquent Arabic idiom, used to draw attention to that action. It occurs in the Qur'an. God says: "And when you strike, you strike as tyrants" (al-Shu'ara' 26:130). And He says: "And when they pass by idle talk, they pass by with dignity" (al-Furqan 25:72).

His words "ahsantum ahsantum li-anfusikum" (if you do good, you do good for yourselves) follow the method of tajrid (abstraction), in that the self of the doer of good is treated as a person to whom good is done. Thus the "li-" (for) makes transitive the verb "ahsantum," as in the expression "ahsantu li-fulan" (I did good to so-and-so).

Likewise His words "wa-in asa'tum fa-laha" (and if you do evil, then it is for them): "fa-laha" is attached to a verb omitted after the answer particle "fa," with the estimated meaning "asa'tum laha" (you did evil to it). The prepositional phrase is not a settled adverbial predicate of an omitted subject, implied by the verb "asa'tum," because if it were, he would have said "fa-'alayha" (then it is against them), as in His words in Surat Fussilat: "Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own self; and whoever does evil, it is against it" (Fussilat 41:46).

[Page 34]

The difference between the style of the two verses is that the verse of Fussilat contains no abstraction. Its estimated sense is: "fa-'amaluhu li-nafsihi, wa-isa'atuhu 'alayha" (his deed is for himself, and his evil is against it). Since the omitted element is a noun, the prepositional phrase after it is a settled adverbial and not a transitive particle. It follows what the statement requires: when the thing spoken of is beneficial, it is described with a phrase introduced by "li-" (for); when it is harmful, it is described with a phrase introduced by "'ala" (against). In the verse of al-Isra', however, the verbs "ahsantum" and "asa'tum," which occur in the two answer clauses, require abstraction. So they come in their original transitive construction with "li-," not to indicate benefit or harm.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 17, verses 7–8:**

﴿So when the promise of the second [transgression] comes, [We will send them to] disfigure your faces and enter the place of worship as they entered it the first time, and to destroy what they had conquered with complete destruction.﴾ ﴿It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you; but if you return [to sin], We will return [to punishment]. And We have made Hell a prison for the disbelievers.﴾

This is a resultant clause (tafri') built upon His saying, "And if you do evil, then it is for yourselves." The sense of the discourse is: "So when you do evil, and the promise of the second time comes..."

By this resultant construction, an admirable concision (ijaz) is achieved. It fulfils the requirement of the first division in His saying, "So when the promise of the first of them comes," and the requirement of conveying that the arrival of the promise of the second [transgression] is consequent upon the evil-doing. Had it been conjoined with the particle "and" (wa), as the apparent form of the division into two times would require, the implication of sequence and consequence would have been lost.

Al-Akhirah ("the second/last") is an attribute of an elided noun indicated by His saying "two times" (marratayn). That is, "the promise of the second time."

This statement is part of what was decreed in the Book, as indicated by its being connected with the particle fa' (so).

[p. 36]

Al-akhirah is the opposite of al-ula ("the first").

The lam-particles in liyasu'u, liyadkhulu and liyutabbiru are lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil), not lam of command (lam al-amr). This is because the widely-transmitted readings agree on the kasra of the second and third lams. Had they been lams of command, they would have been jussive/sukun after the conjunctive wa, so it is necessarily the first lam that is the lam of command—not the lam of the genitive (lam al-jarr). The sense is: "So when the promise of the second comes, We send against you servants of Ours, to disfigure your faces," and so on.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Hafs, Abu Ja'far and Ya'qub read liyasu'u with the plural pronoun, like its four sister verbs. The pronouns refer to an elided noun indicated by the lam of causation in liyasu'u, since it is connected to what is indicated by His saying, "When the promise of the first of them comes, We send against you servants of Ours" (17:5). The sense is: "So when the promise of the second comes, We send against you servants of Ours, to disfigure your faces." The pronouns do not refer back to "servants of Ours" explicitly mentioned in "When the promise of the first of them comes, We send against you servants of Ours possessing mighty might," because those who did evil and entered the place of worship this time were a people other than those who roamed through the homes, according to the testimony of history and the statements of the exegetes, as will come.

Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, Abu Bakr (from 'Asim), and Khalaf read liyasu'a in the singular, with the pronoun referring to God Most High. Al-Kisa'i read linasu'a with the "We" of majesty (nun al-'azamah). The justification for these two readings from the standpoint of conformity with the Qur'anic orthography (rasm al-mushaf) is that the open hamza after the wa may be written in the form of an alif. Thus the script permits reading it as the plural wa, with the alif being the alif of differentiation (alif al-farq), and it also permits the two singular readings, with the alif being the sign of the hamza.

The pronouns of liyasu'u and liyudkhilu refer to "servants of Ours" in terms of its wording, not in terms of the actual referents of the return (ma-sadaq al-ma'ad), in the manner of their saying: "I have a dirham and its half," meaning "the half of the one who bears the name dirham." This relies upon the context, since the wording requires a long interval of time between the two times. Therefore this elision is a form of concision.

[p. 37]

The pronoun in "as they entered it" refers to the servants mentioned in the mention of the first time, by the context that the meaning requires the referents of pronouns, as in His saying, "And they stirred up the earth and cultivated it more than they had cultivated it" (30:9). And as in the verse of 'Abbas ibn Mirdas:

"We returned, and had it not been for us, their host would have encircled the Muslims,
And they would have secured what they had gathered."

The context indicates the referents of "they secured" and "they gathered."

The disfiguring of faces (sau' al-wujuh) is placing harm upon them, that is, imposing causes of distress and sorrow upon you until they appear on your faces. For whatever a person feels of grief and sorrow, or joy and gladness, its effect appears on the face and not on any other part of the body, as in the words of al-A'sha:

"And I advance when the eyes of the people shrink in fear."

He meant: when the people scatter, and the signs of fear appear in their eyes.

The entering of the place of worship is the entering of raiding, by the indication of the comparison in His saying, "as they entered it the first time," the meaning of which is His saying, "and they roamed through the homes."

Al-tatbir is destruction and corruption.

[*ma 'alaw*] is a relative pronoun serving as the object of yutabbiru, and the returning pronoun of the relative clause is elided, since it is attached and in the accusative. The sense is: "what they had conquered (ma 'alawhu)." Ulu (elevation) is figurative elevation, which is domination and conquest.

God did not promise them in this time except the expectation of mercy, without the return of the turn of power. This is an allusion that they will have no dominion after this time. By this it becomes clear that what is referred to by "this last time" is what the Jews committed of corruption and rebellion, the killing of prophets and the righteous, and their aggression against Jesus and his followers. The prophet (Malachi) warned them in the third and fourth chapters of his book, and Zechariah, John (Yahya) and Jesus warned them too, but they did not heed. So God struck them with the decisive blow at the hands of the Romans.

[p. 38]

The explanation of this is that the Jews, after they returned to Jerusalem and renewed their kingdom and their sanctuary in the time of Darius, and were permitted to manage their affairs in their lands which the Babylonians had conquered from them, and were under the authority of the kingdom of Persia, remained so for two hundred years, from 530 to 330 BC. Then their kingdom began to dissolve with the assault of the Ptolemies, kings of Egypt, upon Jerusalem, so they came under their authority until 166 BC. Then a leader from Israel named (Mithya), who was of the Levites, arose, triumphed for the Jews, and took charge over them. Rule passed successively to his sons in a time full of strife until 40 BC, when the kingdom came under the authority of the Romans, who set over it Jewish princes, the most famous of whom was (Herod). Then they rebelled to break away from the Romans, so the Caesar of Rome sent the commander Cestius with his son, the commander Titus, with armies around the year 40 AD. Jerusalem was ruined and the sanctuary was burned. Titus captured some ninety-odd thousand Jews, and killed in those wars about a million Jews. Then they recovered the city, and a small remnant of them remained in it until the Roman emperor Hadrian came to them, destroyed and ruined it, and threw loads of salt upon its soil so that it would not return to being fit for agriculture. That was in the year 135 AD. With that the affair of the Jews ended and they were extinct, and they were scattered over the earth. Jerusalem did not leave Roman rule until the Muslims conquered it in the time of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab in the year 16 AH, by treaty with its people. It was then called Aelia (Iliya').

His saying, "And if you return, We return" (wa in 'udtum 'udna), may be a conjunction joining it to the clause "It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you," as a conjunction of warning upon encouragement.

It may also be a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradiyyah), with the wa being parenthetical, and the meaning being: after your Lord has shown you mercy and granted you security in the lands to which you flee, if you return to corruption, We return to punishing you—that is, We return to the like of the punishments of the worldly life that came before.

[p. 39]

The clause "And We have made Hell a prison for the disbelievers" is joined to the clause "It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you," in order to convey that the punishment mentioned before it is a worldly punishment, and that behind it is the punishment of the Hereafter.

It carries the sense of a concluding appendage (tadhyil), because the definite article in "the disbelievers" encompasses those addressed and others. This points to the fact that their punishment in this world is not restricted to the sins of disbelief, but is tied to corruption on earth and transgression of the bounds of the Law. As for disbelief through denying the messengers, this occurred in the last time, for they denied Jesus. In the first time, messengers had not come to them, but they killed the prophets, such as Isaiah (Ash'ya') and Jeremiah (Irmiya'), and the killing of prophets is disbelief.

Al-hasir is the place in which one is confined so that escape from it is not possible. It is either a form of fa'il in the sense of the active participle, or in the sense of the passive participle, on the presumption of an implied complement: that is, "confined within it."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 9–10:

﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright and gives good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds that they will have a great reward﴾ ﴿And that those who do not believe in the Hereafter, We have prepared for them a painful punishment﴾ This is an initiating resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i), by which the discourse returns to the most important purpose of this surah, which is the confirmation of the Prophet ﷺ with signs and miracles, and the giving to him of signs, the greatest of which is the sign of the Qur'an, as we presented earlier at the words of His, exalted is He, ﴿And We gave Moses the Book﴾ [al-Isra': 2]. This is followed by mention of what was sent down to the Children of Israel of books for guidance and warning, and what befell them of the recompense for their opposition to what Allah had commanded them, and their deviation from the ways of their forefathers since the time of Noah. In this is the benefit of warning against the Muslims falling into what the Children of Israel fell into, and this is the greatest benefit of mentioning the stories of the Qur'an, namely the benefit of history.

And the emphasis (ta'kid) of the sentence takes into account the state of some of the addressees, who did not submit to it, and the state of the believers in their concern with this report. So the emphasis is used in both its meanings: removing denial (daf' al-inkar) and expressing concern (al-ihtimam), and there is no contradiction between the two considerations.

His saying (hadha al-Qur'an) is a pointing to what is present in people's minds of the portion of the Qur'an revealed before this verse.

The demonstrative is clarified by the noun that follows it, as an honoring of the status of the Qur'an.

This verse came as a relief for the believers from the effect of the frightening stories that were recounted about the Children of Israel and the calamities that befell them, which would stir in the souls of the Muslims fear that the like of what happened to those would befall them. So they were informed that in the Qur'an is that which protects them from falling into what the Children of Israel fell into, since it guides to the way that is more upright than what the Children of Israel followed. For this reason, along with guidance, it mentions the good tidings to the believers who do righteous deeds, and the warning to those who do not believe in the Hereafter. In the expression with (allati hiya aqwamu) there is a subtle point that will come, and this is the Qur'an's custom of following fear with hope and the reverse.

(allati hiya aqwamu) is an attribute (sifah) of an omitted noun indicated by yahdi, i.e., to the way that is most upright; because guidance is among the concomitants of journeying and the path. Or it is to the creed that is most upright. In omitting the described noun there is brevity on one hand, and magnification on the other, which favors omission over mention.

Al-aqwam is the elative of al-qawim, and the meaning is: it guides to that which is more upright than the guidance of the Book of the Children of Israel which is in His saying (﴿And We made it a guidance for the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Isra': 2]). So in this there is an allusion to the securing of the community of the Qur'an from deviating from the most upright path, because the Qur'an came with a method of guidance that is upright, rich in branches, that nothing stands between it and entering the intellects, and it does not leave any avenue to any aspect of morals and dispositions except that it leads to it by encouragement or warning, such that the reflecting person in its meanings does not fail to gather the fruits of its branches. And by those methods which the earlier books did not reach, the way to which it guides is more upright than the other ways, even if the intended goal to reach is one.

This is a general description of the meaning of its guidance to that which is most upright; were its detail to be intended, it would require volumes. Let it suffice as an example of this the methods of the Qur'an in blocking the paths of polytheism, such that this verse in all its stages was safe from confusion between human sanctification and divine glorification, so it never descended to the depths of polytheism in any way. Thus the locus of preference is the means of reaching the goal of truth and sincerity, and the locus of preference is not that goal itself, so that it might be said: truth does not vary.

The great reward has been explained as Paradise, and the painful punishment as Hell. The more evident view is that it be taken in the general sense of reward and punishment, so that it includes the reward and punishment of this world, and this is more fitting to what preceded of the happiness and misery of the life of the Children of Israel, so the difference of the two states in them is made an admonition for the states of the Muslims and the polytheists.

(﴿And that those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾) is conjoined (ma'tuf) to (﴿that they will have a great reward﴾), because it is among the content of the good tidings, since by those who do not believe in the Hereafter is meant the polytheists of Quraysh, who were the enemies of the believers, so there is no doubt that the punishment of the enemy is good tidings to whoever opposes him.

Restricting the discourse to these two groups is what the context requires, given the connection to the polytheists' denial of the Night Journey (al-Isra'), so there is no purpose in informing about the condition of the People of the Book.
