Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 11:

﴿And man prays for evil as he prays for good, and man has always been hasty.﴾

The position of this verse here is obscure, and extracting its meaning from its composition and wording is likewise difficult. The exegetes have not offered anything that truly satisfies the heart. What appears to me is that:

The verse before it, since it contained glad tidings and warning, and since those who were warned, when they heard the threat and the warning, mocked it and said (﴿When will this promise be fulfilled, if you are truthful?﴾ [al-Anbiya': 38]), this statement was joined to what preceded it as an alert that this promise has a specified term. Thus, by "man" is meant the man who does not believe in the Hereafter, as in His Exalted saying: (﴿And man says, "When I have died, shall I really be brought forth alive?"﴾ [Maryam: 66]) and (﴿Does man not remember that We created him before, while he was nothing?﴾ [Maryam: 67]). The application of "man" to the disbeliever is frequent in the Qur'an.

The verb (yad'u, "prays/calls") is used in the sense of seeking and desiring, as in the saying of Labid:

I call upon them for a barren she-camel or one with a young calf, whose meat has been distributed among the neighbours of all of them.

His saying (﴿du'a'ahu bil-khayr﴾, "his prayer for good") is a verbal noun conveying a comparison: that is, he seeks evil hastily just as he seeks good hastily, meaning he is slow to accept the arrival of the threatened punishment, just as one is slow to accept the delay of a news he was promised.

His saying: (﴿And man has always been hasty﴾) is a concluding statement (tadhyil). Here "man" refers to the species, since that is what suits the concluding statement; that is, these disbelievers who do not believe in the Hereafter are only of the kind of man, and hastiness is in the nature of man. The particle (kana, "has been") indicates that its subject is characterized by its predicate in a firmly established way, as in His Exalted saying: (﴿And man has been most quarrelsome of all things﴾ [al-Kahf: 54]).

The intended meaning of His saying (﴿And man has always been hasty﴾) is a kinayah (allusion) to his lack of insight, and that God knows best what wisdom requires regarding the timing of things: (﴿And if God were to hasten for people the evil as they seek to hasten the good, their term would have been decreed for them﴾ [Yunus: 11]). Rather, He has gradually allowed the arrival of good and evil to them, out of kindness toward them in both states.

The letter bi' in His saying (bil-sharr wa bil-khayr) serves to emphasize the attachment of the governing verb to its object, like the one in His Exalted saying: (﴿and wipe over your heads﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6]); or it is to imply the meaning of hastening within the root of "calling," so it is like His Exalted saying: (﴿Those who do not believe in it seek to hasten it﴾ [al-Shura: 18]).

"'Ajul" is an intensive form of "'ajil" (hasty). It is said: "'ajila" so he is "'ajil" and "'ajul."

In the Mushaf, (wa-yad'u) was written without a waw after the 'ayn, in accordance with writing the word as it is pronounced when connected, just as (sanad'u al-zabaniyah) and similar examples were written. Al-Farra' said: had it been written with a waw, it would have been correct.

**Verse 12 of Surah al-Isra' (17):**

﴿And We made the night and the day two signs. Then We effaced the sign of the night, and We made the sign of the day to give sight, that you might seek bounty from your Lord, and that you might know the number of years and the reckoning. And everything We have detailed with full detail.﴾

It is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "and man prays for evil..." and so on. The connection (munāsaba) is that the clause "and man prays for evil" implies that delay does not lift the postponement of the promise, and that hastening does not benefit the one who hastens, because for everything there is a term (ajal). Since the term consists of periods of time, it comprises a night and a day passing one after another. This is common among people, in that time passes away, however long it lasts.

When the intention was to draw attention to this, there was inserted (udmija) into it what is more important in the lesson drawn from the two periods of time: that they are two signs of the existence of the Creator and of His great power; that they are two favours upon people; that people sometimes dislike the night because of its darkness and hasten its end by the dawn breaking, as in the verses of poets and others; then, with further lesson, that they are opposites, and that in each of them are the effects of different blessings. The blessing of movement during the day is one of these, and after it he dispensed with mentioning the blessing of rest at night, because that is evident by contrast. Through this contrast there is obtained the blessing of knowing the number of years and the reckoning, because if the whole of time were darkness or whole light, the distinction between its parts would not occur.

In this, after all that, there is also an allusion to the coining of a parable for disbelief and belief, and for misguidance and guidance. Therefore it follows with it His saying (﴿And We gave Moses the Book﴾ [al-Isra': 2]) and the verse, and His saying ﴿Indeed this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ [al-Isra': 9] up to His saying ﴿and We have prepared for them a painful punishment﴾ [al-Isra': 10]. For the same reason, after it he follows with His saying ﴿Whoever is guided, is only guided for his own soul﴾ [al-Isra': 15], and the verse. All this insertion (idmaj) adds to the verse abundant meanings, in keeping with the eloquence and conciseness of the Qur'an.

The branching of the clause ﴿So We effaced the sign of the night﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtiraḍ) which came with the fāʾ between the clause ﴿We made the night and the day﴾ and its dependent element, which is "that you might seek" (li-tabtaghū).

The annexation (iḍāfa) of "sign" to "the night" and to "the day" may be explanatory (bayaniyya), meaning "the sign which is the night" and "the sign which is the day". It may also be that "the sign of the night" is the sign that accompanies it, which is the moon, and "the sign of the day" is the sun. Then the repetition of the word "sign" in both is a reminder that the meaning of "sign" here is another meaning, and the annexation is real (ḥaqīqiyya). This becomes another proof of the wondrous workmanship of God, the Exalted, and a reminder of the blessing of the creation of these two great creations. The meaning of effacement (maḥw) is that the moon is obscured, with no light in its body, but it acquires illumination through the reflection of the sun's rays on its sphere. The meaning of the day being "giving sight" (mubṣira) is that the light of the sun was made the cause of people's seeing things. So "mubṣira" is the active participle of "abṣara" (to make see), which is transitive, meaning He made others see. This is the more precise meaning, and deeper in its eloquence and knowledge regarding the inimitability of the Qur'an, for this is a truth of the science of astronomy, and the word "sign" was only repeated for its sake.

Maḥw means obliteration, and it was applied to the absence of light because light makes things apparent, while in darkness things do not appear. So the disappearance of things was likened to effacement, as is shown by His saying in contrast to it ﴿And We made the sign of the day giving sight﴾, meaning: We made darkness a sign, and We made the cause of sight a sign. The description "giving sight" was applied to the day by way of metaphor of the mind (majāz ʿaqlī), by attributing to it the cause.

His saying ﴿that you might seek bounty from your Lord﴾ is the reason for specifically the sign of the day, from His saying "two signs".

The reason for the wisdom of the sign of the day specifically was given, not what corresponds to it, the wisdom of the night, because the favour in it is clearer, and because through attention to it there is attained awareness of its opposite, which is the wisdom of rest at night, as He said ﴿that you may rest therein, and the day giving sight﴾ [Yunus: 67], as was mentioned earlier in Surah Yunus.

Then another wisdom was mentioned, arising from both signs, which is the wisdom of calculating years. It is clearer in the sign of the night, because the majority of mankind reckon months and years by nights, that is, the reckoning of the moon.

Reckoning (ḥisāb) includes the reckoning of days, months and seasons, so its coordination with "the number of years" is coordination of the general with the particular (ʿaṭf al-ʿāmm ʿalā al-khāṣṣ), for generalisation after mention of the particular, out of concern for it.

The clause ﴿and everything We have detailed with full detail﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyīl) to His saying ﴿We made the night and the day two signs﴾, in view of what preceded it regarding the allusion to the fact that for evil and for good promised by them there is a term at which they end. The meaning is: that term is determined in the knowledge of God, the Exalted, and does not exceed it, so hastening does not bring it closer, nor does delay postpone it, because God has made for everything a measure with no ambiguity in it and no doubt with Him.

Indeed for good and for evil there is a term . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . so do not suppose that this is a promise left in vain.

Tafṣīl means clarification and distinction, and it is derived from faṣl in the sense of cutting, because clarification requires that a thing not be confused with another. It was already mentioned in His saying, the Exalted, ﴿A Book whose verses are made firm, then detailed﴾ [Hud: 1], at the beginning of Surah Hud.

Detailing of things occurs in their creation, their order, God's knowledge of them, and His informing about them. So the detailing that is in God's knowledge, in His creation, and in the laws of the worlds is general for everything, and this is what the generality requires here. As for what God detailed for people of rulings and reports, that is part of things, and among it is His saying, the Exalted, ﴿He details the signs that perhaps you may meet your Lord with certainty﴾ [al-Ra'd: 2], and His saying ﴿We have detailed the signs for a people who know﴾ [al-An'am: 97]. That occurs through the conveying by the tongues of the Messengers and through what God created in people of the faculties of understanding, and among what He detailed for people is guidance to monotheism, righteous deeds, and warning against disobedience. In this there is an indirect reference (taʿrīḍ) of threat.

[Page 46]

"Kulla shay'" (everything) is in the accusative by a suppressed verb, which is explained by "faṣṣalnāhu" (We detailed it), because the mentioned element is occupied with the pronoun of the omitted object.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verses 13–14:

﴿And every person We have fastened his bird (fate) to his neck, and We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a record which he will find spread open.﴾ ﴿"Read your record. Your own self suffices as a reckoner against you this Day."﴾

Since the context of the speech has been running along the path of encouraging righteous deeds and warning against disbelief and misdeeds, beginning with His saying, ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most suitable and gives good tidings to the believers﴾ [al-Isra: 9], up to His saying, ﴿a painful punishment﴾ [al-Isra: 10], and what follows it concerning good tidings and warning, and what has been interwoven within that of reminders, there is a point which indicates that the knowledge of Allah encompasses everything in detail, and the most important of things in this station is the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of all deeds. So after mentioning what Allah has detailed of things, He follows it with an alert to the detailing of people's deeds, a detailing that admits neither doubt nor concealment, which is the detailing resembling being recorded in writing. Thus the conjunction of His saying "And every person…" etc. upon His saying ﴿And everything We have detailed in detail﴾ [al-Isra: 12] is a specific conjunction upon the general, for the sake of giving attention to this specific matter.

The meaning: And every person – We have decreed for him his deed in Our decree, so he is certainly doing it. This is among the conditions of this world.

The "ṭā'ir" (bird): it is applied to the arrow, or to the slip (qirtas) in which is designated the one who has a share in a gift or in a lottery for a division, or to the portions of the slaughtered camel in the game of maysir (qimar). It is said: "They divided the land, and such-and-such fell (ṭāra) to so-and-so." From this is the saying of Umm al-'Ala al-Ansariyya in the hadith of the Hijra: "The Ansar cast lots among the Muhajirun, and 'Uthman ibn Maz'un fell (ṭāra) to us..." and she mentioned the story of his death.

The origin of applying "ṭā'ir" to this is either: because they used to throw arrows inscribed with the names of the sharers upon the piles of the thing to be divided, prepared for distribution, so whoever the arrow inscribed with his name fell upon, took that; and they used to call the throwing of the arrow "flying" (ṭayarān), because they would place feathers on its vanes so that its piercing of the air would be light when shot from the bow. Thus "ṭā'ir" here is applied to a person's portion of deeds, just as the name "arrow" is applied to a person's portion of something.
Or it is from the augury of birds, to know fortune or misfortune of the augur from the state of the bird that crosses him on his path; and most often they did this on their journeys, and this spread in speech, so "ṭā'ir" was applied to a person's portion of good or evil.

"Ilzam" (binding): making it necessary for him, i.e., not separating from him; it is said: "lazimahu" when he does not part from it.

His saying "fi 'unuqihi" (on his neck) may be a metaphor for close attachment and nearness, i.e., his deed is necessary for him like a necklace, and from this is the Arabs' saying "you hang it like the collar of the dove"; thus it is specifically connected to the neck, because a necklace is placed on the neck of a woman. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"And poetry, I have hung it upon Salama, the one of Fa'ish, and a thing wherever it is placed..."

It may also be an illustration of a situation which was perhaps known among the Arabs, namely the placing of marks hung upon the necks of those who are designated for some task or from whom something is to be taken; and in Islam this was done to the People of the Dhimma, as Bashshar said:

"Love has written for her upon my neck, in the place of the seal, from among the people of the covenants (dhimam)."

It is also possible that "fi 'unuqihi" is an illustration with the camel that is branded on its neck with a mark so it does not get mixed with others, or the one upon whose neck a bell is placed so that it does not stray from its owner.

The meaning in all of these is that every person is dealt with according to his deed, good or evil, none of it being diminished for him; and this is other than the writing of deeds which will be mentioned right after this with His saying ﴿And We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a record﴾ ... the verse.

The conjunction of the clause "And We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a record" is information that those deeds expressed by the "ṭā'ir" will appear on the Day of Resurrection detailed and specified, leaving nothing small or great unrecorded except that it is counted for requital.

Al-Jumhur read "wa-nukhriju" with the nun of majesty and with a kasra on the ra'; Ya'qub read it with the ya' of the third person and a kasra on the ra', the pronoun returning to Allah, known from the context, and this is an iltifat (shift). Abu Ja'far read it with a ya' of the third person at its beginning in the passive form, with a deputy subject, and "kitaban" in the accusative as object, and that is permissible.

"Kitab" (record): that in which is mention of the deeds and their enumeration; and "nashr" (spreading): the opposite of folding (tayy).

The meaning of "yalqahu" is "yajiduhu" (finds it); the verb "yalqa" has been used metaphorically for the sense of "yajidu" (finds), likening the finding of a relation to meeting a person. And "nashr" is a metaphor for the speed of his becoming aware of all that he did, such that the record appears before its owner arrives, open for reading.

Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read "yulaqqahu" with a damma on the ya' and a shadda on the qaf, in the passive, on the basis that it is the doubled form of laqiya, for transitivity, i.e., making him one who encounters it, like His saying ﴿And He has given them radiance and joy﴾ [al-Insan: 11], and it is attributed to the object in the sense of "making him encounter," like His saying ﴿And none receives it except those who are patient﴾ [Fussilat: 35] and His saying ﴿And they will be met therein with greeting and peace﴾ [al-Furqan: 75].

The "nashr" of the record is its being displayed so that it may be read; He, Exalted, said: ﴿And when the pages are spread﴾.

The clause "Read your record" is a quoted speech of an omitted saying, indicated by the context.

The imperative in "iqra'" is used for taskhir (compelling/subjugation), and is a metaphor for giving them an excuse and for arguing against them, as His saying ﴿Your own self suffices as a reckoner against you this Day﴾ indicates; and for this reason the knowledge of those deeds from that record is attained by the reader.

Reading is used for knowing what has been recorded for the person of deeds, or for understanding the particular inscriptions if there are inscriptions there, and these are extraordinary occurrences (khawariq al-'adat).

The "ba'" in "bi-nafsika" is an emphatic extra particle entering upon the subject of "kafa," as already mentioned in His saying ﴿And Allah suffices as a witness﴾ [al-Nisa: 79] in Surat al-Nisa.

"Hasiban" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) of the attribution of sufficiency to the self, i.e., in respect of a reckoner. "Hasib" is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of fa'il, like "darib al-qidah" meaning its striker, and "sarim" meaning "sarim" (sharp), i.e., the one who reckons and keeps account. The occurrence of the specification after "kafa bi-kadha" is frequent, and it is transitivized with "'ala" for including the sense of "shahid" (witness). The referent of "nafs" is the person in His saying ﴿And every person We have fastened his bird﴾, and therefore "hasib" came in the masculine form.

It is said: "They divided the land, and such-and-such fell (ṭāra) to so-and-so." From this is the saying of Umm al-'Ala al-Ansariyya in the hadith of the Hijra: "The Ansar cast lots among the Muhajirun, and 'Uthman ibn Maz'un fell (ṭāra) to us..." and she mentioned the story of his death.

The origin of applying "ṭā'ir" to this is either: because they used to throw arrows inscribed with the names of the sharers upon the piles of the thing to be divided, prepared for distribution, so whoever the arrow inscribed with his name fell upon, took that; and they used to call the throwing of the arrow "flying" (ṭayarān), because they would place feathers on its vanes so that its piercing of the air would be light when shot from the bow. Thus "ṭā'ir" here is applied to a person's portion of deeds, just as the name "arrow" is applied to a person's portion of something.
Or it is from the augury of birds, to know fortune or misfortune of the augur from the state of the bird that crosses him on his path; and most often they did this on their journeys, and this spread in speech, so "ṭā'ir" was applied to a person's portion of good or evil.

"Ilzam" (binding): making it necessary for him, i.e., not separating from him; it is said: "lazimahu" when he does not part from it.

His saying "fi 'unuqihi" (on his neck) may be a metaphor for close attachment and nearness, i.e., his deed is necessary for him like a necklace, and from this is the Arabs' saying "you hang it like the collar of the dove"; thus it is specifically connected to the neck, because a necklace is placed on the neck of a woman. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"And poetry, I have hung it upon Salama, the one of Fa'ish, and a thing wherever it is placed..."

It may also be an illustration of a situation which was perhaps known among the Arabs, namely the placing of marks hung upon the necks of those who are designated for some task or from whom something is to be taken; and in Islam this was done to the People of the Dhimma, as Bashshar said:

"Love has written for her upon my neck, in the place of the seal, from among the people of the covenants (dhimam)."

It is also possible that "fi 'unuqihi" is an illustration with the camel that is branded on its neck with a mark so it does not get mixed with others, or the one upon whose neck a bell is placed so that it does not stray from its owner.

The meaning in all of these is that every person is dealt with according to his deed, good or evil, none of it being diminished for him; and this is other than the writing of deeds which will be mentioned right after this with His saying ﴿And We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a record﴾ ... the verse.

The conjunction of the clause "And We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a record" is information that those deeds expressed by the "ṭā'ir" will appear on the Day of Resurrection detailed and specified, leaving nothing small or great unrecorded except that it is counted for requital.

Al-Jumhur read "wa-nukhriju" with the nun of majesty and with a kasra on the ra'; Ya'qub read it with the ya' of the third person and a kasra on the ra', the pronoun returning to Allah, known from the context, and this is an iltifat (shift). Abu Ja'far read it with a ya' of the third person at its beginning in the passive form, with a deputy subject, and "kitaban" in the accusative as object, and that is permissible.

"Kitab" (record): that in which is mention of the deeds and their enumeration; and "nashr" (spreading): the opposite of folding (tayy).

The meaning of "yalqahu" is "yajiduhu" (finds it); the verb "yalqa" has been used metaphorically for the sense of "yajidu" (finds), likening the finding of a relation to meeting a person. And "nashr" is a metaphor for the speed of his becoming aware of all that he did, such that the record appears before its owner arrives, open for reading.

Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read "yulaqqahu" with a damma on the ya' and a shadda on the qaf, in the passive, on the basis that it is the doubled form of laqiya, for transitivity, i.e., making him one who encounters it, like His saying ﴿And He has given them radiance and joy﴾ [al-Insan: 11], and it is attributed to the object in the sense of "making him encounter," like His saying ﴿And none receives it except those who are patient﴾ [Fussilat: 35] and His saying ﴿And they will be met therein with greeting and peace﴾ [al-Furqan: 75].

The "nashr" of the record is its being displayed so that it may be read; He, Exalted, said: ﴿And when the pages are spread﴾.

The clause "Read your record" is a quoted speech of an omitted saying, indicated by the context.

The imperative in "iqra'" is used for taskhir (compelling/subjugation), and is a metaphor for giving them an excuse and for arguing against them, as His saying ﴿Your own self suffices as a reckoner against you this Day﴾ indicates; and for this reason the knowledge of those deeds from that record is attained by the reader.

Reading is used for knowing what has been recorded for the person of deeds, or for understanding the particular inscriptions if there are inscriptions there, and these are extraordinary occurrences (khawariq al-'adat).

The "ba'" in "bi-nafsika" is an emphatic extra particle entering upon the subject of "kafa," as already mentioned in His saying ﴿And Allah suffices as a witness﴾ [al-Nisa: 79] in Surat al-Nisa.

"Hasiban" is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) of the attribution of sufficiency to the self, i.e., in respect of a reckoner. "Hasib" is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of fa'il, like "darib al-qidah" meaning its striker, and "sarim" meaning "sarim" (sharp), i.e., the one who reckons and keeps account. The occurrence of the specification after "kafa bi-kadha" is frequent, and it is transitivized with "'ala" for including the sense of "shahid" (witness). The referent of "nafs" is the person in His saying ﴿And every person We have fastened his bird﴾, and therefore "hasib" came in the masculine form.

[Page 50]

This sentence is either an explanation (bayan) of, or a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for, the sentence ﴿And every human being – We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾ [al-Isra: 13] together with what follows it. It clarifies that the "bird" differs between what benefits and what harms: the bird of guidance benefits its bearer, and the bird of misguidance harms its bearer. Because the sentence is of this kind, it was disjoined (fusila) and not joined by a conjunction to the one before it.

The sentence ﴿No bearer bears the burden of another﴾ stands in the position of a causal explanation (ta'lil) for the content of the sentence ﴿And whoever goes astray, he only goes astray to his own detriment﴾, because of the generality of the ruling it contains: no one's deed's benefit or harm reaches anyone else.

Since the content of this sentence is an important meaning, it was regarded as providing new information (ifadah anafan) to the hearer. For this reason the sentence was joined by a conjunction and not disjoined. In it, the refutation is intended of the delusions of a people who think that others will carry their burdens for them. It is narrated that al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, one of the leaders of disbelief, used to say to the Quraysh: "Disbelieve in Muhammad, and my burdens (awzar) will be upon me," meaning: your consequences and your being held to account for denying him, if there is any consequence in it. Perhaps he said this when he saw their hesitation regarding Islam and their inclination to examine the proofs of the Qur'an, out of fear of recompense on the Day of Resurrection. So he wanted to deceive them by claiming that he would bear their sins if it became clear that Muhammad was upon the truth. This could have been persuasive to their common folk, because they were accustomed to bearing liabilities (hamalat), to guarantees (kafalat) and to pledges (rahain). So God made clear to people the refutation of this, to rescue them from being deceived by it, which would plunge them into ruin. Along with this explanation comes the teaching of a great principle in the religion, which is: no bearer bears the burden of another. Thus this verse became a great foundation in the Sharia, and many rulings branched out from it.

When Ibn 'Umar narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that the dead person is punished for the weeping of his family over him, 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "May Allah have mercy on Abu 'Abd al-Rahman. The Messenger of Allah did not say that, and Allah says: ﴿No bearer bears the burden of another﴾."

And when a funeral of a Jewish woman passed by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), her family were weeping over her, and he said: "They are weeping over her, while she is being punished."

The meaning is that no one's burden is carried by another. If someone, by his own burden, has caused another to fall into a burden, then the burden of that other is laid upon him, because he is its cause. This is not the carrying of another's burden upon him, but rather the carrying of his own burden upon himself, which is the burden of causing others to sin. God the Exalted has said: ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full on the Day of Resurrection, and some of the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge. Unquestionably, evil is what they bear﴾ [al-Nahl: 25]. Likewise is the burden of one who establishes for people a bad practice (sunnah) which they had not done before. In the Sahih it is recorded: "No soul is killed unjustly except that a share of its blood falls upon the first son of Adam, because he was the first to establish killing."

The verse is silent about whether anyone may benefit from the good deeds of another, since there is no need to explain it, as this does not give rise to delusion. It teaches equality through the implicit sense of the address (lahn al-khitab) or its implication (fahwa).

The Qur'an has indeed contained what points to the fact that one who causes another to be guided obtains a share of the reward of the one guided. God the Exalted has said: ﴿And make us leaders for the God-fearing﴾ [al-Furqan: 74]. And in a hadith: "When the son of Adam dies, his deeds are cut off except for three: a continuous charity (sadaqah jariyah), knowledge which he spread among the hearts of men, and a righteous child who prays for him."

From confusion is the supposition that the imposition of blood money (diyah) for accidental killing upon the paternal kin ('aqilah) contradicts this verse. That is a branch of another principle, namely the principle of mutual cooperation and solidarity (ta'awun wa muwasah), and it is not from the transfer of liabilities.

"Tazir" means to carry a burden (wizr), which is a heavy weight. The "wazirah" is the one who carries. Its feminine form is due to considering it a self (nafs), in accordance with His saying before it: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own self, and whoever does evil, it is against it﴾ [Fussilat: 46]. It was applied to the self as "wazirah" in the sense of supposition and assumption: that is, if a self bearing a burden were supposed, it would not have added to its burden the burden of another. So it is understood that a self which has no burden does not bear the burden of another, all the more so.

"Wizr" is sin, because it is likened to a heavy load for the toil it brings its bearer in the Hereafter, just as it was also applied to it the word "thiql" (weight). God the Exalted has said: ﴿And they will surely bear their own burdens and burdens along with their burdens﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 13].

* * *

﴿And We would not punish until We sent a messenger﴾

This is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon the verse ﴿Whoever is guided, he is only guided to his own benefit﴾, and so on.

This is an extended emphasis on giving excuse to the people of misguidance, in addition to negating their being held to account for the crimes of others. For this reason it was restricted to His saying "And We would not punish", without saying "nor would We reward," because the context is one of giving excuse and cutting off argument, not one of bestowing favour through guidance.

The punishment here is the punishment of this world, by the indication of the context and by the conjunction of ﴿And when We intend to destroy a city, We command its affluent ones﴾ [al-Isra: 16], and by many verses. God the Exalted said: ﴿And We never destroyed a city except that it had warners as a reminder, and We were not unjust﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 208], and He said: ﴿So when their messenger comes, judgment will be made between them with justice, and they will not be wronged﴾ [Yunus: 47]. Moreover, the meaning of "hatta" (until) indicates that the sending of the messenger is connected to the punishment in the manner of a limit (ghayah). This connection is customary, in accordance with what the sending requires of a period for conveying the message, of persistence in their denial of the messenger, and of granting respite to the deniers. For this reason it appears that the punishment here is the punishment of this world, and this is what the transition to the following verse requires.

Furthermore, if we consider an extension in the limit, it is correct to take the punishment as covering both the punishment of this world and of the Hereafter.

The occurrence of the verb "mu'adhdhibin" (punishing) in the context of negation conveys generality. Thus the sending of messengers is for clarifying what God wants from the community in terms of actions.

The verse indicates that God does not hold people to account except after He guides them, as a mercy from Him to them. It is a clear proof for the negation of holding anyone accountable when the call of a messenger from God has not reached his people. Thus it is an argument for the Ash'arites, which stands against the Maturidites and the Mu'tazilites, who agreed that reason leads to knowledge of the existence of God. This is what Sadr al-Shari'ah (Sadr al-Shari'ah) stated explicitly in al-Tawdih in the four premises: the existence of God and His unity are, according to them, obligatory by reason. So there is no excuse for one who associates partners with God or denies Him, and there is no excuse for him after the sending of a messenger.

The Mu'tazilites' interpretation, that "the messenger" means (reason) ('aql), is a deviation from the usage of the language, and an overlooking of the fact that it is the object of the verb "nab'ath" (We send). One does not say "ba'atha 'aqlan" in the sense of "ja'ala" (made). This was discussed earlier in the explanation of His saying: ﴿So that people will not have an argument against God after the messengers﴾ in Surat al-Nisa.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 16:

[Page 53]
﴿And when We intend to destroy a town, We command its affluent ones, and they commit sin therein; then the word becomes due against it, and We destroy it with complete destruction.﴾ This is a detailed explanation of the ruling mentioned earlier. It is intended to threaten the leaders of the polytheists and to hold them responsible for the misguidance of those whom they misled. It is a branching-out (tafri') to clarify the causes for the descent of punishment after the sending of the Messenger, into which the threat to the misleaders has been incorporated. The apparent requirement would have been that it be conjoined with the fa' (fa, "then") to His saying ﴿And We would not punish until We have sent a messenger﴾ [al-Isra': 15]. However, it is conjoined with the waw (wa, "and") in order to draw attention to the fact that it is a statement intended for its own sake, in view of what it contains of warning against falling into a state like the one described. The meaning of the branching-out becomes apparent from the nature of the discourse, so the conjunction with waw here is an departure from what the apparent requirement would be in terms of separation and connection (al-fasl wa al-wasl).

So this verse is a threat to the polytheists of Makkah, and an instruction to the Muslims.

The meaning is that the sending of a messenger entails a command concerning a law, and that the cause of the destruction of the people to whom a messenger is sent, after the messenger has been sent to them, is their failure to comply with what Allah commands them through that messenger.

The meaning of Allah's intending to destroy a town is the immediate attachment (al-ta'alluq al-tanjizi) of His will, and that will is directed toward the object willed when its causes are present, and these are indicated by His saying "We command its affluent ones," to the end of the verse.

The object of "amarna" (We commanded) is omitted, meaning: We commanded them with what We command them, i.e., We sent to them the messenger, and We commanded them with what We command them through their messenger, so they disobeyed the messenger, and they committed sin in their town.

Know that the introduction of this sentence with "idha" (when) caused the meaning to be obscure in the linking between the conditional clause of "idha" and its response clause, because the nature of "idha" is that it is a temporal adverb of the future and includes the meaning of a condition, i.e., the linking between its two clauses. So the apparent position of "idha" requires that His saying "We commanded its affluent ones" is the response of "idha," which implies that Allah's will to destroy it precedes the occurrence of the command to the affluent, the condition preceding its response. This would imply that Allah's will attaches to the destruction of the town from the outset, so He commands the affluent of the town's people, and they commit sin therein; then the word becomes due against it, which is the manifestation of Allah's will to destroy them. Yet the course of reason requires that the sinfulness and disbelief of the town's people be the cause of the occurrence of Allah's will to destroy them, and that Allah's will does not attach to destroying a people except after they have done what He threatened them for, not the reverse. It is not befitting of Allah that He wills their destruction before they bring about what causes it, nor is it of wisdom that He drive them toward what leads to their being called to account, in order to produce a cause for their destruction.

The contextual indication is clear in this. Thus, if we make the waw conjunctive, the verb "amarna mutrafiha" (We commanded its affluent ones) is coordinated with "nab'atha rasulan" (We send a messenger), since verbs are coordinated with one another whether or not they share their implications. The original arrangement of the discourse would then be: ﴿And We would not punish until We have sent a messenger﴾ [al-Isra': 15], and We command the affluent of a town with what We command them through the messenger, so they transgress Our command; then the threat becomes due against them, so We destroy them when We intend to destroy them.

Thus, "idha aradna an nuhlika qaryatan" is conditioned on the occurrence of the destruction, i.e., that is by the will of Allah, and no one can compel Him, as many verses indicate, such as His saying ﴿Or He will defeat them so they return disappointed﴾ [Al 'Imran: 127], ﴿You have no part in the matter; or He will relent toward them or punish them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 128], His saying ﴿If We willed, We would have smitten them for their sins﴾ [al-A'raf: 100], His saying ﴿And when We will, We will replace their likes with a complete replacement﴾ [al-Insan: 28], and His saying ﴿We hasten for him therein what We will, for whom We desire﴾ [al-Isra': 18]. Thus He mentioned the condition of His will twice.

Allah deviated from the arrangement of the discourse to this style, which is the style in which the verse came, in order to incorporate an allusive threat to the people of Makkah that they are exposed to the like of this which befell the people of the towns that denied Allah's messengers.

The commentators have many methods of interpreting this verse, exceeding eight, which are varied; some are far-fetched or corrupt, and the closest of them is the view of the one who made the clause "amarna mutrafiha" etc. a qualifier of "qaryatan" and made the response of "idha" omitted.

[Page 55]
Al-mutraf: the passive participle of "atrafahu," meaning he gave him the turfah (with a dammah on the ta' and sukun on the ra'), i.e., luxury/bounty. The mutrafun are the people of bounty and ease of life, and they are the majority of the polytheists in Makkah, while most of the believers at that time were weak. Allah the Exalted said ﴿Leave Me with the deniers, the possessors of bounty, and give them respite a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11].

Restricting the command to the affluent in particular, although the messengers address all people, is because their disobedience of the command directed at them is the cause of their sinfulness and the sinfulness of the rest of their people, since they are the leaders of the common folk and the chiefs of disbelief. Thus the address mostly turns toward them; when they transgress the command, the masses follow them, and sinfulness becomes general or prevails over the town, so it deserves destruction.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and the majority read "amarna" with a single hamzah and a light mim. Ya'qub read "amarna" (with a long alif) with two hamzahs: the hamzah of transitivity and the hamzah of the verb's first radical, meaning: We made them commanders, i.e., calling their people to misguidance. The second hamzah became an alif by lightening, or the alif is the alif of mufa'alah, and mufa'alah is used for intensification, like 'afahu Allah.

Al-fisq: going out of the place of settlement and out of the path. Its meaning in the terminology of the Qur'an is going out of what Allah has commanded, and it was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿And He leads astray thereby none but the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-qawl is what Allah conveys to people of speech through the messengers, and it is the word of threat, as He said ﴿So the word of our Lord has come due against us; indeed we are tasting [it]﴾ [al-Saffat: 31].

Al-tadmir: the demolition of a building and the removal of its trace. It is used here metaphorically for total annihilation, since the intent is the destruction of its people, even if their buildings remain, as in His saying "and ask the town" [Yusuf: 82]. Tadmir was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿And We destroyed what Pharaoh and his people were making﴾ [al-A'raf: 137] in al-A'raf. The emphasis of "dammarnaha" with the verbal noun (ta'kid bi al-masdar) is intended to indicate the magnitude of the destruction, not to negate the possibility of metaphor.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 17:

Page 56
﴿And how many generations have We destroyed after Noah! And sufficient is your Lord as Knower and Seer of the sins of His servants.﴾

An example is given for the destruction of towns, whose cause and manner were described in the preceding verse, and so it is followed by its illustration, because it is more revealing and more effective in conveying the intended warning. In this there is confirmation that the descent of punishment upon the towns is preceded by the sending of a messenger to the people of the town, then by the directing of commands to the affluent (al-mutrafun, the wealthy and comfortable), then by their defiance of those commands. The leaders of the disbelievers among the people of Noah were among the affluent, and they are the ones who said (﴿And we do not see you followed except by those who are the lowest of us, in immature judgment﴾ [Hud: 27]), and Noah, peace be upon him, said to them ﴿Nor do I say of those whom your eyes look down upon that God will never give them any good﴾ [Hud: 31].

The apparent requirement would have been to join this sentence with the particle fa' (so), since it is like a branch (consequence) of the sentence before it. However, it is joined with waw (and), to show that it is independent in the event of warning from another aspect. Thus this is a deviation from what the apparent requirement would dictate, for this appropriate consideration.

And (kam) is originally an interrogative about number, and it is used as a declarative indicating a large, indefinite number of a kind, and therefore it requires a specifier (tamyiz) for the type of number. Here it is declarative, in a position of nasb (accusative) by the verb following it, because it is obligatory that it be placed before the verb, in view of its origin being interrogative, and interrogatives have precedence at the beginning of speech. "From the generations" (min al-qurun) is a specifier clarifying the ambiguity that (kam) entails.

Al-qurun is the plural of qarn, which originally means a long period of time; it may be estimated at a hundred years or forty years, and it is applied to the people who exist during that period, as here. In the hadith, "The best of generations is my generation, then those who follow them," he meant the people of my generation, that is, the people of the era in which I am. And God Most High said ﴿And 'Ad and Thamud and the people of the Rass, and many generations between those﴾ [al-Furqan: 38].

Page 57
The specification "after Noah" is an abbreviation, as if it were said: "from the people of Noah and those after them." The time of Noah has been made the starting point for the narratives of the nations, because he is the first messenger, and the narrative is considered to begin after him, because the time of Noah became as if cut off due to the renewal of the earth's habitation after the Flood, and because the punishment that befell his people was a terrifying punishment, namely the drowning that encompassed the world.

The purpose of mentioning it is to remind the polytheists of it, and that God's punishment has no limit, and to alert them that misguidance prevents taking lessons from consequences and from being admonished by what befell those who came before; and sufficient is what befell the people of Noah of the terrifying punishment.

The sentence ﴿And sufficient is your Lord as Knower and Seer of the sins of His servants﴾ turns to address the Prophet ﷺ specifically, because everything preceding of threat and warning ultimately aims at bringing people to affirm Muhammad ﷺ in what he brought of the Qur'an, after they had persisted in disbelief and varied in denial. Therefore it concluded that with reassuring the Prophet that God is aware of the sins of the people, and this is an allusion that He will recompense them for their sins in a manner proportionate to their enormity. For this reason it came with the verb kafa (suffice) and with the two descriptions khabiran basiran (Knower and Seer), which by mentioning them implies the non-escape of anything of their sins, whether visible or known from their inner selves, that is to say their deeds and their intentions.

He placed first what relates to the inner selves and intentions, because beliefs are the root of deeds in corruption and righteousness. In the hadith: "Verily, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Verily, it is the heart."

In the mention of the verb (kafa) there is an indication that the Prophet does not need anyone other than his Lord to defend him; He is sufficient for him and is his Protector, as He said ﴿So God will suffice you against them, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 137]; or an indication that he is free from concern about their affair, as in His saying to Noah ﴿So do not ask Me about what you have no knowledge of﴾ [Hud: 46]. So this is either a consolation for him regarding their harm, or a turning away of him from grieving over them. And in addressing the Prophet with this there is an allusion to a threat to those disbelievers who hear it.

[p. 58]

This is an explanation of the phrase ﴿Whoever is guided is only guided for his own self﴾ [al-Isra': 15]. It also refers back to the phrase ﴿And every person We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾ [al-Isra': 13], gradually clarifying for people that their deeds are their own acquisition and choice. He first informed them that Allah has made them bear the consequences of their deeds, with His words ﴿And every person We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾ [al-Isra': 13]. Then He left their affairs to them, and [informed them] that the one who walks [on his path] does not harm anyone else by his misdeed, nor does anyone else bear it for him. So He said ﴿Whoever is guided is only guided for his own self﴾ [al-Isra': 15], and so on. Then He left them without excuse, [declaring] that He does not seize them unawares, and does not seize them except for the evil of their deeds, with His words ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾ up to His words ﴿Knowing and Seeing of His servants﴾ [al-Isra': 15–17]. Then He disclosed to them their intentions in their deeds, and that they are of two kinds:

One kind wants only the worldly life, so their deeds are for the pleasure of their desires, believing that this world is the ultimate pasture of souls and that they have no share except what they obtain during the span of life, because they do not believe in the Resurrection, so they limit their deeds to that.

The other kind knows that the true success lies in what comes after this life, so they act for the Hereafter, following what Allah guided them to of deeds through His messengers. Allah treats each group according to the measure of its aspiration.

So the meaning of ﴿Whoever desires the immediate [worldly life]﴾ is that he desires nothing but the immediate [life], that is, [he desires it] instead of the Hereafter, as indicated by its contrast with His words ﴿and whoever desires the Hereafter﴾. This contrast takes the place of a relative restriction (ḥaṣr idafi), since a relative restriction is nothing but two sentences: an affirmation of one thing and a negation of its opposite. The use of the verb "to be" (kāna) here indicates that this is his habit and the ultimate concern of his aspiration. For this reason the predicate of kāna was made a present-tense verb, to indicate continuity, further confirming that his will is purely directed toward this.

[p. 59]

"Al-'ājila" is an attribute of an omitted noun understood from the context, that is, "al-ḥayāt al-'ājila" (the immediate life), as in His words ﴿Whoever desires the worldly life and its adornment, We will pay them in full for their deeds therein﴾ [Hud: 15]. The intended meaning of "hastening" (ta'jīl) is customary hastening, that is, the prompt provision that is commonly understood, namely that it is given in this world before the Hereafter. That is hastening relative to the worldly life, and the indication of this is His words "therein". He added the two restrictions ﴿what We will, for whom We intend﴾, because what is given to those who desire the immediate [life] is given to some of them according to the measures that Allah willed to give.

Mashī'a (will) means submission and the absence of compulsion.

His words ﴿for whom We intend﴾ are a substitute for His words ﴿for him﴾, a partial substitution (badal ba'd min kull) with the repetition of the governing particle. The pronoun in "lahu" refers to "man" according to its wording, and it is general for every desirer of the immediate [life]; then some of them were substituted for it, that is, "We hasten for those among you whom We intend." The object of "intend" is omitted, indicated by what precedes it, that is, "for whom We intend to hasten it." This is like the object of "will", which is often omitted because of an earlier statement. In this there is the particularity of clarification after vagueness. Had the intended meaning been otherwise, the rules of speech would have required it to be stated explicitly.

Irada (intention) is a synonym of mashī'a (will). So using it after "what We will" is a variation of expression (tafannun). The repetition of the preposition governing the substitute is to emphasize the meaning of dependence, and to dispense with linking it to a pronoun referring back to the substituted noun, such as saying "for whom We intend among them."

The meaning is: this group, which desires only the worldly life, may be given some of what it desires according to Our will and intention, for various reasons. No one in this world is free from having some of what he loves of worldly pleasures hastened for him.

[p. 60]

The clause ﴿then We made for him Hell﴾ is conjoined with the particle "thumma" (then) to indicate a rank-based delay (tarākhī rutbī). "Lahu" is a fixed adverbial phrase, the second object of "ja'alnā" (We made), placed before the first object for emphasis. The clause ﴿which he will burn in﴾ is an explanation or a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimāl) for the clause ﴿We made for him Hell﴾. "Reproached and banished" are two circumstantial accusatives (ḥāl) of the subject pronoun in "yaṣlāhā". One says "ṣalā al-nār" when it has afflicted him with its burning.

Dhamm (reproach) is describing someone with the faults that are in the one described.

Mad'ūr (banished) means expelled. One says "daḥarahu" (he expelled him). The verbal noun is "duḥūr". It was previously mentioned in the words of Allah the Exalted ﴿He said: Get out of it, reproached and banished﴾ [al-A'raf: 18] in Surat al-A'raf.

The difference between the clause ﴿Whoever desires the immediate [life]﴾ and the clause ﴿and whoever desires the Hereafter﴾ is that the verb is in the present tense in the first, and in the past tense in the second. This is to suggest that people's desire for the immediate [life] is repeated and renewed, and it is a warning that the affairs of the immediate [life] pass away and vanish. The verb of desiring the Hereafter was made past tense, because the past tense indicates firmness; this is a reminder that the good of the Hereafter deserves to be desired. For this reason the clause was stripped of "kāna" and of the present tense. The only condition for this is that he strives for the Hereafter with its striving, and that he be a believer.

The literal meaning of sa'y (striving) is walking short of running. So the striving for the Hereafter is good deeds, because they are the means of attaining the bliss of the Hereafter. The one who performs good deeds is as if he travels swiftly toward the Hereafter, in order to reach what he desires from it. Its attribution to the pronoun of the Hereafter is an attribution of a verbal noun to its object in meaning, that is, "striving for it," and it is an absolute object (maf'ūl muṭlaq) to specify the type.

In the verse there is a reminder that desiring the good of the Hereafter without striving is delusion, and that desiring anything requires striving in the means of attaining it. 'Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said:

*You hope for salvation, but you do not take its paths;*
*Indeed, a ship does not sail on dry land.*

[p. 61]

The clause ﴿and he is a believer﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of the subject of "sa'ā" (strove). It was expressed as a nominal sentence to indicate permanence and continuity, that is, "and he had already been firm in faith." It has the same meaning as His words ﴿Then he was among those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17], because "kāna" indicates that faith has become a settled quality for him.

The use of the demonstrative in ﴿those—their striving has been appreciated﴾ is to call attention to the fact that those referred to are deserving of what He will report about them, because of what they were described with before the mention of the demonstrative.

"Appreciated striving" means that its doer is appreciated; so describing it with this is a rational metaphor (majāz 'aqlī), since "appreciated" means one who is pleased with. The intended meaning is to report the reward of the deed of one who desires the Hereafter and strives for it with its striving, not to report the goodness of his deed. This is because it is the counterpart to the reward of one who desires the immediate [life] and turns away from the Hereafter. But the attribute was given to the deed because it is more eloquent in reporting that its doer is pleased with, since it has the sense of a metonymy (kināya), which returns to affirming a thing through affirming what necessarily accompanies it.

The use of "kāna" in ﴿their striving was appreciated﴾ is to indicate that the attribute was realized in it previously, that is, from the worldly life; because obedience requires that gratitude be granted promptly and reward be deferred. His making their striving appreciated includes many good things whose detailed description would be lengthy, if one wished to detail it.

[p. 58]

This is an explanation of the phrase ﴿Whoever is guided is only guided for his own self﴾ [al-Isra': 15]. It also refers back to the phrase ﴿And every person We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾ [al-Isra': 13], gradually clarifying for people that their deeds are their own acquisition and choice. He first informed them that Allah has made them bear the consequences of their deeds, with His words ﴿And every person We have fastened his bird to his neck﴾ [al-Isra': 13]. Then He left their affairs to them, and [informed them] that the one who walks [on his path] does not harm anyone else by his misdeed, nor does anyone else bear it for him. So He said ﴿Whoever is guided is only guided for his own self﴾ [al-Isra': 15], and so on. Then He left them without excuse, [declaring] that He does not seize them unawares, and does not seize them except for the evil of their deeds, with His words ﴿And We would never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾ up to His words ﴿Knowing and Seeing of His servants﴾ [al-Isra': 15–17]. Then He disclosed to them their intentions in their deeds, and that they are of two kinds:

One kind wants only the worldly life, so their deeds are for the pleasure of their desires, believing that this world is the ultimate pasture of souls and that they have no share except what they obtain during the span of life, because they do not believe in the Resurrection, so they limit their deeds to that.

The other kind knows that the true success lies in what comes after this life, so they act for the Hereafter, following what Allah guided them to of deeds through His messengers. Allah treats each group according to the measure of its aspiration.

So the meaning of ﴿Whoever desires the immediate [worldly life]﴾ is that he desires nothing but the immediate [life], that is, [he desires it] instead of the Hereafter, as indicated by its contrast with His words ﴿and whoever desires the Hereafter﴾. This contrast takes the place of a relative restriction (ḥaṣr idafi), since a relative restriction is nothing but two sentences: an affirmation of one thing and a negation of its opposite. The use of the verb "to be" (kāna) here indicates that this is his habit and the ultimate concern of his aspiration. For this reason the predicate of kāna was made a present-tense verb, to indicate continuity, further confirming that his will is purely directed toward this.

[p. 59]

"Al-'ājila" is an attribute of an omitted noun understood from the context, that is, "al-ḥayāt al-'ājila" (the immediate life), as in His words ﴿Whoever desires the worldly life and its adornment, We will pay them in full for their deeds therein﴾ [Hud: 15]. The intended meaning of "hastening" (ta'jīl) is customary hastening, that is, the prompt provision that is commonly understood, namely that it is given in this world before the Hereafter.
