﴿كُلًّا نُمِدُّ هَؤُلاءِ وهَؤُلاءِ مِن عَطاءِ رَبِّكَ وما كانَ عَطاءُ رَبِّكَ مَحْظُورًا﴾ *tadhyil* (a concluding summary that closes the preceding argument) for the verse ﴿مَن كانَ يُرِيدُ العاجِلَةَ﴾ [al-Isra': 18] to its end.

This verse is a *fadhlaka* (a summarizing recapitulation) that draws attention to the fact that God, exalted is He, has not deprived His creatures of the effects of His mercy, even the disbelievers among them who do not believe in meeting Him. He has given them some of the blessings of this world according to what He decreed for them, and He has given the believers the good of both this world and the Hereafter. This is the confirmation of His saying ﴿ورَحْمَتِي وسِعَتْ كُلَّ شَيْءٍ﴾ [al-A'raf: 156] and of His saying, as related from Him by His Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed My mercy precedes My wrath."

The *tanwin* of ﴿كُلًّا﴾ is *tanwin al-'iwad* (the nunation that replaces an omitted element), replacing the genitive noun that follows it, i.e., "each of the two groups." It is in the accusative as the object of the verb ﴿نُمِدُّ﴾.

The phrase ﴿هَؤُلاءِ وهَؤُلاءِ﴾ is an *badal* (apposition) for ﴿كُلًّا﴾, specifically *badal mufassal min mujmal* (a detailed apposition following a general term).

The conjoined pair together with the element they are conjoined to forms the *badal*, as in the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "Follow the two after me, Abu Bakr and 'Umar." The purpose of this substitution is to express wonder at the vastness of God's mercy.

The demonstrative ﴿هَؤُلاءِ﴾ in both places refers to "he who desires the immediate" and "he who desires the Hereafter." The principle is that the first-mentioned item returns to the first, when something that specifies its referent is connected to one of the two nouns. Both matters are combined in the verse of al-Mutalammis:

"None accepts oppression inflicted upon him except the two most humiliated: the non-tribesman and the stake.
This one is bound to his halter in humiliation, while that one is split open, and no one pities him."

*Al-imdad* (provision of continuous support): the continuous flow of giving and its succession, and making the new part of it a supply for what preceded, such that it never ceases. The clause ﴿وما كانَ عَطاءُ رَبِّكَ مَحْظُورًا﴾ is either a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraD*) or a *tadhyil*. The phrase ﴿عَطاءُ رَبِّكَ﴾ denotes the genus of giving, and *al-mahzur* means "the prohibited," i.e., that it was never entirely withheld; rather, every created being has a share of it.

[Page 62]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 21:

Page 63
﴿Look how We have favored some of them over others; and the Hereafter is greater in degrees and greater in favoring.﴾ Since the bounty bestowed on both groups is the bounty of this world, and people are favored in it in a manner whose wisdom they can perceive, God drew the attention of His Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, to this with a call to consideration and reflection. Then He reminded him that the bounty of the Hereafter is the greatest bounty, and that God has favored the believers with it.

The command to look (al-nazar) is addressed to the Prophet ﷺ, as an elevation in the ranks of his knowledge, and through it the lesson is directed to others as well.

The basic meaning of al-nazar (looking) is the directing of the faculty of physical sight toward the seen object. It has become common in the speech of the Arabs to use it for looking accompanied by reflection and repeated observation of things in pursuit of a purpose, so that it takes the place of conjecture (zann), and it is used in that sense on this basis. For this reason, the use of "nazar" in the science of kalam (theology) to mean the reasoning that leads to knowledge or conjecture became widespread, and it is so here. A parallel of this was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿Look how they invent lies against God﴾ [al-Nisa larger: 50] in Surat al-Nisa.

"Kayfa" (how) is an interrogative noun used for drawing attention. It suspends the verb "unzur" (look) from acting upon its two objects. The intended meaning is favoring in the bounty of this world, because it is what reflection perceives, and by the context of its contrast with His saying ﴿and the Hereafter is greater in degrees﴾.

The purpose of this comparison is to draw attention to the fact that the bounty of this world is not tied to the goodness of deeds. Do you not see that within it there is variation among people of the same action? The Muslim may be favored over the disbelievers, the disbeliever may be favored over the Muslim, some Muslims may be favored over others, and some disbelievers over others. That is sufficient guidance that the basis of worldly bounty lies in causes that are not of the valley of righteous deeds, nor of what is driven toward good souls.

Page 64
"Darajat" (degrees) and "tafdilan" (favoring) are in the accusative as specifications (tamyiz) of a greater ratio in both places, and the one favored over is the bounty of this world.

"Darajat" is used metaphorically for the greatness of nobility, and "tafdil" means the bestowing of excess, which is wealth and blessing. In the hadith: "and they give in charity from the surplus (fudul) of their wealth." The meaning is: the blessing in the Hereafter is greater than the blessings of this world.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 22:**

﴿Do not set up with God another god, lest you sit down reproached and forsaken.﴾ It is a *tadhyil* (a concluding generalization that follows a statement and confirms it) and a *fadhlaka* (a summary or recapitulation) of the differing conditions of the believers and the polytheists. The essence of the causes of success is abandoning shirk, because that is the starting point of turning toward righteous deeds, and it is the first step in the striving of one who desires the Hereafter. Shirk is the foundation of disordered thinking and the misguidance of minds. God Most High said, concerning the gods of the polytheists, ﴿And they added nothing to them but ruin﴾ [Hud: 101].

The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, following the address in His words ﴿See how We have preferred some of them over others﴾ [al-Isra: 21]. The intended purpose is to make the address heard by others, with an indication that confirms that the Prophet is standing firmly in rejecting shirk, and a rebuke directed at those who worship another god alongside God.

*Taqud* (تَقْعُدَ, "you sit") is used metaphorically for the meaning of remaining and continuing. By this metaphor, the sense of the prohibition is stripped down to being a prohibition in the form of an indirect allusion to the polytheists, because they are already afflicted with reproach and forsaken. If they do not desist from shirk, they will remain in reproach and abandonment.

*Madhmum* (مَذْمُومًا): the one who is mentioned with evil and blame.

*Makhdhul* (مَخْذُولًا): the one whose helper has abandoned him.

As for his being reproached, it comes from people of intellect, for it is among the greatest absurdities that a person should take a stone or a piece of wood as his lord and worship it, as Abraham, peace be upon him, said, ﴿Do you worship what you carve?﴾ [al-Saffat: 95]. His reproach is also from God, through the tongue of the revealed laws.

[Page 65]

As for his being forsaken, it is because he has taken for himself a protector who cannot avail him anything: ﴿If you call upon them, they do not hear your call, and even if they heard, they would not respond to you﴾ [Fatir: 14]. Abraham, peace be upon him, also said, ﴿O my father, why do you worship that which hears not, sees not, and avails you nothing?﴾ [Maryam: 42]. His being forsaken is from God, because He does not take as a protector one who does not take Him as protector. He said, ﴿That is because God is the protector of those who believe, and the disbelievers have no protector﴾ [Muhammad: 11], and He said, ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾ [al-Ra'd: 14].

[Page 66]

﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him.﴾ This is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the preceding discourse, a coordination of one purpose with another. It is a transition (takhallus) to some of the pillars of the Islamic law (sharīʿah), prompted by the preceding recapitulation (fadhlakah, summary). It alerts the reader that the reform of conduct is a consequence of renouncing associationism (shirk), as God the Exalted said: ﴿But he has not attempted the steep path. And what can make you comprehend what the steep path is? It is the freeing of a slave, or feeding on a day of hunger an orphan near of kin, or a needy person in misery; then being among those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 11–17].

Legislation has begun for the Muslims, with great rulings for the reform of their community and the building of its foundations, so that they may grow in certainty of their elevation above the people of associationism and of the lowliness of those people relative to them. All of these rulings contain an allusion (taʿrīḍ) to the associators, who were immersed in what was forbidden. These verses are the first detailed exposition of the law for the Muslims that took place in Mecca. What is mentioned in these verses is intended to teach the Muslims, and for this reason its style differs from the style of its counterpart in Surat al-Anʿām, in which the address was directed to the associators in order to confront them with the principles of their misguidance.

Among the differences between the two styles: this verse opens with the verb of decree (qaḍāʾ), which implies obligation, and this suits addressing a community that obeys the command of its Lord. The address of Surat al-Anʿām opens with ﴿Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you﴾ [al-Anʿām: 151], as was discussed there.

Another difference: this verse makes the thing decreed the singling out of God in worship, because this suits the condition of the Muslims, so it warns them against worshipping other than God. The verse of al-Anʿām made the forbidden thing there the associating of others with God in divinity, which suits what they were upon of associationism, since they had no worship (of God) at all.

Another difference: this verse details the ruling on kindness to the two parents, the ruling on killing, and the ruling on spending, whereas the verses of al-Anʿām did not detail these.

The rulings mentioned in these verses were fifteen legislations, which are the principles of the legislation pertaining to the organisation of society.

I reckon that these verses became well known among people in Mecca, and that the Arabs transmitted them throughout the horizons. For this reason al-Aʿshā alluded to some of them in his well-transmitted qaṣīdah composed to praise the Prophet (ﷺ) when he came seeking faith and Quraysh turned him away from it. It is the qaṣīdah rhyming in dāl, in which he says:

*Is it that you have not heard the charge of Muhammad,*
*the Prophet of God, when he charged and bore witness?*

*So beware of carrion, do not eat it,*
*and do not take an iron arrow to shoot with;*

*and the erected stone, do not sacrifice to it,*
*and do not worship Satan, but worship God;*

*and the near kin, do not sever them*
*in their poverty, nor the captive bound;*

*do not mock a wretched man of distress,*
*and do not think wealth makes a man immortal;*

*do not approach a neighbour woman, for her secret*
*is forbidden to you; so marry, or remain celibate.*

These rulings and charges were introduced with the verb of decree, out of concern for it and because it is among what God commanded with a firm command and a binding judgment. It does not mean "determination" (taqdīr), as in His saying ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 4], because it is evident that what is mentioned here is of the kind that happens and of the kind that does not happen.

The ʾan (that) may be explanatory (tafsīriyyah), interpreting what is implied in qaḍā of the sense of saying; it may also be a verbal-infinitive particle (maṣdariyyah) in the genitive by a suppressed preposition bāʾ, meaning "decreed that you not worship." The legislation began with mention of the root of the whole law, which is the monotheism of God, and this is a preparation for what will be mentioned after it of rulings.

The address in His saying ﴿that you worship none but Him﴾ is in the plural, because the prohibition concerns all people, and it is an allusion to the associators.

The address in His saying "your Lord" is to the Prophet (ﷺ), like that in His earlier saying ﴿from the gift of your Lord﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 20]. The indication is clear. It is also possible that it is addressed to an unspecified person, so it generalises to the community, and the final outcome is the same.

The legislation began with the prohibition of worshipping other than God, because this is the root of reform, since the reform of thought takes precedence over the reform of action; the intellect does not strive towards seeking good deeds unless it is itself sound. In a hadith: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart." I have explained this at length in my book entitled *Uṣūl al-Niẓām al-Ijtimāʿī fī al-Islām* (The Principles of the Social Order in Islam).

* * *

﴿And to parents, kindness. Whether one or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them "uff," nor rebuke them, but speak to them a noble word. And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy, and say: "My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me when I was small."﴾

This is the second principle of the law, which is kindness to parents.

The word *iḥsānan* (kindness) is in the accusative as an absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq), a verbal noun standing in for its verb. The estimate is: "And be kind, kindness to parents," as the coordination with ﴿that you worship none but Him﴾ requires, meaning: "And [He] decreed kindness to parents."

*Bi-al-wālidayni* (to the parents) is connected to *iḥsānan*, and the bāʾ in it marks transitivity; it is said *aḥsin bi-fulān* as one says *aḥsin ilayhi* (be kind to him). His saying "And He has been kind to me" [Yūsuf: 100] has already been mentioned in Surat Yūsuf. Its being placed before its complement is for emphasis on it. The definiteness in *al-wālidayn* is for comprehensiveness (istighrāq), with regard to the parents of every responsible person included in the plural in ﴿that you worship none but Him﴾.

The coordination of the command of kindness to parents with what is in the sense of the command to worship God is because God is the Creator and therefore deserves worship, since He brought people into existence. When God made the two parents the locus of the bringing forth of people, He commanded kindness to them. The Creator deserves worship for His self-sufficiency from kindness; and because worship is the greatest thanks for the greatest favour. The cause of existence, other than that, deserves kindness and not worship, because it is in need of kindness and not of worship, and because it is not a true originator, and because God created the parents with compassion for their offspring, so He commanded the child to requite that with kindness to his parents, as will come later: ﴿and say, "My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me when I was small."﴾

Kindness includes everything to which this genus truly applies of sayings and deeds, and of giving and consolation.

The clause ﴿Whether one or both of them reach old age﴾ explains the clause "kindness." The particle *immā* is composed of *in* (if), the conditional particle, and *mā*, the superfluous particle that prepares for the emphatic nūn. It should properly be written with a nūn after the hamzah and after it *mā*, but they took into account the pronunciation of it as assimilated, so they wrote it that way in the codices (maṣāḥif), and people's writing generally followed it. The meaning: if one of the parents or both reach the limit of old age, while they are with you, that is, in your care, then prepare your character for them and soften your side.

The address "with you" is to an unspecified person, so it generalises to every addressee by the indication of the conjunction with ﴿that you worship none but Him﴾.

It is not an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), since he had no parents at that time. The use of the singular pronoun here rather than the plural pronoun is because it is an address specific to whoever has parents among the group addressed by ﴿that you worship none but Him﴾, so the singular is more suitable for it, although singular and plural are equal in the intended meaning, because the address to an unspecified person equals the address to the plural.

He singled out this condition for explanation, because it is the likely context for the absence of kindness, due to the hardship the child meets from his father and mother in the task of caring for their affairs, and due to bad character on their part.

The reason why the subject of *yablughanna* is expressed as a noun rather than as a dual pronoun, such as *immā yablughānni ʿindaka al-kibar*, is to give attention to specifying each state of the two parents with mention, and one of the two states does not suffice without the other. This is because each state has motives for neglecting the obligation of kindness to them. The state of their being together with the child may require tolerance from them for the sake of respecting one of them, whom the child loves more, in a way that differs from the case where one of them is alone with him without the other, whose inclination towards him is stronger. So the need to mention one of them in this case is to alert to the obligation of guarding kindness towards him. Also, the state of one parent being alone with the child may be less burdensome to him than the state of their being together, so the need for ﴿or both of them﴾ in this case is a warning against the child excusing himself for falling short on the grounds that the state of the parents together is more embarrassing to him. Therefore both states are mentioned, and the ruling is applied to both equally. So the whole clause ﴿then do not say to them, "uff"﴾ is the answer to *immā*.

The conditional verb is emphasised by the emphatic nūn to establish the connection between the content of the answer and the content of the condition in existence. Al-Jumhūr (the majority) read *immā yablughanna* taking *aḥaduhumā* as its subject, so the verb receives no marker, because its subject is an explicit noun.

Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read *yablughānni* with the dual alif and a doubled nūn, the pronoun being the subject referring to the parents in ﴿and to the parents, kindness﴾. Then *aḥaduhumā aw kilāhumā* is a substitute (badal) for the alif of the dual, as an indication that the ruling is not for their being together only, but applies to both states, distributively.

The address with *ʿindaka* is to everyone who is fit to hear speech, so it generalises to every addressee by the indication of the preceding ﴿that you worship none but Him﴾ and the following saying ﴿your Lord knows best what is in your souls﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 25].

*Uff* is a verb-like particle (ism fiʿl) of the present tense, meaning "I am annoyed." It has many dialectal variants; the most famous of them all is the pronunciation with a damma on the hamzah and a doubled fāʾ. The disagreement concerns the vowel of the fāʾ: Nāfiʿ, Abū Jaʿfar and Ḥafs from ʿĀṣim read it with a kasra on the fāʾ, nunated; Ibn Kathīr, Ibn ʿĀmir and Yaʿqūb read it with a fatḥa on the fāʾ, not nunated; and the rest read it with a kasra on the fāʾ, not nunated.

The purpose of the prohibition is not specifically to forbid saying *uff* to them. Rather, the purpose is the prohibition of harm, the least of which is harm by the tongue, expressed in the briefest word, and in that it indicates no more than the arising of annoyance in the one who says it, without insult or blame. From it is understood the prohibition of what is more harmful, by way of the implication of the discourse (fahwā al-khiṭāb) a fortiori.

Then the prohibition of rebuking them is coordinated with it, lest one think that this is discipline for their good and not harm. *Al-nahr* is rebuke; it is said *nahara-hu* and *intahara-hu*.

Then he commanded the honouring of speech to them. *Al-karīm* of anything is what is elevated in its kind. It was mentioned earlier at His saying ﴿and forgiveness and a generous provision﴾ [al-Anfāl: 4] in Surat al-Anfāl.

With this command, the excuse is cut off, so that when the child sees fit to advise one of his parents, or to warn him against what may harm him, he conveys that with gentle speech that has a good effect.

Then he ascended in the charge concerning parents to commanding the child to humble himself before them with a humility reaching the limit of abasement before them, to remove any alienation of their souls should they come to need the child's assistance. This is because parents wish to be the ones who benefit their child. The purpose of this is to adopt the disposition of gratitude for their past favours upon him.

The expression of humility is phrased by depicting it in the form of the bird's submission when fear of a stronger bird comes upon it, when it lowers its wing in abasement. So in the construction there is a implied metaphor (istiʿārah makniyyah), and the "wing" is an imaginative image (takhyīl), like the claws of death in the verse of Abū Dhuʾayb:

*And when death sinks its claws in, you find that every amulet is of no use.*

And like the imaginative image of the hand for the north wind, with the vowel of the shīn opened, and the halter for the cold in the verse of Labīd:

*And on a day of wind that had uncovered the cold,*
*when the north wind's hand held its reins.*

The whole of this metaphor is a representation (tamthīl). It was discussed before at His saying ﴿and lower your wing to the believers﴾ [al-Ḥijr: 88] in Surat al-Ḥijr.

The definiteness in *al-raḥmah* (the mercy) is a substitute for the genitive complement, meaning "of your mercy towards them." *Min* is initial (ibtidāʾiyyah), i.e., the abasement arising from mercy, not from fear, nor from flattery. The aim is that the soul become accustomed to adopting mercy, by keeping in mind the obligation of treating them with it, until it becomes a trait for him, as it is said:

*Indeed, the adopting of a disposition comes before the disposition itself.*

[Page 71 continues]

These are general rulings concerning parents, even if they are polytheists. They are not to be obeyed in disobedience or in disbelief, as in the verse in Surah al-'Ankabut.

The implication of the verse is equality between the two parents in filial piety (al-birr, dutiful goodness), and pleasing both of them together in this matter. This is because its subject is an action that proceeds from the child toward his parents, and such an action is capable of being equalized. It does not address what lies beyond this, where the two parents differ and contend over what they want the child to do. This happens when their wishes cannot be combined, such as when one parent orders him to do the opposite of what the other orders. It appears that this falls under circumstances in which the evidences seem to conflict, so that he should seek to carry out both requests if he is able.

In the authentic hadith from Abu Hurayrah: "A man asked the Prophet ﷺ, 'Who among people deserves my good companionship the most?' He said, 'Your mother.' He said, 'Then who?' He said, 'Then your mother.' He said, 'Then who?' He said, 'Then your mother.' He said, 'Then who?' He said, 'Then your father.'"

This is clear in giving precedence to the mother's side, because the questioner's question indicates that he was asking about the goodness of his treatment of his parents.

The scholars have several opinions. The first: the mother is given precedence over the father. This was the view of al-Layth ibn Sa'd, al-Muhasibi and Abu Hanifah, and it is the apparent position of Malik. Al-Qarafi, in al-Furuq (23), reports from Mukhtasar al-Jami' that a man asked Malik, "My father is in the land of the Sudan and has written to me to come to him, but my mother prevents me from doing so?" Malik said, "Obey your father and do not disobey your mother." Al-Qarafi mentioned in the seventh question of that same Furuq that Malik intended to forbid the son from traveling to the Sudan without his mother's permission.

The second: the view of the Shafi'is, that the two parents are equal in filial piety. This opinion requires that one seek to weigh between them when they order their son with two contrary commands.

Al-Qurtubi reported from al-Muhasibi in his book al-Ri'ayah that he said: "There is no disagreement among the scholars that the mother has three quarters of filial piety, and the father one quarter." Al-Qurtubi also reported from al-Layth that the mother has two thirds of filial piety and the father one third, based on the difference in the transmission of the hadith mentioned, in that he said, "Then your father," after the second time or after the third time.

The correct view is that fixing this by a precise measure refers the matter to something that cannot be pinned down, and that the meaning of the hadith, despite the difference between its two transmissions, is that the mother takes precedence in general.

Then He commanded him to supplicate for them, asking God's mercy upon them, which is the mercy that the child cannot convey to his parents except by earnestly turning to God, exalted is He.

He moved to this in a remarkable transition from His words: ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾. So mentioning the mercy of the servant served as a transition to the mercy of God, and as an alert that adopting the character of loving good for one's parents drives the child to treat them with it, both in what they know and in what is hidden from them, even what reaches them after their death. In the hadith: "When the son of Adam dies, his deeds are cut off except for three: ongoing charity, knowledge that he spread among men, and a righteous child who prays for him."

In the verse there is an indication that supplication for them is answered, because God permitted it, and the hadith mentioned supports this, since it made a child's supplication a deed credited to his parents.

The ruling of this supplication is specific to believing parents, by other evidences that indicate the specification, such as His words: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 113], and the rest of the verse.

The kaf in His words ﴿as they raised me when I was small﴾ is for figurative comparison, which the grammarians express as the meaning of causation in the kaf. An example is His words, exalted is He: ﴿And remember Him as He guided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198], meaning: have mercy on them with a mercy that repays what they did in raising me when I was small.

"Small" (saghir) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) relating to the first-person pronoun (ya' al-mutakallim).

What is intended by it is depicting a particular situation, in which there is an indication of an upbringing shaped by complete mercy. Fatherhood necessitates the father's mercy, and the child's smallness necessitates mercy toward him, even if he were not a child. So His words ﴿as they raised me when I was small﴾ stand in place of saying: "as they raised me and showed mercy to me through their upbringing." Upbringing completes existence, and by itself it calls for gratitude for it, while mercy is the preservation of existence from being violated, and this is what gratitude requires. So He gathered all of that gratitude into the supplication for them for mercy.

The command necessitates obligation. As for the occasions of supplicating for them, these cannot be pinned down; they depend on the state of each person at the times of his earnest turning to God. It is reported from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah that if one supplicates for them in every tashahhud, he has fulfilled the command.

The aim of Islam in commanding filial piety and maintaining the ties of kinship (silat al-rahim) resolves into two aims. The first is psychological: training the souls of the community to acknowledge a kindness to its author, which is gratitude, adopting the character of the Creator, exalted is He, in His name al-Shakur (the Most Appreciative). Just as He commanded gratitude to God for the blessing of creation and provision, He commanded gratitude to parents for the blessing of bringing into existence in form, and the blessing of upbringing and mercy. Commanding gratitude for virtues is also a way of honoring them and an alert to competing in bestowing them.

The second aim is civilizational: that the bonds of the family be strong in their knots, firmly tied in trust. So He commanded what achieves that trust among members of the family, which is good companionship, so that in their souls there would grow love and affection that stands in place of the natural maternal compassion in the mother, and then the paternal compassion that arises from a feeling, part of which is natural and weak, and part of which is rational and strong, to the point that the effect of that feeling in its totality equals the effect of the mother's natural compassion, or exceeds it when the child grows old. Then Islam distributed what it called for of this among the rest of the ranks of kinship according to closeness in relational proximity, through what it legislated of maintaining ties of kinship. God has strengthened the readiness of souls to be carried along by that legislation.

It came in a hadith: "When God created the womb (rahim), it grasped one of the pillars of the Throne and said, 'This is the station of one who seeks refuge in You from severance.' God said, 'Are you not pleased that I join with whoever joins with you, and sever from whoever severs you?'" And in another hadith: "God has made the womb one of His names, the Merciful (al-Rahim)."

In this formation of the bonds of kinship there is great benefit for the community, whose effects appear in comforting one another and in unity among some with others. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O mankind, We created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13].

Islam has further strengthened this by what is in the midst of the Shari'ah of emphasis on tightening the bonds of kinship, more than any previous religion attempted. We have explained this in its chapter in our book on the Objectives of the Islamic Shari'ah.

[Page 66]

﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him.﴾ This is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the preceding discourse, a coordination of one purpose with another. It is a transition (takhallus) to some of the pillars of the Islamic law (sharīʿah), prompted by the preceding recapitulation (fadhlakah, summary). It alerts the reader that the reform of conduct is a consequence of renouncing associationism (shirk), as God the Exalted said: ﴿But he has not attempted the steep path. And what can make you comprehend what the steep path is? It is the freeing of a slave, or feeding on a day of hunger an orphan near of kin, or a needy person in misery; then being among those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 11–17].

Legislation has begun for the Muslims, with great rulings for the reform of their community and the building of its foundations, so that they may grow in certainty of their elevation above the people of associationism and of the lowliness of those people relative to them. All of these rulings contain an allusion (taʿrīḍ) to the associators, who were immersed in what was forbidden. These verses are the first detailed exposition of the law for the Muslims that took place in Mecca. What is mentioned in these verses is intended to teach the Muslims, and for this reason its style differs from the style of its counterpart in Surat al-Anʿām, in which the address was directed to the associators in order to confront them with the principles of their misguidance.

Among the differences between the two styles: this verse opens with the verb of decree (qaḍāʾ), which implies obligation, and this suits addressing a community that obeys the command of its Lord. The address of Surat al-Anʿām opens with ﴿Come, I will recite what your Lord has forbidden you﴾ [al-Anʿām: 151], as was discussed there.

Another difference: this verse makes the thing decreed the singling out of God in worship, because this suits the condition of the Muslims, so it warns them against worshipping other than God. The verse of al-Anʿām made the forbidden thing there the associating of others with God in divinity, which suits what they were upon of associationism, since they had no worship (of God) at all.

Another difference: this verse details the ruling on kindness to the two parents, the ruling on killing, and the ruling on spending, whereas the verses of al-Anʿām did not detail these.

The rulings mentioned in these verses were fifteen legislations, which are the principles of the legislation pertaining to the organisation of society.

I reckon that these verses became well known among people in Mecca, and that the Arabs transmitted them throughout the horizons. For this reason al-Aʿshā alluded to some of them in his well-transmitted qaṣīdah composed to praise the Prophet (ﷺ) when he came seeking faith and Quraysh turned him away from it. It is the qaṣīdah rhyming in dāl, in which he says:

*Is it that you have not heard the charge of Muhammad,*
*the Prophet of God, when he charged and bore witness?*

*So beware of carrion, do not eat it,*
*and do not take an iron arrow to shoot with;*

*and the erected stone, do not sacrifice to it,*
*and do not worship Satan, but worship God;*

*and the near kin, do not sever them*
*in their poverty, nor the captive bound;*

*do not mock a wretched man of distress,*
*and do not think wealth makes a man immortal;*

*do not approach a neighbour woman, for her secret*
*is forbidden to you; so marry, or remain celibate.*

These rulings and charges were introduced with the verb of decree, out of concern for it and because it is among what God commanded with a firm command and a binding judgment. It does not mean "determination" (taqdīr), as in His saying ﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 4], because it is evident that what is mentioned here is of the kind that happens and of the kind that does not happen.

The ʾan (that) may be explanatory (tafsīriyyah), interpreting what is implied in qaḍā of the sense of saying; it may also be a verbal-infinitive particle (maṣdariyyah) in the genitive by a suppressed preposition bāʾ, meaning "decreed that you not worship." The legislation began with mention of the root of the whole law, which is the monotheism of God, and this is a preparation for what will be mentioned after it of rulings.

The address in His saying ﴿that you worship none but Him﴾ is in the plural, because the prohibition concerns all people, and it is an allusion to the associators.

The address in His saying "your Lord" is to the Prophet (ﷺ), like that in His earlier saying ﴿from the gift of your Lord﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 20]. The indication is clear. It is also possible that it is addressed to an unspecified person, so it generalises to the community, and the final outcome is the same.

The legislation began with the prohibition of worshipping other than God, because this is the root of reform, since the reform of thought takes precedence over the reform of action; the intellect does not strive towards seeking good deeds unless it is itself sound. In a hadith: "Indeed, in the body there is a piece of flesh; if it is sound, the whole body is sound, and if it is corrupt, the whole body is corrupt. Indeed, it is the heart." I have explained this at length in my book entitled *Uṣūl al-Niẓām al-Ijtimāʿī fī al-Islām* (The Principles of the Social Order in Islam).

﴿And to parents, kindness. Whether one or both of them reach old age with you, do not say to them "uff," nor rebuke them, but speak to them a noble word. And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy, and say: "My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me when I was small."﴾

This is clear in giving precedence to the mother's side, because the questioner's question indicates that he was asking about the goodness of his treatment of his parents.

The scholars have several opinions. The first: the mother is given precedence over the father. This was the view of al-Layth ibn Sa'd, al-Muhasibi and Abu Hanifah, and it is the apparent position of Malik. Al-Qarafi, in al-Furuq (23), reports from Mukhtasar al-Jami' that a man asked Malik, "My father is in the land of the Sudan and has written to me to come to him, but my mother prevents me from doing so?" Malik said, "Obey your father and do not disobey your mother." Al-Qarafi mentioned in the seventh question of that same Furuq that Malik intended to forbid the son from traveling to the Sudan without his mother's permission.

The second: the view of the Shafi'is, that the two parents are equal in filial piety. This opinion requires that one seek to weigh between them when they order their son with two contrary commands.

Al-Qurtubi reported from al-Muhasibi in his book al-Ri'ayah that he said: "There is no disagreement among the scholars that the mother has three quarters of filial piety, and the father one quarter." Al-Qurtubi also reported from al-Layth that the mother has two thirds of filial piety and the father one third, based on the difference in the transmission of the hadith mentioned, in that he said, "Then your father," after the second time or after the third time.

The correct view is that fixing this by a precise measure refers the matter to something that cannot be pinned down, and that the meaning of the hadith, despite the difference between its two transmissions, is that the mother takes precedence in general.

Then He commanded him to supplicate for them, asking God's mercy upon them, which is the mercy that the child cannot convey to his parents except by earnestly turning to God, exalted is He.

He moved to this in a remarkable transition from His words: ﴿And lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy﴾. So mentioning the mercy of the servant served as a transition to the mercy of God, and as an alert that adopting the character of loving good for one's parents drives the child to treat them with it, both in what they know and in what is hidden from them, even what reaches them after their death. In the hadith: "When the son of Adam dies, his deeds are cut off except for three: ongoing charity, knowledge that he spread among men, and a righteous child who prays for him."

In the verse there is an indication that supplication for them is answered, because God permitted it, and the hadith mentioned supports this, since it made a child's supplication a deed credited to his parents.

The ruling of this supplication is specific to believing parents, by other evidences that indicate the specification, such as His words: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ [al-Tawbah: 113], and the rest of the verse.

The kaf in His words ﴿as they raised me when I was small﴾ is for figurative comparison, which the grammarians express as the meaning of causation in the kaf. An example is His words, exalted is He: ﴿And remember Him as He guided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 198], meaning: have mercy on them with a mercy that repays what they did in raising me when I was small.

"Small" (saghir) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) relating to the first-person pronoun (ya' al-mutakallim).

What is intended by it is depicting a particular situation, in which there is an indication of an upbringing shaped by complete mercy. Fatherhood necessitates the father's mercy, and the child's smallness necessitates mercy toward him, even if he were not a child. So His words ﴿as they raised me when I was small﴾ stand in place of saying: "as they raised me and showed mercy to me through their upbringing." Upbringing completes existence, and by itself it calls for gratitude for it, while mercy is the preservation of existence from being violated, and this is what gratitude requires. So He gathered all of that gratitude into the supplication for them for mercy.

The command necessitates obligation. As for the occasions of supplicating for them, these cannot be pinned down; they depend on the state of each person at the times of his earnest turning to God. It is reported from Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah that if one supplicates for them in every tashahhud, he has fulfilled the command.

The aim of Islam in commanding filial piety and maintaining the ties of kinship (silat al-rahim) resolves into two aims. The first is psychological: training the souls of the community to acknowledge a kindness to its author, which is gratitude, adopting the character of the Creator, exalted is He, in His name al-Shakur (the Most Appreciative). Just as He commanded gratitude to God for the blessing of creation and provision, He commanded gratitude to parents for the blessing of bringing into existence in form, and the blessing of upbringing and mercy. Commanding gratitude for virtues is also a way of honoring them and an alert to competing in bestowing them.

The second aim is civilizational: that the bonds of the family be strong in their knots, firmly tied in trust. So He commanded what achieves that trust among members of the family, which is good companionship, so that in their souls there would grow love and affection that stands in place of the natural maternal compassion in the mother, and then the paternal compassion that arises from a feeling, part of which is natural and weak, and part of which is rational and strong, to the point that the effect of that feeling in its totality equals the effect of the mother's natural compassion, or exceeds it when the child grows old. Then Islam distributed what it called for of this among the rest of the ranks of kinship according to closeness in relational proximity, through what it legislated of maintaining ties of kinship. God has strengthened the readiness of souls to be carried along by that legislation.

It came in a hadith: "When God created the womb (rahim), it grasped one of the pillars of the Throne and said, 'This is the station of one who seeks refuge in You from severance.' God said, 'Are you not pleased that I join with whoever joins with you, and sever from whoever severs you?'" And in another hadith: "God has made the womb one of His names, the Merciful (al-Rahim)."

In this formation of the bonds of kinship there is great benefit for the community, whose effects appear in comforting one another and in unity among some with others. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿O mankind, We created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13].

Islam has further strengthened this by what is in the midst of the Shari'ah of emphasis on tightening the bonds of kinship, more than any previous religion attempted. We have explained this in its chapter in our book on the Objectives of the Islamic Shari'ah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 25:

﴿Your Lord knows best what is in your souls. If you are righteous, then indeed He is ever Forgiving to those who turn back (to Him) in repentance.﴾ This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) for the verse on kindness to one's parents, what it explains, and what the command requires: that the addressees differ in their states before this command arrives, between one who conforms to its requirement and one who goes to excess in it, and that they differ in their states after it arrives, between one who guards its observance and one who falls short, either deliberately or through a moment of heedlessness.

Since what has been mentioned within this discussion, and what it requires, depends on sincerity of intention, so that the action proceeds upon that sincerity in its completeness, without affectation or laziness, He concluded it by stating that He is the One who knows souls and intentions. He promised the child forgiveness if he fulfils what Allah has commanded him toward his parents fully and completely. This is among what the word "righteousness" (salah) includes in His saying ﴿if you are righteous﴾, meaning, obedient to what you have been commanded. The mode of the pronoun was changed and returned to the plural pronoun addressing the group, because this applies to all people, so the plural pronoun is more fitting for it.

Since "righteousness" includes complete righteousness and righteousness mixed with shortcoming, He concluded it with the description of those who turn back (al-awwabin), which by its generality conveys the meaning of returning to Allah, that is, returning to His command and to what pleases Him. Thus there is understood from the speech a meaning of ihtibak by way of contrast, and the implied sense is: "If you are righteous and turn back to Allah, then indeed He is ever Good-doing to the righteous and Forgiving to those who turn back." This applies to the addressees and others, and with this generality it serves as a concluding statement.

This turning back may be continuous, and it may be exposed to shortcoming and negligence, so it requires seeking to desist from whatever spoils it, by returning to the pleasing state. All of that is a turning back, and its doer is one who turns back. The intensive form (awwab) is used for it, because the intensive pattern suits the strength of the quality's manner and the strength of its quantity. Thus one who constantly adheres to obedience in all circumstances and watches over himself is an awwab, because of the intensity of his guarding the return to Allah. And one who is overcome by negligence returns each time he reconsiders himself and remembers his Lord, so he is an awwab because of the frequency of his returning to his Lord's command. Each of the righteous is of this kind.

In His saying ﴿Your Lord knows best what is in your souls﴾ there is something that encompasses all the states of souls, especially the state of negligence and the first stirrings of disobedience, and this is from Allah's mercy toward His creation.

This verse has gathered, together with its brevity, ease after difficulty, mixed with restriction and warning, so that the Muslim may be a watchful observer over himself.

[76]

﴿Give the near of kin his due, and the needy, and the wayfarer.﴾ All kinship branches out from fatherhood, so the discourse moved naturally from the rights of the two parents to the rights of kinship.

Kinship has two rights: the right of maintaining ties (ḥaqq al-ṣilah) and the right of material assistance (ḥaqq al-muwāsāh). The word ḥaqq ("his due") in His words "his due" comprises both. The derivation of this is known, and it rests on other proofs as well.

The address is to an unspecified person, as in His words ﴿Should old age reach them with you﴾ [al-Isrā': 23].

The shift from the plural address in His words ﴿Your Lord knows best what is in your souls, if you are righteous﴾ [al-Isrā': 25] to the singular address in ﴿Give the near of kin his due﴾ is a stylistic variation (tafannun), to avoid the disliked repetition of the same form several times. The one addressed is unspecified, so in meaning he is plural. The sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isrā': 23], since it is part of what God has decreed.

Al-īttā' (giving) means bestowing. It is literally used for giving things, and it is a common figurative usage for empowering one in non-material matters, such as good treatment and support. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "And a man whom God has given wisdom, so he judges by it," the hadith continuing.

Using "giving" here is suitable for both meanings, as is the Qur'an's method of gathering meanings and condensing expressions.

Legal proofs have clarified the rights of the near of kin and their grades: some are obligatory, such as part of the maintenance of certain relatives, whose conditions are specified by the jurists, and some are non-obligatory, such as kindness.

These do not relate to the rights of the relatives of the Prophet ﷺ, because their rights in property were established after the Hijrah, when zakāt (obligatory alms) was prescribed and the spoils of war (maghānim) and the fay' (property taken without battle) and its distribution were legislated. For this reason, the majority of scholars understood this verse as referring to the rights of blood relatives among people. It is reported from 'Alī Zayn al-'Ābidīn that it includes the relatives of the Prophet ﷺ.

[77]
The definite article in "the near of kin" is the definite article of the category, meaning "the kin who are near to you." This is what is expressed by saying that "al-" is a substitute for the genitive complement. Because the giving of the near of kin is mentioned, the one who is similar to them in deserving material support is joined to them.

The right of the needy (miskīn) is charity, as God said: ﴿nor do you urge the feeding of the needy﴾ [al-Fajr: 18], and His words ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger an orphan near of kin, or a needy person in misery﴾ [al-Balad: 14–16]. Many verses and hadiths have clarified the rights of the needy, the greatest of which is the verse on zakāt, and the grades of obligatory and other charities.

The wayfarer (ibn al-sabīl) is the traveller who passes by a settlement; he has the right of hospitality from the settlement he passes through.

The rights of guests in the speech of the Prophet ﷺ are like his saying: "Whoever believes in God and the Last Day, let him honour his guest, his reward being a day and a night."

The hospitality of the wayfarer was among the principles of the ḥanīfiyyah (the primordial monotheistic faith), one of the practices prescribed by Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him). Al-Ḥarīrī said: "And the sanctity of the old man who established hospitality."

A share of zakāt has been assigned to the wayfarer.

This verse gathers three injunctions which God enjoined by His words ﴿Your Lord has decreed﴾ [al-Isrā': 23] … and so on.

As for giving to the near of kin, its aim is close to the aim of kindness to the two parents, in observing the unity of the close origin and strengthening the bond of the clan from which the tribe is formed. In this there is great benefit for the order and security of the tribe and for defending its domain.

As for giving to the needy, its purpose is the organisation of society so that none of its members is in misery and wretchedness. Moreover, that needy person is in most cases from the tribe, whom incapacity to work and poverty in lacking sufficiency has left in need.

[78]
As for giving to the wayfarer, it is for the completion of the social order, since the passer-by from outside his people has a great need of lodging at night, to protect him from the assaults of wild beasts and thieves, and of food and warmth, or shade, against the harm of hunger, poverty or heat.

* * *

﴿And do not squander wastefully. Indeed, the squanderers are brothers of the devils, and the devil has ever been ungrateful to his Lord.﴾

When praiseworthy giving was mentioned, and its opposite was well known among the Arabs, He followed it with mention of the opposite for the sake of relevance.

Also, restraining oneself from the blameworthy giving that is squandering (tabdhīr) is a preservation of the wealth that suffices for the commanded giving. Thus restraint from this facilitates and assists that. Although this is an important aim of the legislation in these verses, it has come as a digression amid the injunctions concerning the giving of wealth, to show that it is a means to giving wealth to its rightful recipients, and that it is also itself intended by the injunction for its own sake. For this reason, the discourse will return to giving wealth to its rightful recipients after finishing the prohibition of squandering, with His words ﴿And if you turn away from them﴾ [al-Isrā': 28] … and so on. Then the discourse returns to the rulings on squandering with His words ﴿And do not keep your hand chained to your neck﴾ [al-Isrā': 29].

His words ﴿And do not squander wastefully﴾ are not connected to His words ﴿Give the near of kin his due﴾ etc., because squandering is not a description applied to giving wealth to its rightful recipient, even if it is more than the giver's need.

So the sentence ﴿And do not squander wastefully﴾ is conjoined to the sentence ﴿that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isrā': 23], since it is part of what God has decreed. It is interposed between the sentence ﴿Give the near of kin his due﴾ … and the sentence ﴿And if you turn away from them﴾ [al-Isrā': 28]. Thus this sentence contains a sixth injunction of what God has decreed.

[79]
Tabdhīr is distributing wealth in other than its proper way, and it is synonymous with isrāf (extravagance). So spending it on corruption is squandering, even if the amount is small. Spending it on what is permissible, when it reaches the limit of extravagance, is squandering. Spending it on the paths of righteousness and goodness is not squandering. Someone said to a man who saw him spending on good causes: "There is no good in extravagance," and the spender replied: "There is no extravagance in good." So in this there is a wonderful eloquence of rhetorical inversion (ḥusn al-ʿaks).

The reason for the prohibition of squandering is that wealth is made the means for acquiring what a person needs in life, of necessities, needs and embellishments. The organised measure in spending it guarantees sufficiency in most circumstances, such that if it is spent in its proper way according to that order between the necessary, the needed and the embellishing, the owner is secure from poverty in what he needs most. Going beyond this limit in it is called squandering in relation to owners of wealth who have just enough. As for people of abundance and riches, that abundance comes from doors which have opened for one person and necessarily narrowed for another, because wealth is limited. So that abundance must be preserved for supporting the weak and those in need, whose number increases in proportion to the abundance of wealth in the hands of the rich and the affluent. It is thus reserved for maintaining the interests of the family, the tribe, and consequently the interests of the nation.

The best use of abundant wealth is acquiring nearness to God, as God said: ﴿And strive with your wealth and your selves in the way of God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 41], and acquiring praise among one's people. Long ago the Arab proverb said: "The best aid to manliness is affluence." It has been said: "O God, grant me praise and grant me glory, for there is no praise except through deeds, and no deeds except through wealth."

The legal aim is that the wealth of the nation should be a provision for it and a strength for building the foundation of its glory and preserving its standing, so that it is feared, respected, and not in need of anyone who may exploit its need, seize its benefits, and bring it under the yoke of his authority.

[80]
For this reason God attributed wealth to the pronoun of the addressees in His words ﴿And do not give the foolish your wealth, which God has made for you a means of support﴾ [al-Nisā': 5], and He did not say "their wealth," although it is the wealth of the foolish, because of His words after it ﴿But if you find in them sound judgement, hand over their wealth to them﴾ [al-Nisā': 6], so He attributed it to them when they became sound of judgement.

What prevented the foolish from disposing of their wealth was only fear of squandering. For this reason, if the foolish person disposed of some of his wealth in a manner of soundness and righteousness, it would be valid.

He mentioned the absolute object tabdhīran after ﴿do not squander﴾ to emphasise the prohibition, as if it were said: "Do not squander, do not squander," along with what the verbal noun carries of evoking the category of what is forbidden, evoking the reality of it with what it involves of corruptions.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, the squanderers﴾ is a definition of the category, meaning: those who are known by this reality, like the definition in His words ﴿guidance for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2].

Ikhwān is the plural of akh (brother), and here it is used metaphorically for the constant companion who does not separate, since that is the character of a brother. Like the saying: "akhū al-ʿilm" (a brother of knowledge), meaning one who is constantly with it and characterised by it; "akhū al-safar" (a brother of travel), for one who travels much. And like the words of ʿAdī ibn Zayd:

*And the brother of al-Ḥaḍar, when he built it, and the Tigris gathers its produce to him, and the Khābūr.*

He means the owner of the palace of al-Ḥaḍar, who was the king of the land of al-Ḥaḍar called al-Ḍayzan ibn Muʿāwiyah al-Quḍāʿī, known as al-Saṭrūn.

The meaning is that they are followers of the devils and their allies, as a brother follows his brother.

This meaning is further emphasised by the word kānū (they were), which indicates that this brotherhood is an established characteristic in them. And the reality of the devil is enough to make people hate it and find it repugnant.

[81]
The meaning of this is that squandering is what the devil calls one to, because it is either spending on corruption, or extravagance that drains wealth on trivialities and pleasures, thereby disabling spending on good. All of this pleases the devil, so there is no doubt that those characterised by squandering are of the army of the devil and his brothers.

This is a warning against squandering, for when a person does it, he becomes habituated to it and addicted to it until it becomes a trait for him, which does not leave him, in the manner of blameworthy traits, which easily attach themselves to souls. As is reported in the hadith: "A man continues to lie until he is recorded with God as a liar." So when a person squanders, it will not be long before he becomes one of the squanderers, that is, those known by this description. And the squanderers are brothers of the devils. So let a person beware of an act which is characteristic of the brothers of the devils, and let him beware of turning into one of the brothers of the devils.

Thereby it becomes clear that there is an elliptical concision (ījāz ḥadhf) in the speech, its estimate being: "And do not squander wastefully, lest you become one of the squanderers; indeed the squanderers have been brothers of the devils." What indicates the omitted part is that a person is truly called a squanderer when he squanders once or twice.

Then He reinforced the warning with the sentence ﴿and the devil has ever been ungrateful to his Lord﴾. This is a severe warning that squandering may lead its doer, step by step, to disbelief through adopting satanic dispositions, so that he goes down in a steady decline into the pits of error until it brings him to disbelief, as God said: ﴿Indeed, the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you, and if you obey them, you will indeed be polytheists﴾ [al-An'ām: 121]. It is also permissible to understand disbelief here as ingratitude for blessings (kufr al-niʿmah), in which case it is the nearest degree to the state of adopting squandering, because squandering is spending wealth on other than what God has commanded, so it is ingratitude for God's blessing of wealth. Thus adopting it leads to the habit and habituation of ingratitude for blessings.

On either interpretation, the statement follows what is known in logic as the syllogism of equivalence (qiyās al-musāwāh): since the squanderer is a brother of the devil, and the devil is ungrateful, the squanderer is ungrateful in outcome or at the nearest degree.

[82]
Squandering was among the characteristics of the people of ignorance (jāhiliyyah). For this reason they boasted of the quality of destroying and ruining wealth. Gambling (maysir) was among the means of such destruction for them. So God warned the believers against taking on the attributes of the people of disbelief, which are among the blameworthy qualities, and taught them the etiquette of wisdom and perfection.

It is thus reserved for maintaining the interests of the family, the tribe, and consequently the interests of the nation.

The best use of abundant wealth is acquiring nearness to God, as God said: ﴿And strive with your wealth and your selves in the way of God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 41], and acquiring praise among one's people. Long ago the Arab proverb said: "The best aid to manliness is affluence." It has been said: "O God, grant me praise and grant me glory, for there is no praise except through deeds, and no deeds except through wealth."

The legal aim is that the wealth of the nation should be a provision for it and a strength for building the foundation of its glory and preserving its standing, so that it is feared, respected, and not in need of anyone who may exploit its need, seize its benefits, and bring it under the yoke of his authority.

[80]
For this reason God attributed wealth to the pronoun of the addressees in His words ﴿And do not give the foolish your wealth, which God has made for you a means of support﴾ [al-Nisā': 5], and He did not say "their wealth," although it is the wealth of the foolish, because of His words after it ﴿But if you find in them sound judgement, hand over their wealth to them﴾ [al-Nisā': 6], so He attributed it to them when they became sound of judgement.

What prevented the foolish from disposing of their wealth was only fear of squandering. For this reason, if the foolish person disposed of some of his wealth in a manner of soundness and righteousness, it would be valid.

He mentioned the absolute object tabdhīran after ﴿do not squander﴾ to emphasise the prohibition, as if it were said: "Do not squander, do not squander," along with what the verbal noun carries of evoking the category of what is forbidden, evoking the reality of it with what it involves of corruptions.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, the squanderers﴾ is a definition of the category, meaning: those who are known by this reality, like the definition in His words ﴿guidance for the God-conscious﴾ [al-Baqarah: 2].

Ikhwān is the plural of akh (brother), and here it is used metaphorically for the constant companion who does not separate, since that is the character of a brother. Like the saying: "akhū al-ʿilm" (a brother of knowledge), meaning one who is constantly with it and characterised by it; "akhū al-safar" (a brother of travel), for one who travels much. And like the words of ʿAdī ibn Zayd:

*And the brother of al-Ḥaḍar, when he built it, and the Tigris gathers its produce to him, and the Khābūr.*

He means the owner of the palace of al-Ḥaḍar, who was the king of the land of al-Ḥaḍar called al-Ḍayzan ibn Muʿāwiyah al-Quḍāʿī, known as al-Saṭrūn.

The meaning is that they are followers of the devils and their allies, as a brother follows his brother.

This meaning is further emphasised by the word kānū (they were), which indicates that this brotherhood is an established characteristic in them. And the reality of the devil is enough to make people hate it and find it repugnant.

[81]
The meaning of this is that squandering is what the devil calls one to, because it is either spending on corruption, or extravagance that drains wealth on trivialities and pleasures, thereby disabling spending on good. All of this pleases the devil, so there is no doubt that those characterised by squandering are of the army of the devil and his brothers.

This is a warning against squandering, for when a person does it, he becomes habituated to it and addicted to it until it becomes a trait for him, which does not leave him, in the manner of blameworthy traits, which easily attach themselves to souls. As is reported in the hadith: "A man continues to lie until he is recorded with God as a liar." So when a person squanders, it will not be long before he becomes one of the squanderers, that is, those known by this description. And the squanderers are brothers of the devils. So let a person beware of an act which is characteristic of the brothers of the devils, and let him beware of turning into one of the brothers of the devils.

Thereby it becomes clear that there is an elliptical concision (ījāz ḥadhf) in the speech, its estimate being: "And do not squander wastefully, lest you become one of the squanderers; indeed the squanderers have been brothers of the devils." What indicates the omitted part is that a person is truly called a squanderer when he squanders once or twice.

Then He reinforced the warning with the sentence ﴿and the devil has ever been ungrateful to his Lord﴾. This is a severe warning that squandering may lead its doer, step by step, to disbelief through adopting satanic dispositions, so that he goes down in a steady decline into the pits of error until it brings him to disbelief, as God said: ﴿Indeed, the devils inspire their allies to dispute with you, and if you obey them, you will indeed be polytheists﴾ [al-An'ām: 121]. It is also permissible to understand disbelief here as ingratitude for blessings (kufr al-niʿmah), in which case it is the nearest degree to the state of adopting squandering, because squandering is spending wealth on other than what God has commanded, so it is ingratitude for God's blessing of wealth. Thus adopting it leads to the habit and habituation of ingratitude for blessings.

On either interpretation, the statement follows what is known in logic as the syllogism of equivalence (qiyās al-musāwāh): since the squanderer is a brother of the devil, and the devil is ungrateful, the squanderer is ungrateful in outcome or at the nearest degree.

[82]
Squandering was among the characteristics of the people of ignorance (jāhiliyyah). For this reason they boasted of the quality of destroying and ruining wealth. Gambling (maysir) was among the means of such destruction for them. So God warned the believers against taking on the attributes of the people of disbelief, which are among the blameworthy qualities, and taught them the etiquette of wisdom and perfection.

﴿And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord which you hope for, then speak to them a gentle word﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf, conjunction) with His saying ﴿And give to the near of kin his right, and to the needy and the wayfarer﴾ [al-Isra': 26], because it is part of it.

The address is to an unspecified addressee so that it covers every person addressed, and the intended addressee is the Prophet (ﷺ). This is because it follows the same structure as His saying ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isra': 23]. Address with "your Lord" (rabbuka) in the Qur'an generally came in speaking to the Prophet (ﷺ). This is supported by what is reported: "The Prophet (ﷺ), whenever someone asked him for wealth and he did not have what he could give, would turn away from him out of modesty." So God directed him to a more perfect courtesy than the one he had been accustomed to, and through this there is instruction for the rest of the community.

The pronoun in ﴿from them﴾ refers to the near of kin, the needy and the wayfarer.

Al-iʿrāḍ (turning away) originally means the opposite of turning toward. It is derived from al-ʿurḍ, with the ʿayn vowelled with a ḍamma, meaning the side. So aʿraḍa means he gave his side. ﴿And when We bestow favour upon man, he turns away and withdraws to his side﴾ [al-Isra': 83]. Here it is used figuratively for not giving, or it is a metonymy for it, because withholding is accompanied by turning away. That is, if one of them asks you for a gift and you do not grant it to him, or if you do not visit them with the customary gift, and you turn away from meeting them out of modesty before them, because you would meet them empty-handed, then ﴿speak to them a gentle word﴾.

Al-maysūr (that which is made easy) is a past participle from al-yusr, which is ease. Its verb is in the passive voice: it is said yusira al-amr, with a ḍamma on the yāʾ and a kasra on the sīn, just as it is said suʿida al-rajul (the man was made fortunate) and nuḥisa (he was made unfortunate). The meaning is that it was made easy and not difficult. Likewise, it is said ʿasīr (difficult). The "gentle word" (al-qawl al-maysūr) is soft, good speech that is acceptable to them. Acceptable speech is likened to the easy, because the soul accepts it, since unacceptable speech is difficult. God commanded that the lack of giving, owing to the lack of means, be softened with a gentle, good word, through an apology and a promise for when one has means, so that turning away is not taken to indicate indifference or stinginess.

He has made turning away conditional on two conditions: that it be turning away in pursuit of provision from God, that is, turning away due to lack of means, not refusal out of miserliness toward them; and that it be accompanied by a gentle word of apology. It is understood from His saying ﴿seeking mercy from your Lord﴾ that the apology is sincere and not a pretext, as Bashshār said:

*For the miser, regarding his wealth, there are excuses,*
*with blue eyes, and upon them are black faces.*

So His saying ﴿seeking mercy from your Lord﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿you turn away﴾, introduced with a descriptive form, meaning "seeking mercy from your Lord." ﴿Which you hope for﴾ is a descriptor (ṣifa) of ﴿mercy﴾. Here "mercy" is the provision from which giving comes, by the context of the passage. In this is an indication that provision is a cause of mercy, because when one gives it to one who deserves it, one is rewarded for it. This is an incorporation (idmāj), a bringing in of a related matter.

Within this condition is an instruction to the believer who lacks what would enable him to do good: he should hope from God for the facilitation of its means, and his stinginess should not lead him to rejoice at the loss of provision for the sake of relief from giving. Rather, he should not withhold giving unless he hopes that it will become easy for him in the future, out of eagerness for its virtue. It is also that one should not turn away from the near of kin, the needy and the wayfarer except in the state of hoping for the attainment of a blessing. If it is attained, he gives to them.

Page 83

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 29:

[84]
﴿And do not let your hand be chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched, lest you sit down blameworthy and destitute.﴾

This returns to the explanation of extravagance (tabdhir) and stinginess (shuhh). The sentence is coordinated (ʿatf) with the sentence ﴿And do not be wastefully extravagant, wasteful extravagance﴾ [al-Isra': 26]. Were it not for the intervening separation between them, by His saying ﴿And if you turn away from them, seeking mercy from your Lord﴾ [al-Isra': 28] and what follows, the sentence ﴿do not let your hand be chained to your neck﴾ would not be joined by the conjunction "wa" (and), because it is the nature of an explanatory clause (bayan) not to be coordinated with what it explains. Moreover, coordinating it carries an emphasis that makes it stand independent in purpose, since it contains an addition beyond the explanation, namely the prohibition against stinginess, which is the counterpart of extravagance.

This verse came as a teaching for understanding one of the subtle realities, so it was among wisdom (hikmah), and its composition came by way of illustration (tamthil), so the wisdom was cast in the mold of eloquence (balaghah).

As for the wisdom: it shows that what is praiseworthy in giving is the middle course lying between the two extremes of excess and deficiency. These praiseworthy middles between blameworthy things exist in every reality that has two extremes. It is established in the wisdom of ethics (hikmat al-akhlaq) that every trait has two extremes and a middle: the two extremes are excess (ifrat) and deficiency (tafrit), and both produce corruption in its source and its object. The middle is justice (ʿadl). Thus giving and spending have, as one extreme, stinginess (shuhh), which corrupts the needy and also the owner of wealth, since it draws to him people's dislike of him and his dislike of them. The other extreme is extravagance (tabdhir) and profligacy (israf), which entails corruption for the owner of wealth and his kin, because he diverts his wealth from its rightful recipient to channels not deserving of it. The middle is placing wealth in its proper places, and this is the limit which the verse expresses by negating two states between "lā … wa-lā" (neither … nor).

As for the eloquence: it lies in depicting stinginess and withholding by the chaining of the hand to the neck. This is an illustration built upon imagining the hand as the source of giving and bestowal, and imagining its extending and chaining as stinginess,

[85]
and this is an imagery well known to the eloquent and the poets. God Most High said: ﴿And the Jews said: "God's hand is chained." Rather, His hands are outstretched﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64]. The poet al-A'sha said:

Your two hands are hands of truth: one palm is beneficial, and another palm, when wealth is withheld, spends.

From this usage they say: "He has a hand over so-and-so," meaning a favour and bounty. So the illustration in the verse came built upon a free handling of this meaning, by depicting the one who is stingy with wealth as one whose hand is chained to his neck, that is, bound with a shackle (ghull), which is a leather strap by which a captive is bound. When the hand is chained to the neck, its use becomes impossible, so benefit from it is nullified, and the source of giving is rendered inoperative. In its opposite, the spendthrift is like one who extends his hand to the utmost extent and its limit, and this is what is conveyed by His saying ﴿fully outstretched﴾, that is, all of the outstretching beyond which there is no further outstretching, which is the meaning of the limit. Of this same meaning was His saying Most High, ﴿And the Jews said: "God's hand is chained." … Rather, His hands are outstretched; He spends as He wills﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64], in Surat al-'Uqud. This is the mold of eloquence cast in that wisdom.

His saying ﴿then you sit down blameworthy and destitute﴾ is the answer to both prohibitions, distributed by the method of orderly correspondence (al-nashr al-murattab). "Blameworthy" refers back to the prohibition against stinginess, and "destitute" refers back to the prohibition against extravagance, for the stingy person is blamed and reproached. It has been said:

Indeed the miser is blamed wherever he may be.

Zuhayr said:
Whoever possesses bounty and withholds his bounty from his people will be left without them and will be disparaged.

"Mahsur" means one whose strength is exhausted. It is said: "a camel that is ḥasīr," when travel has worn it out so that no strength remains in it. From this is His saying Most High: ﴿Then return your gaze, it will come back to you humbled and weary (ḥasīr)﴾ [al-Mulk: 4]. The meaning is: unable to sustain your affairs. The address is to an unspecified person. The discussion of "taqʿud" has already passed above.

Page 86

﴿Indeed your Lord extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it. Indeed He is ever, of His servants, All-Aware, All-Seeing.﴾ The position of this sentence is that of an interjected clause (i'tiraḍ) giving the reason (ta'līl) for what preceded: the command to give to the near of kin and the needy, the prohibition of wastefulness, and the prohibition of miserliness, which implies the command to moderation. The reason is that this is the duty of people regarding their wealth and their duty toward their relatives and the weak among their kinsfolk. They must therefore comply with what God has commanded them in this matter. Stinginess does not preserve the miser's wealth for himself, and wastefulness does not enrich those among whom he squanders wealth, for God has decreed for every soul its provision.

It is possible that the speech continues in the manner of the preceding address, which is directed at an unspecified person. It is also possible that the speech has shifted to address the Prophet (ﷺ), so the address is directed to the Prophet, because he is the most worthy of knowing these lofty truths, although his community is also intended by the address, following him. In that case, these exhortations are interwoven with a turn toward addressing the Prophet (ﷺ).

"Yaqdir" is the opposite of "yabsut." It was previously discussed at His words, ﴿God extends provision to whom He wills and restricts it﴾ [al-Ra'd: 26], in Surat al-Ra'd.

The clause ﴿Indeed He is ever, of His servants, All-Aware, All-Seeing﴾ [al-Isra': 96] gives the reason for the clause ﴿Indeed your Lord extends provision﴾ to its end. That is, He does this because He knows the circumstances of His servants and what befits each of them according to the natures they were created with, and the circumstances surrounding them from the systems of the world that divine wisdom has required and deposited in this world.

Al-Khabir is the one who knows matters of news and information, and al-Basir is the one who knows visible things. These two noble names return to the meaning of some aspects of the relation of divine knowledge.

[p. 87]

﴿Do not kill your children for fear of poverty. We provide for them and for you. Indeed, killing them is a great sin.﴾ This verse links one ruling to another, prohibiting an act that arises from despair of God's provision. It is the seventh of the injunctions mentioned in the verse ﴿Your Lord has decreed﴾ [al-Isra: 23] and what follows it. The pronoun shifts from the singular to the plural, because the prohibited act here belongs to the practices of the Age of Ignorance (jahiliyyah), and the address is a rebuke to them for this blameworthy sin. The discussion of a parallel verse in Surat al-An'am has already passed, but there is a difference in composition (nazm) between the two verses in two respects.

The first: here it says ﴿for fear of poverty﴾ (khashyata imlaq), while in the verse of al-An'am it says ﴿out of poverty﴾ (min imlaq) [al-An'am: 151]. This implies that those who buried their daughters (wa'd, burying alive) did so for one of two reasons. Either they were poor and could not afford to support a daughter, nor did they hope that she would help them earn a living if she grew up. They buried her for that reason, and this is the context of the words in al-An'am ﴿out of poverty﴾ [al-An'am: 151], since the causal min ("out of") implies that poverty was the cause of killing them, and so poverty must have existed at the time of the killing.

Or the motive was not the father's poverty, but fear that poverty might befall him, or that it might befall the daughter upon her father's death, since in their ignorance they did not give daughters inheritance. Thus the impulse to bury was the anticipation of poverty, as the early Islamic poet Ishaq ibn Khalaf said:

When I recall my daughter as she laments for me,
my tears flow with blood for my daughter's tears.

I fear poverty will one day befall her,
so the veil is torn from flesh upon bone.

She loves my life, and I love her death out of compassion,
and death is the most honorable guest for the free.

I fear the harshness of an uncle, or the rudeness of a brother,
and I used to fear for her the harm of harsh words.
