[p. 88]

So, to warn the Muslims against the consequences of these thoughts, they were reminded of the prohibition of burying (wa'd) and what has the same meaning. This was among the things taken as a condition in the pledge (bay'ah) of believing women, as in the verse of Surat al-Mumtahanah. Among the sayings of the people of ignorance was: "Burying daughters is among the noble deeds." Both of these situations, as causes of killing children, imply each other, and the directing of attention is only to what is primarily considered at the outset.

The second aspect: because of this consideration in the first difference, there it was said ﴿We provide for you and for them﴾ [al-An'am: 151], with the pronoun of the fathers placed before the pronoun of the children. This is because the poverty that drove the burying mentioned in the verse of al-An'am was the poverty of the fathers. So it first announced that God is their provider, and then completed it by saying that He is the provider of their daughters.

As for the poverty mentioned in this verse, it is the poverty feared to occur, and most often it was the anticipation of the daughters' poverty, as you have seen in the verses. Therefore it first mentioned that God is the provider of the children, and then completed it by saying that He is the provider of their fathers. This is one of the subtleties (nukat) of the Qur'an.

Al-imlaq means destitution (al-iftiqar). The discussion of burying (wa'd) has already passed at the words of the Exalted ﴿Likewise their partners have made attractive to many of the polytheists the killing of their children﴾ [al-An'am: 137] in Surat al-An'am.

The clause ﴿We provide for them﴾ is a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ) between the conjoined clauses. The clause ﴿Indeed, killing them is a great sin﴾ is an emphasis on the prohibition and a warning against falling into what is forbidden. The verb kana ("was") is an emphasis of the clause.

By "children" (awlad) is meant specifically daughters, because they are the ones they used to kill by burying. However, the Qur'an expressed them with the word "children" in this verse and its parallels, because a daughter is also called a walad (child). The pronoun follows the grammatical form in the phrase ﴿We provide for them﴾.

The word khiṭ' (with a kasrah on the kha' and a sukun on the ta') is the verbal noun of khati'a on the pattern of fariḥa, meaning he committed a sin. Sin only occurs through intention, as the Exalted said ﴿Indeed, Pharaoh and Haman and their soldiers were sinners﴾ [al-Qasas: 8], and He said ﴿a lying, sinning forelock﴾ [al-'Alaq: 16].

[p. 89]

As for khaṭa' (with a fatḥah on both the kha' and the ta'), it is the opposite of intention (al-'amd), and its verb is akhṭa'a, with the active participle mukhṭi'. The Exalted said ﴿There is no blame upon you for what you have done in error, but for what your hearts have intended﴾ [al-Ahzab: 5]. This distinction is the secret of the Arabic language, and the verifying scholars among its imams hold to it.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read khiṭ'an with a kasrah on the kha' and a sukun on the ta' followed by a hamzah, meaning sin. Ibn Dhakwan on the authority of Ibn 'Amir and Abu Ja'far read khaṭa'an with a fatḥah on the kha' and a fatḥah on the ta', and khaṭa' is the opposite of correctness, meaning that their killing is pure error with nothing in it that would excuse its doer.

Ibn Kathir read khiṭa'an with a kasrah on the kha', a fatḥah on the ta', and an alif after the ta', followed by a hamzah, lengthened, and it is the pattern fi'al from khati'a when one commits a crime. It is a dialectal variant of khaṭa', and it seems that the fi'al pattern here is for intensification. It is emphasized by "indeed" (inna) to confirm it, as a refutation of the people of ignorance, who used to claim that burying daughters was correct and would say: "Burying daughters is among the noble deeds." It is also emphasized by the verb kana, because kana indicates that its being a sin is a settled matter.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 32:

﴿And do not approach adultery. Indeed, it is ever an immorality and evil as a way.﴾ The conjoining of this prohibition with the prohibition of burying daughters alive (*wa'd*) is an indication that they used to count among their excuses for burying daughters alive the fear of the shame that may befall them as a result of neglecting daughters, which arises from poverty, which casts them into the pits of prostitution (*'uhr*). Also, adultery involves the loss of lineage (*nasab*), such that the offspring has no known origin to which it can return, and this resembles burying alive in its destruction.

The pronoun here is in the plural form, as it is in His saying ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾ [al-Isra: 31], for the same reason that the change of style was explained there, since what is prohibited here was among the common practices of the people of ignorance (*jahiliyyah*).

[p. 90]

This is the eighth of the divine injunctions, by His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him﴾ [al-Isra: 23].

The "approach" that is prohibited is the least degree of involvement, and it is a metonymy (*kinayah*) for the intensity of the prohibition of involvement in adultery. Close to this meaning is the saying: "He almost did it" (*ma kada yafʿalu*).

In the technical usage of Islam, *zina* (adultery/fornication) is a man's intercourse with a woman who is not his wife, nor a slave-woman who is not married. In the pre-Islamic period, *zina* was a man's intercourse with a free woman who was not his wife; as for intercourse with a slave-woman not owned by the man, that was called *bigha'* (prostitution).

The clause ﴿Indeed, it is ever an immorality﴾ is a justification for the prohibition of involvement in it, an emphatic justification from several aspects: by describing it as an immorality (*fahishah*), which denotes an act that has reached the utmost limit of ugliness; by emphasizing that with the particle of emphasis; and by inserting the verb *kana* (was), which indicates that its predicate is a firmly established and settled attribute, as has been explained earlier, in His saying ﴿Indeed, the squanderers were brothers of the devils﴾ [al-Isra: 27].

The meaning is that this is an attribute established in itself, whether people knew it before or did not know it except after the revelation of the verse.

He follows this with the verb of blame, *sa'a sabilan* (and evil as a way). *Sabil* means "road/way." It is used here metaphorically for the act that a person persists in and makes his habit. This is a compound metaphor (*isti'arah mabniyyah*) built upon the metaphor of traveling for action, as in His saying ﴿We shall return it to its former state﴾ [Ta-Ha: 21]. Upon the metaphor of "travel" for action is built the metaphor of "way" for it, by the relation of constancy. A parallel to it has been mentioned earlier, in His saying ﴿Indeed, it was an immorality and hatred and evil as a way﴾ [an-Nisa: 22], in Surat an-Nisa.

Islam's concern with prohibiting adultery is because it involves the loss of lineage and exposes offspring to neglect, if the adultery is with an unmarried woman, and this is a grave corruption within society. It also involves corrupting women against their husbands and virgins against their guardians. It further involves exposing the woman to neglect, through people turning away from marrying her and her husband divorcing her, and because of the jealousy that arises from it, with its chaos and killing. Imru' al-Qays said:

*"Eager against me, were they to conceal my slaying..."*

[p. 91]

Thus adultery is a *mi'nnah* (a cause/means that leads) to the loss of lineages and a *mazinnah* (a likely occasion) for killing and lewd chaos. It was therefore fitting that its prohibition be made severe, both as an end in itself and as a means. Whoever reflects and considers will be certain of the corruptions that adultery entails. Even if the one who reflects was among those who committed it in the pre-Islamic period, its ugliness is established in its own nature, but intellects differ in perceiving it and in the degree of their perception. So when the prohibition woke them, no excuse remained for people.

Some exegetes have claimed that this verse is Medinan, as was mentioned at the beginning of the surah, but there is no basis for that claim, and we have already pointed out its refutation at the beginning of the surah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 33:

﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden, except by right. And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have certainly given his heir authority, but let him not commit excess in killing. Indeed, he is supported.﴾

The condition of the Arabs in the pre-Islamic era is well known for their haste to kill souls. Therefore the preservation of souls is among the greatest universal principles of the Islamic law (shari'ah), and for this reason the prohibition of killing the soul is among the most important of the injunctions that Islam enjoined upon its followers in these comprehensive verses. This is the ninth of these injunctions.

The word "soul" (nafs) here means the self (dhat), as in His saying, ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa': 29], and His saying, ﴿Whoever kills a soul without a soul having been killed or corruption done in the land, it is as if he had killed mankind entirely﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 32], and His saying, ﴿And no soul knows in what land it will die﴾ [Luqman: 34]. The word nafs is also applied to the human spirit, which is the rational soul (al-nafs al-natiqah).

Qatl (killing) is causing death by the action of an agent, that is, the removal of life from the self.

His saying ﴿Allah has forbidden﴾: the returning pronoun (al-'a'id) from the relative clause to the relative pronoun has been omitted, because it is an object pronoun governed by the verb of the relative clause, and its omission is common. The estimated sense is: "which Allah has forbidden it." The prohibition is attached to the very soul, while what is intended is the prohibition of killing it.

The soul is described by the relative pronoun and the relative clause in accordance with the fact that the prohibition of its killing was well known before this prohibition, either because it had been established earlier by other verses revealed before this verse and before the verse of al-An'am, as gradual injunctions, and this verse and the verse of al-An'am gathered those rulings together; or because the relative clause is treated as if it were known, since it is something that one should not be ignorant of. This thus implies a rebuke of the people of the pre-Islamic era, who treated the killing of a soul lightly, on the grounds that they were ignorant of what they ought to have known, and it serves to emphasize this ruling. This is because reflection on the creation of this world guides the intellects to the fact that Allah brought man into existence in order that he might populate the earth, as He said, ﴿He produced you from the earth and made you inhabit it﴾ [Hud: 61]. Therefore, proceeding to destroy a soul is a demolition of what Allah intended to build. Moreover, it has been widely transmitted and has spread among the nations in all ages and religions since the time of Adam that souls are to be protected from being attacked by execution. Hence it is described as "which Allah has forbidden," meaning that it is recognized through the content of this relative clause.

Excepted from the generality of the prohibition is killing that accompanies right (al-haqq), that is, killing in which the right testifies that a specific soul deserved execution by the community. This is a general statement which, at the time of revelation, was explained by what was known of the laws of retaliation (qawad) in general terms.

Since these verses were brought forth in the manner of legislation for the community, and as an indication that there would be judicature and rule in the community in the future, the matter was left general until it would be explained by the rulings introduced later, such as the verse ﴿It is not for a believer to kill a believer except by mistake﴾ [al-Nisa': 92], up to His saying ﴿and has prepared for him a great punishment﴾ [al-Nisa': 93].

The bi' in His saying "bi-l-haqq" is for accompaniment (lil-musahabah), and it is connected to the meaning of the exception, that is: "except a killing accompanied by right."

Al-haqq means justice, or it means entitlement, that is, the right to kill, as in the hadith: "When they say it, that is, 'There is no god but Allah,' they have secured from me their blood and their property, except by its right."

Since the address of the prohibition is to the whole community, as the verb in the context of the prohibition indicates, the specification of the right that permits the killing of a soul is left to those who have the authority to specify rights.

Since this verse was revealed before the Hijrah, the specification of the right follows what was customary among the tribes, which is what is mentioned in His saying immediately after this, ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully﴾, and so on.

At the time this verse was revealed, the Muslims were mixed in Makkah with the polytheists, and the polytheists were not trustworthy in obeying just laws. It might happen that one of the polytheists would attack one of the Muslims by killing him unjustly. Allah therefore commanded the Muslims that the wronged one should not wrong in return, so He said, ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully, We have certainly given his heir authority﴾, meaning that He has given the heir of the slain the right to act against the killer by retaliation (qawad) or by blood-money (diyah).

Al-sultan: a verbal noun from "al-sultah," like "al-ghufran," and what is meant by it is the ruling of retaliation that was established in their customs.

That it is a right of the heir of the slain, who may take it, pardon, or accept blood-money, is something Allah inspired to them, lest the heirs of the slain pounce upon the killer or his kin, to kill from among them one whose hands had committed no killing. Thus the feuds continue between taking and returning, and this too was among their customs.

Therefore, the "making" (al-ja'l) refers to what Allah guided the people of the pre-Islamic era to, namely the custom of retaliation.

Retaliation (qawad) is among the things covered by His saying "except by right," because retaliation against the wrongful killer is a killing of the soul by right. This is a case which Allah singled out for mention because of the frequency of aggression in the rest of the days of the pre-Islamic era. So Allah commanded the Muslims to accept retaliation. This is a great principle of reform in the Islamic community, namely training its members to follow what is right and just, so that corruption does not come from both sides and thus grow worse. That was a pre-Islamic custom. Al-Shamaydhar al-Harithi said:

We are not like those of you who strike a single blow, and then we accept oppression or appoint a judge;
But the rule of the sword is imposed upon us, so we are content when the sword becomes content.

Allah therefore forbade the Muslims from becoming a bad example, returning injustice with injustice as the pre-Islamic custom did; rather, they must follow the path of equity by accepting retaliation. Hence He said, ﴿but let him not commit excess in killing﴾.

Excess (israf) is exceeding what right requires, and it is not specific to wealth as is understood from the statements of the lexicographers. Excess in killing is that someone other than the killer be killed. As for killing the killer himself, it is clear, as al-Muhalhil said concerning taking vengeance for his brother Kulayb:

Every slain man of Kulayb is a precious stake, until killing encompasses the family of Murrah.

As for killing someone other than the killer when unable to kill the killer, they used to be content, when unable to reach the killer, with killing a man from the killer's tribe, and they would "measure out" blood, that is, make its measure vary according to the nobility of the slain, as Kabshah bint Ma'di Karib said:

He kills, forcibly, a man who was not his equal in blood, but there is no measuring out of blood.

Ba' (equal) means one who is equal in blood. She means: he kills the killer, who is called "jabr," even if he was not an equal to 'Abd Allah, her brother. But Islam abolished the measuring out of blood.

The pronoun in "yusrif" with the ya' of the third person, according to the reading of the majority, refers to the heir, who is the likely source of excess in killing according to what they had become accustomed to. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with the ta' of the second person, addressing the heir. The clause "Indeed, he was supported" is a resumptive statement: the heir of the slain was supported by the ruling of retaliation, so why would he exceed the limit of support into aggression and wrongdoing by excess in killing? Allah warned them against excess in killing and reminded them that He has given the heir authority over the killer.

This is emphasized by the particle of emphasis and by the insertion of "kana" which indicates that the report is firmly established; and in it is an allusion that whoever exceeds the limit of justice into excess in killing will not be supported.

One of the subtleties, eloquence, and hidden inimitability of the Qur'an is the use here of the word "sultan," which in this context apparently means a verbal noun, that is, authority, right, and what is suitable for the will to establish rule. It refers to the imam who takes rights from aggressors for those who were wronged, once the community of the Muslims is organized after the Hijrah. In it is an allusion that Allah will make for the Muslims a lasting state, whereas the Muslims did not have authority on the day this verse was revealed.

This ruling is attached to killing that occurs between individuals, namely killing by aggression. As for killing that protects the homeland and defends the territory, which is jihad, it has other rulings. By this you know the reason for the use of the plural addressee pronoun, as was mentioned earlier in His saying ﴿And do not kill your children for fear of poverty﴾ [al-Isra': 31] and the pronouns coordinated with it.

Know that the clause ﴿And whoever is killed wrongfully﴾ is coordinated with the clause ﴿And do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right﴾ [al-An'am: 151], as a coordination of one narrative to another narrative, out of concern for this ruling, so that it is made independent; it is coordinated with another ruling. Otherwise, the apparent requirement would be that it be separated, either as a resumptive statement explaining the ruling of a frequent case, or as a substitute for part of the clause ﴿except by right﴾.

"Man" is a relative pronoun, the subject of the nominal sentence, intended in a general sense, that is, "and everyone who is killed wrongfully." The fa' was inserted in the predicate clause because the relative pronoun is treated like a conditional when it is intended in a general sense, and because of the link between it and its predicate.

His saying ﴿then We have certainly given his heir authority﴾ is in meaning an introduction to the predicate, by hastening what reassures the soul of the heir of the slain. The intended purpose of the predicate is the consequence stated in His saying ﴿so let him not commit excess in killing﴾. So the mention of ﴿We have certainly given his heir authority﴾ first served as a preparation for accepting the prohibition of excess in killing, since if He has given him authority, the ruling is in his hand, and this suffices to heal his anguish.

Among the implications by indication is that His saying ﴿We have certainly given his heir authority﴾ points to the invalidity of the heir of the slain taking the killer's life without a ruling from the authority, because that is liable to error in establishing who the killer is, and a pretext for another killing through mutual retaliation between the heirs of the slain and the family of the killer, and it leads to the excess in killing that occurred in the pre-Islamic era only through such pretexts. Therefore the pronoun in "so let him not commit excess" refers to the heir.

The clause ﴿Indeed, he was supported﴾ is a justification for restraint from excess in killing, and the pronoun refers to the heir.

The "fi" in "fi al-qatl" is for figurative containment, since excess roams in gain, wealth and the like, so it is as if it were contained within the whole of what it roams in.

Since some exegetes saw that the ruling contained in this verse suits only the circumstances of sincere Muslims, they judged it unlikely that the verse was revealed in Makkah and claimed that it is Madinan. We have explained the way in which it fits, and we have refuted the claim that it is Makkan at the beginning of this surah.

[Page 97]

﴿And do not approach the property of the orphan except in the best manner, until he reaches his maturity.﴾

This is one of the most important of the injunctions that God enjoins in these verses, because the Arabs in the pre-Islamic period (al-Jahiliyya) used to consider the property of orphans lawful to take, since the orphans were too weak to notice who was consuming their wealth and had few supporters to secure their rights. God therefore warned the Muslims against this in order to remove any trace of that pre-Islamic period that might remain in their souls. The discussion of the parallel of this verse has already preceded in Surat al-An'am. This is the tenth injunction.

The discussion regarding the use of the plural addressee pronoun is the same as the discussion regarding the preceding injunctions, because what is forbidden is a practice of the people of the pre-Islamic period.

* * *

[Page 97]

﴿And fulfill the covenant, for the covenant will be questioned about.﴾ They were commanded to fulfill the covenant. The definite article in "al-'ahd" (the covenant) is for the genus, which conveys comprehensiveness, and so it includes the covenant that they made with the Prophet (ﷺ), namely the pledge of allegiance (bay'a) upon faith and support. This has already been discussed at His words, exalted is He, ﴿And fulfill the covenant of God when you have taken it﴾ [al-Nahl: 91] in Surat al-Nahl, and at His words ﴿And fulfill the covenant of God﴾ [al-An'am: 152] in Surat al-An'am.

This legislation is among the foundations of the community's honor in the view of other nations, and of the trust placed in it, so that they may take refuge under its authority. The discussion of this has already passed in Surat al-An'am. The sentence is conjoined to the one before it, and it is among those that came after the explanatory "an" in His words ﴿that you not worship﴾ [al-Isra': 23] and the following verses. This is the eleventh injunction.

The sentence ﴿for the covenant will be questioned about﴾ is a reason for the command, meaning for the obligation that it entails. Repeating the word "covenant" in a place where a pronoun could have been used is for the sake of emphasis on it, and so that this sentence stands independently, to spread like a proverb.

The complement of "mas'ulan" (questioned) is omitted because it is evident, meaning "questioned about it," that is, God will question you about it on the Day of Resurrection.

[Page 98]

Qur'an 17:35: ﴿Give full measure when you measure, and weigh with a true, upright balance. That is better and more excellent in outcome.﴾ These are two of the rulings, the twelfth and thirteenth of the injunctions that God has decreed, and what is said about their counterpart has already been discussed in Surat al-An'am.

The addition of the temporal clause in this verse, ﴿when you measure﴾, without mentioning its counterpart in the verse of al-An'am, is because the particle (idhā) carries the sense of a conditional. It therefore requires that the command it contains be renewed at every time the condition of the temporal conditional clause occurs. This draws attention to not being lax about any shortfall in measuring at each act of measuring. This is because this is an address to the Muslims, unlike the verse of (al-An'am), whose content is an allusion to the polytheists and their evil practices. Here it was more fitting to emphasize the legislation.

The verb kāla (to measure out for others) indicates that its doer is the one directly engaged in measuring, the one who hands over the measured commodity, and he holds the position of the seller. The one who receives the measured commodity is called muktāl (one who takes a measure). It is among the cognates of bā'a (sold) and ibtā'a (bought), shará (sold) and ishtará (bought), and rahana (pledged) and irtahana (took in pledge). God says: ﴿Those who, when they take a measure from people, take it in full﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 2] ﴿but when they measure or weigh for them, they cause loss﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 3].

Al-qusṭās, with a ḍamma on the qāf, is the reading of the majority, while Ḥafṣ, Ḥamza, al-Kisā'ī and Khalaf read it with a kasra. Both are dialectal forms of the word. It is a term for the balance, that is, the instrument of weighing, and also a term for justice. It is said that it is an arabicized word from Greek (al-Rūmiyya), composed of two words: qasaṭa, meaning "he was just," and ṭās, which is the pan of the balance. In Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, Mujāhid said: "al-qisṭās: justice in Greek." Perhaps the word qasaṭa is an abbreviation of qisṭās, because most Greek words end with the letter sīn. Originally in Greek the first letter is vowelled with a ḍamma, but the Arabs changed it to a kasra as a permissible variant, because they were not careful in vowelling foreign words. Among their proverbs is: "It is foreign, so play with it as you wish."

The meanings of justice and balance are both suitable here. But in al-An'am the word used was ﴿with justice﴾ [al-An'am: 152], which means justice, because that verse was presented in the manner of a reminder to the polytheists of the corruptions they were engaged in, so it was fitting that they be reminded of justice so that they would know that what they were doing is injustice. The bā' there is for accompaniment (mulābasa). This verse, however, is an address to the Muslims, so it was more fitting that it use a word suitable for the meaning of an instrument of weighing, because the nature of legislation is to specify the precise measure of the action, while also alluding to the meaning of justice, through the use of a homonym (mushtarak) in both of its meanings. Thus the bā' here clearly signifies instrumentality and the means, and it also conveys accompaniment.

[Page 99]

Al-mustaqīm means upright, straight, sound, derived from al-qawām (with a fatḥa on the qāf), which is the balance of the essence. It is said: "I straightened it and it became straight." Describing the balance as such is clear. As for justice, it is a descriptive attribute that reveals its nature, because justice in its entirety is uprightness.

The clause ﴿That is better﴾ is a new (independent) sentence, and the demonstrative refers to what was mentioned, namely the measuring and weighing derived from the two verbs (measure and weigh).

Khayr here is the comparative (tafḍīl, elative form), meaning: better than cheating (tatfīf, defrauding in measure), that is, better for you. It is preferred over cheating in the sense that the good of the Hereafter that results from the reward of obedience is preferred over the good of this world that results from the surplus gained by the cheater. And it is also better for him in this world, because the tranquility of soul that a person gains from acting justly is better than the elation that comes from gaining some surplus of wealth.

Al-ta'wīl (interpretation, explanation, outcome) is a form (taf'īl) derived from al-awal, which means return. It is said: "awwalahu" when one returns it, that is, one returns it in the best manner, when a contemplator returns it to its origins and its consequences. For when a person reflects, he moves through the reality of a thing across the various states of its goodness and corruption. If the reality is good, the reflector's opinion settles on its goodness, as though he has returned it, after circling, to its proper place, which is its abode. So the settling of opinion after reflection is called ta'wīl by way of figurative expression (tamthīl), and this usage became so common that it came to equal the literal meaning.

The meaning of "that is better in outcome" is this: when the mind roams through the benefits of cheating in measuring and weighing, and the harms of giving full measure in them, and then returns to roam through the harms of cheating and the benefits of giving full measure, it settles and arrives at the conclusion that giving full measure in both is better than cheating. This is because cheating brings the defrauder the acquisition of a small portion of wealth, but it earns him dislike, blame among people, God's anger, and unlawful gain (suḥt) in his wealth, along with contempt for himself in his own eyes. Giving full measure, by contrast, earns him people's affection, God's pleasure, his own satisfaction with himself, and blessing in his wealth.

[Page 100]

Thus it is "better in outcome." The meaning of ta'wīl with its various senses has already been mentioned in the first introduction of this commentary.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 36:

﴿And do not follow that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — about all of these one will be questioned.﴾

Al-qafw (following, pursuing): it means ittiba' (following). One says qafāhu yaqfūhu when he follows him. It is derived from the noun al-qafā (the back of the neck, that which is behind the neck). This verb is used here metaphorically for acting. What is meant by ﴿that of which you have no knowledge﴾ is a mere inner notion for which there is no evidence and no preponderant assumption (ghalabat zann).

Many kinds fall under this. Among them is a vice of the Jahiliyyah: slandering people's lineages. They would accuse women of relations with men who were not their husbands, and they would attribute some children to other than their fathers, as a false charge, or out of ill opinion, when they saw a wide difference in resemblance between the son and his father, or saw his resemblance to another man of the tribe, or saw a colour different from the colour of the father or the mother. This was based on conjecture and ignorance of the causes of formation, for offspring tend in resemblance and colour toward ancestors in the chain of fathers or mothers, nearer or more distant, and in ignorance of the resemblance arising from the womb. A Bedouin came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "My wife has given birth to a black child; he wants to disown him." The Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Do you have camels?" He said: "Yes." He said: "What are their colours?" He said: "Grey." He said: "Is there among them a black male camel?" He said: "Yes." He said: "From where is that?" He said: "Perhaps it is a hereditary strain that pulled it." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Then perhaps your son is a hereditary strain that pulled him." And he forbade him from disowning him. This practice was widespread in the societies of the Jahiliyyah, so Allah forbade the Muslims from it.

Among them is slander with fornication and other vices without witnessing. Often they would accuse neighbours, men and women, of this. Their practice was likewise: when a woman's husband was absent, they would not delay in attaching to her an accusation involving one of her neighbours. They would do the same when an old man married a young woman, or half-grown girl, and she bore him a child; they would attach the child to one of the neighbours. For this reason, when the Prophet (ﷺ) said one day: "Ask me," the people present were so eager that a man would ask: "Who is my father?" and he would say: "Your father is so-and-so." The Arabs in the Jahiliyyah used to challenge the lineage of Usama ibn Zayd from his father Zayd ibn Harithah, because Usama was black in colour, while his father Zayd was white and bright. The Prophet (ﷺ) affirmed that Usama was the son of Zayd ibn Harithah. This was a false custom that was rampant in the Jahiliyyah, and Allah forbade the Muslims from its evil effect.

Among them is avoiding lying. Qatadah said: ﴿do not follow﴾ means: do not say, "I saw," when you did not see; or "I heard," when you did not hear; or "I know," when you do not know.

Among them is false testimony, and this prohibition includes it. Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah and a group [of scholars] interpreted it accordingly.

What confirms that all these meanings are intended is the rationale for the prohibition given by the sentence ﴿Indeed, the hearing, the sight, and the heart — about all of these one will be questioned.﴾ The position of this sentence is that of a justification, meaning: you, O human, will be questioned about what you attribute to your hearing, your sight, and your intellect. The prohibited following refers back to an attribution to hearing, sight, or intellect, regarding what is heard, seen, and believed.

This is a great moral discipline, and it is also a noble intellectual reform that teaches the community to distinguish between the levels of mental impressions, so that what is known, what is assumed, and what is imagined are not mixed up for them. Furthermore, it is a noble social reform that protects the community from falling into harms and ruin, and from causing them, as a result of relying on imagined proofs.

The sentence ﴿all of these one will be questioned﴾ has been formed in this arrangement by placing ﴿all﴾ first, to indicate comprehensiveness of the means of proof from the very beginning. The demonstrative was used rather than a pronoun, so that one would not say "all of them" (kulluhā), because the demonstrative carries additional distinction. The verb kāna was inserted to indicate the firmness of the predicate, as has been mentioned more than once above.

ʿAnhu (about it) is a prepositional phrase in the position of the deputy of the subject of the passive participle (maf'ūl), like His saying ﴿not of those who have incurred wrath﴾ [al-Fatihah: 7]. It was placed before the noun for emphasis and for preserving the rhyme (al-fāṣilah). The estimated structure is: kāna masʾūlan ʿanhu (he was questioned about it), as one says: kāna masʾūlan Zaydun (Zayd was questioned). There is no harm in placing a prepositional phrase that functions as the deputy of the subject before it, even though placing the deputy of the subject itself before the verb is prohibited, because the Arabs make wide use of adverbials and prepositional phrases, and because placing an explicit deputy of the subject first would make it a subject of a nominal sentence, and a prepositional phrase cannot be a subject; thus the reason for prohibiting the fronting is removed.

The meaning: the entirety of the hearing, the sight, and the heart was questioned about itself, and was obliged to make clear the source of its owner from its perception.

Su'al (questioning) is a metonymy (kināyah) for being held accountable for shortcoming and transgression of what is right, as in the saying of Ka'b:

It was said that you are attributed [to a lineage], and you are held to account.

That is: you are held accountable for what you committed of satirizing the Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims. In the verse, it is a metonymy of another degree for holding accountable the owner of hearing, sight, and heart for his lying about his senses. It is not a rational metaphor (majāz ʿaqlī), because considering it so would conflict with the emphasis of the attribution by ﴿indeed (inna)﴾ and ﴿all (kull)﴾, with the observation of the demonstrative and ﴿kāna﴾. This meaning is like His saying ﴿On the Day when their tongues, their hands, and their feet will bear witness against them for what they used to do﴾ [al-Nur: 24]. That is: the hearing will be asked: "Did you hear?" It will say: "I did not hear." Then its owner will be held accountable by having attributed to him what did not reach him, and so on.

The demonstrative in His saying ﴿ulā'ika﴾ refers to the hearing, the sight, and the heart. It is one of the uses of the demonstrative which is mostly used for rational beings for non-rational things, treating those faculties as if they were rational beings, because they are worthy of that, since they are the path of reason, and reason itself. Moreover, the use of ulā'ika for non-rational beings is a well-known usage. It has been said that this is a genuine usage, or that this metaphor became so common that it equalled the literal sense. God, exalted, says ﴿None has sent these down except the Lord of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Isra: 102]. And [the poet] said:

The abodes after the dwelling place of al-Liwa have become desolate, and life after those days [is gone].

In it there is tajrid (abstraction) in attributing ﴿questioned (masʾūlan)﴾ to those things, since the intended meaning is the questioning of their owners. This is among the rhetorical subtleties of the Qur'an.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 37:

﴿And do not walk upon the earth exultantly; indeed, you will not tear the earth apart, and you will not reach the mountains in height.﴾

He is forbidden from a trait of the traits of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam), namely the trait of arrogance (kibriya'). The people of the Jahiliyyah would deliberately practice it. This is the fifteenth of the injunctions.

The address is to an unspecified person, so that it encompasses every addressee. It is not an address to the Prophet (ﷺ), since what follows does not suit him.

Al-maraḥ (مَرَحًا), with a fatha on the mim and a fatha on the ra', means the intense self-conceit and exultation of a person in his state of abundant provision. The word ﴿maraḥan﴾ is a verbal noun (maṣdar) functioning as a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿tamshi﴾. The use of a verbal noun as a ḥāl, like its use as an adjective (ṣifah), is intended to express emphasis in the attribute, and it may be interpreted as an active participle: "do not walk as one who is exultant (māriḥan)," that is, in the manner of the exultant walker, which is the gait indicating the walker's arrogance through swaying and strutting. It is also permissible for ﴿maraḥan﴾ to be an absolute object (maf'ūl muṭlaq) clarifying the verb ﴿tamshi﴾, since walking has types, among them those that indicate that the one who walks is possessed of exultation. Thus, attributing exultation to walking is a rational metonymy (majāz 'aqlī). Walking exultantly means that there is great force in the stepping upon the earth and an elongation in the body of the walker.

The clause ﴿indeed, you will not tear the earth apart﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'nāf) arising from the prohibition, by directing a second address with this meaning in the manner of sarcasm (tahakkum), that is: you, O walker in exultation, will not tear with your walking the surface (adīm) of the earth, nor will you reach with your elongation in walking the height of the mountains. So what entices you to this gait?

Al-kharq (الخَرْق) is cutting a thing and separating its layers; so "tearing the earth" is ripping the crust of the soil. The expression is used for emphasis of rebuke, by placing the one who treads the earth with great force in the position of one who seeks to tear the face of the earth, and placing him, in his elongation in walking, in the position of one who wishes to reach the height of the mountains.

The purpose of the sarcasm is to censure this act. This indicates that what is forbidden is unlawful, because it is corruption in the character of its doer, evil in his intention, and humiliation of people by displaying arrogance toward them and terrorizing them with his strength.

It is related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab that he saw a youth swaggering in his walk, and said to him: "Swaggering (al-bakhtarah) is a gait that is disliked, except in the way of Allah," meaning: because by it one terrorizes the enemy, displaying strength against the enemies of the religion in jihad.

The mention of the noun "the earth" in ﴿tear the earth apart﴾ without a pronoun is so that this statement stands independently of other things, operating in the manner of a proverb (mathal).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 38:

﴿All that was evil in the sight of your Lord, detested.﴾

This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) for the preceding sentences, beginning from His saying, ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isra: 23], in view of what those sentences contain of warnings and prohibitions. Every sentence containing a command necessarily implies a prohibition of its opposite, and every sentence containing a prohibition necessarily implies a forbidden matter. So His saying ﴿that you worship none but Him﴾ [al-Isra: 23] implies a blameworthy worship that is forbidden, and His saying ﴿and to parents, good treatment﴾ [al-Isra: 23] implies a bad treatment that is forbidden, and so on by this analogy.

The majority of readers (al-Jumhur) read sayyi'ah with a fatha on the hamza after the letter ya' (with a dot below), and with the feminine ta' (ta' marbutah) at its end, meaning the opposite of hasanah (good).

Page 105
Thus, whatever is described as sayyi'ah and as detested can only be something forbidden, or something whose opposite is commanded, since what is commanded cannot be detested by the one who commands it. By this, the referent of the demonstrative in His saying ﴿All that﴾ becomes clear to the listener.

The meanings of prohibition in the aforementioned matters are considered because the most important thing is to refrain from the corruptions that all of them entail, whether explicitly or by implication, since the averting of corruptions (dar' al-mafasid) takes precedence over the securing of benefits (jalb al-masalih) in consideration, although the two are mutually implicating in cases like this.

His saying ﴿in the sight of your Lord﴾ is connected to ﴿detested﴾, meaning it is blameworthy in the sight of God. The placing of this adverbial phrase before what it governs serves to give importance to the phrase, since it is attached to the Divine Name (ism al-jalalah). Thus the addition of ﴿in the sight of your Lord, detested﴾ serves to condemn the situation, meaning detested in its doing by its doer, and in it there is an implicit allusion that its doer is detested in the sight of God.

Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read ﴿kana sayyi'uhu﴾ with a damma on the hamza and a pronoun ha' at its end, the pronoun referring back to ﴿All that﴾. And ﴿All that﴾ is itself the evil thing, so the annexation of (sayyi') to its pronoun is an explanatory annexation (idafah bayaniyyah), which conveys the intensity of the attribute of evil, to the point that it is as if there were two things, one of which is annexed to the other. This is the subtle point of the explanatory annexation whenever it occurs, meaning: what He forbade of all that was detested in the sight of God.

It is appropriate that ﴿detested﴾ be a second predicate of (kana), since this suits both readings.

﴿That is of what your Lord has revealed to you of wisdom﴾. He turned away from addressing the community with plural second-person pronouns, and with the pronouns of an unspecified addressee, to address the Prophet (ﷺ). This refers back to what came at the beginning of these verses, His saying ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾ [al-Isra: 23], etc. It is a concluding remark (tadhyil) interposed between the prohibitive clauses. The reference to all the commands and prohibitions mentioned is explicit in His saying ﴿And your Lord has decreed﴾ [al-Isra: 23].

[Page 106]
In this concluding remark there is an alert that what the seventeen verses contain is of wisdom, an encouragement to follow what is in them, and that it is a great good. It also contains a favour (imtinan) upon the Prophet (ﷺ), in that God revealed it to him. This is the reason for His saying ﴿of what has been revealed to you﴾, as an alert that the unlettered (al-Ummiyyun) could not reach the like of this were it not for revelation from God, and that He taught him what he did not know and commanded him to teach it to the people.

Wisdom (al-hikmah): knowing realities as they are, without error or confusion. It is also applied to the speech that indicates them. It has been mentioned earlier in His saying, may He be exalted, (﴿He gives wisdom to whom He wills﴾ [al-Baqarah: 269]).

* * *

﴿And do not set up with God another deity, lest you be thrown into Hell, blameworthy and rejected﴾.
This is coordinated (atf) upon the preceding prohibitive clauses. It is an emphasis on the content of the clause ﴿that you not worship except Him﴾ [al-Isra: 23], repeated for the purpose of giving importance to the matter of monotheism (tawhid), by repeating its content and the threat that follows from it, that one will be recompensed with eternal abiding in the Fire, humiliated.

The address is to an unspecified addressee, following the manner of the prohibitions before it, and by the indication of His saying after it ﴿Has your Lord then favoured you with sons?﴾ [al-Isra: 40], the verse.

Ilqa' (casting): throwing a body from above to below, and it indicates humiliation. Malum (blameworthy): one who is rebuked for what he has done.

Madhur (rejected): the one who is driven away, i.e., driven away from the side of God, meaning one upon whom wrath is brought down and who is distanced from His mercy in the Hereafter.

Tulqa is in the accusative as the answer to the prohibition, by the fa' of causation and consequence upon what is forbidden, i.e., the casting of you into Hell is consequent upon your making another deity with God.

[p. 107]

﴿Has your Lord then favored you with sons, and taken for Himself daughters from among the angels? Indeed, you utter a tremendous saying.﴾ This is a consequence drawn from an implied premise, whose intended sense is indicated by the consequence that follows from it. The implied meaning is: "Has Allah then preferred you and given you sons, while taking daughters for Himself?" Its connection to what precedes is that attributing daughters to Allah amounts to claiming deities that stand in a filial relation to Allah. A group of the Arabs worshipped the angels just as they worshipped idols, and they justified their worship by claiming that the angels are the daughters of Allah, as He relates of them in His saying: ﴿And they have made the angels, who are servants of the Most Merciful, into females﴾ (Surah al-Zukhruf 43:19), through to His saying: ﴿And they say: Had the Most Merciful willed, we would not have worshipped them﴾ (Surah al-Zukhruf 43:20). When they were forbidden to set up another god alongside Allah, the warning was specifically directed at the worship of the angels, lest they imagine that worshipping the angels is not like worshipping idols, because the angels are the daughters of Allah, and so they might suppose that Allah is pleased for them to worship His sons.

The invalidity of worshipping the angels has been established by invalidating its root in their belief, namely that the angels are the daughters of Allah. Once it becomes clear that this is false, they will know that making the angels gods is equivalent to making the idols gods.

Thus the sentence ﴿Has your Lord then favored you with sons﴾ up to its end is a consequence derived from the sentence ﴿And do not set up another god alongside Allah﴾ (Surah al-Isra 17:39), as a consequence of the prohibition, as we have explained. This is because the thing prohibited, by its generality, includes this particular kind, which is especially deserving of being singled out for denunciation. It is similar to a substitution of a part (badl al-ba'd). The particle fa (فـ) indicates consequence, and its proper place is at the beginning of its sentence. But it has been placed after the interrogative, because the interrogative particle has precedence at the head of the sentence in Arabic style. This is the preferred usage concerning the placement of the conjunctive particles together with the interrogative hamzah.

Some scholars treat the interrogative in such a case as an interrogation directed at both the conjoined and the conjunction (al-ma'tuf wa al-'atif). The interrogation here expresses denunciation and mockery.

[p. 108]

Al-isfa' (إصفاء) means making something pure (safw), that is, unmixed. The transitivity of asfa to the pronoun of the addressees is by way of ellipsis and conveyance (al-hadhf wa al-iyşal). Its underlying form is: "Has He chosen purely for you?" As for His saying "bil-banin" (بِالبَنِينَ, "with sons"), the bā' here may be either superfluous, to emphasize the close attachment of the verb asfa to its object, the underlying form being "Has your Lord purely chosen the sons for you," as in His saying: ﴿And wipe over your heads﴾ (Surah al-Ma'idah 5:6); or asfa is taken to imply the meaning of "preferred" (āthara), so that the bā' marks transitivity and indicates the sense of exclusivity with its governed noun. Thus asfa together with its complement becomes like two verbs: "He restricted the sons to you, to the exclusion of Himself," meaning that He made sons purely yours, not something He shares with you in their likes, while He made for Himself the females, which you dislike. The invalidity of this is evident upon the slightest reflection. Once its invalidity in this form has become clear, its non-occurrence is established, since it is unfitting for the majesty of Allah. This has already been discussed under His saying: ﴿And they attribute daughters to Allah, glory be to Him, while for themselves is what they desire﴾ (Surah al-Nahl 16:57), and His saying: ﴿They invoke besides Him only females﴾ (Surah al-Nisa 4:117).

The sentence ﴿Indeed, you utter a tremendous saying﴾ is an affirmation of the meaning of the denunciation and an explanation of it. That is, you say: "Allah has taken the angels as daughters." He emphasized the verb "you say" with its verbal noun (masdar) to reinforce the meaning of denunciation, and He described it merely as a "saying" (qawl), because it is nothing more than words uttered without deliberation. For had its speaker reflected upon it even slightly, he would have found it outside the propositions acceptable to reason.

Al-'azim (العظيم) means strong, and what is meant here is that it is great in corruption and falsehood, as indicated by the context of denunciation. No description is more effective in condemning their saying than calling it "great," because it is a saying flawed on all sides: it entails favoring Allah with the lesser of the two kinds of offspring while assigning to them the nobler kind; then what that implies, namely ascribing to Allah the attributes of bodies, such as composition, generation, and need for offspring for assistance and so that they may succeed the source after its passing. What corruption could be greater than this?

In His saying "ittakhadha" (اتَّخَذَ, "has taken"), there is an allusion to another corruption: they say ﴿Allah has taken a son﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah 2:116). Taking implies that He created the one He takes, and this contradicts begetting. How then can this fit with their saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah, [p. 109] from the noblest of the jinn? And how could He create a thing and then it be a son to Him? Such a claim, in its falsehood, is "a handful of grass laid upon a bundle of firewood" (ḍighth ʿalā ibbālah), meaning one corruption piled upon another.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 41:

﴿And We have certainly varied in this Qur'an [their admonition], that they may take heed; but it increases them only in aversion.﴾

When he mentioned the monstrosity of their saying that the angels are the daughters of Allah, he followed that with the statement that the Qur'an contains sufficient guidance, but they increase in aversion from reflecting upon it.

The clause ﴿And We have certainly varied in this Qur'an﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (mu'tarida) joined by the conjunction waw of interjection (waw al-i'tiraD).

The pronoun refers to those who worshipped the angels and claimed them to be daughters of Allah.

Tasrif (variation) originally means the repeated turning (sarf) of something from one direction to another, as in the turning of the winds (tasrif al-riyah). Here it is a metaphor (kinaya) for clarifying [matters] with varied and diverse exposition. It was discussed previously in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Look how We vary the signs, yet they turn away﴾ [al-An'am: 46], in Surat al-An'am.

The object of sarrafna is omitted, because the verb has been made to function as intransitive (manzilat al-lazim), so no object is assumed for it. That is, We made the clarification clear, so that they might take heed through its clarification. Yadhdhakkaru (that they may take heed) originally is yatadhakkaru, and the ta' was assimilated into the dhal because their articulation points are close. This was discussed at the beginning of Surat Yunus. It is from dhikr (with the dhal vowelled with a damma), which is the opposite of forgetfulness.

The pronoun in liyadhdhakkaru refers to something known from the context, indicated by His words ﴿Has your Lord then favoured you with sons?﴾ [al-Isra': 40]; that is, that those who were addressed with the rebuke in His words ﴿Has your Lord then favoured you﴾ [al-Isra': 40] may take heed. This is therefore a shift (iltifat) from address to third-person reference, or from addressing the polytheists to addressing the believers.

His words ﴿but it increases them only in aversion﴾ express wonder at their condition.

Page 110

Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read liyadhkurū with the dhal sukun and the kaf damma, lightened (mukhaffafa), as the imperfect of (dhakara), whose verbal noun is al-dhukr with the dhal damma.

The clause ﴿but it increases them only in aversion﴾ occupies the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and it is an intended circumstance whose purpose is to express wonder at the state of their misguidance, since they were increasing in aversion from a decisive and clear speech meant to remind them. The nature of detail is to bring reassurance to the intended meaning. Nufur (aversion) is the fleeing of a wild animal or a beast in alarm and fear of harm; it is used here metaphorically for their turning away, treating them as beasts and cattle.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 42:**

﴿Say: "If there were other gods with Him, as you say, they would certainly have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne."﴾ This returns to the refutation of the plurality of gods, adding to the uprooting of the beliefs of the polytheists from their very roots. The sentence is an initial resumption (isti'naf ibtida'i) following the sentence ﴿And do not set up with God another god, lest you be thrown into Hell, blamed and rejected﴾ [al-Isra': 39]. The one addressed by the command to "say" is the Prophet (ﷺ), to confound them with a convincing argument against the corruption of their statement. It is opened with "Say" (qul) because of the importance of this argument, singling it out for proclamation, although the entire Qur'an is commanded to be conveyed.

The clause ﴿as you say﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (mu'tarida) to draw attention to the fact that the plurality of gods has no reality. It is merely an empty statement that does not correspond to what is in reality.

Seeking a way (ibtigha' al-sabil) means seeking the path to reach a thing, that is, aiming at it and striving to attain it. Here it is a metaphor for aiming at the means of a thing. It has come in the hadith about Musa and al-Khidr, peace be upon them both, that Musa asked for the way to meet al-Khidr.

(Idhan) indicates the response and the consequence, so it emphasizes the meaning of the response, which is indicated by the lam attached to the answer of (law) of impossibility (law al-imtina'iyya), which denotes that its answer is not realized because its condition is not realized. It is also an intensifier in that it indicates that the answer is a consequence of the statement being answered. The aim is therefore to argue for the negation of divinity from the idols and the angels whom they made gods.

This argument may bear two meanings, whose outcome is one: 

The first meaning: the intended sense of "the way" is the way of striving for dominance and subjugation, i.e., they would have sought to contend with the Lord of the Throne, who is God Most High. This is like His saying, Most High, ﴿No god was ever with Him; otherwise every god would have taken away what he created, and some would have overcome others﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 91]. The basis of the implication on which the argument is built is that it is customary, by convention and habit, for people of power to seek to extend their dominion, and for some to strive against others by raiding, and to combine against the supreme sovereign to strip him of his kingdom or part of it. Rulers and princes have often risen against the King of Kings and stripped him of his kingdom. Thus, if there were gods with God, they would follow the custom of their like.

The complete argument is omitted for brevity, indicated by what is implied by seeking the way in this sense, namely the mutual repulsion and contention that are customary for the state of seeking a route to descend upon a town or tribe for the purpose of raiding. This leads to the disruption of the world, as its governors are occupied with fighting and defending, in the manner found in Greek mythology, with the contention of the gods and the scheming of some against others. Thus this is in the sense of His saying, Most High, ﴿If there were in them gods other than God, they would both have been corrupted﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22]. This is the argument called the argument of mutual prevention (burhan al-tamanu') in the science of the principles of religion (usul al-din). The way in this sense is therefore a metaphor for being able to attain and triumph over the desired object, and seeking in this sense is a seeking born of enmity and aversion.

His saying ﴿as you say﴾ in this sense is an alert to their error, and it is an instance of using the relative construction to alert to an error.

The second meaning: the intended sense of "the way" is the way of arriving at the Lord of the Throne, who is God Most High, arriving through submission, supplication and drawing near. That is, they would have sought what leads them to His good pleasure, like His saying, ﴿They seek the means of access to their Lord﴾ [al-Isra': 57].

The argument is that you have made them gods and said, "We only worship them so that they may be our intercessors with God." If they were gods as you describe their divinity, they would have no independence from submission to God. That is sufficient to show the corruption of your statement, for divinity requires not needing anything. So the outcome of your statement is that they are servants of God, honoured by Him, and this is sufficient for you to become aware of the corruption of the claim of their divinity.

Seeking in this sense is seeking love and desire, like His saying, ﴿Whoever wills, let him take a way to his Lord﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 19]. Close in meaning is His saying, Most High, ﴿And they say, "The Merciful has taken a son." Glory be to Him! Rather, they are honoured servants﴾ [al-Anbiya': 26]. The way in this sense is therefore a metaphor for seeking a means of reaching Him and striving for His good pleasure.

His saying ﴿as you say﴾ in this sense indicates the condition within the phrase ﴿if there were with Him gods﴾, meaning: if there were with Him gods in the state in which you say they are, that is, as you describe their divinity in your saying, ﴿These are our intercessors with God﴾ [Yunus: 18].

The invocation of the Exalted Essence by the description ﴿Lord of the Throne﴾, rather than by His proper name, is because of the lofty dignity contained in the attribution to the Throne, which is the object of the envy of the gods toward Him, and their desire to snatch away His dominion according to the first meaning, or which is the object of the gods' desire to seek from the abundance of what is with Him according to the second meaning.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read ﴿as you say﴾ with the second-person ta' (taa' al-khitab), following the usual practice in quoting a statement that the speaker has been commanded to convey: it is quoted as the one conveying it says it at the time of conveying. Ibn Kathir and Hafs read it with the third-person ya' (ya' al-ghayba), following the other manner in quoting a statement that is commanded to be conveyed to another, which may be quoted in meaning. This is because, while the one commanding addresses the one commanded to convey, the one to whom it is conveyed is absent, and only becomes addressed at the time of conveying. So when his state is considered in this way, he is referred to in the third person, as was recited in His saying, Most High, ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: "You will be overcome"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 12] with ta' and with ya'. Or, according to His saying ﴿as they say﴾, it is a parenthetical insertion between the condition of (law) and its answer.

[Page 113]

﴿Exalted is He, far above what they say, with a great exaltation.﴾ This is a declarative statement (inshā’) of God's transcendence (tanzīh) above what they claimed concerning the existence of partners with Him in divinity.

This is an interjection (i‘tirāḍ) within the speech being related, between its parts, and it is resumed (mustaʼnaf) because it is a consequence of the invalidity of their statement that there are other gods with God. This is established by the proof brought against them in His saying: ﴿Otherwise they would have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne.﴾ [al-Isrā’: 42]. The discussion of its counterpart has already been given in His saying: ﴿Glory be to Him, above what they describe.﴾ [al-An‘ām: 100], in Surat al-An‘ām.

What is meant by "what they say" is what they say of the kind mentioned just before, like His saying: ﴿And We shall inherit from him what he says.﴾ [Maryam: 80].

‘Uluwwan (exaltation) is an absolute object (maf‘ūl muṭlaq) whose verb is the divine "exalted," and it has been brought in a form other than the regular pattern of its verb, to indicate that exaltation here is the actual attribution of loftiness in truth, not merely a claim. This is like the words of Sa‘da, mother of al-Kumayt ibn Ma‘arr:

*You rose high above the truth regarding the family of Fa‘s,*
*and you did not fear among them a reversal today or tomorrow.*

Also His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿This is none but a man like you who wants to make himself superior to you.﴾ [al-Mu’minūn: 24], meaning: he claims superiority, though he has no superiority. It is in the accusative as an absolute object specifying the type.

What is meant by "great" (kabīr) is the complete in its kind. The original sense of kabīr is an attributive adjective (ṣifah mushabbahah): one characterized by greatness. Greatness (kibar) is the massiveness of a thing's body within the reach of people. The meaning is: He is exalted with the most complete exaltation, unmixed with anything of the kind they attributed to Him. The incompatibility between the necessity of His essence and the attribution to Him of a partner, a consort, or a child has reached such clarity that it needs no further elaboration, for necessary existence and permanence negate the signs of need and weakness.

Al-Jumhūr read ﴿ʻammā yaqūlūn﴾ with the third-person yāʼ (of absence). Ḥamzah, al-Kisā’ī and Khalaf read it with the second-person tāʼ (of address), on the basis that it is a shift of person (iltifāt). Or, on this reading, it is part of the speech being related, from His saying: ﴿Say: Had there been with Him gods, as they say...﴾ [al-Isrā’: 42].

[Page 114]

﴿Glorifies Him the seven heavens and the earth and whoever is in them. And there is nothing but that it glorifies Him with His praise, but you do not understand their glorification. Indeed, He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving.﴾

The clause ﴿yusabbihu lahu﴾ (glorifies Him) etc. is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring back to the pronoun in ﴿subḥānahu﴾ (Glory be to Him) [17:43]. The meaning is: "We glorify Him while the worlds and what is in them glorify Him, that is, ﴿glorify Him﴾ and exalt Him above deficiencies."

The lām in His words ﴿lahu﴾ is either the lām of transitivity (lām al-ta'diya) attached to ﴿yusabbihu﴾, which is construed with a meaning of bearing witness to His transcendence, or it is the lām called lām al-tabyīn (the lām of specification), like the one in His words ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [94:1] and in the saying "I praised God for you."

Since glorification is attributed to many things that do not speak, this shows that it is used to signify transcendence by way of indication through the state (dalālat al-ḥāl). This is the meaning of His words ﴿but you do not understand their glorification﴾, in that they turned away from reflecting on them, and so they were not guided to the indication of His transcendence above everything they attributed to Him of states that are incompatible with divinity, an indication that surrounds them.

The address in ﴿lā tafqahūn﴾ (you do not understand) may be directed to the polytheists, following the style of the preceding address in His words ﴿Indeed you say a monstrous saying﴾ [17:40] and His words ﴿If there were gods with Him, as you say﴾ [17:42]. This is because those who failed to understand the indication of existing things to God Most High's transcendence are those who did not affirm for Him transcendence above the deficiencies which existing things bear witness to, wherever one turns to look at them, by declaring Him free of them. Thus none was deprived of being guided to their testimony except those who did not desist from believing their opposites. As for the Muslims, they were guided to that glorification through what the Qur'an directed them to of reflecting on existing things, although the degrees of guidance vary according to the variation of minds and understandings.

It may also be that the address is to all people, in consideration of the absence of complete knowledge of that glorification.

[Page 115]

Imam Fakhr al-Din (al-Razi) has illustrated this, saying: "If you take a single apple, that apple is composed of a large number of indivisible parts (ajzā' lā tatajazza'), that is, single substances (jawāhir fardah). Each one of those indivisible parts is a complete, independent proof for the existence of God. Each of those indivisible parts has particular attributes of nature, taste, color, smell, spatial location (ḥayyiz) and direction (jihah). The specification of that single substance with that particular attribute is among the possibilities, so that specification is not produced except by the specifying action of a Powerful, Wise Specifier. Thus each one of the parts of that apple is a complete proof for the existence of God Most High. Then the number of those parts is unknown, and the states of those attributes are unknown. For this reason God Most High said: ﴿but you do not understand their glorification﴾."

Perhaps the choice of the verb ﴿lā tafqahūn﴾ (you do not understand), rather than saying "lā ta'lamūn" (you do not know), is to indicate that what is negated is a subtle knowledge, which supports what Fakhr al-Din has pointed out.

The majority of reciters (al-Jumhūr) read ﴿yusabbiḥu﴾ with the masculine third-person ya' (yā' al-ghā'ib), while 'Amr, Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī, Ḥafṣ from 'Āṣim, Ya'qūb and Khalaf read it with the feminine plural ta' (tā' jamā'at mu'annath). Both forms are permissible for plurals of non-rational beings and of nouns that are not truly feminine.

The clause ﴿Indeed He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving﴾ is a resumptive sentence (istī'nāf) which implies an allusion (ta'rīḍ) that their saying requires the hastening of punishment for them in this world, were it not that God treats them with forbearance and respite. In this there is an allusion urging them to desist from their saying, so that God may forgive them.

The addition of (kāna) "was/is" serves to indicate that forbearance and forgiveness are two attributes of His that are firmly established.

[Page 116]

This is a conjunction of one sentence to another and of one narrative to another. When he (Allah) praised the Qur'an in His words, ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ [al-Isra' 9], and then followed this with what the context required, namely a reference to what the Qur'an brought of the foundations of belief (al-'aqida), comprehensive acts of worship, and the admonitions and lessons interspersed among them, He returned here to warn that the polytheists do not benefit from the guidance of the Qur'an. This is in connection with the report that they do not comprehend the evidence of the created beings for God's transcendence above deficiencies (al-naqa'id). It is also a warning to the polytheists about the obligation to abandon their stubbornness and obstinacy, and a reassurance to the Prophet ﷺ against their scheming against him and their intention to harm him. His recitation of the Qur'an used to enrage them and stir in their souls the desire for revenge.

The literal meaning of ḥijab (barrier) is the screen that blocks the sight from seeing what is behind it. Here it is used metaphorically for the diversion by which God turns the enemies of the Prophet ﷺ away from harming him, and for the aversion by which they turn away from listening to the Qur'an and understanding it. God made the aforementioned barrier to be the creation of that diverting force within their souls, such that they intend but do not act, through a weakness of will and resolve, such that a thought passes through their minds but they do not resolve upon it, and the meanings of the Qur'an pass through their ears but they do not understand. This is a disposition that spreads into souls gradually. At first, the desire to turn away and the aversion to what is heard plant it in the souls, and then it soon becomes a possession of the soul that it cannot cast off or change.

Applying the term ḥijab to what is suitable for both meanings is either according to the literal sense of the word, or by way of inferring from what has a parallel in the Qur'an. It has come in another verse: ﴿And between us and you is a barrier﴾ [Fussilat 5].

Since their denial of the Resurrection was the root on which they judged the Prophet's ﷺ call to be implausible, to the extent that they claimed he was saying something impossible when he reported the re-creation of creation after death, (God said:) ﴿And those who disbelieve say, "Shall we direct you to a man who will inform you that when you have been completely torn apart, you will indeed be in a new creation?"﴾ [Saba' 7] ﴿"Has he invented a lie against Allah, or is there madness in him?"﴾ [Saba' 8]

In this statement, by means of the relative construction, they brought to mind the reason for placing that barrier between him and them. Therefore He said: ﴿and between those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾.

The description of the barrier as "veiled" (mastur) is an intensification of the reality of its kind, meaning a barrier extremely effective in blocking what it blocks, such that it is as though it were concealed by another screen. This amounts to saying: "We placed a barrier upon a barrier." A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿and they say, "A forbidding forbidden"﴾ [al-Furqan 22].

Alternatively, it is intended that it is a barrier of a kind other than the familiar kinds of barriers, so it is a barrier which the eyes do not see, but they perceive its effects like those of similar things. It is well established in many reports that a group intended to harm the Prophet ﷺ, and every one of them had something happen to him that came between him and his intention, and God sufficed His Prophet against their evil. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿So Allah will suffice you against them﴾ [al-Baqara 137]. These incidents are well known in the reports of the Prophetic biography (al-sira).

In the combination of ﴿ḥijaban﴾ (a barrier) and ﴿mastura﴾ (veiled) there is an instance of the rhetorical device of antithesis (tibaq), which is among the embellishments of badi' (rhetorical ornament).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 46:

﴿And We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it, and in their ears deafness.﴾ This is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) of "ja'ala" upon "ja'ala."

The explicit repetition of the verb of placing (al-ja'l) indicates that this is another placing. Thus it is preferred that the placing of the concealed veil is the placing of diversion (al-ṣarfa) from harm, and that this is the placing of the non-reflection upon the Qur'an as a natural disposition (khilqa) within their souls. The discussion regarding the composition (naẓm) of this verse and its meanings has preceded in its parallel in Surat al-An'am.

* * *

Page 118
﴿And when you mention your Lord alone in the Qur'an, they turn away on their backs in aversion.﴾
Since the preceding report about them implies that they do not comprehend the meanings of the Qur'an, it is followed by the statement that they turn away from understanding what would be good for them. When they hear what nullifies the divinity of their idols, they understand that, and so they turn away on their backs in aversion. That is, that understanding increased them in misguidance, just as the lack of understanding deprived them of guidance. Their state is contradictory: they do not listen to what ought to be listened to, and they listen to what they desire to hear, so that they may increase in disbelief through it.

The meaning of ﴿you mention your Lord alone﴾ apparently is that you mentioned Him restricting yourself to His mention, and did not mention their deities, because "alone" (waḥdahu) is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of "your Lord," who is the object of "you mentioned." The meaning of the ḥāl is the indication that the attribute exists in external reality and actuality; that is, your mention of Him was such that He was described as alone in the existence of the mention. Thus the turning away of the polytheists on their backs at that time is due to anger at the silence about their deities and the disregard for them, based on their knowing that He did not remain silent about mentioning their deities except because He did not acknowledge them. Were it not for this assumption, there would be no cause for their turning away on their backs, because mentioning one thing does not indicate the denial of another. They may mention al-ʿUzzā or al-Lāt, for example, and not mention other idols, so it is not assumed that one who mentions al-ʿUzzā denies Manāt. In this sense is the words of the Exalted: ﴿And when God alone is mentioned, the hearts of those who do not believe in the Hereafter shrink.﴾ [al-Zumar: 45].

It is also possible that the meaning is: when you mention your Lord by His oneness in divinity, and this suits their aversion and turning away, because they only deny God Most High's sole claim to divinity; so the indication of "alone" in this sense is by the help of the context and the verb "you mentioned."

Perhaps the circumstantial phrase following the objects of verbs of speech, mention and the like may admit that its existence is in external reality, or that it is in speech and tongue. Then the meaning of ﴿you mentioned your Lord alone﴾ is that He is singular in your mention and your speech; that is, you mentioned Him described as one.

Page 119
The restriction of the mention to being in the Qur'an is due to its suitability to the discussion of the states of the polytheists in listening to the Qur'an; or because the Qur'an is intended for instruction and calling to the religion, so that the absence of mention of their deities in its verses, together with the mention of God's name, is understood as an allusion that they are not gods. Hence they become angry whenever the mention of God occurs and their deities are not mentioned. Thus its being in the Qur'an is the indication that He intended the denial of their deities.
His saying "alone" has already been discussed at His saying ﴿They said: Have you come to us that we should worship God alone?﴾ [al-A'raf: 70] in Surat al-A'raf.

The tawliya is returning from whence one came, and ﴿on their backs﴾ has been discussed at His saying ﴿and do not turn back on your heels﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 21] in Surat al-'Uqud.

And ﴿nufūran﴾ may be the plural of (nāfir), like sujūd and shuhūd, and the pattern fu'ūl is regular for the plural of fā'il, so the active participle would be in the form of a verbal noun; then nufūran in this case is an accusative circumstantial qualifier from the pronoun in "wallaw." It may also be taken as a verbal noun in the accusative of cause, meaning: they turned away because of their aversion from the Qur'an.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 47:

﴿We know best why they listen when they listen to you, and when they confer privately, when the wrongdoers say, "You follow only a man bewitched."﴾

The polytheists used to surround the Prophet ﷺ in the Sacred Mosque when he recited the Qur'an, listening to what he said in order to seize upon whatever in the Qur'an they denied, such as the Oneness of God and the affirmation of resurrection after death. Then some of them would marvel at it to one another. So the report about them that "veils have been placed over their hearts, lest they understand it, and in their ears is deafness, and that they turn their backs in aversion when God alone is mentioned" (cf. Q. 17:46), and that it arouses in the listener's mind a question about the reason for their gathering to hear the Prophet ﷺ recite, was the answer to that question. Thus the sentence is a resumptive sentence of explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani).

The opening of the sentence with the pronoun of majesty (Allah) is to show concern for its content and its meaning: God knows with true knowledge the motive behind their listening, even if opinions about it multiply, no one knows that cause.

"A'lam" is an elative form (ism al-tafdil) used in the sense of the strength of knowledge and its detail. It is not intended that God is more knowing than others, since the context does not require this.

The "ba'" in His saying ﴿bima yastami'un﴾ serves to transmit the elative to its object, because it is intransitive and cannot take a direct object. The elative derived from knowledge and ignorance is followed by "bi" (with), while in other cases it is followed by "li" (for). One says: "He is more generous to the dirhams" (a'ta li-l-dara-him).

The "ba'" in ﴿yastami'una bihi﴾ denotes association (mulabasah), and the pronoun governed by "bi" refers back to the relative "ma" (that which). That is: We know best the thing that associates with them when they listen to you. It is an adverbial phrase of fixed location (zarf mustaqirr) in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and the implied meaning is: "associated with it."
