The ambiguity of "ma" is resolved by His saying ﴿when they listen to you and when they confer privately﴾, and so on, to the end of the verse.

"Idh" is an adverb governed by ﴿yastami'una bihi﴾.

"Najwa" is a verbal noun of "munajah," which is conversing in secret, and it has already been discussed in His saying ﴿There is no good in much of their secret talk﴾ (Q. 4:114) in Surah al-Nisa'.

He described them with the verbal noun to emphasize the abundance of their private conferring during the hearing of the Qur'an, occupying themselves away from it.

﴿And when they confer privately﴾ is conjoined to ﴿when they listen to you﴾; that is: We know best what they listen to, and We know best their private conferring.

﴿When the wrongdoers say﴾ is a substitute (badal) for ﴿when they confer privately﴾, a substitution of part for whole (badal ba'd min kull), because their private conferring is not restricted to this saying; the saying was singled out for mention because it is more strange than the rest of their slanders, due to the clear gap between the state of the Prophet ﷺ and the state of one who is bewitched.

An explicit noun was used in place of the pronoun in ﴿when the wrongdoers say﴾ instead of "when they say," to indicate that the motive for their saying was wrongdoing, that is, polytheism, for polytheism is wrongdoing. That is: had it not been for their polytheism, no sensible person would have likened the perfect state of the Prophet ﷺ to the state of one who is bewitched. It is also permissible that "wrongdoing" here means aggression, that is, aggression against the Prophet ﷺ by lying.

The Prophet's phrase "ﷺ" should be rendered as (ﷺ).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 48:

﴿Look at how they coin comparisons for you, so they have gone astray and cannot find a way.﴾ This is an independent resumptive clause (jumlah musta'nafah), begun afresh (istinaf ibtida'i), and its counterparts are numerous in the Qur'an.

The use of the verb "to look" (al-nazar) signals that the matter has reached such clarity that it is something visible to be seen.

The interrogative with (kayfa) ("how") expresses wonder at the state of their likening the Prophet (ﷺ) to one who is bewitched, and the like.

The root meaning of (daraba) is to place a thing and fix it, as in "he pitched a tent" (daraba khaymah). It is also applied to shaping a thing into a specific form, as in "he struck dinars" (daraba dana'ir). Here it is used metaphorically for displaying and clarifying, likening the displayed and clarified thing to the fixed thing. This was discussed earlier at His words, ﴿Indeed, God is not ashamed to present an example (an yadriba mathalan)﴾ (al-Baqarah: 26) in Surah al-Baqarah.

The lam in (laka) ("for you") is for causation and purpose, meaning they coined the comparisons on your account, that is, for the sake of your being likened, so they likened you. One says "I struck for you an example with such-and-such" (darabtu laka mathalan bi-kadha), and its underlying sense is "I likened you with such-and-such," meaning "I find such-and-such as an example for you." God, the Exalted, says: ﴿So do not strike for God comparisons (fa la tadribu lillahi al-amthal)﴾ (al-Nahl: 74), and says: ﴿And present to them an example: the people of the town (wa-idrib lahum mathalan ashab al-qaryah)﴾ (Ya Sin: 13), meaning make them an example of their condition.

Here he used the plural (al-amthal), although what is reported of them is that they likened him to one who is bewitched, which is a single comparison. This is because the intent is to express wonder at this comparison and at others like it in what they say: "He is a poet," "He is a soothsayer," "He is a madman," "He is a sorcerer," "He is one who is bewitched." These are called comparisons (amthal) in view of their state, because they were perplexed about what they should describe him as to the people, lest the people believe him to be a prophet. So they went searching in their imagination for the condition most similar to his and attached him to it, like one who places a strange individual within the most similar of kinds, as when someone says of the giraffe that it is one of the horses, or the camels, or the cattle.

Their going astray is made a consequence of their coining of comparisons, because everything they coined as comparisons is utterly false, error, and a strengthening of disbelief. The intended meaning is that their particular going astray is made a consequence of the falsehood of those comparisons, that is, their going astray became manifest in that, as in His words: ﴿The people of Noah denied before them, so they denied Our servant﴾ (al-Qamar: 9).

It is also permissible that "going astray" here be understood in its original sense, namely bewilderment on the road and failure to find guidance. The meaning would then be: they coined many likenesses for you because they were bewildered about what excuse to offer regarding your great affair.

The consequence stated in ﴿so they cannot find a way (fa la yastati'una sabilan)﴾ is a consequence of "they have gone astray" (fa-dallu), indicating that their deep bewilderment follows from their going astray in coining those comparisons.

Al-sabil means the road, and the ability to reach it is the ability to attain it. So "the way" may be understood as the way of guidance, on the first interpretation of "going astray." It may also be a figure for the state of their going astray, likened to the state of one who stands in a wide desert without knowing from which direction to proceed to his destination, on the second interpretation of "going astray."

The meaning on this reading is: they were bewildered as to how to describe your condition to the people, since they expected that the people would deny them. Therefore they kept shifting in describing him from one attribute to another, because they sensed that what they described him with was false and did not correspond to reality.

[Page 122]

[Page 123]

﴿They say, "When we have become bones and crumbling dust, shall we indeed be raised up in a new creation?"﴾ It may be that it is a separate sentence, or that "they say" (wa qalu) is conjoined (ma'tufa) to the sentence ﴿Say: "If there were with Him other gods, as you claim"﴾ [al-Isra': 42], by virtue of what that sentence contains in His words ﴿as you claim﴾ [al-Isra': 42]. The purpose is to eradicate another of their errors with a crushing proof, after having eradicated the one before it with a conclusive proof in His words ﴿Say: "If there were with Him other gods, as you claim"﴾ [al-Isra': 42] and what lies between them, which occupies the position of a parenthetical interjection (i'tiraḍ).

It may also be that it is conjoined to the sentence ﴿when the wrongdoers say, "You follow only a man bewitched"﴾ [al-Isra': 47], whose content is enclosed within the secret conferring (al-najwa). In that case this saying is among what they secretly exchanged among themselves, and then they openly proclaimed it and counted it as their argument for denial.

The interrogative is one of denial (istifham inkari, an interrogative expressing rejection).

The fronting of the adverbial phrase in His words (﴿when we have become bones﴾) serves to draw attention to it, because its content is the proof of impossibility in their view. The denial thus governs the sentence ﴿shall we indeed be raised up﴾, and the strength of their denial of this is restricted to the state of being bones and crumbling dust. The original structure of the sentence is: "Shall we indeed be raised up when we have become bones and crumbling dust?"

The adverbial phrase is not intended to restrict the meaning, because the state of being bones and crumbling dust applies to everyone who dies and is then raised.

Al-ba'th (resurrection, literally "sending forth") is the basic sense of sending, and here it is applied to the revival of the dead, because the dead person resembles one who remains in place without leaving his station.

Al-'izam (bones) is the plural of 'azm (bone), which is that from which the body of humans and animals is built. The meaning of ﴿we have become bones﴾ is that they are bones with no flesh upon them.

[Page 124]

Al-rufat (crumbling dust) refers to things that have been reduced to pieces, i.e., pulverized. It is said: rafata al-shay' when he broke the thing into fine fragments. The pattern fu'al indicates the object of verbs of fragmentation, like al-duqaq (fine powder), al-huṭam (debris), al-judhadh (chips), and al-futat (crumbs).

﴿a new creation﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥal, a state-description) of the pronoun in mab'uthuna (we shall be raised). The state is mentioned to depict the impossibility of resurrection after annihilation, because al-ba'th is revival, so the revival of bones and crumbling dust is impossible in their view. Their being a new creation is more emphatically impossible.

Al-khalq (creation) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used in the sense of the object (maf'ul), and because it is a verbal noun it did not agree with the number of the noun it describes.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verses 50–52 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Say: "Be you stones or iron,﴾ ﴿or a creation of what is greater in your breasts."﴾ ﴿Then they will say, "Who will restore us?" Say, "The One who originated you the first time." Then they will shake their heads toward you and say, "When will that be?" Say, "It may be that it is near."﴾ ﴿On the Day He calls you, you will respond with His praise, and you will think that you remained but a little.﴾

This is a reply to their saying ﴿"When we are bones and crumbled dust, shall we really be resurrected as a new creation?"﴾ [al-Isra' 49]. Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to answer them with this.

The evidence for this is the parallel between the verb "kunna" (we were) in their statement and the phrase "kūnū" (be you) in the reply, and the parallel between ﴿bones and crumbled dust﴾ [al-Isra' 49] in their statement and ﴿stones or iron﴾ in the reply. This is a parallel of frail bodies with hard bodies. The meaning of the reply is that the frailty of a body is equal to its hardness with respect to the power of Allah the Exalted to shape it however He wills.

[Page 125]

For this reason the sentence ﴿Say, "Be you stones"﴾ and what follows is not conjoined (with a coordinating particle), following the manner of dialogue that I explained at His words ﴿They said, "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ [al-Baqarah 30] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Although the words "Say" do not mark the beginning of a dialogue, and the dialogue is conducted through the statement that follows it, the command to answer has been given the ruling of an answer, and so the phrase "Say" is detached.

Know that the connection between the reply to their statement and the words ﴿Be you stones﴾ and what follows is obscure, because they were only asserting, or deeming impossible, the return of life to bodies whose parts had scattered and whose framework had been broken. They did not justify the impossibility by saying that these were weak bodies, so the reply would not be that if they were among the strongest bodies, life would have been restored to them.

So we must explain the connection between the reply to their statement and their rejected statement. In this there are three aspects:

First: The imperative form in His words "Be you" is used to express equality, and it is evidence of an omitted answer whose estimated meaning is: "You will surely be resurrected, whether you are bones and crumbled dust, or stones or iron." This is a reminder that the power of Allah the Exalted is not resisted by anything, and this is an embedding (idmaj) that makes the sentence function as a concluding statement (tadhyil).

The second aspect: The imperative form in His words "Be you" is used in the sense of a supposition: that is, if it were supposed that the bodies were of hard substances, and it were said to you, "You will be resurrected after death," you would deem it impossible and would consider the return of life to them improbable. In both aspects, His words ﴿or a creation of what is greater in your breasts﴾ are the end of the speech. His words ﴿Then they will say, "Who will restore us?"﴾ are a consequence of the statement ﴿They said, "When we are bones...?"﴾ and what follows, as a consequence of a new resumption. The "fa" (then) here is for resumption, and it has the meaning of "wa" (and), according to a difference of opinion about its use for resumption. The speech is a transition to relating another of their denials.

[Page 126]

The third aspect: His words ﴿Say, "Be you stones"﴾ are a new speech that is not a reply to their statement ﴿"When we are bones and crumbled dust"﴾ [al-Isra' 49] and what follows, and the imperative form is used in the sense of equality. In this aspect, His words ﴿Then they will say, "Who will restore us?"﴾ are connected to His words ﴿Be you stones or iron﴾ and what follows, and are a consequence of an omitted statement indicated by His words ﴿Be you stones﴾. That is: "If they were like that, they would say, 'Who will restore us?'" That is, they would have moved, through the stages of sophistry, from deeming the restoration impossible to claiming that there is no one capable of restoring life to them, because their bodies are hard. By these aspects the composition of the verse is coherent, and its obscurity is uncovered.

The word "al-hadid" (iron): it is a metallic earth, meaning it is found only in the caverns of the earth. It is a thick earth of varying thickness, heavy, dark in color. It is either compact in its parts or flaky, that is, like leaves.

Its varieties are eighteen, according to the differences in the composition of its parts. Their colors differ. The noblest of its varieties is the pure one, which is free of foreign matter in all its parts, and this is rarely found. Its most famous color is red. It is divided, according to its hardness, into two original types called the male and the female. The hard one is the male, and the soft one is the female. The Arabs used to describe a hard, cutting sword as "male." When iron is melted by fire, its parts mix together, it softens and becomes like a sweet confection. Some of it is cast iron, some is wrought iron, and some is steel. Each type is suitable for what its casting is suited to, according to the varying need for great hardness, such as swords and coats of mail. Among the properties of iron is that rust settles on it. It is like green filth, and then it gradually turns into an oxide (a chemical term indicating that oxygen particles attach to a body and corrupt it). If iron is not cared for with polishing and oil, rust begins to eat into its surface. This metal is found in most lands, and it is most abundant in Abyssinia and in the desert of Egypt. Deposits of iron have been found in Tunisian lands.

[Page 127]

The use of iron dates back to ancient eras, for the second phase of the stages of history is known as the Iron Age, meaning the period in which humans used tools made of iron. This is a result of the art of ironworking, and it was before the age of recording history. The age before it is known as the Stone Age.

Traditions concerning the time when the making of iron began are connected to unreliable legends, and its history cannot be fixed by them. What is certain is that iron was in use among humans before the beginning of writing history. Because it is eaten by rust when exposed to air and moisture, only a little of its ancient tools has remained. In Thebes and in the burial grounds of the Pharaohs at Memphis in Egypt, images have been found on the monuments depicting the storerooms of sharpeners of their knives, painted in the pictures with blue, the color of steel. This was in the twenty-first century before the Christian era. The Torah and the hadith mention the story of the sacrifice, and the story of Abraham's circumcision with an adze. It is not mentioned that the knife or the adze was made of flint, so it is most apparent that it was made of iron. Chains for binding and maces for striking are made of iron, and His words the Exalted ﴿And for them are maces of iron﴾ [al-Hajj 21] will come in Surat al-Hajj.

"Al-khalq" (creation): in the sense of "al-makhluq" (the created thing). That is: "or another creation which is great in your souls, from accepting life, and which you deem impossible for Allah to revive, such as steel or copper."

His words ﴿of what is greater in your breasts﴾ are an attribute of "khalq" (creation). The meaning of "yakburu" (is great) is that it becomes large, and this greatness is figurative, meaning strong in its kind and its attributes. "Al-suduur" (breasts) means the intellects. That is: of what you regard as great and unchanging.

In the speech there is an omission indicated by the rejected statement, which is their saying ﴿"When we are bones and crumbled dust, shall we really be resurrected?"﴾ [al-Isra' 49]. The estimate is: "Be you things further from accepting life than bones and crumbled dust."

[Page 128]

The meaning is: "Even if you were stones or iron, Allah would revive you." This is because they made their being bones a proof of the impossibility of restoration, so He replied that restoration is within the power of Allah the Exalted, and even if you were stones or iron, because stones and iron are further from accepting life than bones and crumbled dust, since life has never previously dwelt in them at all, unlike crumbled dust and bones.

The consequence in His words ﴿then they will say, "Who will restore us?"﴾ follows His words ﴿Say, "Be you stones"﴾. That is: "Say to them this, and they will say to you, 'Who will restore us?'"

Their question here was made about the one who restores, not about the act of restoration itself, because searching for the restorer is more inclusive of impossibility than searching for the act of restoration. It is like answering with a dialectical concession after answering with a denial, for they first denied the possibility of reviving the dead, and then moved to a dialectical concession, because a dialectical concession is stronger in opposing a claim than a denial.

The interrogative in "Who will restore us?" is mocking. Since their statement was certain to occur in the future, the Prophet was commanded to revive them when they say it, by answering with a specification of who will restore them, nullifying the implication of the mockery, which is their deeming it impossible, with His words ﴿Say, "The One who originated you the first time."﴾ This is applying the apparent form of their interrogation to its original meaning by taking it contrary to their intention, because that is more fitting to the wise mode of discourse for increasing the argument, like His words concerning Moses' argument against Pharaoh: ﴿He said to those around him, "Do you not listen?" He said, "Your Lord and the Lord of your forefathers, the first ones."﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 25].

The subject is expressed as a relative pronoun (al-ladhi) to indicate what is in the relative clause of an allusion to the reason for the judgment: that the One who originated you the first time is capable of restoring your creation. Like His words the Exalted ﴿And He is the One who begins creation, then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum 27], for by His power with which He began creating you the first time, He is capable of creating you a second time.

"Al-infaad" (shaking): the movement from top to bottom and the reverse. So "infaad al-ra's" is moving the head in that way, and it is the movement of mockery.

[Page 129]

They asked about its time with their words ﴿"When will that be?"﴾, as an interrogative of mockery also, so He commanded the Messenger to answer them with a true answer, to nullify the implication of mockery, as was previously mentioned in its like.

The pronoun in ﴿"When will that be?"﴾ refers to the restoration implied by His words "who will restore us". Like His words ﴿Be just, that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Ma'idah 8]. And "'asa" (it may be) is for hope on the tongue of the Messenger (ﷺ). The meaning is: "It is not far that it may be near."

﴿"On the Day He calls you"﴾ is a substitute for the hidden pronoun in "yakun" (it may be) in His words ﴿"that it may be near"﴾. Its vowel is the vowel of indeclinability, because it is attached to a verbal clause. It is also permissible that it be an adverb of "yakun", that is: "it may be on the Day He calls you", and its vowel is the vowel of the accusative of place.

"Al-du'a" (calling) may be taken in its literal sense: that is, Allah calling people through the angels who drive people to the place of gathering.

It may also be taken as a creative command to revive them, and calling is applied to it because calling entails the reviving of the one called and his presence. So it is a metaphor for reviving and compelling them to be present for the reckoning.

"Al-istijaba" (responding) is a metaphor for the compliance with the meaning of "yad'ukum" (calls you). That is: "you will come to life and stand before the reckoning," that is, He calls you while you are bones and crumbled dust. Bones and crumbled dust have no perception or hearing, and there is no response, because response is a consequence of hearing. Rather, it is a depiction of the swiftness of revival and summoning, and the swiftness of rising and presence for the reckoning, in such a way that it occurs like the occurrence of hearing a call and responding to it, in that there is no effort in bringing it about and no delay or slowness in its timing.

[Page 130]

On this view, the pronouns of address are an address to the disbelievers who said ﴿"Who will restore us?"﴾ and who said ﴿"When will that be?"﴾.

The "ba'" in "bi-hamdihi" (with His praise) denotes accompaniment, so it has the meaning of a state, that is: "praising." So when they are raised, the perception of realities is created in them, and they know that the truth belongs to Allah.

It is also permissible that "bi-hamdihi" be connected to an omitted word, on the basis that it is part of the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ). The estimate is: "Speak with His praise," as one says "bi-ismi Allah" (in the name of Allah), meaning "I begin," and as one says to the groom, "with blessing and prosperity," meaning "praise Allah for the manifestation of the truth of what I have informed you." This would be a parenthetical statement between the coordinated phrases.

It has also been said that His words ﴿"On the Day He calls you"﴾ begin a speech addressed to the believers, so "on the Day He calls you" is connected to an omitted verb, meaning: "Remember the Day He calls you." The praise on this view is taken literally, meaning: "you will respond praising Allah for what He has bestowed upon you of faith, and for what He has prepared for you, which you witness at the time of your resurrection, of signs of honor and favor."

The clause ﴿And you will think that you stayed only a little﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf, grammatical conjunction) with "they will respond" (tastajībūn). The meaning is: "and you will suppose that you remained on earth only a little." The purpose is to express wonder at this state. For this reason, another passage mentions the Lord (al-Mawla) asking them, when they are raised, how long they stayed, in wonder at their condition. He, may He be exalted, says: ﴿He will say: "How many years did you remain on earth?" They will say: "We remained a day or part of a day, so ask those who count." He will say: "You remained only a little, if only you knew."﴾ [al-Muʾminun: 112]. And He says: ﴿So God caused him to die for a hundred years, then raised him. He said: "How long did you remain?" He said: "I remained a day or part of a day." He said: "Rather, you remained a hundred years."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 259]. This wonder is a rebuke to the polytheists and a confirmation for the believers. What is intended here is that they held a mistaken assumption, and that is the object of wonder. This is a reply to their saying ﴿"When we are bones and crumbled dust, shall we really be resurrected as a new creation?"﴾ [al-Isra' 49]. Allah commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to answer them with this.

The evidence for this is the parallel between the verb "kunna" (we were) in their statement and the phrase "kūnū" (be you) in the reply, and the parallel between ﴿bones and crumbled dust﴾ [al-Isra' 49] in their statement and ﴿stones or iron﴾ in the reply. [Page 125]

For this reason the sentence ﴿Say, "Be you stones"﴾ and what follows is not conjoined (with a coordinating particle), following the manner of dialogue that I explained at His words ﴿They said, "Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ [al-Baqarah 30] in Surat al-Baqarah.

Although the words "Say" do not mark the beginning of a dialogue, and the dialogue is conducted through the statement that follows it, the command to answer has been given the ruling of an answer, and so the phrase "Say" is detached.

So we must explain the connection between the reply to their statement and their rejected statement. In this there are three aspects:

First: The imperative form in His words "Be you" is used to express equality, and it is evidence of an omitted answer whose estimated meaning is: "You will surely be resurrected, whether you are bones and crumbled dust, or stones or iron." This is a reminder that the power of Allah the Exalted is not resisted by anything, and this is an embedding (idmaj) that makes the sentence function as a concluding statement (tadhyil).

The second aspect: The imperative form in His words "Be you" is used in the sense of a supposition: that is, if it were supposed that the bodies were of hard substances, and it were said to you, "You will be resurrected after death," you would deem it impossible and would consider the return of life to them improbable. In both aspects, His words ﴿or a creation of what is greater in your breasts﴾ are the end of the speech. The speech is a transition to relating another of their denials.

[Page 126]

The third aspect: His words ﴿Say, "Be you stones"﴾ are a new speech that is not a reply to their statement ﴿"When we are bones and crumbled dust"﴾ [al-Isra' 49] and what follows, and the imperative form is used in the sense of equality. In this aspect, His words ﴿Then they will say, "Who will restore us?"﴾ are connected to His words ﴿Be you stones or iron﴾ and what follows, and are a consequence of an omitted statement indicated by His words ﴿Be you stones﴾. That is: "If they were like that, they would say, 'Who will restore us?'" That is, they would have moved, through the stages of sophistry, from deeming the restoration impossible to claiming that there is no one capable of restoring life to them, because their bodies are hard. By these aspects the composition of the verse is coherent, and its obscurity is uncovered.

The word "al-hadid" (iron): it is a metallic earth, meaning it is found only in the caverns of the earth. It is a thick earth of varying thickness, heavy, dark in color. It is either compact in its parts or flaky, that is, like leaves.

Its varieties are eighteen, according to the differences in the composition of its parts. Their colors differ. The noblest of its varieties is the pure one, which is free of foreign matter in all its parts, and this is rarely found. Its most famous color is red. The Arabs used to describe a hard, cutting sword as "male." When iron is melted by fire, its parts mix together, it softens and becomes like a sweet confection. Some of it is cast iron, some is wrought iron, and some is steel. Each type is suitable for what its casting is suited to, according to the varying need for great hardness, such as swords and coats of mail. Among the properties of iron is that rust settles on it. It is like green filth, and then it gradually turns into an oxide (a chemical term indicating that oxygen particles attach to a body and corrupt it). If iron is not cared for with polishing and oil, rust begins to eat into its surface. This metal is found in most lands, and it is most abundant in Abyssinia and in the desert of Egypt. Deposits of iron have been found in Tunisian lands.

[Page 127]

The use of iron dates back to ancient eras, for the second phase of the stages of history is known as the Iron Age, meaning the period in which humans used tools made of iron. This is a result of the art of ironworking, and it was before the age of recording history. The age before it is known as the Stone Age.

The meaning of "yakburu" (is great) is that it becomes large, and this greatness is figurative, meaning strong in its kind and its attributes. "Al-suduur" (breasts) means the intellects. That is: of what you regard as great and unchanging.

[Page 128]

The meaning is: "Even if you were stones or iron, Allah would revive you." This is because they made their being bones a proof of the impossibility of restoration, so He replied that restoration is within the power of Allah the Exalted, and even if you were stones or iron, because stones and iron are further from accepting life than bones and crumbled dust, since life has never previously dwelt in them at all, unlike crumbled dust and bones.

The consequence in His words ﴿then they will say, "Who will restore us?"﴾ follows His words ﴿Say, "Be you stones"﴾. That is: "Say to them this, and they will say to you, 'Who will restore us?'"

Their question here was made about the one who restores, not about the act of restoration itself, because searching for the restorer is more inclusive of impossibility than searching for the act of restoration. It is like answering with a dialectical concession after answering with a denial, for they first denied the possibility of reviving the dead, and then moved to a dialectical concession, because a dialectical concession is stronger in opposing a claim than a denial.

The interrogative in "Who will restore us?" is mocking. Since their statement was certain to occur in the future, the Prophet was commanded to revive them when they say it, by answering with a specification of who will restore them, nullifying the implication of the mockery, which is their deeming it impossible, with His words ﴿Say, "The One who originated you the first time."﴾ This is applying the apparent form of their interrogation to its original meaning by taking it contrary to their intention, because that is more fitting to the wise mode of discourse for increasing the argument, like His words concerning Moses' argument against Pharaoh: ﴿He said to those around him, "Do you not listen?" The subject is expressed as a relative pronoun (al-ladhi) to indicate what is in the relative clause of an allusion to the reason for the judgment: that the One who originated you the first time is capable of restoring your creation. Like His words the Exalted ﴿And He is the One who begins creation, then repeats it, and that is easier for Him﴾ [al-Rum 27], for by His power with which He began creating you the first time, He is capable of creating you a second time.

"Al-infaad" (shaking): the movement from top to bottom and the reverse. So "infaad al-ra's" is moving the head in that way, and it is the movement of mockery.

[Page 129]

They asked about its time with their words ﴿"When will that be?"﴾, as an interrogative of mockery also, so He commanded the Messenger to answer them with a true answer, to nullify the implication of mockery, as was previously mentioned in its like.

The pronoun in ﴿"When will that be?"﴾ refers to the restoration implied by His words "who will restore us". Like His words ﴿Be just, that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Ma'idah 8]. And "'asa" (it may be) is for hope on the tongue of the Messenger (ﷺ). The meaning is: "It is not far that it may be near."

﴿"On the Day He calls you"﴾ is a substitute for the hidden pronoun in "yakun" (it may be) in His words ﴿"that it may be near"﴾. Its vowel is the vowel of indeclinability, because it is attached to a verbal clause. It is also permissible that it be an adverb of "yakun", that is: "it may be on the Day He calls you", and its vowel is the vowel of the accusative of place.

"Al-du'a" (calling) may be taken in its literal sense: that is, Allah calling people through the angels who drive people to the place of gathering.

It may also be taken as a creative command to revive them, and calling is applied to it because calling entails the reviving of the one called and his presence. So it is a metaphor for reviving and compelling them to be present for the reckoning.

"Al-istijaba" (responding) is a metaphor for the compliance with the meaning of "yad'ukum" (calls you). That is: "you will come to life and stand before the reckoning," that is, He calls you while you are bones and crumbled dust. Bones and crumbled dust have no perception or hearing, and there is no response, because response is a consequence of hearing. Rather, it is a depiction of the swiftness of revival and summoning, and the swiftness of rising and presence for the reckoning, in such a way that it occurs like the occurrence of hearing a call and responding to it, in that there is no effort in bringing it about and no delay or slowness in its timing.

[Page 130]

On this view, the pronouns of address are an address to the disbelievers who said ﴿"Who will restore us?"﴾ and who said ﴿"When will that be?"﴾.

It is also permissible that "bi-hamdihi" be connected to an omitted word, on the basis that it is part of the speech of the Prophet (ﷺ). The estimate is: "Speak with His praise," as one says "bi-ismi Allah" (in the name of Allah), meaning "I begin," and as one says to the groom, "with blessing and prosperity," meaning "praise Allah for the manifestation of the truth of what I have informed you."
