﴿And say to My servants that they should speak in the manner that is best. Indeed, Satan incites discord among them. Indeed, Satan has ever been to mankind a clear enemy.﴾ When He had followed what He commanded the Prophet ﷺ to convey to the polytheists, namely the statements that admonish and forbid them, from His saying, ﴿Say, "If there were with Him other gods, as you claim..."﴾ [al-Isra': 42], and His saying, ﴿Say, "Be stones or iron"﴾ [al-Isra': 50], and His saying, ﴿Say, "It may be that it is near"﴾ [al-Isra': 51], the reins were turned to the command to convey to the believers, as a form of instruction that benefits them in this situation. This follows the Qur'an's custom of varying its aims and alternating some of them with their opposites, in order to cover the full range of guidance, its different methods, and the benefit to different kinds of people.

Since what preceded, the recounting of the polytheists' statements, indicated the error of their belief that speech should be conveyed to the Commander of the Believers (ʾAmīr al-Mu'minīn), [the Qur'an commands] that they say things that express good intention and pure souls. They were given in this matter a comprehensive phrase, which is ﴿the manner that is best﴾.

﴿The manner that is best﴾ (allatī hiya aḥsan) is an attribute of an omitted noun that is indicated by the verb "yaqūlū" (they say). Its estimated form is: "with that which is best." The intended meaning is not a single statement.

The elative form (ism al-tafḍīl, the comparative/superlative form) is used here with the force of the simple adjective "good." Its parallel is His saying, ﴿Argue with them in the manner that is best﴾ [al-Naḥl: 125], meaning: with arguments that reach the utmost degree of goodness, since argument is not carried out with one word.

This verse is very closely connected to the one before it, and it does not need a search for a cause of its revelation. It is a great instruction concerning guarding the tongue and what proceeds from it. In the authentic hadith from Mu'ādh ibn Jabal: "The Prophet ﷺ commanded him to do deeds that would admit him to Paradise, then said to him, 'Shall I not inform you of the foundation of all that?' I said, 'Yes, O Messenger of God.' So he took hold of his tongue and said, 'Restrain this.' I said, 'O Messenger of God, will we be held accountable for what we say?' He said, 'May your mother be bereaved of you! Will people be thrown into the Fire on their faces, or he said on their noses, except for the harvest of their tongues?'"

[Page 132]

The more important aim of this instruction is to train the community in treating one another with good conduct and gentleness of speech, because speech reveals intentions, as indicated by His saying, ﴿Indeed, Satan incites discord among them﴾. Then [the instruction] trains them in arguing with the polytheists, avoiding what harshness and severity stir up of increased obstinacy and stubbornness among the polytheists. Such [harshness] is from Satan's incitement between them and their enemy. He, the Exalted, said, ﴿Repel [evil] with that which is better; and thereupon the one between whom and you there is enmity will become as though he was a devoted friend﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 34]. The Muslims in Mecca at that time were a small group, and God had turned away from them the harm of their enemies through various kindnesses of His, so that they might be secure. Therefore He commanded them not to become a cause of corrupting that state.

By His saying "to My servants," what is meant is the believers, as is well known in the Qur'an's usage of this designation. It is narrated that the phrase "the manner that is best" means that they should say to the polytheists: "May God guide you," "May God have mercy on you," meaning by faith. And from al-Kalbī: "The polytheists used to harm the Companions of the Messenger of God ﷺ with speech and deeds. They complained of that to the Messenger of God ﷺ, so God revealed this verse."

The verb "yaqūlū" is in the jussive mood by the omission of the lam of command (lām al-amr, the particle of command). This is very common after a command to speak. You may also treat "yaqūlū" as an answer in the accusative following the imperative, with the object of the verb "say" omitted because the answer indicates it. The estimated meaning is: "Say to them: Speak the manner that is best, and they will say that." In that case it is a metonymy (kināya) indicating that compliance is their characteristic: when they are commanded, they comply. A parallel to this was mentioned before in His saying, ﴿Say to My servants who believe that they should establish prayer﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 31], in the Surah of Ibrahim.

The root nazgh (incitement) originally means a quick stab, and here it is used for quick-acting corruption. It was mentioned before in His saying, ﴿after Satan had incited discord between me and my brothers﴾ [Yūsuf: 100], in the Surah of Yusuf.

The clause ﴿Indeed, Satan incites discord among them﴾ is a justification (taʿlīl) for the command to speak the manner that is best. The purpose of the justification is that they should not treat corrupt speech lightly, since it stirs up corruptions that are the work of Satan.

[Page 133]

Since the pronoun in "among them" refers to "My servants," the meaning is a warning against Satan's casting enmity among the believers, in realization of the Sharia's aim of spreading Islamic brotherhood.

Al-Wāḥidī narrated: "'Umar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb was insulted by a Bedouin among the polytheists, and 'Umar insulted him back and intended to kill him, and it nearly stirred up strife, so this verse was revealed." Whatever the cause of revelation, it does not restrict the unrestricted form of the command to the Muslims, that they should speak the manner that is best in every situation.

The clause ﴿Indeed, Satan has ever been to mankind a clear enemy﴾ is a justification for the clause ﴿he incites discord among them﴾, and upon the justification is another justification.

The mention of "has ever been" (kāna) indicates that the attribute of enmity is a fixed matter in his creation, something he was made with. His enmity toward mankind has been established since the time of the creation of Adam, peace be upon him. He also tempts the Muslims to be harsh with the disbelievers, by making them imagine that this is support for the religion, in order to throw them into strife. The greatest of Satan's schemes is to cause the believer to fall into evil while he imagines that he is doing good.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 54:

﴿Your Lord knows you best. If He wills, He will have mercy upon you; or if He wills, He will punish you. And We have not sent you as a guardian over them.﴾ This statement is connected to His saying ﴿We know best what they listen to when they listen to you﴾ [al-Isra: 47] up to His saying ﴿so they cannot find a way﴾ [al-Isra: 48], for that includes what their secret talk concerns: their determination to persist in obstinacy and their insistence upon disbelief. This grieves the Prophet (ﷺ) and saddens him that they do not find guidance, so this statement was addressed to him as consolation for him. What confirms this is that it is followed by His saying ﴿And We have not sent you as a guardian over them.﴾

The meaning of ﴿If He wills, He will have mercy upon you, or if He wills, He will punish you﴾ according to this is a metonymy for His will to guide them, which is the cause of mercy, or His will to leave them and their own affairs. This is the best way to explain this verse and to show its place in the context; what has been said other than this, I think, does not fit.

The Subject is mentioned by the word (al-Rabb) ("the Lord"), attached to the pronoun of the believers, which includes the Messenger, as a reminder that choosing for good is among the meanings of lordship (rububiyyah), which is the management of the affairs of those who are nurtured in a manner befitting their condition. Thus the predicate falling upon the subject afterward, in His saying "knows you best," has a wonderful effect, because the one who is the Lord is the one who knows best the inner dispositions of souls and their readiness for being chosen.

This sentence serves as an introduction to what follows it, namely the sentence ﴿If He wills, He will have mercy upon you﴾ and the rest of the verse. That is: He knows best what suits the condition of each person regarding deserving mercy and deserving punishment.

The meaning of "knows you best" is "knows your condition," because the condition is what is appropriate for the attachment of knowledge.

Thus the sentence ﴿If He wills, He will have mercy upon you, or if He wills, He will punish you﴾ clarifies the intended meaning of the sentence ﴿Your Lord knows you best﴾.

Mercy and punishment are used metonymically for guidance and misguidance, by the indication of their being juxtaposed with His saying ﴿Your Lord knows you best﴾, which functions as an introduction. He adopted the path of metonymy with them to convey two benefits: their literal and their metonymic meanings, and to show that He is not questioned about what He does, because He knows best what befits the conditions of His creatures. So when He attached mercy to its causes and punishment to its causes, by His wisdom and justice, it is known that the meaning of His will for mercy or punishment is the will to bring about their causes. The verb of the condition is elided, and the estimate is: "If He wills to show you mercy, He will have mercy upon you, or if He wills to punish you, He will punish you," according to the rule of eliding the object of the verb of willing in usage.

The conjunction "or" (aw), which indicates one of two things, is used because mercy and punishment do not coexist, so "or" is for division.

Mentioning the condition of will here serves the teaching that He, exalted is He, has no compeller. Thus the verse gathers an indication of the attribute of knowledge and wisdom and of the attribute of will and choice.

Repeating the condition of will in the coordinated sentence is to emphasize the dominion of will over both states.

The sentence ﴿And We have not sent you as a guardian over them﴾ is an addition to clarify that guidance and misguidance are by the appointment of God, exalted is He, and that the Prophet is not responsible for the persistence of those who persist in error. This removes distress from him regarding what he finds of the non-guidance of those he calls. That is: We have not sent you to compel them to faith; We sent you only as a caller.

A "wakil" over a thing is one who is held responsible for it. The meaning is: We sent you as a warner and caller to them, and We have not sent you as a guardian over them. This conveys the sense of restriction, because his being a caller and warner is known by observation, so when it is denied that he be a guardian and one who bears responsibility, it returns to the meaning: you are only a warner.

The pronoun in "over them" refers back to the polytheists, just as the pronouns of "upon their hearts" [al-Isra: 46] and the pronouns that follow it appropriate to them returned to them.

"Over them" is connected to "guardian" (wakilan), and it was placed before its complement for emphasis and for the sake of observing the rhyme (fasilah).

﴿Your Lord knows best who is in the heavens and the earth. We have certainly favoured some of the prophets over others, and We gave David the Psalms (al-Zabur).﴾ The parallelism of the two rhyme-endings in this verse, namely the word "wal-ardi" (and the earth) and the phrase "ʿalā baʿḍin" (over others), clearly indicates that the two parts are connected to one another, and that the statement ﴿Your Lord knows best who is in the heavens and the earth﴾ is not a continuation of the verse ﴿Your Lord knows best about you﴾ [al-Isra: 54].

The change of address in ﴿Your Lord knows best﴾ after ﴿Your Lord knows best about you﴾ [al-Isra: 54] suggests that the purpose of this sentence relates to a matter concerning the Prophet ﷺ that has a particular connection with him. It follows the refutation of the polytheists' claims about the divine attributes with a refutation of their claims about the condition of the Prophet ﷺ. In their arrogance, they considered that he was not one of the great men of their land and its leaders, and they said: "Has God sent the orphan of Abu Talib as a messenger? Has God sent a mere human as a messenger?" God silenced them with this response in His words ﴿Your Lord knows best who is in the heavens and the earth﴾, meaning that He is the One who knows where to place His message.

The statement ﴿Your Lord knows best who is in the heavens and the earth﴾ served as an introduction to His words ﴿We have certainly favoured some of the prophets﴾ and what follows. It reminded them that God knows better than they do who is fit for the message, according to the qualities that He has prepared in that person for it, as He said concerning them (﴿They said: "We will not believe until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of God"﴾ [al-An'am: 124], ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am: 124]) in Surat al-An'am.

The judgment in this introduction applies to all existing things in general, so that it serves as a universal premise from which every ruling on its particulars is derived. This is because the claims of the polytheists that were to be refuted encompass many forms of the conditions of existing things, both humans and angels and their circumstances. Some of the polytheists denied that a human could be sent as a messenger, some denied that someone who was not among their great men could be sent, and some denied that someone who did not bring the like of what Moses (peace be upon him) brought could be sent. This raises many conditions of eras, men, and nations, living and dead. Therefore, the generalisation in His words ﴿who is in the heavens and the earth﴾ has a great significance. It is also an introduction to the sentence ﴿We have certainly favoured some of the prophets over others﴾, indicating that the preference of the prophets arises from what God has deposited in them of the requirements of preference. This is a concise statement that includes the affirmation and establishment of prophethood in the past, which they cannot deny, and the multiplicity of prophets, which makes Muhammad ﷺ not a novelty among the messengers, and the affirmation of preference among individual humans, some of whom are messengers and some of whom are sent to people, and the affirmation of preference among individuals of the excellent category. This has been established in the past with an established fact that no one can deny except the arrogant one who is stubborn. Even among the most excellent there is a divine custom that is established and cannot be denied.

From this it is known that their criticism of the prophethood of Muhammad ﷺ is criticism born of arrogance and envy.

As God said concerning the Jews: ﴿Or do they envy people for what God has given them of His bounty? We had already given the family of Abraham the Scripture and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingdom﴾ [al-Nisa: 54] in Surat al-Nisa.

The singling out of David (peace be upon him) for mention immediately after this general matter has been explained by the author of al-Kashshaf and those who followed him as meaning that the purpose of this allusion is that Muhammad ﷺ is the most excellent of the prophets, and his community is the most excellent of nations, because in the Psalms (there is the statement) ﴿that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾ [al-Anbiya: 105]. This is good. However, I see that the reason for this specific mention is an allusion to the fact that many of the conditions that are regarded as disgraceful in the eyes of the ignorant and the short-sighted are conditions that do not prevent their possessors from ascending the levels of perfection to which God has chosen them, and that preference through prophethood and messengership does not arise from prior greatness. David (peace be upon him) was a shepherd among the shepherds of the Children of Israel, and he had strength in throwing stones. God commanded Saul (Shaul), king of the Children of Israel, to choose David to fight Goliath (Jalut) the Canaanite. When David killed Goliath, God gave him prophethood and made him king over Israel. He is the prophet in whom God's choice of one who had no greatness or lordship was manifested.

Mention of God giving him the Psalms is the point of indirect reference to the polytheists that the Muslims will inherit their land and triumph over them, because that is written in the Psalms, as was mentioned just before. David was given the Psalms, and none of the prophets of the Children of Israel after Moses (peace be upon him) was given a scripture. The mention of David has already occurred in Surat al-An'am and at the end of Surat al-Nisa.

As for the Psalms (al-Zabur), they were mentioned at His words, exalted is He, ﴿We gave David the Psalms﴾ at the end of Surat al-Nisa.

Al-Zabur is the name for the collection of the sayings of David (peace be upon him), some of which were revealed to him and some of which were inspired in him as supplications and intimate prayers. It is what is known today as the Book of Psalms (al-Mazamir) among the books of the Old Testament.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 56:

﴿Say: "Call upon those you claim besides Him; they do not possess the removal of harm from you, nor any transformation."﴾ I have not seen for this verse an explanation that brings ease to the heart, and bewilderment is evident in the statements of the commentators regarding its meaning and the coherence of its placement with what precedes it. There is no need to survey their words. Their views return to two approaches regarding the sense of ﴿those you claim besides Him﴾. One is found in the Tafsir of al-Tabari and in Ibn 'Atiyya, on the authority of Ibn Mas'ud and al-Hasan. The second is found in the Tafsir of al-Qurtubi and al-Fakhr, without attribution to a specific speaker.

What appears to me in its explanation is that the sentence ﴿Say: call upon those you claim besides Him﴾ up to ﴿transformation﴾ is a parenthetical sentence between the sentence ﴿And We have certainly preferred some of the prophets﴾ [al-Isra': 55] and the sentence ﴿Those whom they call upon﴾ [al-Isra': 57]. This is because, when mention was made of the most excellent of the prophets in the course of the verse refuting the polytheists' claim regarding the choosing of Muhammad (ﷺ) for the message, and the choosing of his followers for his guardianship and his religion, which is the verse ﴿And your Lord knows best who is in the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Isra': 55] to its end, the occasion arose to refute another of their false claims: their excuse for worshipping idols, that they only worship them so that they may bring them near to God in proximity (zulfa). Thus they made them servants brought near and intermediaries for them to God. When the mention of those truly brought near was made, the occasion of their mention was seized, so that it would be a means of nullifying what they claimed about the intercession of their idols, following the Qur'an's custom of seizing occasions for admonition, which is part of the style of preachers. Accordingly, this verse is connected in meaning with the verse ﴿Say: if there were with Him other gods, as you say, they would certainly have sought a way to the Lord of the Throne﴾ [al-Isra': 42]. After it had refuted, by the proof of reason, that there could be gods with God, it returned to nullifying their supposed divinity by the proof of sense, which is the observation that they do not avail them in the removal of harm.

The underlying connection of the discourse is thus: "And We have certainly preferred some of the prophets over others, and We gave David the Psalms. Those whom they call upon seek..." (the verse). By way of praising them for their supplication to their Lord, He mentioned the opposite of that: the supplication of the polytheists to their gods. He placed this before the statement that provoked the occasion, out of concern for nullifying their act, so that its nullification would be like the intended aim, and the mention of its counterpart would be like the proof for that aim. Perhaps this verse was revealed during the period when the famine afflicted the Quraysh in Makkah, which was the seven years of which the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed: "O God, make it upon them as years of Joseph." The debate continued, one part drawing on another, until it reached this occasion.

"Al-mulk" here means capability and power, as in His saying ﴿Say: who can prevail against God in anything?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 17], and His saying ﴿Say: do you worship besides God what possesses for you neither harm nor benefit?﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 76] in Surat al-'Uqud.

The purpose of this is to show the difference between true supplication and false supplication. Among the parallels of this meaning in the Qur'an is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, my guardian is God, who revealed the Book, and He takes charge of the righteous. And those you call upon besides Him are unable to help you, nor can they help themselves﴾ [al-A'raf: 196] in Surat al-A'raf.

"Al-kashf" (removal): used metaphorically for removal.

"Al-tahwil" (transformation): the moving of a thing from one place to another, i.e., they cannot remove harm from all, nor remove it from one person to another.

[Page 140]

﴿Those whom they call upon seek means of access to their Lord, [each] of them striving to be nearest [to Him], and they hope for His mercy and fear His punishment. Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is something to be feared.﴾

The demonstrative in ﴿Those whom they call upon﴾ refers to the prophets, in order to make their distinction clearer.

The meaning is: those who, if they call upon [God], are answered and have harm removed from them, and they are not like those whom you call upon, who cannot remove harm from you by themselves, nor by their intercession with God, as you have seen, since they did not avail you in removing harm or averting it.

The clause ﴿seek﴾ (yabtaghūna) is either a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the pronoun in ﴿call upon﴾ (yadʿūna), or an explanatory clause (bayān) for the clause ﴿call upon﴾.

Al-wasīlah (means of access) is a high rank close to a great sovereign, such as a king.

The phrase ﴿which of them is nearest﴾ (ayyuhum aqrab) may be a partial substitution (badal baʿḍ) for the pronoun in ﴿seek﴾. In that case (ayy) is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah) meaning "the one who," and the sense is: [each] one who is nearest to God seeks to increase the means of access to Him, that is, he increases in deeds so as to increase in God's good pleasure toward him and in His choosing him.

It may also be a substitution for the whole clause ﴿they seek means of access to their Lord﴾, in which case (ayy) is interrogative, meaning that they seek to know the answer to: "Which of them is nearest to God?"

Aqrab is an elative noun (ism tafḍīl), and its complement is omitted, indicated by the context; the implied sense is: "which of them is nearest to their Lord."

The mention of fear after the hope for mercy serves to indicate that they stand in a posture of courtesy toward their Lord; so drawing nearer to His good pleasure only increases them in reverence for Him and in fear of His wrath. This is an allusion to the polytheists who ran headlong into error and went deep into delusion, claiming that their associates are their intercessors with God.

[Page 141]

The clause ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is something to be feared﴾ is a concluding remark (tadhyīl), and the meaning of ﴿is something to be feared﴾ (kāna maḥdhūran) is that its very reality calls for the caution of those who are granted success, since it is worthy of that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 58:

﴿And there is no city but that We will destroy it before the Day of Resurrection, or punish it with a severe punishment. That was in the Book inscribed.﴾

When he had alluded to a threat against the polytheists in His saying ﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is something to be feared﴾ [al-Isra': 57], and had challenged them in His saying ﴿Call upon those you claim besides Him; they have no power to remove the harm from you﴾ [al-Isra': 56], He came with an explicit threat, audibly addressed to them, that every city like their city in polytheism will not escape the punishment of annihilation (al-isti'sal), which comes upon the city and its people, or the punishment of retribution (al-intiqam) by the sword, humiliation, captivity, fear and hunger, which comes upon the people of the city, like the slain of Badr. All of this is in this world. Thus, the intended meaning is the cities whose people are disbelievers; this is supported by His saying ﴿And your Lord would never destroy the cities unjustly while their people are reformers﴾ [Hud: 117] in Surah Hud, and His saying ﴿We would never destroy the cities unless their people were wrongdoers﴾ [al-Qasas: 59] in Surah al-Qasas.

The omission of the qualifier in such a context is well known, as in His saying ﴿who seizes every ship by force﴾ [al-Kahf: 79], meaning every sound ship, indicated by His saying ﴿so I wanted to damage it﴾ [al-Kahf: 79].

The intended meaning is not the inclusion of believing cities, in the sense that cities must inevitably perish and vanish according to the law of God in this world; because that would contradict other verses, and because it would conflict with the purpose of warning the polytheists against persisting in polytheism.

Even if we grant that this judgment admits no exception among cities, by the law of God that everything created ends in annihilation, we would not grant that mentioning it here has any benefit.

The restriction by the phrase ﴿before the Day of Resurrection﴾ is an addition to the warning and threat, like His saying ﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is greater and more lasting﴾ [Ta-Ha: 127].

Page 142

The particle (min) is extra (mazidah) after the negative (in), to emphasize the comprehensiveness of what it governs according to the implied qualifier, i.e., all disbelieving cities; so that the people of Makkah do not suppose that they are not included.

"Al-Kitab" is metaphorically used for the knowledge of God and His preordained decree, so its definiteness is for a specific reference (al-'ahd). Or it may be intended to mean the books revealed to the prophets, in which case its definiteness is generic (lil-jins), and it includes the Qur'an and others.

"Al-mastur" means the written, as it is said: "sattara al-kitab" when he wrote it in lines (sutur). God said ﴿By the pen and what they inscribe﴾ [al-Qalam: 1].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 59:

﴿And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs except that the former peoples denied them. And We gave Thamud the she-camel as a visible sign, but they wronged her by it.﴾ This is the dispelling of another doubt among the doubts of their denial, for they used to ask the Prophet to bring them signs according to their own proposals, and they would say: "If he were truthful, and he demands that we believe in him, he would have brought us the signs we asked for," out of self-conceit, believing that Allah would stoop to their challenges.

The sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿And there is no town but We will destroy it﴾ [al-Isra: 58], meaning: We only gave respite to those who persisted in disbelief until the appointed time of the descent of the punishment, and We did not respond to them with what they requested of the signs, because sending signs according to their proposals would be of no benefit, as it did not benefit the former peoples before them who disbelieved, so they denied the signs.

The real meaning of "man'" (prevention) is the restraining of the doer from an act that he wants to do or is striving to do, and this is impossible with respect to Allah the Exalted, since there is no one who can compel the Almighty, the Free Chooser. So "man'" here is used metaphorically for diverting from the act and preventing its occurrence without an attempt to bring it about.

The sending (al-irsal) may be literal, in which case the object of ﴿an nursila﴾ is omitted, indicated by the verb nursil, and the estimate is: "that We send Our messenger," so the particle "bi" in His saying "bi-al-ayat" is for accompaniment, meaning accompanied by the signs that the polytheists proposed. It is also permissible that the sending is used metaphorically for the manifesting and bringing into being of the signs, in which case the "bi" is superfluous, to emphasise the connection of the verb "nursil bi-al-ayat," and "al-ayat" is in meaning the object, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and wipe your heads﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6].

The definiteness in "al-ayat" in both cases is for the known (al-'ahd), meaning the signs known from their proposals, as in their saying ﴿We will not believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾ [al-Isra: 90], and ﴿They said: Why was he not given the like of what was given to Moses?﴾ [al-Qasas: 48], and ﴿They said: We will not believe until we are given the like of what was given to the messengers of Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 124], according to one of the two interpretations.

The first "an" (that) yields a verbal noun in the accusative by removal of the preposition, and it is of those through which the verb of prevention is transitive, and this deletion is regular with "an."

The second "an" has as its verbal noun the subject of "manaʿana" in the exceptive construction of the incomplete type (al-istithna' al-mufarragh).

Attributing the prevention to the denial of the former peoples by the signs is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), because the denial is the cause of the diversion.

The meaning: We know that they will not believe, just as those disbelievers before them did not believe when similar signs came to them. So people knew that persistence in disbelief is a disposition of the polytheist which the manifestation of signs does not uproot. Had the former peoples believed when the signs were shown to them, these latter would have made their belief contingent upon the bringing into being of the signs they asked for. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has come into effect will not believe, even if every sign should come to them﴾.

It is most apparent that this is a strengthening of the hearts of the believers, lest Satan tempt them, and a consolation for the Prophet ﷺ because of his eagerness for the faith of his people, for he may wish that Allah would answer them regarding what they asked of the signs, and because of his grief lest they think him a liar.

The sentence ﴿And We gave Thamud the she-camel﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of majesty in "manaʿana," meaning: and We had indeed given Thamud a sign as they asked, but they increased in disbelief because of it, until the punishment was hastened upon them.

The meaning of "mubsirah" is clear in indication. It is the active participle of "absara," which is transitive to an object, meaning it made another seeing and possessed of insight. So the meaning is: it conveys insight, that is certainty, meaning it makes whoever sees it possessed of insight and informs him that it is a sign. From this is His saying, exalted is He, ﴿So when Our signs came to them as visible, they said: This is manifest magic﴾ [al-Naml: 13].

Thamud and their sign were singled out for mention because of the fame of their affair among the Arabs, and because the traces of their destruction in the lands of the Arabs are near to the people of Makkah, whose travellers and arrivers see them during their journeys between Makkah and Syria.

His saying ﴿but they wronged her by it﴾ may be that wrong (zulm) is used in the sense of disbelief, since it is wronging oneself, and the "bi" is for transitivity, since the act of disbelief is transitive to the one disbelieved in by means of "bi." It is also permissible that wrong is implicitly construed with the meaning of denial, meaning they were obstinate regarding its being a sign, as in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and they denied them, though their souls were convinced of them, out of wrongdoing and arrogance﴾ [al-Naml: 14]. It is also permissible that wrong remains in its true sense, which is transgression without right, and the "bi" is a complement for emphasising transitivity, like the "bi" in ﴿and wipe your heads﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6], meaning they wronged the she-camel when they hamstrung her, and she had not committed any offence against them, so her hamstringing was wrong, and aggression against dumb creatures is wrong when it is not permitted by the Law, as in hunting.

* * *

﴿And We send not the signs except as a warning﴾

This is an explanation of another wisdom in not sending the signs to Quraysh, pointing out that Allah the Exalted intended to spare them so that many of them would enter Islam, and so that the spreading of Islam would be through the hand of many of them.

That is a noble honour for the Prophet ﷺ, for if Allah had sent them the signs as they asked, despite their natural disposition towards obstinacy, they would have persisted in disbelief, and the sunnah of Allah which has passed concerning His servants would have come into effect against them, namely annihilation following the manifestation of the signs, because the manifestation of the signs

is a warning of the punishment, and Allah intended to spare this nation. He said: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [al-Anfal: 33], and so We substituted their warning in place of sending the signs they had proposed.

The discussion regarding the transitivity of ﴿And We send not the signs﴾ is like the discussion regarding ﴿And nothing prevented Us from sending the signs﴾, in meaning and estimate according to both interpretations. Takhwif (warning) is making a person fearful.

The restriction in His saying ﴿except as a warning﴾ restricts the sending of signs to the cause of warning. It is a restriction relative to a particular context, meaning there is no contest between the messengers and their peoples, nor is there hope for the faith of the peoples, for We have known that they will not believe.

[Page 146]

﴿And when We told you, "Indeed, your Lord has encompassed the people."﴾ This is a consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning his grief over his people's denial of him, and over God's allowing the obstinate enemies of the religion, who persecuted the believers, to remain unpunished. So God reminded him of His promise to support him.

The fact that the predicate is attributed to the word "Lord" (al-Rabb), in the form of an annexed noun with the Messenger's pronoun, indicates that this statement is delivered in a manner of honour for the Prophet and of encouragement to patience, and that he is under God's special care, since He is his Lord and his Supporter. God says, ﴿So be patient for the judgment of your Lord, for indeed you are within Our eyes﴾ [al-Tur: 48].

The clause ﴿And when We told you﴾ etc. may be coordinated with the clause ﴿And We do not refrain from sending signs except that the former peoples denied them﴾ [al-Isra': 59], and it may also be parenthetical.

The word (idh) ("when") is connected to a verb that is omitted, meaning: "Remember when We told you," a statement that is a promise of patience; that is, "Mention that to them, and repeat it to their ears." Or it may be the verb "remember" (udhkur), understood as derived from dhikr (with a dammah on the dhal), which is the restoration of information to the mind's power of recollection.

Since the verb "encompass" (ihata) here is applied to the very persons of the people and not to some of their states, it is established that it is used in the sense of domination, as in God's words ﴿And they thought that they had been encompassed﴾ [Yunus: 22] in Surat Yunus. He expressed it in the past tense to draw attention to the certainty of God's encompassing of the people in the near future. Perhaps this is an allusion to God's words ﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its outlying parts?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 41].

The meaning is: "So do not grieve over their slander and arrogance, for We shall surely take vengeance upon them."

* * *

﴿And We did not make the vision which We showed you except as a trial for the people﴾

This is coordinated with the clause ﴿And We do not refrain from sending signs﴾ [al-Isra': 59], and what lies between them consists of parenthetical clauses.

The word "vision" (ru'ya) is most commonly used for a dream, but it is also used for seeing with the eye, as is reported from Ibn 'Abbas concerning this verse. He said: "It was a vision of the eye that the Prophet (ﷺ) was shown on the night he was taken by night to Bayt al-Maqdis." This is related by al-Tirmidhi, who said: "This is also the view of 'A'isha, Mu'awiya, and seven of the Successors," whom al-Tirmidhi named. Some scholars interpreted it to mean what he saw on the night of the Isra', when he saw Bayt al-Maqdis and began to describe it to the polytheists, and he saw their caravan arriving at a specific place on the road, and he described to them the condition of men in it, and it was as he described. This view is supported by God's words ﴿which We showed you﴾, for it is a description of the vision, to make known that it was a vision of the eye. It was also said: he saw that he would enter Mecca in the year of al-Hudaybiyya, but the polytheists turned him back, so he did not enter, and some of those who had embraced Islam were thrown into turmoil; then when the following year came, he entered it.

It was also said: it was a vision of the slaying of the chiefs of Quraysh at Badr, which the Prophet (ﷺ) was shown before that, that is, in Mecca. According to these two views, it was a vision of sleep, and the visions of the prophets are revelation.

Fitna (trial) is the disturbance of opinion and the disruption of the order of life. It is also applied to a repeated torment that cannot be borne, as God says ﴿Indeed, those who tormented the believing men and women﴾ [al-Buruj: 10], and ﴿On the day they will be tormented over the Fire﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 13]. So the meaning according to the first of the two views concerning the vision is that what was seen, namely their punishment by the sword, was a trial for them.

* * *

﴿And the accursed tree in the Qur'an﴾

"And the tree" is coordinated with "the vision," meaning: We did not make the mention of the accursed tree in the Qur'an except as a trial for the people. This is an allusion to God's words ﴿Indeed, it is a tree that springs from the root of the Hellfire; its fruit is like the heads of devils. Indeed, they will eat from it and fill their bellies with it﴾ [al-Saffat: 64–66] in Surat al-Saffat, and His words ﴿Indeed, the tree of zaqqum is the food of the sinful﴾ [al-Dukhan: 43] in Surat al-Dukhan, and His words ﴿Indeed you, O astray deniers, will surely eat from a tree of zaqqum﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 51] in Surat al-Waqi'a.

It is reported that Abu Jahl said: "Your companion claims that the fire of Hell burns stones, then he says that there is a tree in the fire that the fire does not burn." They failed to realise that God creates in the fire a tree that the fire does not consume. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas and his companions in the asbab al-nuzul (occasions of revelation) of al-Wahidi and in the tafsir of al-Tabari. It is also reported that Ibn al-Zib'ara said: "Zaqqum means dates with butter in the dialect of Yemen," and that Abu Jahl ordered a slave girl, who brought dates and butter, and said to his companions: "Eat zaqqum!" According to this interpretation, the meaning is that the tree of zaqqum was the cause of the trial of their disbelief and their turning away from faith. And on this interpretation, the meaning of making the tree of zaqqum a trial must be that its mention was a cause of trial, with an omitted noun, namely "mention," indicated by the context of His words ﴿accursed in the Qur'an﴾; for what it was described with in the verses of the Qur'an is a curse upon it.

It may also be that the meaning is: its creation is a trial, that is, a repeated punishment, as He said ﴿Indeed, We have made it a trial for the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Saffat: 63].

The accursed (al-mal'una): that is, the condemned in the Qur'an, in His words ﴿the food of the sinful﴾ [al-Dukhan: 44], and His words ﴿its fruit is like the heads of devils﴾ [al-Saffat: 65], and His words ((﴿like molten brass, boiling in the bellies﴾ [al-Dukhan: 45], ﴿like the boiling of scalding water﴾ [al-Dukhan: 46])). It was also said that the meaning of "accursed" is that it is placed in a place of curse, which is distance from mercy, because it was created in a place of punishment. In al-Kashshaf it is said: the Arabs call every harmful food "accursed."

* * *

﴿And We warn them, but it only increases them in great transgression﴾

This is coordinated with the clause ﴿And We do not refrain from sending signs except that the former peoples denied them﴾ [al-Isra': 59], which indicates that they are firm in their disbelief, stubborn and obstinate. This is an additional consolation for the Prophet (ﷺ), so that he will not be distressed that God has not shown them signs; for the Prophet (ﷺ) is eager for their faith, just as Moses (peace be upon him) said ﴿So they will not believe until they see the painful punishment﴾ [Yunus: 88].

It is found in some tafsir works that Ibn 'Abbas said concerning the accursed tree that it is the Banu Umayya. This is one of the fabricated reports attributed to Ibn 'Abbas, and I do not think it was anything but what the forgers invented in the time of the 'Abbasid call, to increase the repulsive things said about the Banu Umayya. The description of the tree as "accursed in the Qur'an" is an explicit statement that there are verses in the Qur'an that mention an accursed tree, namely the tree of zaqqum, as you know. Such fabrication is a departure from the Qur'an's admonitions in His words ﴿And do not defame one another, nor insult one another with nicknames; wretched is the name of defiance after faith﴾ [al-Hujurat: 11].

The present tense is used in "We warn them" to indicate a warning that is ongoing, for God warned them with drought and famine until they saw smoke between the heaven and the earth, and asked God to remove it, and He said ﴿Indeed, We will remove the punishment a little; indeed you will return﴾ [al-Dukhan: 15]. That, and other warnings that preceded it, did not increase them except in transgression. So it is apparent that this verse was revealed during the period in which some of these warnings were occurring.

The present-tense verbs "We warn them" and "it increases them" have been chosen because they imply the repetition and renewal of the warning, and that whenever the warning is renewed, their transgression is renewed and grows.

"Great" (kabir) is used metaphorically for the sense of intense and powerful in the kind of transgression. It was previously discussed at His words ﴿Say: fighting therein is a great [sin]﴾ [al-Baqara: 217] in Surat al-Baqara.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 17, verses 61–62:**

﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis. He said, "Shall I prostrate to one whom You created from clay?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Do You see this one whom You have honored above me? If You delay me until the Day of Resurrection, I will surely seize control of his descendants, except for a few."﴾

This is an attachment (ʿatf) to the clause, ﴿And when We said to you, "Indeed your Lord has encompassed the people"﴾ (Al-Isra, 60). The meaning is: "And mention when We said to the angels." The purpose of this is to remind the Prophet ﷺ of what the prophets before him suffered from the opposition of enemies and envious people, from the time of Adam, when Iblis envied him for his favor. Yet despite this, they never lacked people who acknowledged their merit, and these were the best of their times, just as the angels were toward Adam (peace be upon him). Both groups, in every age, trace back to one of the two groups of the time of Adam: the believers belong to the group of the angels, and the disbelievers belong to the group of Satan. This is what His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿He said, "Go, and whoever follows you among them..."﴾ (Al-Isra, 63), hints at. In this there is consolation for the Prophet ﷺ. God commanded His Prophet to mention this, which implies a reminder of it to him. The Prophet ﷺ also mentioned it as an admonition to the people, by means of the condition of the two groups, so that the intelligent person may consider where he places himself.

The explanation of the story of Adam and the details of its words has already passed in Surat al-Baqarah and what follows it.

The interrogative in ﴿Shall I prostrate?﴾ is a denial, meaning: it is not to be.

The clause ﴿He said, "Shall I prostrate...?"﴾ is a resumptive clause introduced as an explanatory resumption (istinaf bayani), because the exception of Iblis from the ruling of prostration conveyed no more than the fact that he did not prostrate. This raises in the listener's mind the question of the cause of his failure to comply with this ruling. The answer is given by what came from him at the time of his failing to prostrate: it was disobedience to God's command, arising from his ignorance and conceit.

His saying ﴿clay﴾ (ṭīnan) is a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the relative pronoun, meaning: "the one whom You created while being clay." It conveys the meaning that You created him from clay. The reason he made the genus of clay a circumstantial state of him is to indicate the predominance of the earthly element in him, because that is more severe in belittling him in Iblis's view.

The clause ﴿He said, "Do You see..."﴾ is a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for the clause ﴿Shall I prostrate to one whom You created from clay?﴾, in terms of what it includes of belittling Adam and deeming the preference for him a mistaken choice. The denial of preference is repeated with the words ﴿Do You see this one...﴾, which convey denial. He justified the denial by implying a scheme against his descendants. For this reason the clause ﴿He said, "Do You see..."﴾ is separated from the clause ﴿He said, "Shall I prostrate?"﴾, as occurs in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Then Satan whispered to him, saying, "O Adam, shall I direct you to the tree of eternity?"﴾ (Ta-Ha, 120).

The expression ﴿Ara'aytaka﴾ (Do you see you?) is a formula with which speech is opened when what follows is intended to be emphasized and given importance. Its meaning is: "Inform me of what I have seen." It is composed of the interrogative hamzah, the verb ra'a (meaning ʿalima, "to know"), and the suffix of the second person singular in the nominative case (the taʾ of address). Then a particle of address, the kaf, is added to the pronoun of address, resembling the accusative pronoun of address, according to whether the addressee is singular or plural. One says: ﴿Ara'aytaka﴾ and ﴿Ara'aytakum﴾, as already mentioned in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Say, "Have you considered: if the punishment of God comes upon you, or the Hour comes to you..."﴾ (Al-An'am, 40), in Surat al-An'am. This kaf, according to the Basrans, is an emphasis of the meaning of address conveyed by the taʾ of address, which is in a position of nominative case, and it resembles verbal emphasis. Al-Farra' said: the kaf is an accusative pronoun, and the construction means "you saw yourself." This is closer to usage, and it is supported by the fact that verbs of opinion and knowledge may take as their object a pronoun referring to their own subject, as in the verse of Tarafa:

*"What is it with me that I see myself and my paternal cousin Malik? When I approach him, he moves away from me and keeps his distance."*

That is: "I see myself."

The demonstrative ﴿this﴾ (hadha) is used in a belittling sense, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Is this the one who mentions your gods?﴾ (Al-Anbiya, 36). The meaning is: "Inform me of your intention: is this the one whom You honored over me without any justification?"

The clause ﴿If You delay me until the Day of Resurrection...﴾ and so on is a resumption of the initial kind (istinaf ibtida'i). It is a sworn clause (jumlah qasamiyyah). The lam is a preparatory particle (muwatta'ah) for the omitted oath together with the condition, and the predicate (the apodosis) is used in the sense of a supplication. It is thus equivalent to His saying, ﴿He said, "My Lord, then reprieve me until the day they are resurrected"﴾ (Al-Hijr, 36).

This speech came from Iblis as an expression of what was in his inner self. He specified the delay until the Day of Resurrection so that his misguidance would encompass all generations of Adam's descendants, so that no generation would be safe from his misguidance.

This came from Iblis out of a conviction that was cast into his soul, which coincided with God's purpose concerning him. When God created him, He decreed that he would be a source of misguidance until the Day of Resurrection, and that he would misguide many of mankind, while only a few would be spared from him.

The reason it was limited to misleading the descendants of Adam, without mentioning misleading Adam himself, even though Adam would have been more appropriate to mention, is that Adam was the root of Satan's enmity, which arose from envy of his being preferred over him. This is either because he said these words after he had misled Adam and he had been expelled from the Garden, so he had already satisfied his rancor against him, and the enmity remained spread among Adam's descendants. God, Exalted is He, said, ﴿Indeed, Satan is an enemy to you﴾ (Fatir, 6).

The word ﴿ihtinak﴾ (to seize, or to take control) means: the rider placing the bridle in the mouth (ḥanak) of the horse in order to ride it and guide it. So here it is a metaphor for drawing Adam's descendants toward his purpose of corruption and misguidance, by guiding them as one guides a horse toward what its rider wishes.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 63–64:

[p. 152]
﴿He said, "Go! Whoever among them follows you, indeed Hell is your recompense, an ample recompense.﴾ ﴿And incite whom you can among them with your voice, and urge upon them your cavalry and your infantry, and share with them in wealth and children, and make promises to them. But Satan promises them nothing except delusion.﴾

This is a reply from God, exalted is He, to Iblis's request for a delay until the Day of Resurrection. For this reason the clause (qala, "He said") is detached (fusilat) in the manner of dialogues that we mentioned at His words, exalted is He, ﴿They said, "Will You place therein..."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30].

The word "dhahab" (go) is not meant in the sense of departing; rather, it is used for persisting in an action, i.e., "proceed with your affair which you intended." The imperative form is used for equivalence (al-taswiyah), as in the saying of al-Nabhani, one of the poets of the Hamasah:

"If you were our lord, we would have made you lord; and if you were a fool, then go and be foolish."

His words ﴿whoever among them follows you﴾ are a consequence (tafri') of the equivalence and the rebuke, like His words, exalted is He, ﴿He said, "Go, for it is yours in life to say, 'No touching'"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 97].

"Al-jaza'" is a verbal noun of "jazahu 'ala 'amal," meaning he gave him a return for his deed. Here it has the meaning of the passive participle, like "al-khalq" in the sense of "al-makhluq."

"Al-mawfur" is a passive participle from "wafarahu," when he made it abundant.

"Jaza'an" is repeated for emphasis, out of concern and eloquence, like His words ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [Yusuf: 2]. It is also because it is better for the attribute "al-mawfur" to follow directly the noun it qualifies without separation. The original sentence is: "Indeed Hell is your recompense, ample." So "jaza'an" is in the accusative as a preparatory circumstantial (al-hal al-muwatti'ah), and "mawfuran" is its adjective, and it is in meaning the circumstantial (al-hal), i.e., a recompense not diminished.

[p. 153]
"Al-istifzaz" is seeking to cause agitation (fazz), which is lightness, disturbance, and abandonment of heaviness. The sin and ta' in it are for making (al-ja'l) arising from intensity of seeking and urging, which is the basic meaning of the sin and ta'; i.e., "provoke them and disturb them."

"Al-sawt" (voice) is often applied to speech, since speech is a sound from the mouth. It is used here metaphorically for casting whispering into people's souls. It may also be that it is used here as a figure for the state of Iblis by the state of a army commander, and it would then be connected to His words ﴿and urge upon them your cavalry﴾, as will come.

"Al-ijlab" is gathering an army and driving it, derived from "al-jalabah" (with two fathas), which is shouting, because when the commander of an army wishes to gather the army he calls out to them for mobilization or for raid and assault.

"Al-khayl" is a collective noun for horse, and what is meant by it, when there is mention of what indicates the army, is the horsemen. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ, "O cavalry of God, ride!" It is a figure for the state of dispersing his power and capacity to misguide by the state of an army commander who gathers his horsemen and his foot soldiers.

Since the army commander calls out to the army when ordering a raid, it is permissible that His words ﴿and incite whom you can among them with your voice﴾ be part of this figure.

"Al-rajl" is a collective noun of "al-rijal" like "sahb." The armies of the Arabs were composed of foot soldiers who fought with swords, and of companies of horsemen who fought by shooting arrows; when they engaged, they all fought with swords. Unayf ibn Zabban al-Nabhani said:

"Beneath the chests of horses is a rough stone, a foot-soldier whose arrows are given to the hearts' kernels."
Then he said:

"When we met, the sword made clear between us, for one asking about us, whose question is pressing."

[p. 154]
The meaning: gather for those who follow you from the offspring of Adam, both means of temptation and whispering to mislead them. The means of whispering are made, by adorning corruptions and making benefits appear abhorrent, like the differing kinds of an army. So this is a figure for the state of Satan and the state of his followers among the offspring of Adam, by the state of one who raids a people with a great army of horsemen and foot soldiers.

Hafs, on the authority of 'Asim, read "wa rajilika" with a kasrah on the jim, and it is a dialect of "rajul" with a dammah on the jim, which is one man of the men; the intended meaning is the genus, and the meaning: "with your horsemen and your men," i.e., the horsemen and the infantry.

The ba' in "bikhaylika" is either to emphasize the attachment of the verb to its object, so it is merely for emphasis, and its governed noun is in meaning the object of the verb "ajlib," like ﴿and wipe over your heads﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6]; or to make the verb "ajlib" imply the meaning of "ghazhum" (raid them), so the verb is implicitly carrying the meaning of an intransitive verb, and the ba' is for accompaniment.

"Sharing in wealth" means that Satan has a share in their wealth, which is their livestock and crops, since he embellished for them that they should set aside a share of the produce and the tilth for the idols, and these are among the channels of Satan; for Satan is the one who embellishes for people the adopting of them. God, exalted is He, says ﴿And they assign to God a share of what He has produced of tilth and livestock, and they say, "This is for God, by their claim, and this is for our partners."﴾ [al-An'am: 136].

As for sharing in children, it means that Satan has a share in the affairs of their children, like his embellishing for them to bury their daughters alive, and to have children by fornication, and to name them after idol-worshippers, like their saying: "'Abd al-'Uzza," "'Abd al-Lat," "Zayd Manat," and his being attributed to that idol.

The meaning of "make promises to them" is give them promises of obtaining what they desire, as he embellishes to them that if they dedicate their children to the idols, the fathers are spared bereavement and the children are spared illnesses; and he embellishes to them that the idols will intercede for them with God in this world, and guarantee for them

[p. 155]
victory over enemies, as Abu Sufyan said on the day of Uhud: "Exalt Hubal!" And from it is his promising them that they need not fear punishment after death, by denial of resurrection, and promising the sinners the attainment of the pleasures sought from sins, such as fornication, theft, wine, and gambling.

The object of "wa'adahum" is omitted for generality regarding what is promised, and the context indicates that the intent is that he promises them what they desire; for promise (al-'idah) is the undertaking to give what is desired. He called it a promise (wa'd) because it makes them imagine its occurrence in the future, so they continue awaiting it, as is the habit of a liar who avoids reporting the immediate, since his exposure is near; so he makes all his promises concern the future.

For this reason the clause ﴿But Satan promises them nothing except delusion﴾ is inserted parenthetically. "Al-ghurur" is showing a disliked thing in the form of a beloved, fine thing. It was discussed earlier at His words, exalted is He, ﴿Let not the movement of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 196] in Al 'Imran, and at His words ﴿deceptive embellished speech﴾ [al-An'am: 112] in al-An'am. The meaning: what Satan embellishes to them concerning the attainment of what is desired is either false and does not occur, like the corrupt beliefs he embellishes to people, and its being delusion is because it shows what does not occur in the form of what occurs, so it is deception; or it is attained but disliked and not praiseworthy in its outcome, like what he embellishes to people of satisfying the urges of anger and desire and love of the immediate without reflection on the deferred. All of this is never free from the disliked matter accompanying it, or its leading to harm.

Al-Ghazali expounded this in the book on "Delusion" (al-Ghurur) in his (Ihya' 'Ulum al-Din).

Also, this sentence functions like a proverb, so it is not fitting for it to contain a pronoun that is not part of its components.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 63–64:

[p. 152]
﴿He said, "Go! Whoever among them follows you, indeed Hell is your recompense, an ample recompense.﴾ ﴿And incite whom you can among them with your voice, and urge upon them your cavalry and your infantry, and share with them in wealth and children, and make promises to them. But Satan promises them nothing except delusion.﴾

This is a reply from God, exalted is He, to Iblis's request for a delay until the Day of Resurrection. For this reason the clause (qala, "He said") is detached (fusilat) in the manner of dialogues that we mentioned at His words, exalted is He, ﴿They said, "Will You place therein..."﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30].

The word "dhahab" (go) is not meant in the sense of departing; rather, it is used for persisting in an action, i.e., "proceed with your affair which you intended." The imperative form is used for equivalence (al-taswiyah), as in the saying of al-Nabhani, one of the poets of the Hamasah:

"If you were our lord, we would have made you lord; and if you were a fool, then go and be foolish."

His words ﴿whoever among them follows you﴾ are a consequence (tafri') of the equivalence and the rebuke, like His words, exalted is He, ﴿He said, "Go, for it is yours in life to say, 'No touching'"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 97].

"Al-jaza'" is a verbal noun of "jazahu 'ala 'amal," meaning he gave him a return for his deed. Here it has the meaning of the passive participle, like "al-khalq" in the sense of "al-makhluq."

"Al-mawfur" is a passive participle from "wafarahu," when he made it abundant.

"Jaza'an" is repeated for emphasis, out of concern and eloquence, like His words ﴿Indeed, We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [Yusuf: 2]. It is also because it is better for the attribute "al-mawfur" to follow directly the noun it qualifies without separation. The original sentence is: "Indeed Hell is your recompense, ample." So "jaza'an" is in the accusative as a preparatory circumstantial (al-hal al-muwatti'ah), and "mawfuran" is its adjective, and it is in meaning the circumstantial (al-hal), i.e., a recompense not diminished.

[p. 153]
"Al-istifzaz" is seeking to cause agitation (fazz), which is lightness, disturbance, and abandonment of heaviness. The sin and ta' in it are for making (al-ja'l) arising from intensity of seeking and urging, which is the basic meaning of the sin and ta'; i.e., "provoke them and disturb them."

"Al-sawt" (voice) is often applied to speech, since speech is a sound from the mouth. It is used here metaphorically for casting whispering into people's souls. It may also be that it is used here as a figure for the state of Iblis by the state of a army commander, and it would then be connected to His words ﴿and urge upon them your cavalry﴾, as will come.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 65:

Page 156
﴿Indeed, My servants—you have no authority over them. And sufficient is your Lord as a Guardian.﴾

The clause ﴿Indeed, My servants—you have no authority over them﴾ is part of the speech reported by ﴿He said, "Go!"﴾ [al-Isra: 63]. It is a resumptive clause (mustaʾnafa) of explanatory resumption (istiʾnaf bayani), arising from His saying ﴿So whoever of them follows you﴾ [al-Isra: 63] and His saying ﴿And incite whomever you can among them﴾ [al-Isra: 64]. The implied meaning (mafhum) of "whoever follows you" and of ﴿whomever you can﴾ [al-Isra: 64] is of the category of the implied meaning of a qualifier (mafhum al-sifa). It therefore indicates that a group of the descendants of Adam do not follow Iblis, so he does not ensnare them. This implied meaning indicates that God has protected or safeguarded this group from Satan. That raises a question in the mind of Iblis, so that he may learn what stands between him and that group, after he had come to know in himself, in a general way, that a group would not be ensnared by him, from His saying ﴿I will surely ensnare his descendants, except for a few﴾ [al-Isra: 62]. Thus the indication to identify this group came through a description and through a cause.

As for the description, it is in His saying "My servants" (ʿibadi), which indicates that they have wholly devoted themselves to the worship of God, Exalted, as the idafa (genitive construction) shows. Thus it is known that those who worshipped idols and jinn and turned away from the worship of God, Exalted, are not among them.

As for the cause, it is in His saying ﴿And sufficient is your Lord as a Guardian﴾, which indicates that they put their trust in God and sought refuge in Him from Satan. So He was the best guardian for them, since He encompassed them from Satan and protected them from him.

In this trust there are degrees of turning away from Satan's ensnarement, and these are the degrees of the believers in taking up obedience to God, as is the truth according to the People of the Sunna.

So the authority negated in His saying ﴿you have no authority over them﴾ is the continuous rule by which they would become his subjects and soldiers. As for others, Satan may beguile them, but they will not remain long before returning to righteous deeds. It suffices as evidence of this that their monotheism to God endures, and their affirmation of His Messenger,

Page 157
and their regarding themselves as servants of God, seeking to be thankful for His blessing. How far apart they are from the people of polytheism, even if the creed of the Mu'tazila is weak regarding them. The meaning of this has already been mentioned at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe and rely upon their Lord. His authority is only over those who take him as an ally and those who associate others with Him﴾ [al-Nahl: 99], in Surat al-Nahl.

The believer never takes Satan as an ally, but he may be deceived by his whisperings; and yet he curses him for the grave sins into which he has caused him to fall. In proportion to that deception, he draws closer to his authority. This is the meaning of the words of the Prophet ﷺ in the Farewell Pilgrimage sermon: "Indeed, Satan has despaired of being worshipped in this land of yours, but he is content with what is less than that, of the deeds you consider trivial."

The clause ﴿And sufficient is your Lord as a Guardian﴾ may be a completion of the rebuke of Satan, in which case the kaf of address (kaf al-khitab) is the pronoun referring to Satan, recording against him that he is a servant of God. It may also be a parenthetical clause at the end of the speech, in which case the kaf of address is the pronoun referring to the Prophet ﷺ, bringing him near by its attachment to the pronoun of God. The final meaning is one under both aspects, though the consideration differs.

**Commentary of Ibn ʿAshur (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Surah 17, verse 66:**

﴿Your Lord is the One who drives the ship for you through the sea, that you may seek of His bounty. Indeed, He is ever Merciful to you.﴾ This is an *istiʾnāf ibtidāʾī* (an independent resumptive sentence), and it returns to establishing the proofs of God's sole control over the affairs of the world. These proofs are mixed with the blessings in it for creation, and by that mixture they point to the perfection of the making and the firm arrangement of the system of this world, and to the dominion of humankind within it and over it. It is likely that this statement returns to His saying ﴿And man prays for evil as he prays for good﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 11], as was mentioned there, so refer back to it.

[Page 158]

When the discourse had addressed warning and caution, it was followed here by argument for the soundness of the warning and caution.

The address is to the group of polytheists, as indicated by His saying after it, ﴿So when He delivers you to the land, you turn away﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 67], that is, you turn away from calling upon Him and call upon the idols. And His saying ﴿Those whom you invoke vanish except Him﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 67].

The sentence opens with the subject (*al-musnad ilayh*) defined by a construct (*iḍāfa*) and brought to mind through the attribute of lordship (*rubūbiyya*). This is to draw the listeners' attention to the predicate, and it signals its importance, since it begins with what is awaited to be a great report, because it concerns the affairs of the true God, the Creator of creation, and the Manager of their affairs with the management of the Subtle, the Merciful. This compels the listener to attend with his whole being, whether he is a believer who remembers or a polytheist who looks and reflects.

The sentence is nominal (*jumla ismiyya*), because it indicates permanence and stability.

By defining both its parts, it indicates exclusivity (*inḥiṣār*): your Lord is the One who drives the ship for you, not anyone else among those you worship falsely. And He is the One who continually does this for you.

The relative clause is a verb in the present tense (*fiʿl muḍāriʿ*), to indicate the repetition and renewal of this act. Thus this sentence, despite its brevity, contains many specific meanings, and this is among the limits of inimitability (*iʿjāz*).

*Yuzjī* means to drive gently, slowly. It likens the subjecting of the ship to movement on water to the driving of a laden animal.

*Al-fulk* here is a collective noun, not a singular. *Al-baḥr* means a large body of water, so it includes rivers such as the Euphrates and the Tigris. It was discussed at His saying ﴿And the ships that run in the sea﴾ [al-Baqara: 164] in Surah al-Baqara.

*Al-ibtighāʾ* means seeking, and *al-faḍl* means provision, that is, for trade. It was discussed at His saying ﴿There is no blame upon you for seeking bounty from your Lord﴾ [al-Baqara: 198] in Surah al-Baqara. This favour upon all people is appropriate to the generality of the call, because the people of Makkah did not benefit from riding the sea. Only the Arabs of Yemen, the Arabs of Iraq, and other peoples benefit from that.

The clause ﴿Indeed, He is ever Merciful to you﴾ is a justification and an alert to the place of the favour, so that they would reject the worship of other than Him, since what is other than Him has no effect in this favour.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 67:

﴿When harm touches you at sea, those you call upon vanish, except Him. But when He delivers you to the land, you turn away. And man has always been ungrateful.﴾ After He had established the proof, through what is among the distinctive features of His creation and through their own acknowledgment, of the truth of Allah the Exalted's divinity, He followed it with another proof from their own circumstances. This proof includes their affirmation that He alone has sole authority over affairs, and then an expression of wonder at the contradiction within themselves once their dire need has passed.

The clause ﴿When harm touches you at sea, those you call upon vanish, except Him﴾ is a statement used for confirmation and for imposing the proof, since no one reports about his own act in a literal sense of reporting.

The clause ﴿But when He delivers you to the land, you turn away﴾ is a statement used for wonder and reproach.

The "harm of the sea" is the state of being on the brink of drowning, because it unsettles the souls with fear, so it is a harm to them. The verb ﴿ضَلَّ﴾ (ḍalla), with a fallen ḍād, is a verb from ḍalāl, which is following a path that does not lead to the intended goal, in error.

The shift to the relative form (al-mawṣūliyyah), with what the relative clause implies of the action of the tongue, is for the sake of concision. That is, "those whom you habitually call upon", as the present tense indicates. The meaning is that the names of those you were accustomed to calling upon have vanished and departed from your tongues, so you do not call upon them. This is shown by the mention here of supplication, whose object is the tongue. Thus it is determined that their going astray is the going astray of the mention of their names. This is a wonderful concision.

[p. 160]

The exception is from the generality of the relative pronoun, because the name of Allah is among what occasionally runs on their tongues in supplication, just as the names of the idols do. Therefore the exception is connected (istithnāʾ muttaṣil).

It is also permissible that the relative pronoun in His saying ﴿those you call upon﴾ be specific to their idols, because they frequently call upon them, rather than the name of Allah the Exalted, as the implication of recurrence requires. When harm presses them hard, they call upon Allah, as the Exalted said: ﴿So when they board a ship, they call upon Allah, sincerely devoting religion to Him. But when He delivers them to the land, at once they associate others with Him﴾ [al-ʿAnkabūt: 65]. In this case the exception is disconnected (istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ). The accusative case of the excepted noun does not differ in the two readings, in accordance with standard (fuṣḥā) usage. Perhaps this reading is preferable, because it is more fitting with His saying "you turn away".

The turning away (iʿrāḍ) is abandonment, that is, you abandoned the supplication of Allah. This is indicated by the combination of the implication of the present tense of renewal and the implication of the exception that supplication is restricted to calling upon Him by His name, the Exalted.

His saying ﴿to the land﴾ takes the particle ﴿إلى﴾ (ilā) because the verb ﴿نَجّاكم﴾ (najjākum) is construed with the meaning of "brought you to" and "connected you to".

The clause ﴿And man has always been ungrateful﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ) and a concluding statement (tadhyīl), to increase the wonder at them and at those like them. The word ﴿kafūr﴾ is an intensive form, meaning one who is extremely ungrateful, and kufr is the opposite of shukr (gratitude).

The definite article in ﴿al-insān﴾ (man) is the definite article of genus, and it conveys comprehensiveness (istighrāq). This comprehensiveness may be customary (istighrāq ʿurfī), by taking it to refer to the majority of the human species, namely those who associate partners with Allah, who were the majority of people at that time. In that case the intensive form in His saying ﴿kafūr﴾ refers to the intensity of the attribute of ingratitude or lack of gratitude, for the highest degree of it is associating with Allah a non-benefactor alongside the Benefactor in a blessing in which that non-benefactor has no share.

It is also permissible that the comprehensiveness is literal, meaning that the species of man is ungrateful, that is, not free of ingratitude. In that case the intensive form refers to the multiplicity of states of ingratitude, though they vary, and the frequency of man's ingratitude is the repetition of his turning away from gratitude at the place of gratitude, through error, forgetfulness or heedlessness, in that he attributes blessings to their proximate causes and not to their Giver, and in that he imagines benefactors who have no share in bestowing.

[p. 161]

The mention of the verb ﴿kāna﴾ (was) indicates that ingratitude is firmly established in the disposition of this man, because man rarely perceives what lies beyond the world of the senses. The senses occupy him with what they perceive, distracting him from reflecting on other meanings that are stored in memory and those derived by thought.

Since gratitude for a blessing depends on remembering the blessing, his preoccupations hide the blessings of the past from his awareness. Also, among what the senses perceive is what is agreeable to the soul, which is the usual case, and what is repugnant to it. When man perceives what is agreeable, he does not feel its value, because of its frequent recurrence until it becomes a habit, and so he is heedless of the benefit in it. When he perceives what is repugnant, he recalls the loss of what was agreeable, and so he cries out and is distressed. This is the meaning of the Exalted's saying: ﴿And when We bestow blessing upon man, he turns away and withdraws to one side; but when harm touches him, he is full of lengthy supplication﴾ [Fuṣṣilat: 51]. For this reason the wise said: "Well-being is a crown upon the heads of the healthy, which only the sick can see." This consideration is what this verse, together with the one following it, ﴿Do you feel secure that He will not cause the side of the land to swallow you?﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 68], points to. For this reason it was among the principles of the soul in the Sharia to remind it of the blessings of Allah. The Exalted said: ﴿And remind them of the days of Allah﴾ [Ibrāhīm: 5], so that the remembrance of the blessing takes the place of guarding it.

[Page 162]

This is a consequence (tafri') of the clause "you turned away" (a'radtum), and what lies between them is a parenthetical digression (i'tiraD). The reproachful interrogative is a consequence of their turning away from gratitude and their returning to disbelief.

Al-khasf (the sinking of the earth) is the overturning of the earth's surface into its interior through an earthquake. It was mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿Do those who devised evil deeds feel secure that God will cause the earth to swallow them?﴾ [al-Nahl: 45], in Surah al-Nahl.

In this there is a reminder that safety on land is a great blessing which you forget. If the earth were to sink beneath you, you would perish with a destruction from which there is no escape, unlike the terror of the sea. But since the value of safety on land is not fully perceived, souls rarely feel its blessing, nor do they feel the danger of the terror of the sea. Therefore one should train oneself to remember the blessing of being safe from harm. Moreover, the place of safety is itself exposed to dangers.

The interrogation in His words ﴿Do you feel secure?﴾ (afa-amintum) is one of denunciation and reproach.

Al-janib (the side) means the shore. Making the land a "side" intends the edge to which they are carried for deliverance, namely the shore on which they come to rest. This is an indication that fear may befall them merely by their arriving on land, such that God may cause that very shore to sink beneath them. That is, land and sea are equal in God's power, so the rational person should keep his fear of God equal on land and on sea. The annexation of "side" to "land" is an explicative annexation (idafah bayaniyyah).

The preposition ba' in ﴿to swallow you﴾ (yakhsifa bikum) is for transitivity, with yakhsifa carrying the sense of accompaniment (musahabah).

Al-hasib is the one who pelts with pebbles, namely hasba (gravel/pebbles). It is an adjective here: He sends upon you a cloud (arid) pelting with stones, likening it to one who throws pebbles, that is, a rain of stones, that is, hail resembling stones. It has also been said that al-hasib here means "possessor of pebbles," and so the active participle is formed from it by the pattern fa'il, which conveys the sense of a relative adjective, like laban (having milk) and tamir (having dates).

Al-wakil is the one entrusted with the task of his principal and who defends his principal's right. That is, you will find no one among yourselves who will dispute with Us on your behalf, or demand from Us what We have inflicted on you of sinking or destruction by the hasib. That is, you will find among your people and your allies none who will avenge you, as is the case with one who suffers harm among his people: that they defend him and that his kin and his band demand retribution for his blood. This meaning is suitable to what befalls people on land of calamities.

[Page 163]

The particle am here is the interrogative am that introduces a transitional turn (idrab intiqali), meaning "rather, do you feel secure?" The interrogative is thus implied alongside am, because am is specific to it. The sense is: "Or were you secure from returning to riding the sea another time, so that He would send upon you a violent wind (qasif) from the wind?"

Al-tarah is a repeated occurrence. It has been said its root is a hamza, which was then lightened due to frequent usage. It has also been said it is a waw, but the first is more evident, since it occurs with a hamza, and they do not pronounce the hamza in the weak letter in classical Arabic. As for the lightening of the hamza, it is common, as in fa's and fas, and ka's and kas.

Al-qasif is that which breaks, that is, shatters. The root of qasf is breaking. The description of the wind by it prevailed, so it is treated as one of the attributes specific to the feminine, and they did not attach to it the feminine marker, like 'asif in His words ﴿a violent wind came upon them﴾ [Yunus: 22] in Surah Yunus.
