The majority read min al-rih (from the wind) in the singular. Abu Ja'far read min al-riyah (from the winds) in the plural.

The ba' in ﴿because you disbelieved﴾ (bima kafartum) is causal, and ma is verbal (masdariyyah), meaning "because of your disbelief," that is, your polytheism.

Thumma (then) is for graded sequence (al-tartib al-rutbi), as is its custom in conjoining sentences. It is an escalation in the threat by the absence of any rescuer for them, after threatening them with drowning, because the drowning person may find a rescuer.

Al-tabi' is an intensive form of the one who follows, that is, one who pursues another and demands something from him. That is, you will find none who will go after Us, nor anyone who will demand vengeance for you.

[Page 164]

The description "tabi'" (pursuer) suits the state of harm that befalls them at sea, because the men of their tribe and their allies cannot reach it. So if they were to seek vengeance for them, they would ride the sea to follow the traces of the one who inflicted harm upon them. Therefore it is said here "tabi'an," and in the preceding verse "wakil," as already mentioned.

The pronoun in bihi refers either to the drowning implied by "He drowns you," or to what was mentioned of sending the violent wind and other things.

The majority read the verbs yakhsifa, yursila, yu'idakum, fayursila, and fayughriqakum, all five, with the yaʾ of the third person. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read them with the nun of majesty (nun al-'azamah), by way of iltifat (shift) from the third-person pronoun in His words ﴿when He brought you safe to land﴾ [al-Isra': 67] to the first-person pronoun. Abu Ja'far and Ruways from Ya'qub read ﴿fa-tughriqakum﴾ with the feminine ta', the pronoun referring to the wind on account of its feminine grammatical gender, or to "the winds" in the reading of Abu Ja'far.

[Page 162]

This is a consequence (tafri') of the clause "you turned away" (a'radtum), and what lies between them is a parenthetical digression (i'tiraD). The reproachful interrogative is a consequence of their turning away from gratitude and their returning to disbelief.

Al-khasf (the sinking of the earth) is the overturning of the earth's surface into its interior through an earthquake. It was mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿Do those who devised evil deeds feel secure that God will cause the earth to swallow them?﴾ [al-Nahl: 45], in Surah al-Nahl.

In this there is a reminder that safety on land is a great blessing which you forget. If the earth were to sink beneath you, you would perish with a destruction from which there is no escape, unlike the terror of the sea. But since the value of safety on land is not fully perceived, souls rarely feel its blessing, nor do they feel the danger of the terror of the sea. Therefore one should train oneself to remember the blessing of being safe from harm. Moreover, the place of safety is itself exposed to dangers.

The interrogation in His words ﴿Do you feel secure?﴾ (afa-amintum) is one of denunciation and reproach.

That is, land and sea are equal in God's power, so the rational person should keep his fear of God equal on land and on sea. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 70:

﴿And We have certainly honoured the children of Adam, and carried them on land and sea, and provided for them of the good things, and preferred them above much of what We have created, with a definite preference.﴾

This is an interjection (i'tiraḍ) that came in connection with the lesson and the favour directed at the polytheists. It interjects by mentioning His blessing upon all people, so it resembles a conclusion (tadhyil), because what is mentioned in it includes what came before.

By "the children of Adam" is meant the whole species, so the attributes affirmed here are rulings concerning the species as such, as is the case with rulings that are ascribed to collectivities.

The verse gathers five favours: the honouring, the subjugation of mounts on land, the subjugation of vessels at sea, provision from the good things, and preference over many of the created beings.

Page 165
As for the favour of honouring, it is a distinction which God singled out for the children of Adam from among all the earthly creatures.
Honouring (al-takrim) means making him noble (karim), that is, precious, not cheapened nor debased in his form, nor in the movement of his walking and in his skin. All animals do not know cleanliness, nor clothing, nor the refinement of resting places and food, nor the goodness of the manner of taking food and drink, nor preparation for what benefits them and the repelling of what harms them, nor awareness of what is in their essence and intellect of virtues, so that they seek more of them, and of vices, so that they conceal and repel them; not to mention being free of knowledge and crafts, and of accepting development in the methods of their life and civilisation. Ibn 'Abbas illustrated honouring by saying that man eats with his fingers, meaning that he does not tear food with his mouth but raises it to his mouth with his hand, and does not drink from water by lapping but raises it to his mouth with his hand. For raising food with a ladle and drink with a cup is part of the increase of honouring, and it is still taking with the hand.

Carrying (al-haml) is placing upon a vehicle from among the riding beasts, so the rider is carried upon the mount. Its original meaning is in riding on land, by His subjugating the mounts for them and inspiring them to use them.

As for carrying at sea, it is being inside the ship, and the application of "carrying" to that state is a metaphor drawn from carrying upon a mount, which became so common that it became almost literal. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, when the water rose high, We carried you in the sailing ship﴾ [al-Haqqah: 11]. The meaning of God carrying people at sea is His inspiring them to use ships, sails and oars, so the facilitation of that is treated as carrying.

As for provision from the good things, it is because God, exalted is He, inspired man to eat what he wishes of what pleases him, and placed in foods signs of benefit, and made what man takes of foodstuffs far more numerous than what other animals take, which eat only things they are accustomed to. Moreover, the animal closest to humanity and civilisation is the one most wide in its consumption of foods.

Page 166
As for preference over many of the created beings, what is meant is the preference that is observed, since it is the place of favour; and its sum is that man is empowered to dominate all earthly creatures by his opinion and his cunning, and that suffices as a preference over the rest.

The difference between preference and honouring is one of generality and specificity: honouring considers his honour in his very essence, while preference considers his elevation above others. Moreover, He preferred him by the intellect through which the improvement of his affairs is achieved and harms are repelled from him, and by the kinds of knowledge and sciences. This is the preference that is meant.

As for the relation of superiority between the human species and kinds of beings hidden from us, such as the angels and the jinn, it is not here; it is known only through textual proofs from the Shari'ah. Therefore the question of the preference of humans over angels, whose details are disputed between us and the Mu'tazilah, is not raised here. Al-Zamakhshari raised it here, in his habit of provoking the people of the Sunnah and forcing the Qur'an to support his school, and he exceeded the bounds of courtesy in this question in this place, so he deserved reproach and censure.

There is no doubt that the insertion of the word "many" in His words, ﴿and preferred them above much of what We have created﴾, is meant to restrict, qualify and teach without deception, so it is understood from it that there are created beings over which the children of Adam are not preferred, and which are equal to them or superior, in general or in detail. Its clarification is taken from the Shari'ah in what it has explained of that, and what it has left silent on we do not investigate.

The use of the absolute object in His words "tafdilan" serves to convey the magnification contained in the indefiniteness, meaning a great preference.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 71–72:

﴿On the Day We shall summon every people with their leader. Whoever is given his record in his right hand—those will read their record, and they will not be wronged even by a thread.﴾ ﴿And whoever was blind in this [life] will be blind in the Hereafter, and further astray from the way.﴾

This is a transition from the theme of warning of the swift punishment in this world, which appears in His words ﴿Your Lord is He who drives for you the ships through the sea﴾ [17:66] up to His words ﴿then you would not find for yourselves against Us any avenger﴾ [17:69], to the mention of the condition of people in the Hereafter, as glad tidings and warning. The speech is therefore a fresh, initiatory resumption (istinaf ibtida'i), and the connection is as you have learned. The word "Day" (yawma) is not appropriate as attached to what precedes it, namely His words ﴿and We have favoured them over many of those We created with [marked] preference﴾ [17:70], such that it would serve as a transition (takhallus) from the mention of preference to the mention of the Day on which the benefits of preference will become apparent. It is therefore preponderant that it is a fresh beginning resuming initiatorily. The fatha on yawma is either the fatha of i'rab, with it being a direct object of a verb widely elided at the beginning of Qur'anic admonitions, namely the verb "remember" (udhkur), so that yawma here is a noun of time functioning as an object of the implied verb, and not an adverb of time.

The fa' in His words ﴿fa-man uti'a﴾ ("so whoever is given") is for consequence (al-tafri'), because the implied verb "remember" (udhkur) requires a great matter stated in general terms, so its detail is given with the fa' and what follows it, since detail branches off from generality.

Or its fatha may be the fatha of construction (bina'), because it is a time noun attached to a verb. It is then either in the position of raf' as subject, with its predicate being the clause ﴿whoever is given his record in his right hand﴾, and the fa' has been added to the predicate according to the opinion of al-Akhfash; Ibn Hisham has related from Ibn Burhan that the fa' is added to the predicate according to all the Basrans except Sibawayh. Or it is an adverbial of time for an elided verb indicated by the division that follows it, namely His words ﴿whoever is given his record in his right hand﴾

Page 168

up to His words ﴿and further astray from the way﴾. The estimated elided element is: people will differ and will be deceived (tataghabbanu), and the detail of that elided element is explained by the branching with His words "whoever is given his record" etc.

Al-Imam: that which is followed, i.e. one acts upon its like or its course. The intended meaning here is the explainer of the religion: of a true religion for the believing nations, and of a religion of disbelief and falsehood for the misguided nations.

The meaning of calling the people is that it is called out: "O nation of so-and-so, O followers of so-and-so," such as: "O nation of Muhammad, O nation of Moses, O nation of Jesus," and such as: "O nation of Zoroaster, O nation of Brahma, O nation of Buddha," and such as: "O worshippers of al-'Uzza, O worshippers of Ba'l, O worshippers of the vulture."

The ba' is for the transitivity of the verb "nad'u" (We call), because it is transitive with the ba', as one says: "I called him by his kunya" and "they called upon one another by their slogan."

The benefit of calling them by their leaders is the hastening of joy for those who followed the guided ones, and of grief for those who followed the deviators, because when they are called by those names they see their leaders in the stations appropriate to them, and so they know their destiny.

Following this, His words ﴿fa-man uti'a kitabahu bi-yaminihi﴾ come as detailed division of what His words ﴿We shall summon every people with their leader﴾ had summarized. That is: among the people are those who are given their record, i.e. the book of their deeds, in their right hand.

His words "fa-man uti'a" are a conjunction over an implied element required by His words ﴿We shall summon every people with their leader﴾. That is: they will be given their books, i.e. the pages of their deeds.

The giving of the book in the right hand is the inspiring of its bearer to take it in his right hand, and that is a sign of care for the one who receives it, because the right hand is what one takes by when resolving a great deed. God the Exalted said: ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ [69:45], and the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever gives a charity from lawful earnings—and God accepts only what is good—the Merciful receives it in His right hand, and both His hands are right" … etc. And al-Shammakh said:

Page 169

"When a banner is raised for glory, 'Araba receives it in the right hand."

As for the people of wretchedness, they will be given their books in their left hands, as in the verse of al-Haqqah: ﴿But as for him who is given his record in his left hand, he will say: "Oh, I wish I had not been given my record"﴾ [69:25].

The use of the demonstrative after the fa' of the answer to "as for" (amma) is to draw attention to the fact that they, and no others, will read their record, because in their being informed of what it contains of good deeds and reward for them there is joy for them and bliss through remembrance and knowledge of its reward. This is the nature of every record that contains what pleases and recalls good deeds, just as a person reads news of the safety of his loved ones and friends and the wellbeing of their condition; so the eagerness to read such books is a well-known trait.

As for the other group, the record is not mentioned here as being read; and in the verse before it in this surah it occurs: ﴿And every person We have fastened his bird to his neck, and We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a record he will find spread open. "Read your record. Sufficient is yourself against you this Day as a reckoner."﴾ [17:13]. The word "wronged" (yuzlamun) is used here in the sense of diminishing, as in His words ﴿Each of the two gardens brought its produce and did not fall short of it in anything﴾ [18:33], because most wronging occurs by seizing part of what belongs to the one wronged, so diminishing follows, and it is then applied to it figuratively by metonymy. From this it is understood that what they are given as reward is of what people desire to increase.

Al-Fatil: a thread-like thing found in the cleft of a date-stone; it was mentioned in His words ﴿Rather, God purifies whom He wills, and they will not be wronged a thread﴾ in Surat al-Nisa'. It is an example for a trivial, insignificant thing, meaning they will not be diminished in anything, even a very little.

The conjunction of "wa-man kana fi hadhihi a'ma" is the conjunction of the counterpart over its counterpart: it falls within the scope of the detailed "as for" (amma). The estimate is: "As for whoever was blind in this [life]..." And since the counterpart conjoined to is those given their books in the right hand, it is understood that the conjoined one is given its book in the left,

Page 170

so this is omitted, and another attribute is brought for him, namely that he is blind, a further judgment of his horrible conditions on that Day.

The demonstrative "hadhihi" refers to something known from the context, namely this world, and it has parallels in the Qur'an. By blindness in this world is meant misguidance in religion, which is called blindness by way of metaphor.

By blindness in the Hereafter is meant what arises from blindness of bewilderment and turmoil of mind; so "blind" here is also a metaphor for something resembling blindness by one of the two relations.

The description "blind" in both instances is intended as mere description, not comparison. Since the aspect of resemblance in the condition of the disbeliever in the Hereafter is stronger than in his condition in this world, this is indicated by His words "and further astray from the way," which stands in place of the comparative form in blindness, because the description "blind" cannot be formed into the comparative form; for it has come in the comparative form in the state of description.

He turned away from the word "ashadd" and similar expressions, which are used to form the comparative when the form af'al cannot be derived, so that mention of "the way" could be made, because in straying from the way there is an illustration and clarification of the state of blindness; for the straying of one who has lost sight from the road makes his walk more harmful than it would be if he sat in his place. So he turned from the concise wording to the expanded structure, because expansion conveys the image of the state, clarifies it, and makes it more dreadful; and this is a masterful expansion. By this it is conveyed that his blindness in both abodes is blindness of straying from the path that leads to the destination. The sense of comparison refers to comparing one of his two states with the other in misguidance and its effect, not to the state of anyone else. So the meaning is: "and further astray from the way than he was in this world."

The reason his misguidance in the Hereafter is greater is that his misguidance in this world was within his power to escape by seeking what would guide him to the path that leads to it, from the guidance of the Messenger and the Qur'an, while being free from the pain befalling him; but his misguidance in the Hereafter is a misguidance from which there is no escape, and it accompanies everlasting punishment. Therefore his misguidance in the Hereafter is more truly and essentially misguidance.

The use of the demonstrative after the fa' of the answer to "as for" (amma) is to draw attention to the fact that they, and no others, will read their record, because in their being informed of what it contains of good deeds and reward for them there is joy for them and bliss through remembrance and knowledge of its reward. This is the nature of every record that contains what pleases and recalls good deeds, just as a person reads news of the safety of his loved ones and friends and the wellbeing of their condition; so the eagerness to read such books is a well-known trait.

As for the other group, the record is not mentioned here as being read; and in the verse before it in this surah it occurs: ﴿And every person We have fastened his bird to his neck, and We will bring out for him on the Day of Resurrection a record he will find spread open. "Read your record. Sufficient is yourself against you this Day as a reckoner."﴾ [17:13]. The word "wronged" (yuzlamun) is used here in the sense of diminishing, as in His words ﴿Each of the two gardens brought its produce and did not fall short of it in anything﴾ [18:33], because most wronging occurs by seizing part of what belongs to the one wronged, so diminishing follows, and it is then applied to it figuratively by metonymy. From this it is understood that what they are given as reward is of what people desire to increase.

Al-Fatil: a thread-like thing found in the cleft of a date-stone; it was mentioned in His words ﴿Rather, God purifies whom He wills, and they will not be wronged a thread﴾ in Surat al-Nisa'. It is an example for a trivial, insignificant thing, meaning they will not be diminished in anything, even a very little.

The conjunction of "wa-man kana fi hadhihi a'ma" is the conjunction of the counterpart over its counterpart: it falls within the scope of the detailed "as for" (amma). The estimate is: "As for whoever was blind in this [life]..." And since the counterpart conjoined to is those given their books in the right hand, it is understood that the conjoined one is given its book in the left,

Page 170

so this is omitted, and another attribute is brought for him, namely that he is blind, a further judgment of his horrible conditions on that Day.

The demonstrative "hadhihi" refers to something known from the context, namely this world, and it has parallels in the Qur'an. By blindness in this world is meant misguidance in religion, which is called blindness by way of metaphor.

By blindness in the Hereafter is meant what arises from blindness of bewilderment and turmoil of mind; so "blind" here is also a metaphor for something resembling blindness by one of the two relations.

The description "blind" in both instances is intended as mere description, not comparison. Since the aspect of resemblance in the condition of the disbeliever in the Hereafter is stronger than in his condition in this world, this is indicated by His words "and further astray from the way," which stands in place of the comparative form in blindness, because the description "blind" cannot be formed into the comparative form; for it has come in the comparative form in the state of description.

He turned away from the word "ashadd" and similar expressions, which are used to form the comparative when the form af'al cannot be derived, so that mention of "the way" could be made, because in straying from the way there is an illustration and clarification of the state of blindness; for the straying of one who has lost sight from the road makes his walk more harmful than it would be if he sat in his place. So he turned from the concise wording to the expanded structure, because expansion conveys the image of the state, clarifies it, and makes it more dreadful; and this is a masterful expansion. By this it is conveyed that his blindness in both abodes is blindness of straying from the path that leads to the destination. The sense of comparison refers to comparing one of his two states with the other in misguidance and its effect, not to the state of anyone else. So the meaning is: "and further astray from the way than he was in this world."

The reason his misguidance in the Hereafter is greater is that his misguidance in this world was within his power to escape by seeking what would guide him to the path that leads to it, from the guidance of the Messenger and the Qur'an, while being free from the pain befalling him; but his misguidance in the Hereafter is a misguidance from which there is no escape, and it accompanies everlasting punishment. Therefore his misguidance in the Hereafter is more truly and essentially misguidance.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 73:

[Page 171]
﴿And indeed, they were about to tempt you away from that which We have revealed to you, so that you would invent other than it against Us; and then they would have taken you as a close friend.﴾ This is a description of one kind of their misguidance and blindness in this world. The sentence is coordinated (ʿatf) with the sentence ﴿And whoever is blind in this [world] will be blind in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Isra: 72]. It is a transition from describing their state and refuting their claim in denying the Prophet ﷺ to mentioning another state of their opposition and aversion, namely their hope that they could bring the Prophet ﷺ down to saying something that would show favour to their gods, so that they would condescend to reconcile with him and agree with him if he agreed with them in some of what they asked of him.

The pronouns of the third person refer to the disbelievers of Quraysh, that is, those who managed the direction of their affairs. The style shifts from the address to them in the verses ﴿It is your Lord who drives the ships for you through the sea﴾ [al-Isra: 66] to addressing the Prophet ﷺ directly, because the situation has changed from a context of argument to a context of favour.

Al-fatn and al-futun (temptation, trial): a dealing from which harm and disturbance of the soul arise, in kinds of dealing that are difficult to repel, through domination over strength and over reason. This was discussed in His saying, ﴿And temptation (fitnah) is worse than killing﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The verb yaftinunaka is followed by the particle (ʿan) because it is construed with a verb whose meaning the temptation serves, namely what has the sense of "they would turn you away."

That which was revealed to him is the Qur'an.

This is the proper way of interpreting the verse, in accordance with what the meanings of its structures give, while observing what the proofs of the Messenger's infallibility (ʿismah) require, namely that thoughts of responding to what the polytheists hope for should not occur to him.

[Page 172]
The exegetes have several other interpretations of this verse, which al-Qurtubi surveyed exhaustively. Some of them have no share of acceptance, because their chains are weak and they do not fit the meanings of the verse. Others have a weak chain and the verse bears them only with strain. Their common root is that the polytheists asked the Prophet ﷺ not to place alongside himself those whom they regarded as inferior to them among the believers who were weak in their eyes, such as Bilal, ʿAmmar ibn Yasir, Khabbab and Suhayb; and that they promised the Prophet ﷺ that if he did this, they would sit with him and listen to the Qur'an at times when nothing in it disparaged their gods; and that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ resolved to show them some leniency, out of desire for their turning to listening to the Qur'an, perhaps they would be guided. Thus "that which We have revealed to you" would mean part of what We have revealed to you, namely what contains the merit of the believers, such as His saying, ﴿And do not drive away those who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾ [al-Anʿam: 52], or what contains the denunciation of the idols.

The marks of conjecture and narrowness of outlook are evident in all these reports when the meaning of the verse is taken in its plain words. Since the books of tafsir are filled with them, it was necessary to interpret the verse in the best manner that suits those reports, lest it become a trial for the readers. We say: the Prophet's ﷺ desire for their drawing near to Islam, and for the security of the Muslims, turned over in his mind the idea of answering them in some of what they called him to, which concerned easing the harshness toward them or granting them respite, or pleasing some of his companions by withdrawing from his gathering when the chiefs of the polytheists attend it, while he knows that they are being appointed to that for the interest of the religion or something similar, in which there is an interest for the spread of the religion and no loss to the Muslims. That is, they were about to turn you away from some of what We revealed to you that is contrary to what they asked.

Accordingly, the relative pronoun in His saying ﴿that which We have revealed to you﴾ is for specific reference (ʿahd), to what was known to the Prophet ﷺ according to what the polytheists asked him to oppose. This verse is therefore couched as a favour bestowed upon the Prophet ﷺ through Allah's protecting him from error in judgment (ijtihad), and also as a display of the polytheists' dismay at the Islamic call and their fear of its consequences. In this there is a strengthening of the Prophet ﷺ and the believers, and a removal of hope from the polytheists that this will ever happen.

[Page 173]
His saying ﴿so that you would invent other than it against Us﴾ is connected to yaftinunaka. The lam is for causation: that is, they do this, hiding their intent and hoping that you would invent other than it against Us, that is, other than what was revealed to you. This is a hope of the polytheists that they might lead the Prophet ﷺ step by step from one request to another, so it relates to their intentions. There is nothing in the speech that requires that the Prophet ﷺ resolved to do this, as some exegetes understood, since the lam of causation requires no more than the purpose of the agent of the causative act; it does not require the purpose of the object, nor its knowledge.

The "in" (إنْ) in His saying ﴿And indeed they were about to tempt you﴾ is the lightened form of the heavy "inna", its subject is an omitted pronoun of matter (ḍamir al-shaʾn), and the lam in la-yaftinunaka is the lam that distinguishes the lightened "in" from the negative "in", so it does not express emphasis of the sentence.

The sentence ﴿and then they would have taken you as a close friend﴾ is coordinated with the sentence "and indeed they were about to tempt you". "Idhan" is a particle of conditional response, and the nun at its end is the nun of the word itself, not the nunation of declension (tanwin tamkin), so that it is a response to the verb yaftinunaka together with its complements, inserted between the two conjoined elements, so that the conjunction wa with idhan conveys the meaning of the particle of consequence (fa').

The reason for its being conjoined with the wa, rather than restricted to the particle of response, is that, since it is among their states in which they argued with the Prophet ﷺ and pressed him, it is fitting to be coordinated with the sentence of their states. The sense is: "If they turned you away from some of what We revealed to you, they would have taken you as a close friend." The lam in His saying "la-attakhadhukum" is the lam that prefaces an oath, since the speech is on the presumption of a condition, namely: "If they turned you away from that which We revealed to you, they would have taken you as a close friend." The lam in "la-attakhadhukum" is the lam of the response of "law", since it is a affirmative past verb.

Al-khalil: the close friend. It was discussed at His saying, ﴿And Allah took Ibrahim as a close friend (khalil)﴾ [al-Nisa: 125], in Surat al-Nisa.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verses 74–75:

[Page 174]
﴿And had We not made you firm, you would have almost inclined toward them a little.﴾ ﴿Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] in life and double [punishment] in death; then you would not find for yourself any helper against Us.﴾

It is permissible that this be an independent statement, not connected to His words ﴿And indeed, they almost tempted you﴾ [al-Isra': 73], based on what we have suggested in explaining the previous verse. This is another favour and another station of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) toward the polytheists. It is also permissible that it be a continuation of what precedes it, so that the inclining (rukun) toward them is inclining to what they asked of him, in the manner of the reports mentioned by the exegetes that have preceded.

"Lawla" (لَوْلا) is a particle of prohibition due to existence (حَرْفُ امْتِناعٍ لِوُجُودٍ), meaning it indicates the prohibition of its answer due to the existence of its condition, i.e., because of the existence of its condition.

"Al-tathbit" (التَّثْبِيتُ): making a thing firm, i.e., settled in its place, neither unsettled nor uprooted. It is used metaphorically for remaining in one's state without change. It was discussed earlier at His words, Exalted is He, ﴿and a strengthening from themselves﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah.

Tathbit is transitive to the pronoun of the Prophet, which denotes his person, but what is intended is the strengthening of his understanding and opinion. This is an attribution of a judgment to the essence, with some of its states intended according to the indication of the context, like ﴿Forbidden to you are your mothers﴾ [al-Nisa': 23]. So the meaning is: Had We not made your opinion firm, confirming it upon what it was in dealing with the polytheists, you would have nearly inclined toward them.

The lam in ﴿laqad kidta tarkanu ilayhim﴾ may be the lam of the answer to "lawla," and it is necessarily attached to its answer to establish the connection between it and the condition.

The meaning according to the first view regarding the placement of this verse: inclining is general over things which are likely to lead to inclining, but inclining is negated from its root, owing to the strengthening through infallibility, just as the polytheists' attempt to tempt him away from what was revealed to him was negated, by Allah's diverting them from carrying out their temptation.

[Page 175]
The meaning according to the second view: Had We not preserved you from error in ijtihad, and shown you that the benefit of firmness in religion and honouring its followers, even if they are of the weak among the people of this world, is not opposed by the benefit of winning over the hearts of the polytheists, even if the Muslims were content with humiliation of themselves for the sake of conciliating the polytheists. Showing leniency in matters of religion makes the polytheists hope to advance to asking for things far beyond what they asked. So the benefit of holding firmly to a resolute stance with them outweighs the benefit of being soft and agreeing with them. That is, there is no benefit in that. Had all this not been the case, you would have nearly inclined toward them a little, that is, you would have leaned toward them, that is, you would have promised them agreement to some of what they asked of you, relying on the evidence of an apparent lesser benefit and neglecting a hidden greater benefit, being deceived by the lightness of some of what they asked in comparison with the greatness of what they promised in return of their faith.

Ruku' (الرُّكُونُ): inclining with a side (rukn), i.e., with a side of the body, and it is used for agreement by the relation of proximity. It was mentioned earlier at His words ﴿And do not incline toward those who have done wrong﴾ in Surat Hud. Its opposite is used for opposition in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿And when We bestow favour upon man, he turns away and distances himself﴾ [al-Isra': 83] in this surah.

"Shay'an" (شَيْئًا) is in the accusative as an absolute object of "tarkanu," meaning some inclining. The reason for departing from the verbal noun of tarkanu is seeking lightness, since the verbal noun of tarkanu, which is al-ruku', is heavy, so leaving it is more eloquent. He did not limit himself to "qalilan" because the indefiniteness of "shay'an" conveys diminution, so mentioning it prepares for emphasising the meaning of diminution. For the word "shay'" (thing), by its deep indefiniteness regarding the kind of what it is attached to or the kind of existence in general, conveys diminution mostly, like His words, Exalted is He, ﴿so do not take from him anything﴾ [al-Nisa': 20].

The second "idhan" (إذَنْ) is the answer to ﴿kidta tarkanu﴾. Because it is an answer, it is separated from conjunction, since there is no requirement for it. The inclining of the Prophet (ﷺ) toward them is not occurring nor approaching occurrence, because the verse has negated it by four matters: "lawla" of prohibition; the verb of approximation, which implies that inclining did not occur, but approaching it did; the belittling derived from "shay'an"; and the diminution derived from "qalilan."

That is, had We not made you understand the face of truth, you would have feared that you might approach a weak, slight inclining. But that did not occur. "Qad" has entered into the sphere of prohibition, so its realisation became non-existent. That is, had We not strengthened you, the closeness of your slight inclination would have been realised, but that did not occur, because We strengthened you.

The clause ﴿Then We would have made you taste double [punishment] in life﴾ is the answer to the clause ﴿you would have almost inclined﴾. The meaning: If you were to incline toward them, We would have made you taste double [punishment] in life and double in death. Because of the meaning of conditionality in "idhan," the clause is left without being linked by a particle of consequence. The meaning is: You nearly inclined, so We would have made you taste.

"Al-dif'" (الضِّعْفُ) with a kasra on the dad: an equivalent of the quantity of a thing that has quantity. It is therefore only ever specified by its kind, verbally or by implication, like His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Whoever of you commits a clear immorality, her punishment will be doubled twofold﴾ [al-Ahzab: 30], i.e., twice what was prepared for that immorality. Since this is so, it is permissible to use it without specification, relying on the specification of the context, as here, for the mention of tasting in the context of warning indicates that it is tasting a punishment described as a double.

Then, "al-dif'" is applied here to the strong and severe, because the dif' cannot be taken in its literal sense, as there is no knowledge of the measure of punishment whose doubling is intended, like His words ﴿so give them a double punishment of the Fire﴾, and this was discussed in Surat al-A'raf.

The attribution of "al-dif'" to "al-hayah" (life) and to "al-mawt" (death) is in the sense of "fi" (in), since the implied sense of "fi" between two terms in a genitive construction is not restricted to the attribution of things attributed to times. So the estimate is: We would have made you taste a double in life and a double in death. The double punishment of life is the accumulation of calamities and afflictions during the period of life, that is, the lifespan, with the removal of what he used to receive of joy and happiness through the completion of his call and the orderliness of his community, namely that his enemies would gain power over him. The punishment of death is that he would die distressed and humiliated among disbelievers who see that they have triumphed over him after having been close to falling before him.

It seems that His words ﴿and double [punishment] of death﴾ are in continuation of the double of life, so the meaning becomes: We would have made you taste a double of life until death. The intended sense of "double of death" is not the punishment of the Hereafter, because if the Prophet (ﷺ) had inclined toward them a little, that would have been from ijtihad and seeking the benefit of religion in his view, and there is no punishment in the Hereafter for ijtihad, since the otherworldly punishment only occurs for opposition in obligation. Allah permitted His Prophet ijtihad and made for the one who errs in his ijtihad a reward, as established in the explanation of His words, Exalted is He, ﴿Had there not been a prior decree from Allah, a great punishment would have touched you for what you took﴾ [al-Anfal: 68] in Surat al-Anfal. As for the calamities and afflictions of this world, they are caused by causes of errors and mistakes, so good intention does not avert them if its holder has erred the right course. So reflect upon these meanings with the reflection of people of understanding. For this reason the customary expression used for the punishment of the Hereafter was departed from, and here it is expressed as ﴿double [punishment] of life and double [punishment] of death﴾.

The clause ﴿then you would not find for yourself any helper against Us﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿We would have made you taste﴾.

Its position is to affirm that there is no escape from that tasting. "Thumma" (ثُمَّ) is for sequence of rank, since the lack of escape from punishment is more important than tasting it, so its rank in importance is higher. "Al-nasir" (النَّصِيرُ): the helper who rescues from defeat, or who avenges the defeated. That is, you would not find for yourself anyone who would support you, so as to turn us away from inflicting that upon you, or avenge you against us.

﴿And they had almost tempted you away from the land to expel you from it; and then they would not have remained after you except a little.﴾ ﴿This is the way [of dealing] with those whom We sent before you of Our messengers, and you will not find any alteration in Our way.﴾

This is a conjunction with the clause ﴿And they had almost tempted you﴾ [al-Isra: 73], enumerating their evil deeds. The pronouns refer to the same subjects.

Al-istifza' (incitement) is to provoke someone to depart. It is an istif'al form from (fazza), meaning he left the place. That is, they almost sought to make you a fāzz, i.e., one who departs from Makkah. The meaning of this verb was discussed earlier at the words ﴿and incite whoever you can﴾ [al-Isra: 64] in this surah. The meaning is: they almost expelled you from your land. They intended to expel him by force, but then Allah turned them away from this, so that his departure would be without compulsion, when he left as an emigrant without their knowledge. For they later decided to keep him among them until they killed him.

The definite article in (al-ard), "the land," is the definite of prior reference (ta'rif al-'ahd), i.e., your land, which is Makkah.

The phrase ﴿to expel you﴾ is a causal clause explaining the incitement, meaning: an incitement with the aim of expulsion.

By "expulsion" is meant departing from the place without return. From this perspective it is made the cause of the incitement, because incitement is more general than expulsion.

The clause (﴿And then they would not remain after you except a little﴾) is either conjoined to the clause ﴿And they had almost﴾, or it is a parenthetical interjection at the end of the speech, in which case the wāw is for interjection, and (idhan) is an adverb of time for the verb ﴿they would not remain﴾, and it is (idh), which is always attached to a clause.

It is also possible that (idhan) is a particle of answer and consequence to a preceding statement. This is the one whose nūn is a letter of the word, but it has frequently been written with an alif in the form of the nunated noun

[Page 179]

and the basic rule is that the verb after it is in the subjunctive, governed by an implied (an). When it comes after a conjunction, the imperfect verb after it may be either in the indicative or the subjunctive. It is also possible that (idhan) is an adverb of time, with its tanwin being a replacement for an omitted clause, according to a group of Kufan grammarians. This is not far-fetched. Do you not see that when it comes after a conjunction, the imperfect verb after it is rarely in the subjunctive, because the sense of causation is absent, and because in that case the sense of answer and consequence does not appear in it?

The estimated meaning is: "And then they would have expelled you," or "And then you would have departed, they would not remain after you except a little."

The majority of readers read (﴿khalfaka﴾), and (khalfaka) is meant to mean "after you." The root meaning of khalf is "behind," and it is used figuratively for "after," i.e., they would not remain after you.

Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Hafs, and Khalaf read (﴿khilafaka﴾), which is a dialectal variant of khalf. It was discussed earlier at the words ﴿in their seat, against the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Tawbah: 81].

Al-lubth is staying in a place. That is, they would not settle in Makkah; rather they would go out from it and not return. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) left after this as an emigrant, and they were the cause of his departure, so it is as if they had expelled him, as was discussed earlier at the words of Allah, ﴿and expel them from where they expelled you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 191] in Surat al-Baqarah. Those who caused his expulsion and incited their people against him did not remain after him except a little, then they went out to the battle of Badr, where they met their death, and did not return. The threat was fulfilled against them. Allah spared the common people and the rabble, because their scheming was weak, so Allah willed that they enter Islam after that.

The verse contains an allusion that the Messenger would go out of Makkah, and that those who would expel him, i.e., those who caused his departure, would not remain in Makkah after him except a little.

Al-sunnah is the custom and the course of conduct that its practitioner adheres to. The discussion of whether it is a fixed noun or a verbal noun was presented earlier at the words of Allah, ﴿Systems have passed before you﴾ [Al 'Imran: 137], i.e., it is Allah's custom with every

[Page 180]

messenger whom his people expelled: they would not remain after him. Hud went out from the homes of 'Ad to Makkah, Salih went out from the homes of Thamud, Ibrahim and Lut went out, and their peoples were destroyed. Thus the idafa (construct) of (sunnah) to ﴿those whom We sent﴾ is a looser connection, meaning: Our custom concerning them, as shown by His saying ﴿and you will not find any alteration in Our way.﴾ Its idafa to the pronoun of majesty (Allah) is the true idafa.

The phrase ﴿the way of those whom We sent﴾ is in the accusative as an absolute object (mafʿul mutlaq). If (sunnah) is a verbal noun, then it is a substitute for its verb, and the estimated meaning is: "We established that for those whom We sent before you of Our messengers," i.e., for their sake. When he turned from the verb to the verbal noun, the verbal noun was made an idafa to what is connected to the verb, as the verbal noun is made an idafa to its object, by way of extension. If (sunnah) is a fixed noun, its accusative status is as a circumstantial (ḥāl), by interpreting it as having a derived meaning.

The clause ﴿the way of those whom We sent﴾ is a resumptive explanatory clause (istinaf bayani), explaining the reason why their remaining after him would be only a little. Allah established this custom for His messengers because the conspiracy of peoples to expel them calls for the wisdom of Allah, so that His will is connected to His command to them to emigrate, lest they remain looked upon with disgrace among their people and neighbors, in a manner similar to what the Arabs called khal' (the disowning of a member of the tribe).

The clause ﴿and you will not find any alteration in Our way﴾ is a parenthetical interjection completing the explanation.

The meaning is: that matter is certain to occur, because We have applied it to the earlier nations, and because Our custom does not change.

The expression ﴿you will not find﴾ is an emphatic negation, as in His saying ﴿and you will not find most of them grateful﴾ [al-A'raf: 17] in Surat al-A'raf.

Al-tahwil (alteration) is the change of a state, which is substitution. Among the strange interpretations is that the meaning is: the Jews said to the Prophet, "Go to the land of Syria, for it is the land of the prophets." The Prophet accepted their statement and set out on the expedition of Tabuk, intending only Syria. When he reached Tabuk, Allah revealed this

[Page 181]

verse. This narration is false. The cause of the expedition of Tabuk is well known in the books of hadith and biography. On account of this narration, a group said that the verse is Medinan, as was mentioned earlier at the beginning of the surah.

[Page 178]
