﴿Establish the prayer at the decline of the sun until the darkness of the night, and the recitation of dawn. Indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed.﴾

The legislation of the five daily prayers for the community occurred on the night of the Isra' (the Night Journey), as is established in the authentic hadith. However, it was not recorded in the widely transmitted legislation (mutawatir). The Prophet only conveyed it to his Companions, so it was likely that it would not be known to others among the Muslims who came after them. Also, the verse specified times for the prayers after their obligation had been established. Therefore, this verse came in this surah, which was revealed after the event of the Isra', to gather the legislation that was prescribed for the community at that time. It begins with His saying, ﴿And your Lord has decreed that you not worship except Him﴾ [Al-Isra: 23], and so on. Thus the sentence is a new independent sentence (isti'naf ibtida'i). Its placement after what precedes it is because Allah, when He bestowed favour upon the Prophet (ﷺ) with protection and victory, reminded him to be grateful for the blessing by commanding him with the greatest worship by which he serves Him, and with increasing in it, seeking an increase of blessing upon him, as indicated by His saying at the end of the verse, ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praised station﴾ [Al-Isra: 79].

The address in the command is to the Prophet (ﷺ), but it has been established in the Qur'anic usage that when the Prophet is addressed with a legislative ruling, his community is included in it, unless there is evidence that the ruling is specific to him. The Muslims knew this, and it was so widespread among them that they would not ask about a ruling's specificity except when there was a strong possibility of it. For example, one of them asked: "Is this for us alone, or for ever?" He said: "Rather, it is for ever."

The word iqamah (establishing) is used metaphorically for persistence and constancy, and it has already been discussed at His saying, ﴿and who establish the prayer﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 3], at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

The lam in ﴿li-dulūk al-shams﴾ is the lam of timing (lam al-tawqit), and it has the meaning of "at" ('inda).

Dulūk (the decline) is one of the states of the sun. It has been used with the meaning of the sun's passing from the middle of an imaginary arc in its daily course. It has also been used with the meaning of the sun's inclination by about three-quarters of that arc, which is the time of 'Asr. And it has been used with the meaning of its setting. Thus the word dulūk has become homonymous (mushtarak) in these three meanings.

Ghasaq is darkness, which is the cessation of the remaining rays of the sun when the darkness of the horizon of sunset becomes equal to the darkness of the rest of the horizon. This is the time of the disappearance of the twilight (shafaq), and that is the time of 'Isha', which is called al-'atamah, meaning darkness.

The verse includes four times. Dulūk encompasses three times through the use of the homonym in its meanings, and the indication (qarinah) is clear. From the particle ilā (until), which denotes an endpoint, it is understood that in those times there are prayers, because the endpoint was for the act "Establish the prayer." So the endpoint requires the repetition of establishing the prayer. The intended meaning is not an endpoint for a single prayer whose time is made wide, because that understanding is rejected by what the lam in His saying ﴿li-dulūk al-shams﴾ indicates, namely the obligation to establish the prayer at the stated time, since that is the obligatory or the most complete (performance). The Prophet's practice (ﷺ) has further clarified the verse.

As for the extent of the time's breadth, it is known from other evidences, and there is disagreement among the jurists about it. The word dulūk has no equivalent in any other word.

It has been established in the hadith of Abu Mas'ud al-Ansari in al-Muwatta' that the beginning of the time is what is intended. It has been established in the mursal hadith of 'Ata' ibn Yasar in al-Muwatta' (mursal: one in which the Successor omits the Companion), and in the connected (mawsul) version from Anas ibn Malik in Ibn 'Abd al-Barr and others: "Indeed, for the dawn prayer there is a time, which has a beginning and an end." This is also established for each prayer through many reports, except for Maghrib, on which the report is silent. Therefore the views of the jurists differed concerning it, between halting at what is narrated and analogizing its time to the times of the other prayers. The latter is more preponderant, because extending the time of the prayer is an ease for the one praying, and it suits the facilitation of the religion.

Since the ghasaq was made the endpoint of the times, it is understood that the intended meaning is the beginning of the ghasaq, as is the customary practice with an endpoint introduced by ilā. Thus it is understood that the beginning of the ghasaq is a time for prayer. This is a wonderful combination.

Then He conjoined ﴿the recitation of dawn﴾ to the prayer. The implied sense is: "and establish the recitation of dawn," meaning the prayer with it. So the reciters and the majority of the commentators (mufassirun) have estimated it, so that it is known that for each of those prayers there is a recitation, like His saying, ﴿So recite what is easy of the Qur'an﴾ [Al-Muzzammil: 20], meaning: pray with it the night voluntary prayer (nafilah).

The mention of this was specified for the dawn prayer rather than others, because in its every rak'ah the Qur'an is recited aloud, and because its sunnah is to recite from the long surahs of the mufassal. Thus listening to the Qur'an by the followers is greater in it, and its recitation by the imam and the solitary worshipper (fadh) is also greater.

It is possible that the conjunction of ﴿and the recitation of dawn﴾ is a conjunction of a whole sentence, and that the speech is an incitement (al-igra'), with the implied sense: "and adhere to the recitation of dawn." This was said by al-Zajjaj. Thus it is understood that the recitation of the Qur'an in every prayer is obligatory (hatm).

This is general concerning the manner of the prayers and the quantities of Qur'an they contain, which was clarified by the widely transmitted Sunnah and by the customary practice in knowing the times of the day and night.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, the recitation of dawn is ever witnessed﴾ is an explanatory resumptive sentence (isti'naf bayani), explaining the reason for specifying the dawn prayer by the name of the Qur'an: that the dawn prayer is witnessed, meaning attended. It has been explained that the angels of the night and the angels of the day attend it, as reported in the hadith: "The angels of the night and the angels of the day gather at the dawn prayer." This is an increase in its excellence and blessing. Also, most worshippers attend it, because its time is a time of vigour, and after it people wait for the sunrise to go out to their work, so the hearing of the Qur'an increases at that time.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 79:

﴿And during the night, perform the tahajjud (night prayer) with it as a supererogatory act for you; it may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station.﴾ It is coordinated (ʿatf) with ﴿and the Qur'an of dawn﴾ [al-Isra': 78], for it is, in implied meaning, a full clause, since it is an object (maʿmul) of the verb aqim (establish).

The prepositional phrase governed by tahajjad (perform the night prayer) has been placed before its complement, out of concern for it and as an encouragement toward it. By this fronting it acquires the sense of a conditional and a consequent, so its complement is treated as the consequent, and the particle of consequence (fa') is introduced upon it. This usage occurs with adverbials and prepositional phrases fronted before what they govern, and it is an eloquent usage. Among its instances is the words of God Most High, ﴿And for that let the competitors compete﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 26], and the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Then in both of them, strive (fa-jahid)." It was discussed previously at the words of God Most High, ﴿So long as they remain upright toward you, be upright toward them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 7], in Surat Bara'ah.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Zamakhshari took His words ﴿And during the night﴾ to carry the sense of incitement (ighra'), on the basis that the accusative of ﴿and the Qur'an of dawn﴾ [al-Isra': 78] is by way of incitement. Thus ﴿perform tahajjud﴾ would be a consequence of the incitement, a consequence of the detailed upon the summary, and min (from) would be a noun meaning "some of" (ba'd), like the one in His words ﴿Among those who are Jews, they distort the words﴾ [al-Nisa': 46]. This is also a good interpretation.

The pronoun in bihi refers to the Qur'an mentioned in His words ﴿and the Qur'an of dawn﴾ [al-Isra': 78], even though the antecedent is restricted by being at dawn, while what is mentioned here is intended in its unrestricted sense, like your saying, "I have a dirham and its half," meaning half a dirham, not half of the dirham you have. The bi' is causal (sababiyyah).

Page 185
Tahajjud means prayer in the course of the night. It is a noun derived from hujud, which is sleep; the root of the tafaʿʿul form in it indicates removal, like taharruj and atamm. Nafilah means an increment of a beloved matter.

The lam in laka is attached to nafilatan and is the lam of cause, meaning "a supererogatory act for your sake." In this there is evidence that the command to perform tahajjud is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ), so the command is for obligation, and by this it is counted among the obligatory prayers: some of them are obligatory upon him and upon the community, and some are obligatory upon him alone. It is known from this that it is encouraged for him, as the verse in Surat al-Muzzammil explicitly states, ﴿Indeed your Lord knows that you stand [in prayer] almost two-thirds of the night, or half of it, or a third of it, and a group of those with you﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20], up to His words ﴿what is easy of it﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 20]. In this imposition upon him there is an increase of honor for him, and for this reason it is followed by the promise that God will raise him to a praiseworthy station. Thus the clause ﴿it may be that your Lord will raise you﴾ is a justification for specifying him with the obligation of tahajjud. The expression of hope (raja') from God Most High is a promise, so the meaning is: "that your Lord will certainly raise you to a praiseworthy station."

Al-Maqam: the place of standing. What is meant by it is a place designated for a great matter, since it is the nature of such a place that people stand in it and do not sit; otherwise it would be a majlis (assembly).

Maqaman is in the accusative as an adverb of place governed by yab'athaka.

The description of the station as "praiseworthy" is a metaphorical description; the praiseworthy one is the one who stands in it, meaning that his effect there is praised, owing to his benefit to those who are in that station. For this reason the praiseworthy station has been explained as the greatest intercession (al-shafa'ah al-'uzma).

In Sahih al-Bukhari, from Ibn 'Umar: "People will become kneeling (juthan), with the jim vowelled with a damma and the thaʾ lightened, meaning in groups, on the Day of Resurrection; every community will follow its prophet, saying: 'O so-and-so, intercede,' until the intercession reaches the Prophet, and that is the day on which God raises him to the praiseworthy station." In Jami' al-Tirmidhi, from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said concerning His words ﴿it may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾: it is the intercession." He said: "This is a hasan sahih hadith."

The description of the intercession has come in detail in Sahih al-Bukhari, and it is that station in which all the people of the gathering praise him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 80:

﴿And say: "My Lord, cause me to enter a sound entrance, and cause me to exit a sound exit, and grant me from Yourself a supporting authority."﴾ When Allah the Exalted commanded him to give thanks through action, He followed it with the command to give thanks through speech, by supplicating Allah to grant success in leaving one place and entering another, so that his enemies would not be able to provoke him from the land to drive him out of it. This is also in keeping with His words, ﴿It may be that your Lord will raise you to a praiseworthy station﴾ [al-Isra' 79]. When He promised him that He would establish him in a praiseworthy station, it was fitting that he ask that this be his condition in every station he occupies. In this instruction there is a divine indication that Allah the Exalted would bring him out of Makkah to a place of emigration (hijrah). Apparently this verse was revealed shortly before the First Pledge of al-'Aqabah, which was the preface to the Hijrah to Madinah.

The mudkhal and mukhraj, with a damma on the mim and a fatha on the third letter, originally denote the place of entering and exiting. The derived noun from the transitive verb is chosen here to indicate that what is sought is an entering and an exiting that are facilitated by Allah the Exalted and occur by His permission. This is a supplication for every entering and exiting to be blessed, so that the one asked for and the one promised, namely the praiseworthy station, may be completed. This request encompasses every place into which he enters and every place from which he exits.

Al-sidq (sound, truthful): here it means the place and whatever is praiseworthy in its kind, because whatever is not praiseworthy is like a liar, since it disappoints the expectation of the one who experiences it.

This supplication embraces all entrances to whatever he is destined to enter and all exits from which he goes out, whether literally or figuratively. He followed it with a request for confirmation and victory in those entrances and exits, and in other regions far away and in the affairs undertaken there by him and by others among his followers and enemies, by granting victory to his followers and abandoning his enemies.

Al-sultan: a noun of the verbal noun form, used for authority, for proof, and for dominion. In this context it is a comprehensive word, following the manner of using a homonym in its several meanings, or it is of the general sense of the homonym. It includes that Allah grant him confirmation, proof, dominance and great dominion. Allah has given him all of that: He gave him victory over his enemies and subjected to him those who did not (yet) recognize the rising of the proof and the manifestation of the signs of truthfulness, and He supported him with awe.

Some interpreters explained the mudkhal and mukhraj as meaning: the exiting refers to the going out for the conquest of Makkah, and the entering refers to entering the land of Makkah as a conqueror. They took the verse to have been revealed shortly before the Conquest, and on this basis they held that it is Madani. But it has been objected from several angles, and it has already been noted that the entire surah is Makki according to the sound opinion.

Al-Nasir: an intensive form of al-nasir (the helper), meaning an authority that gives me victory. Since the work the Prophet was engaged in was the call to Islam, his being supported was confirmation in what he was undertaking. Thus this description becomes a restriction on the authority: he did not ask for an authority for domination over people, but asked for an authority to support him in what requires support, namely the conveying (of the message) and the spreading of Islam among people.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 81:

﴿And say: "The truth has come and falsehood has vanished. Indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish."﴾ This follows his being instructed to supplicate for the rectitude of his affairs and for divine support in them, by teaching him this proclamation, which announces that the answer to the inspired supplication will come about. It does so by presenting the promise of the manifestation of his cause in the form of a report about something already past.

Since the call of the Messenger was to establish the truth and nullify falsehood, the promise of the manifestation of the truth was a promise of the manifestation of the Messenger's cause and of his triumph over his enemies. God entrusted him with this sublime word until he uttered it on the day of the Conquest of Mecca, in the hearing of those who had been his enemies.

[Page 188]

When he entered the Ka'bah and found the idols in it and around it, he began to point at them with a staff and say: ﴿The truth has come and falsehood has vanished. Indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish.﴾ Thereupon those idols fell on their faces.

The "coming" of the truth is used figuratively for people's recognition of it, their acting upon it, and the victory of the one who upholds it over those who oppose him; this is a comparison of an apparent thing to a thing that was absent and then arrived.

(Zahaqa) means to perish after having existed, and its verbal noun is (al-zuhuq) and (al-zahaq). The "vanishing" of falsehood is a metaphor for its abandoning its adherents, as if it had been residing among them and then departed from them. The meaning is: the truth to which the Prophet calls became established and widespread, and the falsehood against which the Prophet ﷺ used to warn came to an end.

The clause ﴿Indeed, falsehood is ever bound to vanish﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyil) to the preceding sentence, because it contains a generality that encompasses every falsehood at every time. If this is the nature of falsehood, then steadfastness and victory are the nature of the truth, since it is the opposite of falsehood: when falsehood is removed, the truth remains.

Accordingly, the clause is a concluding clause for everything the preceding sentence contained. The meaning is: the truth has appeared among this community and falsehood has come to an end among it. This is the nature of falsehood in the earlier religious laws as well: it has no permanence.

The verb (kana) indicates that vanishing is the habit (shinshinah) of falsehood, and its condition in every age is that it appears and then perishes, as was previously explained in His exalted words ﴿Is it a wonder to mankind?﴾ [Yunus: 2] at the beginning of Surah Yunus.

[Page 189]

It is a conjunction (*'atf*) on the sentence ﴿And say: "The truth has come and falsehood has vanished"﴾ [al-Isra: 81], concerning the sense of affirmation (*ta'yid*) for the Prophet (ﷺ) contained in that sentence and the sentences preceding it, and the sense of enraging (*ighaza*) the polytheists, beginning from His saying ﴿And they had almost tempted you away from that which We revealed to you﴾ [al-Isra: 73]. After Allah had graced him by strengthening him with protection (*'isma*) from inclining toward them, and had given him the good news of victory over them and deliverance from their scheming, and after He had warned them that they would soon come to destruction and that their religion would soon collapse, He declared to him and to them in this verse that what causes their rage and fury, namely the Qur'an, which they hoped he would ask the Prophet to replace with a Qur'an that does not mention their idols with evil, is continually renewed and perpetual. In it is healing for the Messenger and his followers, and loss for the wrongdoers. Because the Qur'an is the source of truth and the refuter of falsehood, He followed His saying ﴿The truth has come and falsehood has vanished﴾ [al-Isra: 81] with His saying ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy﴾, and so on. For this reason, the present tense verb derived from the doubled root (*al-fi'l al-mudari' al-mushtaqq min fi'l al-mudda'af*) was chosen to report the sending down, to indicate renewal, repetition and abundance. It is a promise that this sending down will continue for a long time.

﴿ma huwa shifa'un﴾ is the object of *nunazzilu* (We send down). "*Min al-Qur'an*" (of the Qur'an) is an explanation (*bayan*) of the vagueness in *ma* (that which), like the one in His saying ﴿So avoid the abomination of the idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30], meaning: the abomination which is the idols. Placing the explanation first serves the purpose of attention to mentioning the Qur'an, together with the purpose of praising it through the relative construction (*mawsuliyya*) in His saying ﴿that which is a healing and a mercy﴾, etc., to indicate that this attribute is so firmly established in it that it is known by it. The meaning is: We send down healing and mercy, which is the Qur'an. *Min* here is neither partitive (*lil-tab'id*) nor for the beginning of a point (*lil-ibtida'*).

The essential meaning of *shifa'* (healing) is the removal of disease. It is used figuratively for the removal of whatever is deficiency, misguidance, or an obstacle to benefit, such as false beliefs, corrupt deeds, and blameworthy character traits, by likening it to the recovery from sickness, as in the saying of 'Antara:

*"It has healed my soul and cured its sickness, the saying of the knights: 'Woe to you, 'Antar, advance!'"*

The meaning is: the entire Qur'an is a healing and a mercy for the believers, and it increases loss for the disbelievers, because every verse of the Qur'an, of its commands, its prohibitions, its admonitions, its narratives, its parables, its promise and its threat, each verse of these contains guidance and the rectification of the condition of the believers who follow it. 

Page 190

And by contrast, it contains that which increases the rage of those who persist in wrongdoing (*zulm*), i.e., shirk. So they increase in rage, with aversion to the Qur'an, and thereby they increase in loss through the increase of their sins, their persistence in corrupt morals, and the distance between them and faith. This is like His saying ﴿As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice﴾ [al-Tawba: 124], and ﴿As for those in whose hearts is disease, it has increased them in defilement to their defilement, and they died while they were disbelievers﴾ [al-Tawba: 125].

In the verse there is evidence that the Qur'an contains verses by which one is healed from diseases and pains, and their specification has been reported in authentic reports (*al-akhbar al-sahiha*). So the verse includes them by the method of using a homonym (*mushtarak*) in both of its meanings. We have explained the foundation of this in the ninth introduction among the introductions of this tafsir.

As for the authentic reports regarding the recitation of specific verses for healing from described ailments, not to mention seeking refuge through verses of it from misguidance, they are numerous in Sahih al-Bukhari, Jami' al-Tirmidhi, and others. In the authentic hadith from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent us on a detachment (*sariyya*) of thirty riders, and we alighted at a people of the Arabs and asked them to host us, but they refused. Then the chief of the tribe was stung, and they came to us and said: 'Is there among you anyone who can perform *ruqya* for the scorpion sting?' I said: 'Yes, but I will not do it until you give us something.' They said: 'We will give you thirty sheep.' He said: 'So I recited over him the Opening of the Book (al-Fatiha) seven times, and he was healed.'" The hadith continues, and in it: "Until we came to the Messenger of Allah and I informed him. He said: 'How do you know that it is a *ruqya*?' I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, something was cast into my heart' — i.e., inspiration (*ilham*) which Allah inspired — He said: 'Eat, and feed us from the sheep.'" This is an affirmation by the Prophet (ﷺ) of the soundness of Abu Sa'id's (may Allah be pleased with him) inspiration.

[Page 191]

﴿And when We bestow favour upon man, he turns away and withdraws to one side; and when harm touches him, he is despairing.﴾ Since the Qur'an was a great blessing for people, and the turning away of the polytheists from it was a great deprivation for them of many good things, and since it is not the way of people of sound minds to be content with being deprived of good, the report that the wrongdoers increase in loss was a strange one. By its nature it should stir in the hearers' souls the question of its cause. He followed this with an explanation of the psychological cause that throws the intelligent into the pit of this deprivation, after their preoccupation with the blessing they have, which they desire and are infatuated with. This blessing falls short of the summit of those blessings from which they are deprived, were it not for the desire attached to it and the delusion that presents it as the ultimate goal. It is only heading toward a near end, as indicated by His saying, ﴿Leave Me with the deniers, the possessors of luxury, and give them respite a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 11], and His saying, ﴿Let not the strutting of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you; it is a brief enjoyment﴾ [Al 'Imran: 196].

So the content of this sentence is intended in itself, and its clarification was gained by its occurrence after the preceding sentence.

The definite article in "al-insan" (man) is the generic definite article (ta'rif al-jins), and it indicates istighraq (comprehensiveness, i.e., all-inclusiveness). It is a customary ('urfi) istighraq, meaning most individuals of mankind, because most people at that time were disbelievers and most Arabs were polytheists. The meaning is: when We bestow favour upon the polytheists, they turn away, and when harm touches them, they despair. This is the opposite of the state of the people of faith, for whom the Qur'an was a healing for their souls, gratitude for blessing is among their characteristics, and patience in adversity is among their traits.

By "bestowing" (in'am) is meant giving a blessing, not the complete blessings of faith and divine success, as in His saying, ﴿the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour﴾ [al-Fatiha: 7], and His saying, ﴿with those upon whom Allah has bestowed favour of the prophets, the truthful, the martyrs and the righteous﴾ [al-Nisa': 69].

[Page 192]

Al-i'rad (turning away) is avoidance, the opposite of approaching. It was discussed earlier at His saying, ﴿So turn away from them and admonish them﴾ [al-Nisa': 63] in Surat al-Nisa', and at His saying, ﴿And when you see those who engage in vain talk concerning Our verses, turn away from them﴾ [al-An'am: 68] in Surat al-An'am.

Al-nP'i (withdrawing) is distance. It was discussed at His saying, ﴿and they keep away from it﴾ [al-An'am: 26] in Surat al-An'am.

Al-janib (side) is the flank, the part of the body where the hand is, and there are two sides: right and left.

The ba' in His saying bi-janibihi (with his side) denotes accompaniment, meaning he withdraws accompanied by his side, i.e., keeping his side away. Withdrawing with the side is a figure of speech for shrinking back from something. 'Antarah said:

"As if he were drawing away with the side of his wild drum from the lilting of the evening, one who is startled."

So what is conveyed by His saying, ﴿and withdraws to one side﴾, is turning away from worship and gratitude. This is not the meaning conveyed by "turns away", so it is not an emphasis of it. The meaning is: he turned away and went far off.

The object of ﴿turns away and withdraws﴾ is omitted, because the context indicates it from His saying, ﴿When We bestow favour upon man﴾. The meaning is: he turned away from Us and shrank back from Us, that is, from Our worship, Our command and Our prohibition.

Ibn 'Amir, in the transmission of Ibn Dhakwan, and Abu Ja'far read (wa-na'a) with an alif after the nun and then a hamza. This is metathesis (qalb makani), because the Arabs may seek to lighten the hamza when it comes after a consonant that is followed by a long vowel, and so they transpose the long vowel before the hamza, since its occurrence after the long vowel is lighter. Of this is their saying ra'a for ra'a (to see), and their saying aram for arw'am, the plural of ri'm (white gazelle). It was also said that na'a in this reading means "became heavy", i.e., in regard to gratitude, which has the same meaning as His saying, ﴿but he clung to the earth﴾ [al-A'raf: 176].

[Page 193]

The clause ﴿And when harm touches him, he is despairing﴾ is an ihtiras (precautionary qualification), lest the hearer suppose from the restriction in His saying, "And when We bestow favour", that when the blessing is removed from him his condition becomes righteous. So He made clear that his state is constant in ingratitude in both ease and hardship. When the blessing is removed from him, he does not desist from polytheism and disbelief and repent to Allah. Rather, he despairs of good and remains bitter and constricted of breast, not knowing how to remedy his situation.

There is no contradiction between this verse and His saying in Surat Fussilat, ﴿And when harm touches him, he has long supplication﴾ [Fussilat: 51], as will come there.

His saying ﴿he is despairing﴾ (ya'us) indicates the intensity of his despair, since the intensive pattern (mithal al-mubalagha) was formed for it, and with it was inserted the verb "kana" (was), which indicates the firmness of the action, to express wonder at his state at the time harm touched him. This is because the state of adversity is more conducive to thinking about the means of removing it, unlike the state of turning away at a time of blessing, which is a state in which self-conceit over the blessing one has is not surprising.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 84:

﴿Say: Each acts according to his own manner (shakilah), but your Lord knows best who is best guided in the way.﴾ This is a tadhyil (a concluding sentence that reinforces the meaning of what precedes it), and it serves as a conclusion (tanhiyah) to the theme that began with His words ﴿Your Lord is He who drives the ships for you in the sea, that you may seek of His bounty﴾ [al-Isra: 66], which returns to reminding people of God Most High's blessings upon them within the course of proving that He alone is the One who disposes of affairs, and to warning against the consequences of ingratitude for blessings. Since two groups were mentioned within that context, in His words ﴿the Day We shall summon every people with their leader﴾ [al-Isra: 71], and His words ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers, and it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss﴾ [al-Isra: 82],

and because of the generality contained in the word kull (each), the sentence is a tadhyil.

The tanwin (nunation) of kull is the tanwin of 'iwad (compensation) for the omitted genitive complement, meaning: "each person of those covered by the generality of His words ﴿And whoever is blind in this world will be blind in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Isra: 72], and His words ﴿...a mercy for the believers, and it does not increase the wrongdoers except in loss﴾ [al-Isra: 82], and His words ﴿And when We bestow favour upon man﴾ [al-Isra: 83]."

The shakilah (manner) is the way and conduct that a person has become accustomed to and grown up upon. Its origin is shakilat al-tariq (the branch of the road), which is the side path branching off from it. Al-Nabigha said, describing a garment to which he likens the lanes of the road:

"It has side-paths that lead off singly, and turns back to every one with two lights, its branches clearly visible."

This is the best explanation given for shakilah here, and this sentence in the verse functions like a proverb.

Following from it is His words ﴿So your Lord knows best who is best guided in the way﴾, a comprehensive statement that teaches people the all-encompassing knowledge of God, encourages the believers, and warns the polytheists, while casting doubt on the truth of their religion, so that perhaps they will reflect, like His words ﴿And indeed, either we or you are surely upon guidance﴾ [Saba: 24].

[Page 195]

The placement of this verse among the verses around it, as its arrangement suggests, indicates that the referent of the pronoun in ﴿يَسْألُونَكَ﴾ (They ask you) is the referent of the pronouns mentioned earlier. So those who asked about the soul were the Quraysh. al-Tirmidhi narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Quraysh said to the Jews, "Give us something to ask this man about." They said, "Ask him about the soul (al-ruh)." He said: So they asked him about the ruh, and Allah the Exalted revealed ﴿They ask you about the soul﴾, the verse.

The apparent meaning of this is that they asked him only about the soul, and that the verse was revealed because of their question. In that case there is no difficulty in this question being singled out in this verse according to this narration, and thereby the position of this verse between the verses before it and the verses after it is explained as being caused by its revelation between the revelation of those verses.

Know that there were many ties between the Quraysh and the people of Yathrib (Medina): marriage, trade, and companionship. Each Yathribite had a companion in Mecca with whom he would stay when the other came to his city, just as there was between Umayya ibn Khalaf and Sa'd ibn Mu'adh. Their story is mentioned in the hadith of the Battle of Badr in the Sahih of al-Bukhari.

Ibn Ishaq narrated that the Quraysh sent al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and 'Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt to the rabbis of the Jews in Yathrib to ask them about the matter of the Prophet ﷺ. The Jews said to them: Ask him about three things, and they mentioned to them the People of the Cave, Dhu al-Qarnayn, and the soul, as will come in Surat al-Kahf. The Quraysh asked him about them. He answered about the People of the Cave and about Dhu al-Qarnayn with what is in Surat al-Kahf, and he answered about the soul with what is in this surah.

This narration raises a difficulty regarding why the answer to the question about the soul is separated from the answers to the other two questions by mentioning the answer to the soul question in Surat al-Isra', although it was revealed earlier than Surat al-Kahf. What resolves the difficulty is that it is possible that the question about the soul occurred separately the first time, and then was combined with the other two questions the second time.

It is also possible that the verse about the question of the soul was among what was appended to Surat al-Isra', as we will explain in Surat al-Kahf. The majority hold that all of it was revealed in Mecca. al-Tabari said, from 'Ata' ibn Yasar: the words ﴿And you have been given of knowledge only a little﴾ were revealed in Mecca.

As for what is reported in the Sahih of al-Bukhari from Ibn Mas'ud, that he said: "While I was with the Prophet ﷺ in a field in Medina, some Jews passed by. Some of them said to others, 'Ask him about the soul.' So they asked him about the soul, and the Prophet ﷺ remained silent and did not answer them anything. I knew that revelation was coming to him, so I stood in my place. When the revelation descended, he said: ﴿They ask you about the soul﴾, the verse." The reconciliation between this and the earlier hadith of Ibn 'Abbas is that when the Jews asked the Prophet ﷺ, the Prophet ﷺ thought they were closer than the Quraysh to understanding the soul, so he waited for revelation to descend to him with an answer for them clearer than what he had given the Quraysh. So Allah the Exalted repeated the sending down of the verse that had been revealed in Mecca, or commanded him to recite it to them, so that it would be known that they and the Quraysh were equal in their inability to grasp this reality, or that the answer does not change.

That said, what appears to me to be preponderant is that there is confusion in what the biographers (ahl al-siyar) mention, and that the Quraysh took something from the Jews and something from the Christians. The Quraysh had contact with the Christians of Syria during their summer journey to Syria, because the story of the People of the Cave was not among the affairs of the Children of Israel; rather it is among the concerns of the Christians, on the basis that the People of the Cave were Christians, as will come in Surat al-Kahf. Likewise, the story of Dhu al-Qarnayn, if it refers to Alexander the Macedonian, appears to be among what the Christians were concerned with, because his conquests are linked to the history of the lands of the Romans. Therefore it is established that the Jews only instructed the Quraysh to ask about the soul. With this, the reason becomes clear for singling out the question about the soul in this surah, and for mentioning the other two stories in Surat al-Kahf. Moreover, it is possible that a question is repeated on various occasions, and that is the practice of those whose knowledge is limited, for they bring it out in every gathering.

Their question about the soul means that they asked him to explain the quiddity (mahiyyah) of what is expressed in the Arabic language by "the soul (al-ruh)," which everyone knows in general terms to be something that inheres in the body.

The word "al-ruh" is applied to the hidden, pervasive existent that spreads through the whole human body, whose effects are evident in perception and thought. It is what comes into being in the human body when it is an embryo, after one hundred and twenty days have passed since the drop of semen settled in the womb. This usage is the one in His saying, exalted be He: ﴿So when I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My soul﴾ [al-Hijr: 29]. This is also called the self (nafs), as in His saying: ﴿O reassured soul﴾ [al-Fajr: 27].

The word "al-ruh" is also applied to the noble being created by a divine command without an ordinary cause. From this is His saying: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit of Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52], and His saying: ﴿and a spirit from Him﴾ [al-Nisa': 171].

The word "al-ruh" is also applied to the angel who brings revelation to the messengers, namely Jibril, peace be upon him. From this is His saying: ﴿The Trustworthy Spirit has brought it down upon your heart﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 193].

The exegetes differed concerning which of these three meanings is the "soul" about which they asked here. The majority said: what is asked about is the soul in the first sense. They said: because it is the difficult matter whose reality has not become clear. As for the soul in the other two senses, it is likely that asking about it would be asking about the meaning of a Qur'anic technical term. It is established that the Jews asked about the soul in the first sense, because it is the one that occurs at the beginning of their book, which is the Book of Genesis of the Torah, in His saying in the first chapter: "and the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters." The soul in the other two senses does not occur in their books.

It is narrated from Qatada and al-Hasan that they asked about Jibril. But the more correct view is the first. In al-Rawd al-Unuf it is stated that the Prophet ﷺ answered them once, saying to them: "It is Jibril, peace be upon him." We have clarified this in Surat al-Kahf.

They asked only about the reality of the soul and the explanation of its quiddity, for it has occupied philosophers and scholars among the Shari'ah experts, because it is evident that in a living body there is something additional to the physical body, by which a person perceives, and with whose departure the body becomes stripped of will and perception. So it is known by necessity that in the body there is something additional to the outward and inward organs, which is not observed, since dissection has shown that the body of the dead has not lost any of the inward organs it had during life.

Since people's intellects were incapable of grasping the reality of the soul, the manner of its connection to the body, the manner of its removal from it, and its destiny after that removal, they were answered that

[Page 198]

the soul is from the command of Allah, meaning that it is a great being among the noble creatures in the sight of Allah, but it is among the things Allah has kept the knowledge of to Himself. The word "amr" may be synonymous with "shay'" (thing). So the meaning is: the soul is one of the great things that belong to Allah. The attribution of "amr" to the Name of Majesty is in the sense of the lam of specification, that is, a matter specific to Allah in the manner of exclusive knowledge.

The "min" (from) is partitive, so this usage is like His saying: ﴿And thus We have revealed to you a spirit of Our command﴾ [al-Shura: 52]. It may also be that "amr" means the command of creation. Then either the verbal noun itself is intended and "min" is the "min" of origin, as in His saying: ﴿Our command for a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it "Be," and it is﴾ [al-Nahl: 40], meaning the soul issues from Allah's command to bring it into being; or the verbal noun is used in the sense of the object, like "khalq" (creation), and "min" is partitive, meaning the soul is one of the things Allah commands, so the intended meaning of "al-ruh" is Jibril, peace be upon him, that is, the soul is one of the created beings whom Allah commands to convey revelation. On both interpretations, the verse is not an answer to their question.

Ibn al-'Arabi narrated in al-Ahkam from Ibn Wahb, from Malik, that he said: "No answer was given to him on this." That is, the words ﴿Say: The soul is from the command of my Lord﴾ are not an answer explaining what they asked about; rather they are a diversion from seeking it, and an informing them that this is from the knowledge that they have not been given. All the possibilities are intended, and it is a comprehensive statement. In it there is an allusion to defining the soul by genus, which is a descriptive definition (rasm).

The clause ﴿And you have been given of knowledge only a little﴾ may be among what Allah commanded His Messenger to say to the questioners, so the address is to the Quraysh or to the Jews who instructed them. It may also be a concluding remark (tadhyil) or an interjection (i'tiraD), so the address is to everyone who is fit to be addressed, and the addressees vary in the little that is excepted from the knowledge that has been given. It may also be an address to the Muslims.

By "knowledge" here is meant the known, that is, what is capable of being known, or from the things known by Allah. Its description as "little" is in relation to what is capable of being known among existents and realities.

In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi it is said: they, the Jews, said: "We were given much knowledge, the Torah, and whoever has been given the Torah has been given much good." So there was revealed: ﴿Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord are exhausted﴾ [al-Kahf: 109], the verse.

Clearer than this is what al-Tabari narrated: from 'Ata' ibn Yasar, who said: "It was revealed in Mecca: ﴿And you have been given of knowledge only a little﴾. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ emigrated to Medina, the rabbis of the Jews came to him and said: 'O Muhammad, has it not reached us that you say ﴿And you have been given of knowledge only a little﴾? Do you mean us or your people?' He said: 'Both of you are meant.' They said: 'You recite that we were given the Torah, and in it is an explanation of everything.' The Messenger of Allah said: 'It is little in the knowledge of Allah, and He has given you what, if you act upon it, will benefit you.' So Allah revealed: ﴿And if whatever trees on earth were pens and the sea, extended by seven more seas, were ink, the words of Allah would not be exhausted. Indeed Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise﴾ [Luqman: 27]."

This being said: those who tried to bring close an explanation of the quiddity of the soul, from among the philosophers and the Shari'ah scholars, through explanatory statements, produced only deficient descriptive definitions (rusum), taking in them remote genera and approximate properties that are not precisely fixed, and relying on effects some of which are real and some imaginary. All of them vary in closeness to explaining its particular properties and signs, according to the variation of their conceptions of its quiddity, which is based on the variation of the faculties of their perception. None of them amounts to more than imaginative and poetic descriptions expressing the effects of the soul in the human being.

Since the soul has been mentioned in this verse, and the questioners were turned away from their intended meaning for a sound purpose required by their state and the state of their time and place, it is not incumbent upon us to attempt, in general terms, to discover the reality of the soul. Knowledge-seekers now have means of knowledge through which the condition that required turning the questioners away in this verse has changed to some extent, and changes may occur in the future that increase the readiness of the people of knowledge to manifest some of the quiddity of the soul. Therefore we do not follow those who said that the reality of the soul must be withheld from explanation, because the Prophet ﷺ remained silent about it, so one should not go into the matter of the soul beyond its being existent. For the majority of scholars among the theologians (mutakallimun) are of the view

[Page 200]

Among the jurists, Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi in al-'Awasim and al-Nawawi in his commentary on Muslim held that this verse does not prevent scholars from investigating the soul (al-ruh), because it was revealed concerning a specific group of the Jews, and the Muslims were not intended by it. The majority of the theologians (al-mutakallimun) said: it is among the immaterial substances (al-jawahir al-mujarrada), and this is not far from the view of some of them that it is among the subtle bodies (al-ajsam al-latifa). Among the theologians of the Muslims, souls are created (hadithah), and this is the view of Aristotle (Aristaalis). The ancient philosophers (qudama' al-falasifa) said: they are eternal (qadima), and this is close to their intention in the claim that the world is eternal. The meaning of their being created (hadithah) is that they are created by God, Exalted is He. It was said: the souls were created before the creation of the bodies into which they are breathed, and this is the most sound view, in keeping with the apparent sense of the words of the Prophet (ﷺ). So they exist from eternity, like the existence of the angels and the devils. It was also said: they are created at the time God wills to bring life into the body into which they are placed. They agreed that souls remain after the perishing of their bodies, and that they will be present on the Day of Reckoning.

This is connected to His saying, "And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing" [al-Isra: 82]. The connection arose naturally: when His saying "Say: The Spirit is of the command of my Lord" [al-Isra: 85] included a comprehensive word of knowledge being imparted, and implied that the Ummah had been given some knowledge while being denied other knowledge, and that the knowledge of prophethood is among the greatest things it was given, He followed this with an admonition to be grateful for the blessing of knowledge, as a safeguard against the vanity of the self. This is because knowledge of things makes one proud of distinguishing oneself from those who lack it. So the reader is alerted to the fact that the One who granted knowledge is able to take it away. This was addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), because his knowledge is the greatest knowledge. If the existence of his knowledge is subject to the will of God, then what is to be thought of the knowledge of others? This is an allusion to the rest of the scholars. The speech is, on its surface, a warning, and it is a metaphorical expression of favour, as indicated by His saying after it, "Except as a mercy from your Lord; indeed His bounty towards you has been great," and an allusion warning the people of knowledge.

The lam is an introduction to the implied oath before the conditional clause, and the clause "We would surely take away that which We have revealed to you" is the answer to the oath. It is the indication of the answer to the condition and suffices in its place.

"Lanadhhabanna bil-ladhi awhayna" means "We would surely cause it to be taken away from you," and this is more emphatic than "nudhhibuhu," as was mentioned previously in His saying "Glorified is He who took His servant by night" [al-Isra: 1]. The referent of "alladhi" is the Qur'an.

"Thumma" (then) indicates sequence in rank, because the denial of hope of recovering what has been taken away is harder on the soul than its taking away. So mentioning it is more effective in alerting to gratitude and warning against vanity.

Al-wakil: the one to whom important matters are entrusted. What is meant here is the one who defends you and intercedes for you. Because of the sense of overpowering it contains, it is followed by "'ala" (against), and because of the sense of undertaking and pursuing it contains, it is followed by "bi" (with) for the object, meaning one who undertakes responsibility for that which We revealed to you. The sense of undertaking it is the undertaking of its recovery, because it stands in contrast to His saying "We would surely take away that which We have revealed to you," and because undertaking does not apply to the thing itself but to a state of it, so the speech proceeds with brevity.

Here He mentions "wakilan" (a guardian), and in the verse before it "nasiran" (a helper). This is because the meaning of this one is on the supposition of the removal of the blessing of selection, so demanding the return of the blessing is intercession and acting as an agent on his behalf, whereas the verse before it is on the supposition of inflicting punishment upon him, so defending against that punishment or avenging it is victory.

The exception in His saying "except as a mercy from your Lord" is disjunctive (munqati'), so the particle of exception in it carries the meaning of "but" (istidrak), a correction of what the conditional verb implied of the expectation of that, meaning:

but a mercy from your Lord has negated the will to take away that which We revealed to you, so it remains, not taken away.

This is an allusion to the preservation of the Qur'an and its safeguarding, as He said: "Indeed, We sent down the Reminder, and indeed We are its guardians" [al-Hijr: 9].

The position of "Indeed His bounty towards you has been great" is that of a reason for the disjunctive exception, meaning: but a mercy from your Lord prevented the will from attaching to the removal of that which We revealed to you, because His bounty towards you has been great, so He will not deprive you of the bounty of what He revealed to you. The addition of the verb "kana" (was) is for emphasis of the sentence, over and above its emphasis by the particle of emphasis, which is used with the meaning of causation and consequence.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 88:

﴿Say: "Indeed, if mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like, even if they were to one another assistants."﴾ This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) for the sake of increasing the favour (imtinan), and it is an explanatory resumptive sentence (isti'naf bayani) for the content of the clause ﴿Indeed, His favour upon you has been great﴾ [al-Isra': 87]. Its opening with "Say" is for the sake of giving it importance (lil-ihtimam). This is an exaltation (tanwih) that honours the Qur'an, and so this exaltation is a favour (imtinan) upon those who believed in it, who are the ones for whom it was a healing and a mercy, and it is a challenge (tahaddi) by way of incapacity to produce its like, directed at those who turned away from it, who are the ones it increases only in loss. The lam is a preparatory lam (muwatti'ah) for the oath.

The clause ﴿they would not produce its like﴾ is the answer to the omitted oath.

The answer was stripped of the lam that commonly accompanies the answer to an oath, out of disliking the combination of two lams: the lam of the oath and the lam of negation.

صفحة ٢٠٣
The meaning of "gathering" (al-ijtima') is agreement and unity of opinion, i.e., even if the minds of mankind and the jinn converged on each one of them producing the like of this Qur'an, they would not produce its like. Thus it is a gathering of opinion, not a gathering of cooperation, as is indicated by the emphasis in His words that follow: ﴿and even if they were to one another assistants﴾.

The mention of the jinn alongside mankind is for the sake of generalization, as one says, "Even if the people of the heavens and the earth gathered together." Also, because those challenged by the inimitability of the Qur'an used to claim that the jinn are able to perform great deeds.

By likeness to the Qur'an is meant likeness in the totality of eloquence and rhetoric, meanings, manners, and laws, and these are the aspects of the verbal and scientific inimitability of the Qur'an.

The clause "they would not produce" is the answer to the oath preceded by the lam, and the answer to the conditional "in" (in) is omitted, indicated by the answer to the oath.

The clause ﴿and even if they were to one another assistants﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "they would not produce."

And "law" (law) here is wasliyyah (concessive), which indicates that what follows it is something that one would suppose would not be included by what precedes it; its meaning was previously discussed at His words ﴿and even if he offered it in ransom﴾ [Al 'Imran: 91] in Al 'Imran.

Al-zahir means the helper, and the meaning: even if mankind and the jinn cooperated to produce its like, they would not produce its like; so how about them when they attempt that dispersed?

The benefit of this clause is to affirm the meaning of gathering indicated by His words ﴿if mankind and the jinn gathered together to produce the like of this Qur'an﴾: that it is a gathering united upon one work and one aim. And this verse is silencing to the polytheists in the challenge by the inimitability of the Qur'an.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 89:

﴿And We have certainly diversified for the people in this Qur'an every kind of example, but most of the people refused except disbelief.﴾ When Allah challenged the eloquent among the polytheists to produce something like it (i'jaz), He extended to them a mention of the virtues of the Qur'an over all other speech, incorporating within it a reproach to them, for they had deprived themselves of benefiting from what is in the Qur'an of every kind of example. Here is mentioned one aspect of its inimitability (i'jaz), namely what it comprises of the various types of examples (amthal). The word "mathal" was already mentioned in His words, ﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to present an example (mathal) of anything﴾ [al-Baqarah: 26] in Surat al-Baqarah. It is also permissible that "mathal" here means "hal" (state, condition), i.e., of every good state of meanings that is worthy of being illustrated and likened to something, which is further clarified in its kind.

So the clause ﴿And We have certainly diversified﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿Say: If mankind and the jinn gathered to produce the like of this Qur'an﴾ [al-Isra': 88], sharing with it in its previously explained ruling, for added favour and challenge.

Its emphasis with the oath-lam (lam al-qasam) and the particle of confirmation (harf al-tahqiq) is to refute the notions of the polytheists that it is from themselves; so the focus of the emphasis is the verb "sarrafna" (We diversified), which indicates that it is from Allah.

The word "tasrif" (diversification) was already mentioned just before, in His words, ﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an that they may be reminded﴾ [al-Isra': 41].

The qualifier "lil-nas" (for the people) was added in this verse but not in the previous verse, because this verse occurs in the context of challenge and inimitability, so people were intended by it as a primary aim, both its believers and its disbelievers; unlike the previous verse, which occurs in the context of rebuking the polytheists specifically, so they were known, as previously explained.

The reason for placing one of the two complements of the verb "sarrafna" before the other: mentioning the people is more important in this context, because the speech is directed toward challenging them and establishing proof against them. Although the mention of the Qur'an is more important in essence, incidental considerations are placed before essential considerations in eloquent speech, because essential considerations, having become firmly established in souls, become familiar; so incidental considerations are more precious to attain. From this category is the method of departing from what the apparent context requires. The more apparent view is that the definiteness in "al-nas" is for generality, as His words ﴿but most of the people refused﴾ require.

Mention of the complement of "tasrif" with His words ﴿from every kind of example﴾ is unlike the previous verse, because mentioning that is more effective in inimitability: the multiplicity of the purposes of speech is more forceful in rendering one incapable, of one who seeks to oppose it, of producing its like, since an eloquent person among the eloquent may be capable of one purpose but not capable of another. Thus their inability to oppose a single sura of the Qur'an, along with the multiplicity of its purposes, is a clear inability from two aspects: they were unable to produce its like, even in some of its purposes, as indicated by His words in Surat al-Baqarah ﴿then produce a sura like it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23]. Here "min" is partitive, and the tanwin on "mathal" is for magnification and honour, i.e., from every noble example, and what is meant is its nobility in the purpose of the illustration.

The "min" in His words ﴿from every kind of example﴾ is partitive, and "kull" (every) conveys generality; so the Qur'an comprises parts of all types of examples.

The object of "aba" (refused) is omitted for the indicator, i.e., refused to act upon it.

In His words "illa kufuran" there is an emphasis of a thing by what resembles its opposite, i.e., an emphasis in the form of deficiency, because of what it contains of raising hope that their refusal is not consistent. Then the exception comes confirming the meaning of what is excepted from, since disbelief (kufur) is more specific than the omitted object, which was omitted for the indicator. It is an exception of the "mufarragh" type (incomplete exception) on account of the sense of negation in the verb "aba", which is the condition of the incomplete exception, since the basis is the sense of negation, just as the exception from an interrogative used in the sense of negation, as in His words ﴿Was I anything but a human messenger?﴾ [al-Isra': 93].

"Kufur" with a damma on the kaf means the denial, i.e., they rejected what is in the Qur'an of guidance and obstinately opposed it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verses 90–93:

[p. 206]
﴿They say: "We will never believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth,﴾ ﴿or until you have a garden of date palms and grapevines and cause rivers to gush forth within it abundantly,﴾ ﴿or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed, or you bring God and the angels before us as a guarantee,﴾ ﴿or you have a house of gold, or you ascend into the sky. And we will not believe in your ascent until you send down to us a book that we can read." Say: "Glory be to my Lord! Am I anything but a human messenger?"﴾.

[The clause "wa qalu" (and they said) is conjoined to the clause ﴿fa-aba al-zalimuna illa kufuran﴾ [al-Isra' 99], meaning: they disbelieved in the Qur'an and demanded other miracles.]

The pronoun of the plural refers to most of the people who refused except disbelief, in view of this statement having been uttered among them, and they being content with it and colluding upon it whenever they came to know it. Hence it does not necessarily follow that each one of them said this entire statement; rather, some of them said all of it, or some of them said part of it.

Since their statement contains second-person pronouns, it is determined that some of them addressed the Prophet ﷺ directly, either in a single gathering or in several gatherings. Ibn Ishaq mentions that 'Utba ibn Rabi'a, Shayba ibn Rabi'a, Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, Zam'a ibn al-Aswad, al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya, Umayya ibn Khalaf, and others with them gathered after sunset at the Ka'ba and sent to the Prophet ﷺ asking him to come to them.

[p. 207]
So he hastened to them, eager for their guidance. They rebuked him for denigrating their intellects and attacking their religion, and they offered him whatever wealth he wished or leadership. He answered them that he was a messenger from God to them, and it was not fitting for him to seek anything but their counsel. When they saw his steadfastness, they moved on to demanding some of what God related of them in this verse.

It is also narrated that the one who asked for what is related in His words, Exalted is He, ﴿or you ascend into the sky﴾ to the end, was 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya al-Makhzumi. God related their refusal to believe with the particle (lan), which denotes perpetual negation, because that is how they themselves phrased it.

By "the earth" is meant the earth of Makkah, so the definite article is for prior reference. The reason for specifying it is that its land is scarce in water and far from gardens.

Al-tafjir is the verbal noun of fajjara (with doubled ʿayn), intensive of al-fajr, which is splitting with width; from it the dawn is named fajr, because the light splits the darkness in a long, wide cleft. Thus tafjir is stronger than mere fajr, being a severe splitting in view of its breadth. For this reason yanbu' (spring) fits here, and nahr (river) in His words ﴿And We caused a river to gush forth between them﴾ [al-Kahf 33] and His words ﴿so that you cause the rivers to gush forth﴾.

The majority read ﴿tufajjira﴾ with a dammah on the taʾ and a shaddah on the jim, as the imperfect of the doubled fajjara. ʿAsim, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a fatha on the taʾ, a sukun on the fa', and a dammah on the jim, unshaddah, as the imperfect of "fajara" like "nasara"; there is no iltifat in it for intensity, because the yanbu' itself indicates the intended meaning, or it expresses the varied forms of their statements that indicate firm determination in refusal.

The meaning of ﴿lan nu'mina laka﴾ is: "we will never affirm you as God's messenger to us."

Al-iman is at-tasdiq (affirmation), one says amanahu, i.e. saddaqahu, and it is frequently construed with the object introduced by the preposition lam, as He, Exalted, says ﴿You will not believe us﴾ [Yusuf 17] and ﴿So Lut believed him﴾ [al-'Ankabut 26]. This lam is of the kind that the author of Mughni al-Labib named lam al-tabyin (the lam of specification), but he failed to illustrate it with this verse and its like, for the object of the lam after the verb "nu'minu" is a direct object with no ambiguity with the subject. The lam is mentioned only for added clarification and emphasis. It may also be said that it serves to prevent confusion between the object of amana in the sense of saddaqa and the object of amana in the sense of making someone trustworthy; and His words ﴿None believed Musa except a few of his people﴾ [Yunus 83] have preceded in Surat Yunus.

Yanbu' is a name for a spring of abundant flow whose water never runs dry. The pattern yaf'ul is a non-analogical intensive form. Yanbu' is derived from the root n-b-ʿ, but names in this pattern vary: some have clear derivation, like yanbu' and yanbut, and some are obscure, like ya'bub for a horse that runs much. It is said it is derived from the figurative "abb" (pouring). There are also loanwords arabicized on the pattern yaf'ul, such as Yaksum, the name of an Abyssinian commander, and Yarmuk, the name of a river. Al-Hasan al-Saghani surveyed the words in Arabic on the pattern yaf'ul in a concise work arranged by the letters of the alphabet, and al-Suyuti said in al-Muzhir that Ibn Duraid devoted a chapter to it in al-Jamhara.

The garden, the date palms, the grapes and the rivers were discussed in His words ﴿Would any of you like to have a garden of date palms and grapevines with rivers flowing beneath it?﴾ [al-Baqara 266] in Surat al-Baqara.

They specified this garden as belonging to him, because it is the nature of a garden to belong exclusively to one specific owner. Thus they showed him that they did not seek the benefit of themselves through this proposal, but they sought its occurrence even if it were for the benefit of the one to whom it is proposed. The proposal is the gushing of water in barren land. They mentioned the existence of the garden only as a preparation for the gushing of rivers within it, as though they said: "until you cause a spring to gush forth for us, which gives drink to all the people, or you cause rivers to gush forth to water one garden, which will be that garden and its rivers yours. We are content with its occurrence, not seeking any benefit from it." This is like their saying: ﴿or you have a house of gold﴾.

[p. 208]
He mentioned the absolute object with His words "tafjiran" to indicate multiplication, because "tufajjira" had already sufficed to indicate intensity in splitting, so the bringing of its absolute object must be for intensity in number, like His words ﴿And We sent it down in sections﴾ [al-Isra' 106]. This suits His words "khilaluha" (within it), because the garden is threaded through by branches of the river to water the trees, so He gathered "al-anhar" (the rivers) in view of the water of the river dividing into many branches. The consensus of the readers on reading ﴿fa-tufajjira﴾ here with shaddah, despite their disagreement over the preceding word, supports this meaning. This is among the subtle meanings of the readings transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ, and they are among the many facets of the Qur'an's inimitability.

Their statement ﴿or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed﴾ is a transition from his being challenged with marvels containing benefits for them to being challenged with marvels containing harm for them. By this they intend to make him feel constrained, i.e., let him bring us a sign of that even if it harms us. This is a quotation of their words as they said them. Perhaps they intended by it to exaggerate their astonishment at that, so they combined making the falling be of the sky itself, and reinforced their astonishment with the parenthetical clause ﴿as you claimed﴾, indicating that no one would believe that. By this they meant His words ﴿If We will, We shall cause the earth to swallow them, or cause pieces of the sky to fall upon them﴾ [Saba' 9], and His words ﴿And if they see a piece of the sky falling, they would say: "A gathered cloud"﴾ [al-Tur 44], since it is a threat to them with the portents of the Hour and their standing before reckoning. They took "min" in His words ﴿kisfan min al-sama'﴾ [al-Tur 44] as partitive, meaning a fragment of the celestial bodies; therefore they refused to make the verb "tusqita" transitive to the substance of the sky itself. Know that this requires that these two verses, or one of them, were revealed before Surat al-Isra'; and that is not unlikely.

Kisaf (with kasra on the kaf and fatha on the sin) is the plural of kisfa, a piece of a thing, like sidra and sidar. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and Abu Ja'far read it so; the rest read it with a sukun on the sin, in the sense of the passive participle, i.e., "maksuf," meaning "maqtu'" (cut).

[p. 209]
Al-za'm: a statement that is far-fetched or impossible.

Al-qabil: a group of one kind. It is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of "al-malaika," meaning they are a particular unfamiliar group, as though they said: "or you bring a company of the kind of the angels."

Al-zukhruf: gold.

The verb "turqa" was given the locative particle "fi" (in) to indicate that ascent is a gradual progression through the heavens, like one who climbs a ladder or staircase.

Then they became inventive in their proposals and asked him, if he ascended, to send down to them a book from the sky which they could read, containing testimony that he had reached the sky. It is said the one who said this was 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Umayya, who said: "until you bring us a book with you, with four angels testifying for you."

Perhaps they meant that a complete book should descend upon them from the sky all at once, so that they would be denying the gradual revelation of the Qur'an, supposing that its being revealed in portions does not suit its being sent down from God; for gradual revelation, in their view, implies deliberation and contrivance in its composition. For this reason the Qur'an often explains the wisdom of its gradual revelation.

The lam in His words ﴿li-ruqiyyika﴾ may be the lam of specification, with "ruqiyyika" as the object of "nu'minu," like His statement ﴿we will never believe you﴾; so the claim of ascent is denied of him as something they would not affirm until a book descends upon them. It may also be the lam of cause, with the object of "nu'mina" omitted, indicated by His preceding words ﴿we will never believe you﴾, the sense being: "we will never affirm you because of your ascent," namely "that You send down to us a book." The meaning is that if he ascended into the sky, they would disbelieve their own eyes until he sent them a book they could see descending from the sky; and this is a sneer and mockery on their part.

Since their proposal was one of obstinate contention and stubbornness, God commanded him to answer them in a way that expresses wonder at their words with the phrase ﴿Glory be to my Lord!﴾, which is used to express wonder, as was mentioned at the opening of this surah; then with a rhetorical interrogative and the exclusive construction that restricts himself to humanity and messengership, a restriction relative to what they claim (i.e., I am not a lord who disposes of affairs and creates what is demanded of me); so how could I bring God and the angels? And how could I create on earth what has not been created in it?

The majority read "qul" (say) in the imperative form. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read "qala" (he said) with an alif after the qaf, in the past tense, as a report of the Messenger's ﷺ answer to their statement ﴿We will never believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth﴾, in the manner of iltifat (shift of grammatical person).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verses 90–93:

[p. 206]
﴿They say: "We will never believe you until you cause a spring to gush forth for us from the earth,﴾ ﴿or until you have a garden of date palms and grapevines and cause rivers to gush forth within it abundantly,﴾ ﴿or you cause the sky to fall upon us in pieces, as you claimed, or you bring God and the angels before us as a guarantee,﴾ ﴿or you have a house of gold, or you ascend into the sky.
