Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 17, verse 110:

﴿Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful. Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾

There is no doubt that this verse has a specific occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), since there is no reason to mention this option between calling upon God by His proper name and calling upon Him by the attribute al-Rahman specifically, without mentioning any other of God's attributes, such as al-Rahim, al-'Aziz, or other of the most beautiful attributes.

Then, after that, it is necessary to seek the connection (munasaba) with its place in this surah.

As for the occasion of its revelation, al-Tabari and al-Wahidi narrated, "from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: The Prophet ﷺ was prostrating and calling, 'O Merciful! O Compassionate!' The polytheists said: 'This man claims that he calls upon one God, yet he calls upon two, two by two.' So Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful. Whichever you call upon, to Him belong the most beautiful names.﴾" Accordingly, the restriction of the choice in calling upon God to the name Allah or the attribute al-Rahman is by way of sufficiency, meaning: or al-Rahim.

In al-Kashshaf: "From Ibn 'Abbas: Abu Jahl heard the Prophet ﷺ saying, 'O Allah, O Merciful!' Abu Jahl said: 'He forbids us to worship two gods, yet he calls upon another god.'" Ibn Mardawayh also transmitted it. This is more suitable to the verse, because it is restricted to the name Allah and the attribute al-Rahman.

As for its place here, it must be that the occasion of its revelation occurred at the time of the revelation of the verse that precedes it.

The statement is a rebuttal and an instruction that the multiplicity of names does not necessitate the multiplicity of the One named. There is a great difference between this and the calling upon of the polytheists of gods with different names and different named entities. Monotheism (tawhid) and polytheism (shirk) relate to the essences, not to the names.

The word (ayyun) is originally an interrogative noun. When the superfluous (ma) is attached to it, it conveys the meaning of a condition (shart), just as (kayfa) conveys it when the superfluous (ma) is attached to it. For this reason the verb after it, which is ﴿tad'u﴾ ("you call"), is put in the jussive mood as a conditional, and it is given a response (jawab) connected by the particle (fa), which is ﴿fa-lahu al-asma' al-husna﴾ ("to Him belong the most beautiful names").

[Page 237]

The truth is that ﴿fa-lahu al-asma' al-husna﴾ is the reason (ʿilla) for the response. The implied meaning is: whichever of His names, exalted is He, you call upon, there is no harm in calling upon Him with a number of names, since to Him belong the most beautiful names, and since the Named is one.

The meaning of ﴿Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful﴾ is: call upon this name or this name, that is, mention in your calling this or this. The Named is one. According to this interpretation, there is a figurative usage (tajawwuz) in the verb "call upon" (ud'u), used with the meaning of "mention" (udhkuru) or "name" (sammu) in your calling.

It is also possible that "calling" (du'a') is used with the meaning of "name" (sammu). In that case, it is transitive to two objects, and the implied meaning is: name your Lord Allah, or name Him al-Rahman. The first object of both verbs has been omitted, and the second has been retained because the context indicates it.

* * *

﴿And do not recite your prayer aloud, nor recite it in a whisper, but seek a way between that.﴾

There is no doubt that this sentence is connected to the sentence ﴿Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful﴾, which supports what was mentioned before regarding the connection of the statement ﴿Say: Call upon Allah, or call upon the Most Merciful﴾ with the verses that precede it. This was because of the Prophet's ﷺ raising his voice in his calling upon the name al-Rahman.

The word (salah) may mean supplication (du'a'), and it may mean the well-known worship. The early generations (al-salaf) explained it here in both senses. It is known that whoever explained (salah) as the well-known worship meant specifically its recitation, because it is the one described as being done aloud or in a whisper.

On both possibilities, the Prophet ﷺ had raised his voice in mentioning al-Rahman. A group of the polytheists said: "What is al-Rahman?" They also said: "Muhammad calls upon two gods." A group of them stood up and reviled the Qur'an and the one who brought it, or reviled al-Rahman, thinking that He was another lord besides Allah the Exalted and besides their gods.

[Page 238]

So Allah commanded His Messenger not to raise his voice in his calling, or not to raise his voice in reciting his prayer during the audible prayer.

Perhaps the foolish among the polytheists imagined from the Prophet's ﷺ proclaiming the recitation or the calling that he intended by this to provoke them and to exalt himself over them by mentioning Allah the Exalted alone, without mentioning their gods. So they became enraged and reviled. Therefore Allah the Exalted commanded him not to raise his prayer to this degree, avoiding what would stir up their resentment and increase their obstinacy in their disbelief, while the intent is to soften their hearts.

The purpose of the speech is the prohibition of excessive loudness.

As for His saying ﴿nor recite it in a whisper﴾, its purpose is precaution, lest he make his calling secret or his entire prayer secret, so that it does not reach the ears of those prepared to be guided by it. This is because the purpose of the prohibition of loudness is avoiding a loudness from which the unbelievers might imagine provocation or exaltation, as we have said.

Loudness (al-jahr) is the strength of the voice of the one speaking.

The whisper (al-mukhafata) is a form of mufa'ala, from "khafata bi-kalamihi," when he spoke in a low voice. The form of mufa'ala is used with the meaning of intensity, that is, do not make it secret.

His saying "that" (dhalika) is a reference to what was mentioned, that is, the loudness and the whisper known from the two verbs ﴿tajhar﴾ ("you recite aloud") and ﴿tukhafit﴾ ("you recite in a whisper"). That is: seek a way between the two matters, so that the purpose of making the Qur'an heard by the people is achieved, and the supposition of intending to exalt oneself over them is removed.

[p. 239]

﴿Say: "Praise belongs to God, who has not taken a son, and who has no partner in the dominion, and who has no protector out of weakness. And magnify Him with full magnification."﴾

When the prohibition on raising the voice in supplication or in reciting the prayer was issued, as a means of blocking the pretext that it would increase their obstinacy in disbelief, it was followed by a command to proclaim tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness). This was to cut off the root of the illusion of those who imagined that "al-Rahman" (the Most Merciful) is a name for a referent other than the referent of the name "Allah." Some of them imagined it to be a second deity, and some imagined it to be a helper and supporter. The Prophet was commanded to say what uproots all of that, and to glorify Him with various kinds of glorification.

The phrase "Praise belongs to God" (al-hamdu lillah) implies restricting praise to Him, that is, confining the whole category of praise to Him, the Exalted, because He is the greatest deserver of being praised. The restriction is therefore claimed ( idda'i), on the claim that the motives for praising anyone other than God, the Exalted, are, in comparison with the motives for praising God, as nothing, as was mentioned in the commentary on Surat al-Fatihah.

The "min" in His saying "out of weakness" (min al-dhull) carries the sense of the causal "li" (for, because of). Dhull means incapacity and need; it is the opposite of 'izz (might). The meaning is that He has no supporter because of weakness. What is intended is the negation of a supporter for Him in an emphatic manner, since the need for a supporter arises only from inability to defend oneself. It is also permissible to take "al-waliyy" (the protector) as implying the meaning of "one who prevents," so that "min" marks the transitivity of the name thus implied.

The meaning of "magnify Him" (kabbirhu) is: believe that He is Great, that is, great in the immaterial greatness that encompasses necessary existence (wujub al-wujud), absolute self-sufficiency, and all attributes of perfection in their complete and far-reaching scope; for being characterized by all of that is perfection, while being characterized by their opposites is deficiency and immaterial abasement.

[p. 240]

The placing of these three relative clauses after the divine name (Allah), which is the object of praise, is because these clauses contain an allusion to the reason for restricting praise to Him.

The use of the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq) after "kabbirhu" (magnify Him) serves emphasis, and because of the tanwin (nunation) it carries the sense of magnification, and because He who has these attributes is the One who is able to bestow blessings which others are unable to bestow.

[p. 241]

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

Surat al-Kahf (The Cave).

The Messenger of God (ﷺ) named it Surat al-Kahf.

Muslim and Abu Dawud narrated from Abu al-Darda', from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever memorizes ten verses from the beginning of Surat al-Kahf" (and in a narration of Muslim: "from the end of al-Kahf") "will be protected from the trial of the Dajjal (the Antichrist)."

al-Tirmidhi also narrated it from Abu al-Darda' with the wording: "Whoever recites three verses from the beginning of al-Kahf will be protected from the trial of the Dajjal." al-Tirmidhi said: "A hadith, hasan sahih."

Likewise its naming is attested from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib in Sahih al-Bukhari, who said: "A man was reciting Surat al-Kahf, and beside him was a horse tied with two ropes. A cloud covered him and began to draw near, and draw near, and his horse began to shy. When morning came he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and mentioned that to him. He said: 'That was the tranquility (al-sakinah) that descended with the Qur'an.'"

In a hadith narrated by Ibn Mardawayh from the Prophet (ﷺ), he named it Surat Ashab al-Kahf (The Surah of the Companions of the Cave).

It is Meccan by consensus, as Ibn 'Atiyyah reported. He said: "It was narrated from Farqad that the beginning of the surah up to His saying 'barren (juruzan)' was revealed at Medina." He said: "The first view is more sound."

[p. 242]

It was also said that His saying "And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord" [18:28] and the two verses following it were revealed at Medina, and it was said that His saying "Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them are the Gardens of Paradise as a lodging" [18:107] to the end of the surah was revealed at Medina. All of that is weak, as will be pointed out in its proper places.

It was revealed after Surat al-Ghashiyah and before Surat al-Shura.

It is the sixty-eighth in the order of revelation of the surahs according to Jabir ibn Zayd.

Varied hadiths have been transmitted concerning its virtues; the most sound of them are the hadiths already mentioned. It is among the surahs that were revealed all at once. al-Daylami narrated in Musnad al-Firdaws "from Anas, who said: 'Surat al-Kahf was revealed all at once, with seventy thousand angels accompanying it.'" The author of al-Itqan (al-Suyuti) has overlooked this.

Its verses were counted, according to the reckoning of the reciters of Medina and Mecca, as one hundred and five; according to the reckoning of the reciters of Syria, one hundred and six; according to the reckoning of the reciters of Basra, one hundred and eleven; and according to the reckoning of the reciters of Kufa, one hundred and ten, based on their difference over dividing some verses into two.

The occasion of its revelation is what many exegetes have mentioned. Ibn Ishaq expanded on it in his Sirah without a chain of transmission, and al-Tabari traced it to Ibn 'Abbas through a chain in which there is an unknown man: "When the polytheists were troubled by the affair of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the increase of the Muslims with him, and the questions of the delegations arriving at Mecca from the tribes of the Arabs about the matter of his call became frequent, they sent al-Nadr ibn al-Harith and 'Uqbah ibn Abi Mu'it to the rabbis of the Jews in Medina, Yathrib, asking them their opinion about his call, hoping that the rabbis would find for them something they had not found, by which they could direct their denial of him. They said: 'The Jews are the People of the Earlier Scripture, and they have knowledge of the prophets, that is, their attributes and signs, knowledge that we do not have.' So al-Nadr and 'Uqbah came to Medina and described to the Jews the call of the Prophet (ﷺ)

[p. 243]

and related some of what he had said. The rabbis of the Jews said to them: 'Ask him about three things. If he informs you of them, then he is a prophet; and if he does not do so, then the man is inventing speech. Ask him about youths who went forth in the former age, what their affair was; ask him about a wandering man who reached the easts and wests of the earth; and ask him about the Spirit (al-Ruh), what it is.' Al-Nadr and 'Uqbah returned and informed the Quraysh of what the rabbis of the Jews had said. A group of the polytheists came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and asked him about these three things. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to them: 'I will inform you of what you asked about tomorrow,' and he was waiting for the time of the revelation's descent upon him according to a habit he knew, and he did not say 'if God wills.' So the Messenger of God remained three days without revelation coming to him. Ibn Ishaq said: fifteen days. The people of Mecca spread rumors and said: 'Muhammad promised us tomorrow, and today we have passed several days, and he tells us nothing of what we asked him about,' until that grieved the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and weighed heavily upon him. Then Gabriel (peace be upon him) came to him with Surat al-Kahf, in which was their answer concerning the youths, who are the People of the Cave, and concerning the wandering man, who is Dhu al-Qarnayn; and there was revealed to him concerning what they had asked about the Spirit: 'And they ask you about the Spirit. Say: The Spirit is of the command of my Lord, and you have been given of knowledge only a little' [17:85] in Surat al-Isra'."

al-Suhayli said: "In a narration from Ibn Ishaq, other than through al-Bakka'i, that is Ziyad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Bakka'i, from whom Ibn Hisham narrates, he said in this report: 'The Messenger of God (ﷺ) called out to them: He, that is the Spirit, is Gabriel.' This contradicts what others have narrated, that the Jews told the Quraysh: 'Ask him about the Spirit. If he informs you of it, he is not a prophet; and if he does not inform you of it, he is a prophet.'" End of quotation.

I say: The two narrations may be reconciled by saying that the Prophet (ﷺ), after he had answered them about the matter of the Spirit with His saying "Say: The Spirit is of the command of my Lord" [17:85], according to what they meant by the Spirit, turned them to an answer about a matter of which they ought to have had knowledge, namely the Spirit that is mentioned repeatedly in the Qur'an, such as His saying "The Trustworthy Spirit has descended with it" [26:193] and His saying "The Spirit descends therein" [97:4] (and it is one of the titles of Gabriel), following the method of wise discourse, together with what it contains of provoking the Jews, because they are enemies of Gabriel, as His saying indicates: "Say: Whoever is an enemy to Gabriel..." [2:97], and the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Salam clarifies it, in his saying to the Prophet (ﷺ) when Gabriel (peace be upon him) was mentioned: "That is the enemy of the Jews among the angels." Thus the Prophet (ﷺ) left the Jews no outlet through which they might cast doubt upon the Quraysh except that he closed it to them.

It may be objected here: the verse that was revealed about the matter of the Spirit is from Surat al-Isra', so it was not contemporaneous with the verse revealed concerning the youths and the wandering man. What then distinguishes the two verses? And it is reported that Surat al-Isra' was revealed before Surat al-Kahf, for it is counted as the fifty-sixth in the order of revelation of the surahs, while Surat al-Kahf is counted as the sixty-eighth in revelation. It may be answered that the verse about the Spirit may have been revealed so as to be joined to Surat al-Isra', for it was revealed in the style of Surat al-Isra' and on a pattern like its verse-endings, and because the answer in it is an answer by committing knowledge to God, which is a context that calls for conciseness, unlike the answer concerning the People of the Cave and concerning Dhu al-Qarnayn, which requires elaboration and lengthy exposition. Thus the verse about the Spirit was distinguished from the two narratives.

Furthermore, it is permissible that the revelation of Surat al-Isra' continued until the time of the revelation of Surat al-Kahf, so a Qur'an distributed between it and Surat al-Kahf was revealed. This is according to one of the two interpretations of the sense of the Spirit being "of the command of my Lord," as was mentioned in Surat al-Isra'. What the majority of narrators hold is that the verse "And they ask you about the Spirit" [17:85] is Meccan, except what is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, and you have already known its interpretation in Surat al-Isra'.

It thus becomes clear that the most important purpose for which Surat al-Kahf was revealed is the explanation of the story of the People of the Cave and the story of Dhu al-Qarnayn. The first of them is mentioned at the beginning of the surah, and the other is mentioned at its end.

A Qur'anic marvel (karamah qur'aniyyah):

For placing this surah in this position in the mushaf there is a fine correspondence, which God inspired

[p. 245]

in the Companions of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) when they arranged the mushaf. It approximates the midpoint of the mushaf, for in its early part there is a point which is said to be the midpoint of the letters of the Qur'an, namely the letter "ta'" (ت) in His saying "and let him be gentle" [18:19]. It is also said that the midpoint of the letters of the Qur'an is the letter "nun" (ن) in His saying "You have certainly produced a thing unthinkable" [18:74], within the surah. That is the end of the fifteenth juz' of the juz's of the Qur'an, which is the midpoint of its juz's, namely His saying "He said: Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?" [18:75]. Thus this surah was placed at approximately the middle of the mushaf.

It also begins with praise, so that the beginning of the second half of the Qur'an is with "Praise belongs to God," just as the beginning of the first half was with "Praise belongs to God," and just as the beginning of the fourth quarter of it approximately was with "Praise belongs to God, Originator of the heavens and the earth" [35:1].

The aims of the surah:

The aims of the surah:

It opens with praise for the sending down of the Book, to exalt the Qur'an, as a lofty affirmation from God against the polytheists and their instructors from among the People of the Book.

Included in it is a warning to the obstinate who attributed a son to God, and good tidings to the believers, and consolation for the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concerning their sayings, when the revelation was delayed, in accordance with what God's sunnah required in His dealings with His friends, namely the display of His displeasure at neglecting to observe the complete etiquettes.

It mentions the polytheists' infatuation with the life of this world and its adornments, and that these do not bring souls purification.

It moves on to the story of the People of the Cave, the subject of the question.

It warns them against Satan and his enmity toward the children of Adam, so that they may be on guard against his scheming.

It presents, before the story of Dhu al-Qarnayn, a story more important than it, namely the story of Musa and al-Khidr (peace be upon them both), because both stories are alike in the journey for a noble purpose: Dhu al-Qarnayn set out to extend his dominion over the earth, while Musa (peace be upon him) set out seeking knowledge.

[p. 246]

In the mention of the story of Musa there is an indirect rebuke of the rabbis of the Children of Israel, for they were preoccupied with the report of a king who was not of their people nor of their religion, and they forgot a report from the biography of their own prophet.

Interspersed within this were digressions containing guidance for the Prophet ﷺ and affirmation of him, and [the affirmation] that the truth is in what he reported, and that his companions who stayed constantly with him are better than the chieftains of the polytheists; and [they contained] promise and warning, and the illustration of the believer and the disbeliever, and the illustration of the worldly life and its passing away, and what follows it of resurrection and gathering, and the reminder of the consequences for the nations that denied the messengers, and [the surah] concluded with the nullification of polytheism, the warning to its adherents, and the promise to the believers of the opposite of their fate, and the illustration of the vastness of God Most High's knowledge; and it concluded with the confirmation that the Qur'an is a revelation from God Most High to His Messenger ﷺ. Thus in this conclusion there is the rhetorical device of *radd al-'ajuz 'ala al-sadr* (the return of the final part to the beginning).
